articles.title: Fourth central moment bound for Bernstein weights
articles.statement:
The fourth central moment of the Bernstein weights is at most `1 / n ^ 2`, uniformly in
`x ∈ [0, 1]`.

articles.title: Fourth central moment of the Bernstein weights
articles.statement:
For `n ≠ 0`,
`∑ k : Fin (n + 1), (x - k / n) ^ 4 * bernstein n k x = x (1 - x) (1 + 3 (n - 2) x (1 - x)) / n³`,
i.e. `E[(S - n x) ^ 4] = n x (1 - x) (1 + 3 (n - 2) x (1 - x))` for `S ~ Bin(n, x)`.

articles.title: First central moment of the Bernstein weights
articles.statement:
For `n ≠ 0`,
`∑ k : Fin (n + 1), (x - k / n) * bernstein n k x = 0`: the binomial frequency `S / n` has
mean `x`.

articles.title: Voronovskaya's theorem (1932)
articles.statement:
For `f : ℝ → ℝ` of class `C²` and `x ∈ [0, 1]`, the
Bernstein approximations of `f` on `[0, 1]` satisfy
`n · (bernsteinApproximation n f x - f x) → x (1 - x) / 2 · f''(x)` as `n → ∞`.

## Sources

- Voronovskaya (1932); Lorentz, *Bernstein Polynomials* (1953), Chapter 1.

articles.title: Uniqueness of best approximation in strictly convex spaces
articles.statement:
In a strictly convex real normed space, a convex set contains at most one
point nearest to a given point: the midpoint of two distinct nearest points
would be strictly closer, by `norm_midpoint_lt_iff`.

articles.title: Existence of best approximations in finite-dimensional subspaces
articles.statement:
Every point of a normed space has a nearest point in a
finite-dimensional subspace (proximinality). No completeness hypothesis on
the ambient space is needed: completeness enters only through the
finite-dimensional subspace, whose closed balls are compact.

articles.title: Unique best approximation in finite-dimensional subspaces
articles.statement:
Existence plus uniqueness: a finite-dimensional subspace of a strictly
convex real normed space admits a unique best approximation to every
point.

articles.title: De la Vallée Poussin's theorem
articles.statement:
If the error `f - p` of a polynomial
`p` of degree at most `n` alternates with a one-sided lower bound `η` at
`n + 2` strictly increasing points of `[a, b]`,
`η ≤ σ * (-1) ^ i * (f (x i) - p (x i))`, then every polynomial of degree at
most `n` has uniform error at least `η` on `[a, b]`.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the equioscillating best approximation
articles.statement:
If `p` equioscillates against `f` on `[a, b]`, then `p` is the unique
polynomial of degree at most `n` whose uniform error on `[a, b]` is at most `E`.
In particular `p` is the unique best uniform approximation to `f` among
polynomials of degree at most `n`.

articles.title: Equioscillation of a polynomial approximation
articles.statement:
A polynomial `p` of degree at most `n` equioscillates against `f` on `[a, b]`
with amplitude `E` and sign `σ = ±1` at the `n + 2` points `x 0 < ⋯ < x (n+1)`,
if `f (x i) - p (x i) = σ * (-1) ^ i * E` for every `i ≤ n + 1`, and
`|f y - p.eval y| ≤ E` for every `y ∈ [a, b]`.

articles.title: Chebyshev equioscillation theorem (sufficiency)
articles.statement:
If `p` equioscillates against `f`, then no polynomial of degree at most `n`
has uniform error strictly less than `E` on `[a, b]`: `p` is a best uniform
approximation.

articles.title: Kolmogorov–Arnold superposition with a single outer function
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on the unit cube $[0, 1]^n$. Then there exist a
continuous function $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and continuous functions
$\varphi_{k,l} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ for $0 \le k \le 2n$ and $0 \le l < n$ such that for
every $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \in [0, 1]^n$,

$$f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{2n} g\left(\sum_{l=0}^{n-1} \varphi_{k,l}(x_l)\right).$$

Both $g$ and the $\varphi_{k,l}$ may depend on $f$, so this is weaker than the form in which the
inner functions are universal.

## Sources

- A. N. Kolmogorov, *On the representation of continuous functions of several variables by superposition of continuous functions of one variable and addition*, Doklady Akad. Nauk SSSR 114 (1957), 953-956. V. I. Arnold, *On functions of three variables*, Doklady Akad. Nauk SSSR 114 (1957), 679-681. G. G. Lorentz, *Metric entropy, widths, and superpositions of functions*, Amer. Math. Monthly 69 (1962), 469-485 (single-outer-function refinement). Listed as §80 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `kolmogorov_arnold_superposition` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Kolmogorov superposition theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$. There are continuous functions
$\psi_{q,p} : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$ for $0 \le q \le 2n$ and $0 \le p < n$, depending only on
$n$, such that for every continuous function $f : [0,1]^n \to \mathbb{R}$ there are continuous
functions $\varphi_q : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ for $0 \le q \le 2n$ with
$f(x) = \sum_{q=0}^{2n} \varphi_q\left(\sum_{p=0}^{n-1} \psi_{q,p}(x_p)\right)$ for every
$x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \in [0,1]^n$.

## Sources

- Kolmogorov superposition theorem, A. N. Kolmogorov, Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR 114 (1957) 953–956, refined Arnold 1957; see Braun–Griebel, Acta Numer. 2009 review; Lean is n ≥ 2 exact cardinal Fin (2n+1) with inner ψ in C(Icc 0 1, ℝ) independent of f and outer φ in C(ℝ, ℝ), compact-source specialization [0, 1]^n as Fin n → Icc.

articles.title: Positive linear operators bound absolute values
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a real-linear
operator on $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ that is positive: $(L f)(x) \ge 0$ for all
$x \in [0, 1]$ whenever $f(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$. If
$g, h \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ satisfy $|g(y)| \le h(y)$ for all $y \in [0, 1]$, then
$|(L g)(x)| \le (L h)(x)$ for every $x \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: Quadratic bound from a modulus of continuity
articles.statement:
Let $f \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$
have sup norm $\|f\|$, let $x \in [0, 1]$, and let $\delta > 0$, $\varepsilon \ge 0$
and $C \ge 0$ be real numbers with $2\|f\| \le C \delta^2$. If
$|f(y) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for every $y \in [0, 1]$ with $|y - x| < \delta$, then
$|f(y) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon + C (y - x)^2$ for every $y \in [0, 1]$.

Korovkin's theorem applies this with $C = 2\|f\| / \delta^2$.

articles.title: The square test function
articles.statement:
The function $x \mapsto x^2$ on $[0, 1]$, as an element
of $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$.

articles.title: The identity test function
articles.statement:
The function $x \mapsto x$ on $[0, 1]$, as an element
of $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$.

articles.title: Expansion of the shifted square
articles.statement:
Write $e(y) = y$ and $q(y) = y^2$ for the identity
and square functions and $1$ for the constant function one, as elements of
$C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$. For every $x \in [0, 1]$, the function $y \mapsto (y - x)^2$ in
$C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ equals $q - 2x \cdot e + x^2 \cdot 1$.

articles.title: The shifted square
articles.statement:
For $x \in [0, 1]$, the function $y \mapsto (y - x)^2$
on $[0, 1]$, as an element of $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$.

articles.title: Korovkin's theorem
articles.statement:
Write $e_0$, $e_1$ and $e_2$ for the functions $x \mapsto 1$,
$x \mapsto x$ and $x \mapsto x^2$ in $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$.
Let $(L_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be real-linear operators on $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$, each
positive: $(L_n f)(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$ whenever $f(x) \ge 0$ for all
$x \in [0, 1]$. If $L_n e_i \to e_i$ in the sup norm for $i = 0, 1, 2$, then
$L_n f \to f$ in the sup norm for every $f \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$.

articles.title: Positive linear operators are monotone
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a real-linear operator on
$C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ that is positive: $(L f)(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$ whenever
$f(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$. If $g, h \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ satisfy
$g(x) \le h(x)$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$, then $(L g)(x) \le (L h)(x)$
for every $x \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence
articles.statement:
If a sequence $(u_n)$ in
$C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ converges to $e$ in the sup norm, then $u_n(x) \to e(x)$ for every
$x \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: Lagrange basis polynomials vanish at the other nodes
articles.statement:
For real nodes
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and indices $k \ne j$ below $n$, the $k$-th evaluated Lagrange basis
polynomial $\ell_k$ for these nodes satisfies $\ell_k(x_j) = 0$.

The nodes need not be distinct.

articles.title: Lagrange basis polynomials equal one at their own node
articles.statement:
If the real nodes
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct, then $\ell_k(x_k) = 1$ for every $k < n$, where
$\ell_k$ is the $k$-th evaluated Lagrange basis polynomial for these nodes.

articles.title: Evaluated Lagrange basis polynomial
articles.statement:
For real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, an index
$k < n$ and a real number $t$, the value at $t$ of the $k$-th Lagrange basis polynomial is
$\ell_k(t) = \prod_{j \ne k} (x_k - x_j)^{-1} (t - x_j)$, the product running over the indices
$j < n$ with $j \ne k$.

The inverse follows the convention $0^{-1} = 0$, so $\ell_k$ is identically $0$ when some other
node equals $x_k$.

articles.title: The Lagrange interpolant matches the function at the nodes
articles.statement:
If the real nodes
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct, then for every function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$
and every $j < n$, the Lagrange interpolant of $f$ on these nodes satisfies
$\mathcal{L}^n f(x_j) = f(x_j)$.

articles.title: Lagrange interpolant
articles.statement:
For real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, a function
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and a real number $t$, the Lagrange interpolant of $f$ at $t$ is
$\mathcal{L}^n f(t) = \sum_{k < n} f(x_k)\, \ell_k(t)$, where $\ell_k$ is the $k$-th evaluated
Lagrange basis polynomial for these nodes.

articles.title: The Lebesgue function equals one at the nodes
articles.statement:
If the real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$
are pairwise distinct, then their Lebesgue function satisfies $L_n(x_j) = 1$ for every $j < n$.

articles.title: Lebesgue function
articles.statement:
For real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and a real number $t$, the
Lebesgue function of the nodes at $t$ is $L_n(t) = \sum_{k < n} |\ell_k(t)|$, where $\ell_k$ is
the $k$-th evaluated Lagrange basis polynomial for these nodes.

articles.title: Müntz–Szász theorem for integer exponents
articles.statement:
Let $\Lambda : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be
strictly increasing with $\Lambda(0) = 0$. The real linear span of the monomials
$x \mapsto x^{\Lambda(n)}$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, restricted to $[0, 1]$, is dense in
$C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ with the uniform norm if and only if the series
$\sum_{n \ge 0} 1/\Lambda(n+1)$ diverges, that is, the sequence
$(1/\Lambda(n+1))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is not summable.

## Sources

- C. Müntz, Festschrift H. A. Schwarz 1914 303-312 and O. Szász, Math. Ann. 77 (1916) 482-496, Müntz-Szász theorem; Rudin Real & Complex; Lean states integer-exponent `ℕ→ℕ` `StrictMono` with `0∈range` case as closure `= ⊤` iff non-summable reciprocals.

articles.title: Runge's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be compact, let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be
open with $K \subseteq U$, and let $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ be analytic at every point of
$U$. Then for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there are complex polynomials $p$ and $q$ such that
$q(z) \ne 0$ for every $z \in K$ and $|f(z) - p(z)/q(z)| < \varepsilon$ for every $z \in K$.

## Sources

- C. Runge, *Zur Theorie der eindeutigen analytischen Funktionen*, Acta Math. 6 (1885), 229-244. Listed as §64 (additional statement 3) in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `runge_theorem` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Scottish Book Problem 159 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
There is no sequence of real numbers
$a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ with the following property: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural
number $N$ such that for every function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is continuous on
$[0, 1]$ and satisfies $f(0) = 0$ and $0 \le f(x) \le 1$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$, there is a natural
number $n \le N$ with $\left|f(x) - \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k x^k\right| < \varepsilon$ for all
$x \in [0, 1]$.

Sternbach's argument in the addendum Ad 159 uses the functions $\sin^2(2^n \pi x)$. Mazur showed
that for an arbitrary family $\Phi$ of functions of this kind, a power series with this property
exists exactly when the functions of $\Phi$ are equicontinuous.

## Sources

- S. Ruziewicz, Problem 159 of the Scottish Book; Ad 159 in the typescript (Sternbach's negative argument; Mazur's equicontinuity criterion).

articles.title: The claim of Scottish Book Problem 159
articles.statement:
There is a sequence of real numbers
$a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ such that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number $N$ with the
following property: for every function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is continuous on
$[0, 1]$ and satisfies $f(0) = 0$ and $0 \le f(x) \le 1$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$, there is a natural
number $n \le N$ with $|f(x) - P_n(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$, where
$P_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k x^k$ is the $n$-th partial sum of the power series $\sum a_k x^k$.

articles.title: Universal approximation theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ carry its
standard inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$, let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be compact,
and let $\sigma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous and not a polynomial, that is, there is
no real polynomial $p$ with $\sigma(x) = p(x)$ for all real $x$. Then for every function
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ that is continuous on $K$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exist
$m \in \mathbb{N}$, real numbers $c_1, \dots, c_m$ and $b_1, \dots, b_m$, and vectors
$w_1, \dots, w_m \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that
$\left| f(x) - \sum_{i=1}^{m} c_i \, \sigma(\langle w_i, x \rangle + b_i) \right| < \varepsilon$
for every $x \in K$.

In words: single-hidden-layer feedforward networks with a continuous, non-polynomial activation
approximate every continuous function uniformly on every compact set.

## Sources

- `universal-approximation-s1` from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_approximation_theorem; the continuous-activation case of M. Leshno, V. Ya. Lin, A. Pinkus and S. Schocken, *Multilayer feedforward networks with a nonpolynomial activation function can approximate any function*, Neural Networks 6(6) (1993), 861–867, doi:10.1016/S0893-6080(05)80131-5, which allows any locally bounded, piecewise continuous activation that is not almost everywhere equal to a polynomial; for continuous activations this is the same as the pointwise non-polynomial hypothesis.

articles.title: Logarithmic asymptotics of the square-root Poisson series
articles.statement:
For real $x$ let
$S(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} x^k \sqrt{k} / k!$. Then, as $x \to \infty$,

$$\log S(x) = x + \tfrac{1}{2} \log x - \frac{1}{8x} - \frac{1}{16 x^2} + O\left(x^{-3}\right).$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 10, Example 1, printed p. 64 / PDF p. 74.

articles.title: Eventual summability of the square-root Poisson series
articles.statement:
For all sufficiently large
real $x$, the series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} x^k \sqrt{k} / k!$ is summable.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 10, Example 1, printed p. 64 / PDF p. 74.

articles.title: Eventual positivity of the square-root Poisson series
articles.statement:
For all sufficiently large
real $x$, the sum $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} x^k \sqrt{k} / k!$ is strictly positive.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 10, Example 1, printed p. 64 / PDF p. 74.

articles.title: Asymptotics of the logarithmic Poisson series
articles.statement:
There are real constants $C > 0$ and
$x_0$ such that for every real $x \ge x_0$ the series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} x^k \log(k + 1) / k!$
has a sum $S$ satisfying

$$\left| e^{-x} S - \log x - \frac{1}{2x} - \frac{1}{12 x^2} \right| \le \frac{C}{x^3}.$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 10, Example 2, printed p. 65 / PDF p. 75.

articles.title: Summability of the logarithmic Poisson series
articles.statement:
For every real $x$, the series
$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} e^{-x} x^k \log(k + 1) / k!$ is summable.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 10, Example 2, printed p. 65 / PDF p. 75.

articles.title: Asymptotics of the harmonic Poisson series
articles.statement:
Let $H_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} 1/j$ be the $k$-th
harmonic number (so $H_0 = 0$) and let $\gamma$ be the Euler–Mascheroni constant. Then, as
$x \to \infty$,

$$e^{-x} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^k H_k}{k!} = \log x + \gamma + O\left(\frac{1}{x}\right).$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 10, Example 4, printed pp. 65-66 / PDF pp. 75-76.

articles.title: Summability of the harmonic Poisson series
articles.statement:
Let $H_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} 1/j$ be the $k$-th
harmonic number (so $H_0 = 0$). For every real $x$, the series
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} e^{-x} x^k H_k / k!$ is summable.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 10, Example 4, printed pp. 65-66 / PDF pp. 75-76.

articles.title: Ramanujan's asymptotic expansion of Poisson averages
articles.statement:
Let $M \ge 1$ be an integer,
$\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ and $G : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ functions, $A \ge 1$ a
real number and $F$ a finite set of natural numbers. Write $\varphi^{(n)}$ for the $n$-th
iterated derivative of $\varphi$ and $S_2(n, k)$ for the 2-associated Stirling numbers of the
second kind. Assume that there are $C \ge 0$ and $p \in \mathbb{N}$ such that
$|\varphi(x)| \le C x^p$ and $|G(x)| \le C x^p$ for all sufficiently large $x$; that $G(x) \ge 1$
for all sufficiently large $x$; and that for every integer $m \ge 1$ and all sufficiently large
$x$, the derivatives $\varphi^{(0)}, \dots, \varphi^{(m-1)}$ are differentiable at $x$ and
$|\varphi^{(m)}(x)| / m! \le G(x) (A / x)^m$. Then, as $x \to \infty$,

$$e^{-x} \sum_{j \in \mathbb{N} \setminus F} \frac{x^j}{j!} \varphi(j) - \varphi(x) -
\sum_{k=2}^{M} \sum_{n=k}^{2k-2} S_2(n, n + 1 - k) \, x^{n-k+1} \frac{\varphi^{(n)}(x)}{n!}
= O\left(\frac{G(x)}{x^M}\right).$$

Proof: Taylor expansion on the central Poisson range is combined with the associated-Stirling
central-moment identity from Comtet; Berndt's route and even-moment tails control the remainder.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 10, printed pp. 57-58 / PDF pp. 67-68.

articles.title: Eventual summability of the series in Entry 10
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$
be polynomially bounded at infinity, that is, there are a real number $C \ge 0$ and a natural
number $p$ such that $|\varphi(x)| \le C x^p$ for all sufficiently large real $x$. Let $F$ be a
finite set of natural numbers. Then for all sufficiently large real $x$, the family indexed by
the natural numbers $j$ whose $j$-th term is $0$ for $j \in F$ and $x^j \varphi(j) / j!$ for
$j \notin F$ is summable.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 10, printed pp. 57-58 / PDF pp. 67-68.

articles.title: The Entry 10 Stirling numbers are the 2-associated Stirling numbers
articles.statement:
For all natural
numbers $n$ and $k$, the integer $\sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^j \binom{n}{j} S(n - j, k - j)$ used in
Ramanujan's Entry 10, where $S$ denotes the Stirling numbers of the second kind, equals the
2-associated Stirling number of the second kind $S_2(n, k)$.

articles.title: 2-associated Stirling numbers in Ramanujan's Entry 10
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$,
$S_2(n, k)$ is the integer $\sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^j \binom{n}{j} S(n - j, k - j)$, where $S$
denotes the Stirling numbers of the second kind.

$S_2(n, k)$ is the number of partitions of an $n$-element set into $k$ blocks, each containing at
least two elements.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the even-power shift in Catalan asymptotics
articles.statement:
Let
$C_n = \binom{2n}{n} / (n + 1)$ be the $n$-th Catalan number. For a real number $\alpha$, there is
a real sequence $(a_k)_{k \ge 0}$ with $a_{2k+1} = 0$ for every $k$ such that, for every
$N \ge 0$, the difference
$C_n \sqrt{\pi} \, (n + \alpha)^{3/2} / 4^n - \sum_{k=0}^{N} a_k (n + \alpha)^{-k}$ is
$o\left((n + \alpha)^{-N}\right)$ as $n \to \infty$, if and only if $\alpha = 3/4$.

Elezović phrases this as the expansion "containing only odd terms"; the condition meant is that
the odd-indexed coefficients vanish: his displayed series for $\alpha = 3/4$ has only even powers,
and his proof obtains $\alpha = 3/4$ by setting the first odd coefficient to zero.

Proof: The reverse implication exponentiates the all-orders logarithmic expansion of the Catalan
numbers and uses the reflection symmetry of the Bernoulli polynomials to eliminate odd powers. The
first logarithmic coefficient gives uniqueness, following Elezović.

## Sources

- Neven Elezović, "Asymptotic Expansions of Central Binomial Coefficients and Catalan Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 17 (2014), Article 14.2.1, Corollary, lines 568–578, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL17/Elezovic/elezovic5.tex

articles.title: Stirling-type asymptotic expansions of the Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
Let $C_n$ be the $n$-th Catalan
number and $B_k$ the $k$-th Bernoulli number, and let $(E_k)$ be a sequence of integers with
$E_0 = 1$ and $\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \binom{n}{2j} E_{n-2j} = 0$ for every $n > 0$
(these are the Euler numbers $1, 0, -1, 0, 5, \dots$). For $k \ge 1$ put
$c_k = (-1)^{k+1} \left((2^{-k} - 2) B_{k+1} - k - 1\right) / (k (k + 1))$ and
$d_k = 2^{-4k-2} (4 - E_{2k}) / k$. Then for every $m \ge 0$, as $n \to \infty$,
$\log\left(C_n \, n \sqrt{\pi n} / 4^n\right) = \sum_{k=1}^{m} c_k n^{-k} + o(n^{-m})$ and,
writing $x = n + 3/4$,
$\log\left(C_n \sqrt{\pi x^3} / 4^n\right) = \sum_{k=1}^{m} d_k x^{-2k} + o(x^{-2m})$.

The first coefficient is $c_1 = -9/8$, matching the classical expansion
$C_n = \frac{4^n}{\sqrt{\pi} \, n^{3/2}} \left(1 - \frac{9}{8n} + \dots\right)$.

Proof: The Catalan recurrence gives a logarithmic first-difference equation.
Telescoping its Bernoulli-polynomial expansion yields both all-orders formulas.

## Sources

- Neven Elezović, "Asymptotic Expansions of Central Binomial Coefficients and Catalan Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 17 (2014), Article 14.2.1, Catalan Stirling-type theorem (unlabeled, equation 42), lines 626–637, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL17/Elezovic/elezovic5.tex

articles.title: All-orders logarithmic expansion of the Catalan numbers at a real shift
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a real
number, let $C_n$ be the $n$-th Catalan number and $B_k(x)$ the $k$-th Bernoulli polynomial, and
for $j \ge 0$ put
$a_j = (-1)^j \left(B_{j+2}(1/2 - c) - B_{j+2}(2 - c)\right) / ((j + 1)(j + 2))$.
Then for every natural number $M$,
$(n + c)^M \left(\log\left(C_n \sqrt{\pi (n + c)^3} / 4^n\right) -
\sum_{j=0}^{M-1} a_j (n + c)^{-(j+1)}\right) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Bernoulli-polynomial expansion from a logarithmic difference equation
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$, $\beta$
and $c$ be real numbers and let $(u_n)$ be a real sequence with $u_n \to 0$ such that, for all
sufficiently large $n$,
$u_{n+1} - u_n = \log(1 + \alpha/(n + c)) - \log(1 + \beta/(n + c)) +
(\beta - \alpha) \log(1 + 1/(n + c))$.
Let $B_k(x)$ be the $k$-th Bernoulli polynomial and, for $j \ge 0$, put
$a_j = (-1)^j \left(B_{j+2}(\alpha) - B_{j+2}(\beta)\right) / ((j + 1)(j + 2))$. Then for every
natural number $M$, $(n + c)^M \left(u_n - \sum_{j=0}^{M-1} a_j (n + c)^{-(j+1)}\right) \to 0$
as $n \to \infty$.

The normalization $u_n \to 0$ fixes the otherwise undetermined additive constant.

articles.title: Functional equation of Ramanujan's factorial series
articles.statement:
Let
$C(x) = \sum_{j \ge 0} (-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$ be Ramanujan's factorial
series. For every real $x > 0$, $C(x) = \frac{1}{x + 1} - \frac{C(x + 1)}{x + 1}$.

articles.title: Ramanujan's factorial series
articles.statement:
For a real number $x$, $C(x)$ is the sum
$\sum_{j \ge 0} (-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$ of Ramanujan's factorial series,
where a term is read as $0$ when its denominator vanishes and the sum is taken to be $0$ when
the series is not summable.

The series is summable for every $x > 0$.

articles.title: Recursion for the terms of Ramanujan's factorial series
articles.statement:
Write
$c_j(x) = (-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$ for the $j$-th term of Ramanujan's
factorial series, with division by $0$ read as $0$. For every real $x$ and every natural number
$j$, $c_{j+1}(x) = -\frac{1}{x + 1} \, c_j(x + 1)$.

articles.title: Terms of Ramanujan's factorial series
articles.statement:
For a real number $x$ and a natural number $j$,
the $j$-th term of Ramanujan's factorial series is $(-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$,
read as $0$ when the denominator vanishes.

articles.title: Closed form of Ramanujan's product series off the poles
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, x, z \in \mathbb{C}$
with $b \neq 0$, let $0 < \varepsilon < \pi$, and put $w = (z + a)/b$. Suppose that $w \neq 0$,
that $-\pi + \varepsilon \le \arg w \le \pi - \varepsilon$, and that $w + r + 1 \neq 0$ for every
natural number $r$. Then Ramanujan's product series $P$ satisfies

$$P(a, b, x; z) = e^{-x} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{m+1}}{m!\,(z + a + b(m + 1))}.$$

articles.title: Ramanujan's product series
articles.statement:
For complex numbers $a$, $b$, $x$, $z$, Ramanujan's product
series of Entry 9(i) is

$$P(a, b, x; z) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-b)^j x^{j+1}}{\prod_{r=0}^{j} (z + a + b(r + 1))}.$$

The definition is totalized: a quotient with vanishing denominator is taken to be $0$, and the sum
of a non-summable series is taken to be $0$. Hence at a pole of the source expression, for example
$a = 0$, $b = 1$, $x = 1$, $z = -1$, where every product contains the vanishing factor
$z + a + b = 0$, every term and so $P$ itself equals $0$, whereas the source expression has a
singularity there. Off the poles, when $b \neq 0$ and $w = (z + a)/b$ is nonzero and satisfies
$|\arg w| \le \pi - \varepsilon$ for some $0 < \varepsilon < \pi$, the closed form of Ramanujan's
product series identifies $P$ with the source's closed form.

articles.title: Entry 3 coefficients as generalized Bell values
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be Ramanujan's generalized Bell
function. For every complex number $x$ and every natural number $j$, let
$f(x, j) = e^{-x} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(k+1)^j x^{k+1}}{k!}$. Then
$f(x, j) = F(0, 1, x; j)$.

articles.title: Asymptotic expansion of Ramanujan's factorial series
articles.statement:
Let
$C(x) = \sum_{j \ge 0} (-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$ be Ramanujan's factorial
series and let $B_n$ denote the $n$-th Bell number. For every natural number $N$,

$$C(x) - \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \frac{(-1)^j B_{j+1}}{x^{j+1}} = O\left(\frac{1}{x^{N+1}}\right)
\quad \text{as } x \to \infty.$$

articles.title: Ramanujan's factorial series as the Entry 9 product series at $a = 0$, $b = 1$
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be
Ramanujan's Entry 9(i) product series. For all complex numbers $x$ and $z$, let
$\psi(x, z) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} t_j$, where $t_j = \frac{(-1)^j x^{j+1}}{(z+1)(z+2)\cdots(z+j+1)}$
when the product in the denominator is nonzero and $t_j = 0$ otherwise. Then
$\psi(x, z) = P(0, 1, x; z)$.

Since division by zero is taken to give zero, the case distinction in $t_j$ changes nothing.

articles.title: Asymptotic expansion of Ramanujan's factorial series, for every $x$
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a complex
number. For natural numbers $j$ let
$f(x, j) = e^{-x} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(k+1)^j x^{k+1}}{k!}$, and for complex $z$ let
$\psi(x, z) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} t_j$, where
$t_j = \frac{(-1)^j x^{j+1}}{(z+1)(z+2)\cdots(z+j+1)}$ when the denominator is nonzero and
$t_j = 0$ otherwise. Let $\varepsilon$ be a real number with $0 < \varepsilon < \pi$, and let
$S_\varepsilon$ be the set of complex $z$ whose principal argument satisfies
$-\pi + \varepsilon \le \arg z \le \pi - \varepsilon$. Then for every natural number $N$,

$$\psi(x, z) - \sum_{j=0}^{N} \frac{(-1)^j f(x, j)}{z^{j+1}} = O\left(\frac{1}{z^{N+2}}\right)$$

as $|z| \to \infty$ with $z \in S_\varepsilon$.

articles.title: Summability of Ramanujan's factorial series in a sector, for every $x$
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a
complex number and let $\varepsilon > 0$ be a real number. Then there is a real number $R$ such
that for every complex number $z$ with $|z| \ge R$ whose principal argument satisfies
$-\pi + \varepsilon \le \arg z \le \pi - \varepsilon$, the series
$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^j x^{j+1}}{(z+1)(z+2)\cdots(z+j+1)}$ is summable.

articles.title: Summability of Ramanujan's factorial series in a sector
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a nonzero complex
number and let $\varepsilon$ be a real number with $0 < \varepsilon < \pi$. Then there is a real
number $R$ such that for every complex number $z$ with $|z| \ge R$ whose principal argument
satisfies $-\pi + \varepsilon \le \arg z \le \pi - \varepsilon$, the series
$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^j x^{j+1}}{(z+1)(z+2)\cdots(z+j+1)}$ is summable.

The hypotheses $x \neq 0$ and $\varepsilon < \pi$ are not needed for the proof; they are kept to
match the source.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 3, printed p. 47 / PDF p. 57. It follows from `ramanujan_part1_ch3_entry3_psisummable_general`; the hypotheses `x ≠ 0` and `ε < π` are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Ramanujan's asymptotic expansion of a factorial series
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a nonzero complex
number. For natural numbers $j$ let
$f(x, j) = e^{-x} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(k+1)^j x^{k+1}}{k!}$, and for complex $z$ let
$\psi(x, z) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} t_j$, where
$t_j = \frac{(-1)^j x^{j+1}}{(z+1)(z+2)\cdots(z+j+1)}$ when the denominator is nonzero and
$t_j = 0$ otherwise. Let $\varepsilon$ be a real number with $0 < \varepsilon < \pi$, and let
$S_\varepsilon$ be the set of complex $z$ whose principal argument satisfies
$-\pi + \varepsilon \le \arg z \le \pi - \varepsilon$. Then for every natural number $N$,

$$\psi(x, z) - \sum_{j=0}^{N} \frac{(-1)^j f(x, j)}{z^{j+1}} = O\left(\frac{1}{z^{N+2}}\right)$$

as $|z| \to \infty$ with $z \in S_\varepsilon$.

The hypothesis $x \neq 0$ is not needed for the proof; it is kept to match the source.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 3, printed p. 47 / PDF p. 57.

articles.title: Convergence of Ramanujan's product series in a sector
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, x \in \mathbb{C}$ with
$b \neq 0$ and let $0 < \varepsilon < \pi$. Then there is a real number $R$ such that for every
complex $z$ with $|(z + a)/b| \ge R$ and $-\pi + \varepsilon \le \arg((z + a)/b) \le
\pi - \varepsilon$, the series

$$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-b)^j x^{j+1}}{\prod_{r=0}^{j} (z + a + b(r + 1))}$$

converges absolutely.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 9(i), definitions printed p. 53 / PDF p. 63 and result printed p. 54 / PDF p. 64. It follows from `Complex.summable_neg_pow_mul_pow_div_prod_add_mul`: the upper sector bound keeps `(z + a) / b` off the negative real axis, so no factor of the denominator vanishes. The hypothesis `hεlt`, the radius (taken to be `0`) and the lower sector bound are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Asymptotic expansion of Ramanujan's product series
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, x \in \mathbb{C}$ with
$b \neq 0$, let $0 < \varepsilon < \pi$, and let $n$ be a natural number. Write $F(a, b, x; k)$
for Ramanujan's generalized Bell function and $P(a, b, x; z)$ for Ramanujan's product series.
Then

$$P(a, b, x; z) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^k F(a, b, x; k)}{z^{k+1}} + O(|z|^{-n-2})$$

as $|(z + a)/b| \to \infty$ with $-\pi + \varepsilon \le \arg((z + a)/b) \le \pi - \varepsilon$:
there are real numbers $C$ and $R$ such that the difference of the two sides has absolute value
at most $C / |z|^{n+2}$ for every complex $z$ with $|(z + a)/b| \ge R$ and
$-\pi + \varepsilon \le \arg((z + a)/b) \le \pi - \varepsilon$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 9(i), definitions printed p. 53 / PDF p. 63 and result printed p. 54 / PDF p. 64.

articles.title: Asymptotic expansion of a factorial series
articles.statement:
Let $a_0, a_1, \ldots$ be complex numbers, let
$\psi : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$, let $\lambda$ be either a real number or $-\infty$, and let
$0 < \varepsilon < \pi/2$. Suppose that for every complex $z$ that is not a negative integer and
satisfies $\operatorname{Re} z > \lambda$, the series

$$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^j a_j}{(z + 1)(z + 2) \cdots (z + j + 1)}$$

converges absolutely with sum $\psi(z)$. Write $S(n, k)$ for the Stirling numbers of the second
kind and $c_j = \sum_{k=0}^{j} a_k S(j + 1, k + 1)$. Then for every natural number $N$ there are
real numbers $C \ge 0$ and $R > 0$ such that

$$\Big|\psi(z) - \sum_{j=0}^{N} \frac{(-1)^j c_j}{z^{j+1}}\Big| \le \frac{C}{|z|^{N+2}}$$

for every complex $z$ that is not a negative integer, satisfies $\operatorname{Re} z > \lambda$
and $|z| \ge R$, and lies in the sector $|\arg z| \le \pi/2 - \varepsilon$ when
$\lambda = -\infty$, or $|\arg(z - \lambda)| \le \pi/2 - \varepsilon$ when $\lambda$ is real.

For $\lambda = -\infty$ the expansion is stated on the sector $|\arg z| \le \pi/2 - \varepsilon$,
as for real $\lambda$; on the wider sector $|\arg z| \le \pi - \varepsilon$ it fails, for example
for $a_j = j!\,(-2/3)^j$.

Proof: Use convergence at one real point to obtain absolute convergence two units to the right,
then expand each $1/((z + 1)\cdots(z + j + 1))$ termwise in powers of $1/z$ and bound the tail.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Section 8, Example 1, formula (8.1), printed p. 50 / PDF p. 60.

articles.title: Convergence of a factorial series in a sector
articles.statement:
Let $a_0, a_1, \ldots$ be complex numbers,
let $\lambda$ be either a real number or $-\infty$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$, with
$\varepsilon < \pi/2$ when $\lambda$ is real and $\varepsilon < \pi$ when $\lambda = -\infty$.
Suppose that the series

$$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^j a_j}{(z + 1)(z + 2) \cdots (z + j + 1)}$$

converges absolutely for every complex $z$ that is not a negative integer and satisfies
$\operatorname{Re} z > \lambda$. Then there is a real number $R$ such that the series converges
absolutely for every complex $z$ with $|z| > R$ that lies in the sector
$|\arg(z - \lambda)| \le \pi/2 - \varepsilon$ when $\lambda$ is real, or
$|\arg z| \le \pi - \varepsilon$ when $\lambda = -\infty$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Section 8, Example 1, formula (8.1), printed p. 50 / PDF p. 60. It follows from `ramanujan_part1_ch3_section8_example1_summable_general`; the upper bound `heps_lt` is unused and keeps the source's shape.

articles.title: Convergence of a factorial series in a sector, general form
articles.statement:
Let $a_0, a_1, \ldots$ be
complex numbers, let $\lambda$ be either a real number or $-\infty$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$.
Suppose that the series

$$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^j a_j}{(z + 1)(z + 2) \cdots (z + j + 1)}$$

converges absolutely for every complex $z$ that is not a negative integer and satisfies
$\operatorname{Re} z > \lambda$. Then there is a real number $R$ such that the series converges
absolutely for every complex $z$ with $|z| > R$ that lies in the sector
$|\arg(z - \lambda)| \le \pi/2 - \varepsilon$ when $\lambda$ is real, or
$|\arg z| \le \pi - \varepsilon$ when $\lambda = -\infty$.

articles.title: Convergence and asymptotic expansion of Ramanujan's factorial series
articles.statement:
Let
$c_j(x) = (-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$, let $C(x) = \sum_{j \ge 0} c_j(x)$,
and let $B_n$ denote the $n$-th Bell number. For all sufficiently large real $x$, $x > 0$ and the
series $\sum_{j \ge 0} c_j(x)$ is summable; and for every natural number $N$,

$$C(x) - \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \frac{(-1)^j B_{j+1}}{x^{j+1}} = O\left(\frac{1}{x^{N+1}}\right)
\quad \text{as } x \to \infty.$$

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 6.

articles.title: Convergence of Ramanujan's factorial series
articles.statement:
For every real $x > 0$, the series
$\sum_{j \ge 0} (-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$ is summable.

Its $j$-th term is bounded in absolute value by $1 / (j + 1)!$.

articles.title: Remainder bound for the Lambert series $\sum_k 1/(e^{kx}-1)$
articles.statement:
Let $x > 0$ be real and
let $n \ge 1$ be an integer. Let $S(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{e^{kx} - 1}$, let $B_m$ be
the $m$-th Bernoulli number, let $\gamma$ be the Euler–Mascheroni constant, and let
$C_n(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{B_{2k}^2 \, x^{2k-1}}{2k \, (2k)!}$. Then
$\left| S(x) - \left( \frac{\gamma}{x} - \frac{\log x}{x} + \frac14 - C_n(x) \right) \right|
\le \frac{|B_{2n} B_{2n+2}| \, x^{2n}}{(2n)!}
\left( \frac{x^2}{4\pi^2} + \frac{\pi^2}{6} \right)$.

articles.title: Asymptotic expansion of the Lambert series $\sum_k 1/(e^{kx}+1)$
articles.statement:
Let $x > 0$ be real
and let $n \ge 1$ be an integer. Let $B_m$ be the $m$-th Bernoulli number and let
$D_n(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{(2^{2k} - 1) \, B_{2k}^2 \, x^{2k-1}}{2k \, (2k)!}$. Then the
series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{e^{kx} + 1}$ is summable, and its sum $T(x)$ satisfies
$\left| T(x) - \left( \frac{\log 2}{x} - \frac14 + D_n(x) \right) \right|
\le \frac{|B_{2n} B_{2n+2}| \, x^{2n}}{(2n)!} \left( \frac{x^2}{4\pi^2} + \frac{\pi^2}{6} +
2^{2n+1} \left( \frac{x^2}{\pi^2} + \frac{\pi^2}{6} \right) \right)$.

The proof writes this series as the series $\sum_k 1/(e^{kx}-1)$ minus twice the same series
at $2x$, and applies the remainder bound for $\sum_k 1/(e^{kx}-1)$.

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 6.

articles.title: Asymptotic expansion of the Lambert series $\sum_k 1/(e^{kx}-1)$
articles.statement:
Let $x > 0$ be real
and let $n \ge 1$ be an integer. Let $B_m$ be the $m$-th Bernoulli number, let $\gamma$ be the
Euler–Mascheroni constant, and let
$C_n(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{B_{2k}^2 \, x^{2k-1}}{2k \, (2k)!}$. Then the series
$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{e^{kx} - 1}$ is summable, and its sum $S(x)$ satisfies
$\left| S(x) - \left( \frac{\gamma}{x} - \frac{\log x}{x} + \frac14 - C_n(x) \right) \right|
\le \frac{|B_{2n} B_{2n+2}| \, x^{2n}}{(2n)!} \left( \frac{x^2}{4\pi^2} + \frac{\pi^2}{6} \right)$.

The proof applies the Euler–Maclaurin formula to the smooth Mittag-Leffler kernel and bounds
the periodic Bernoulli remainder by its Fourier series.

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 6.

articles.title: Summability of the Lambert series $\sum_k 1/(e^{kx}-1)$
articles.statement:
For every real $x > 0$, the
series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{e^{kx} - 1}$ is summable.

articles.title: Summability of the Lambert series $\sum_k 1/(e^{kx}+1)$
articles.statement:
For every real $x > 0$, the
series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{e^{kx} + 1}$ is summable.

articles.title: Ramanujan's asymptotic expansion of power sums
articles.statement:
Let $r \in \mathbb{C}$ with $r \ne -1$,
and let $N$ be a positive integer with $\mathrm{Re}\, r < 2N$. For natural $n$ put
$A_N(n) = \zeta(-r) + \frac{n^{r+1}}{r+1} + \frac{n^r}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{N} T_k(n)$, where
$T_k(n) = \frac{B_{2k}}{(2k)!}\, r(r-1)\cdots(r-2k+2)\, n^{r-2k+1}$ (a product of $2k - 1$
factors), $\zeta$ is the Riemann zeta function, $B_{2k}$ are the Bernoulli numbers and complex
powers are principal. Then $\sum_{k=1}^{n} k^r - A_N(n) = O(n^{\mathrm{Re}\, r - 2N})$ as
$n \to \infty$.

Proof: Euler--Maclaurin gives the expansion with an integrable periodic-kernel tail. The constant is
identified with the Riemann zeta function first in its convergent half-plane, then everywhere needed
by analytic continuation.

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 7, Entry 1.

articles.title: Ramanujan's asymptotic expansion of a binomial combination of log-power sums
articles.statement:
For natural
numbers $m$ and $x$ let $S_m(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{x} (\log k)^m$, let $c_m = (-1)^m \zeta^{(m)}(0)$,
where $\zeta^{(m)}(0)$ is the $m$-th derivative at $0$ of the real function
$s \mapsto \operatorname{Re} \zeta(s)$, and let $\psi_m(x) = S_m(x) - c_m$. Let $n$ be a natural
number. Then for every $m \le n$,

$$S_m(x) - \int_1^x (\log t)^m \, dt - \frac{(\log x)^m}{2} + (-1)^{m+1} m! \to c_m$$

as $x \to \infty$ through the natural numbers, and

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n+k} \binom{n}{k} (\log x)^k \psi_{n-k}(x) = n! \, x -
\frac{B_{n+1}}{(n+1) x^n} - \frac{n B_{n+2}}{2 (n+2) x^{n+1}} -
\frac{n (n + 5/3) B_{n+3}}{8 (n+3) x^{n+2}} + O\left(\frac{1}{x^{n+3}}\right)$$

as $x \to \infty$ through the natural numbers, where $B_j$ are the Bernoulli numbers with
$B_1 = -1/2$.

Proof: Analytic continuation of ζ to `re s > -1` by Euler–Maclaurin, Cauchy estimates for the
remainder's derivatives, and the Euler–Maclaurin tail expansion of the log-power sums.

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 8.

articles.title: Asymptotic expansion of partial sums of powers times logarithms
articles.statement:
Let $r > -1$ be a real
number. For a natural number $n$ write $\varphi_r(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} k^r \log k$ and
$S_r(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} k^r$, and for a natural number $m$ let
$D_m(r) = \sum_{j=0}^{m} \prod_{0 \le q \le m,\ q \ne j} (r - q)$, the derivative of
$r(r-1)\cdots(r-m)$ with respect to $r$. Let $B_j$ be the Bernoulli numbers and $\zeta$ the Riemann
zeta function. Then there is a real constant $C$ such that for every natural number $N$, as
$n \to \infty$ through the natural numbers,

$$
\varphi_r(n) - \log n \, \bigl(S_r(n) - \zeta(-r)\bigr) = C - \frac{n^{r+1}}{(r+1)^2} +
\sum_{k=1}^{N} \frac{B_{2k}}{(2k)!} D_{2k-2}(r) \, n^{r-2k+1} + O\bigl(n^{r-2N-1}\bigr).
$$

Moreover, if $r > 0$, then $\Gamma(r+1) > 0$, the series $\sum_{n \ge 1} \log n / n^{r+1}$
converges, and

$$
C = \frac{2\Gamma(r+1)\zeta(r+1)}{(2\pi)^{r+1}} \Bigl(\sin\frac{\pi r}{2} \Bigl(\log(2\pi) -
\frac{\Gamma'(r+1)}{\Gamma(r+1)}\Bigr) - \frac{\pi}{2} \cos\frac{\pi r}{2}\Bigr) +
\frac{2\Gamma(r+1)\sin\frac{\pi r}{2}}{(2\pi)^{r+1}} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\log n}{n^{r+1}}.
$$

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 9.

articles.title: Bender's lemma without a radius condition on the second series
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$
be real sequences, let $A(z) = \sum_n a_n z^n$ have radius of convergence $\alpha \in [0, \infty]$,
and let $\beta \ge 0$ be a real number with $\beta < \alpha$. Suppose that $b_n \neq 0$ for all
sufficiently large $n$, that $b_{n-1} / b_n \to \beta$ as $n \to \infty$, and that
$A(\beta) \neq 0$. Then the coefficients $c_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_{n-k}$ of the product of the
formal power series $\sum_n a_n z^n$ and $\sum_n b_n z^n$ satisfy $c_n \sim A(\beta) \, b_n$ as
$n \to \infty$.

Unlike Bender's original lemma, nothing is assumed about the radius of convergence of
$\sum_n b_n z^n$.

articles.title: Bender's lemma on coefficients of a product of power series
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ be
real sequences such that $A(z) = \sum_n a_n z^n$ has radius of convergence $\alpha \in [0, \infty]$
and $\sum_n b_n z^n$ has radius of convergence $\beta$, where $\beta \ge 0$ is a real number with
$\beta < \alpha$. Suppose that $b_n \neq 0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, that
$b_{n-1} / b_n \to \beta$ as $n \to \infty$, and that $A(\beta) \neq 0$. Then the coefficients
$c_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_{n-k}$ of the product of the formal power series $\sum_n a_n z^n$ and
$\sum_n b_n z^n$ satisfy $c_n \sim A(\beta) \, b_n$ as $n \to \infty$.

The hypothesis that $b_n$ is eventually nonzero makes the ratios $b_{n-1} / b_n$ meaningful; with
the convention $x / 0 = 0$ the statement fails at $\beta = 0$ without it: for $A(z) = 1 + z$ and
$b$ vanishing at every even index and growing fast at odd indices, every ratio is $0$ while the
even product coefficients stay nonzero.

## Sources

- Dennis E. Davenport, Louis W. Shapiro, Lara K. Pudwell, and Leon C. Woodson, "The Boundary of Ordered Trees," Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015). Source file: <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Davenport/dav3.tex> (Bender's lemma, lines 521-523). It follows from `bender_product_coefficient_asymptotic_general`; the hypothesis `hB` is unused and keeps the source's shape.

articles.title: The function $e^{-\sqrt{\|x\|}}$ on the plane
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be
$f(x) = e^{-\sqrt{\|x\|}}$, where $\|x\|$ is the Euclidean norm of $x$.

articles.title: Asymptotics of the self-convolution of $e^{-\sqrt{\|x\|}}$
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to
\mathbb{R}$ be $f(x) = e^{-\sqrt{\|x\|}}$, where $\|x\|$ is the Euclidean norm, and let $f * f$ be
the convolution of $f$ with itself with respect to Lebesgue measure. Then

$$\lim_{\|a\| \to \infty} \frac{(f * f)(a)}{f(a)} = 2 \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x)\,dx.$$

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Functional analysis; Measures, integration, derivative, holomorphy), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_90`.

articles.title: Euler–Maclaurin formula
articles.statement:
Let $a < b$ be integers, let $p \ge 1$ be a natural number, and
let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be $p$ times continuously differentiable on $[a, b]$, its
derivatives $f^{(k)}$ being taken relative to $[a, b]$ (one-sided at the endpoints). Let $B_j$
be the Bernoulli numbers with $B_1 = -\tfrac{1}{2}$. Then there are $1$-periodic functions
$P_m : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ for $m \ge 0$ such that $P_p$ agrees on $[0, 1)$ with the
Bernoulli polynomial $\sum_{j=0}^{p} \binom{p}{j} B_j x^{p-j}$, and
$\sum_{n=a}^{b} f(n) = I + E + R$, where $I = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \frac{f(a) + f(b)}{2}$,
$E = \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor p/2 \rfloor} \frac{B_{2k}}{(2k)!} (f^{(2k-1)}(b) - f^{(2k-1)}(a))$
and $R = \frac{(-1)^{p+1}}{p!} \int_a^b P_p(x) f^{(p)}(x)\,dx$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%E2%80%93Maclaurin_formula.

articles.title: Initial-segment mean
articles.statement:
For a sequence $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
the initial-segment mean is the real number $m(a, n) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a(j)$, with
the convention $1 / 0 = 0$, so that $m(a, 0) = 0$.

The source uses $m(a, n)$ only for $n \ge 2$, with indices starting at $1$.

## Sources

- Joel E. Cohen, *Variance Functions of Asymptotically Exponentially Increasing Integer Sequences Go Beyond Taylor's Law*, Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.9.3, mean/variance definitions, lines 119–124, equation `eq:mean` at line 122, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Cohen/cohen13.tex>.

articles.title: Initial-segment sample variance
articles.statement:
For a sequence $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, the unbiased initial-segment sample variance is the real number
$v(a, n) = \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \left(a(j) - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a(k)\right)^2$,
with the convention $1 / 0 = 0$; in particular $v(a, 0) = v(a, 1) = 0$.

The inner average is the initial-segment mean $m(a, n)$. The source uses $v(a, n)$ only for
$n \ge 2$, with indices starting at $1$.

## Sources

- Joel E. Cohen, *Variance Functions of Asymptotically Exponentially Increasing Integer Sequences Go Beyond Taylor's Law*, Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.9.3, mean/variance definitions, lines 119–124, equation at line 122, first equality of the equation at line 123, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Cohen/cohen13.tex>.

articles.title: Admissible sequences for Taylor's law
articles.statement:
A sequence $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, indexed
from $1$ (its value at $0$ is ignored), is admissible when $a(n) > 0$ for every $n \ge 1$ and
there is $n_0 \ge 1$ such that $a(n) < a(n + 1)$ for every $n \ge n_0$.

## Sources

- Joel E. Cohen, *Variance Functions of Asymptotically Exponentially Increasing Integer Sequences Go Beyond Taylor's Law*, Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.9.3, the collection `𝒜` of infinite eventually strictly increasing sequences of natural numbers, lines 113–125, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Cohen/cohen13.tex>.

articles.title: Taylor's law, asymptotic form
articles.statement:
A sequence $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, indexed from
$1$ (its value at $0$ is ignored), satisfies Taylor's law asymptotically when it is admissible
for Taylor's law and, writing $m(a, n)$ and $v(a, n)$ for its initial-segment mean and
initial-segment sample variance, there are real numbers $c > 0$ and $b$ such that
$v(a, n) / m(a, n)^b \to c$ as $n \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Joel E. Cohen, *Variance Functions of Asymptotically Exponentially Increasing Integer Sequences Go Beyond Taylor's Law*, Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.9.3, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Cohen/cohen13.tex>: the collection `𝒜` of admissible sequences with the mean `eq:mean` and variance `eq:varexpanded` definitions (lines 113–125), and the asymptotic power-law definition `eq:TLpower` (lines 152–156).

articles.title: Watson's inverse factorial expansion
articles.statement:
Let $A,B,\rho,\sigma,\alpha,\delta>0$, $\gamma\ge 0$
and $p$ be real numbers with $\alpha+3\delta\lt \pi/2$ and $1\lt p<1+e^{-\pi\cot\alpha}$. Let $S$ be the
sector $\{z\in\mathbb{C} : |z|>\gamma,\ |\arg z|\le\pi/2+\alpha+3\delta\}$, where $\arg$ is the
principal argument. Let $f$ be a complex function that is analytic at every point of the
half-plane $\{z : \mathrm{Re}\,z>0\}$ and at every point of $S$, let $a_0,a_1,\dots$ be complex
numbers with $|a_n|\lt A\rho^n n!$ for every $n\ge 0$, and let $R_0,R_1,\dots$ be complex functions
such that for every $n\ge 0$ and every $z\in S$

$$f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{a_k}{z^k}+R_n(z)\qquad\text{and}\qquad|R_n(z)\,z^{n+1}|\lt B\sigma^n n!.$$

Suppose that $M_0$ is the largest real $x>0$ with

$$e^{-2\cos\alpha/(\rho x)}-2\cos\big(\sin\alpha/(\rho x)\big)e^{-\cos\alpha/(\rho x)}+1-p^2=0.$$

Then for every real $M$ with $0\lt M\le M_0$ and every complex $w$ with $\mathrm{Re}\,w\ge 0$ there
are complex numbers $b_0,b_1,\dots$ such that for every $z$ with $\mathrm{Re}\,z>0$ the series

$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{b_k}{(Mz+w+1)(Mz+w+2)\cdots(Mz+w+k)}$$

converges absolutely and its sum is $f(z)-b_0$.

## Sources

- https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Schumacher/schu9.tex, lines 370-417. Scope exclusion: excludes the `M = 1, w = 0` specialization and the later Stirling-coefficient theorem.

articles.title: Watson's lemma for Laplace integrals
articles.statement:
Let $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and let
$(c_k)_{k \ge 1}$ be real numbers such that for every $N \ge 0$,
$g(s) - \sum_{k=1}^{N} c_k s^k = O(s^{N+1})$ as $s \to 0^+$. Suppose there is $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$
such that $s \mapsto g(s) e^{-ms}$ is integrable on $(0, \infty)$ for every $m \ge m_0$. Then
for every $N \ge 0$,
$\int_0^\infty g(s) e^{-ms} \, ds - \sum_{k=1}^{N} k! \, c_k / m^{k+1} = O(1 / m^{N+2})$ as
$m \to \infty$.

The case $N = 0$ of the hypothesis says $g(s) = O(s)$ as $s \to 0^+$: the expansion of $g$ has no
constant term.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL14/Nemes/nemes4.tex>, lines 142-151.

articles.title: Mazur's Problem 24: additive functionals measurable along curves are continuous
articles.statement:
Let $E$
be a real Banach space and let $F \colon E \to \mathbb{R}$ be additive, that is,
$F(x + y) = F(x) + F(y)$ for all $x, y \in E$. If for every continuous map
$x \colon [0, 1] \to E$ the function $t \mapsto F(x(t))$ on $[0, 1]$ is Borel measurable,
then $F$ is continuous.

## Sources

- S. Mazur, Problem 24 of the Scottish Book (prize: two small beers). Solved affirmatively by I. Labuda and R. D. Mauldin, "Problem 24 of the Scottish Book concerning additive functionals", Colloquium Mathematicum 48, as quoted in Ger (2016); the proof covers additive operators into a Hausdorff topological vector space.

articles.title: Separation, normalized
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a subspace of $E$, and let $x \in E$ lie outside the
topological closure of $S$. Then some continuous linear functional $f$ in the topological
annihilator of $S$ satisfies $f(x) = 1$.

articles.title: Separation
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$
or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a subspace of $E$, and let $x \in E$ lie outside the topological
closure of $S$. Then some continuous linear functional $f$ in the topological annihilator of $S$
satisfies $f(x) \neq 0$.

articles.title: A subspace lies in its double annihilator
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$,
where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Every subspace $S$ of $E$ is contained in the
topological coannihilator of the topological annihilator of $S$.

articles.title: Membership in the topological annihilator
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$,
where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a subspace of $E$, and let
$f : E \to \mathbb{K}$ be a continuous linear functional. Then $f$ lies in the topological
annihilator of $S$ if and only if $f(x) = 0$ for every $x \in S$.

articles.title: Membership in the topological coannihilator
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$,
where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $\Phi$ be a subspace of the continuous dual
of $E$, and let $x \in E$. Then $x$ lies in the topological coannihilator of $\Phi$ if and only if
$f(x) = 0$ for every $f \in \Phi$.

articles.title: The topological annihilator reverses inclusion
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $S \subseteq T$ be
subspaces of $E$. Then the topological annihilator of $T$ is contained in the topological
annihilator of $S$.

articles.title: Topological annihilator of the zero subspace
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$,
where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The topological annihilator of the zero subspace
of $E$ is the whole continuous dual of $E$.

articles.title: Density criterion via the annihilator
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where
$\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $S$ be a subspace of $E$. The topological
annihilator of $S$ is the zero subspace of the continuous dual of $E$ if and only if $S$ is dense
in $E$.

articles.title: The annihilator determines the closure
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where
$\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $S$ and $T$ be subspaces of $E$. Then $S$ and
$T$ have the same topological annihilator if and only if they have the same topological
closure.

articles.title: Topological annihilator of a sum of subspaces
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$,
where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $S$ and $T$ be subspaces of $E$. The
topological annihilator of $S + T$ is the intersection of the topological annihilators of $S$
and $T$.

articles.title: Topological annihilator of the whole space
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with continuous dual $E^*$. The topological
annihilator of $E$, viewed as a subspace of itself, is the zero subspace of $E^*$: a continuous
linear functional vanishing everywhere on $E$ is zero.

articles.title: Topological annihilator of the closure
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For every subspace $S$ of $E$, the topological
annihilator of the topological closure $\overline{S}$ equals the topological annihilator of
$S$: a continuous linear functional vanishing on $S$ vanishes on $\overline{S}$.

articles.title: Bipolar theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$
and let $S$ be a subspace of $E$. The topological coannihilator of the topological annihilator
of $S$, that is, the subspace of vectors of $E$ killed by every continuous linear functional
vanishing on $S$, is the topological closure of $S$.

articles.title: Topological annihilator
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, with continuous dual $E^*$. The topological annihilator of a subspace $S$ of $E$
is the subspace of $E^*$ consisting of the continuous linear functionals $f$ with $f(x) = 0$
for all $x \in S$.

articles.title: The topological coannihilator is antitone
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with continuous dual $E^*$. If $\Phi \subseteq \Psi$
are subspaces of $E^*$, then the topological coannihilator of $\Psi$ is contained in the
topological coannihilator of $\Phi$.

articles.title: Topological coannihilator of the zero subspace
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with continuous dual $E^*$. The topological
coannihilator of the zero subspace of $E^*$ is all of $E$.

articles.title: Topological coannihilator of a sum of subspaces
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with continuous dual $E^*$. For subspaces $\Phi$
and $\Psi$ of $E^*$, the topological coannihilator of their supremum $\Phi + \Psi$ is the
intersection of the topological coannihilators of $\Phi$ and $\Psi$.

articles.title: Topological coannihilator of the whole dual
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with continuous dual $E^*$. The topological
coannihilator of $E^*$ itself is the zero subspace of $E$: a vector killed by every continuous
linear functional is zero.

The proof uses the Hahn–Banach norming functional.

articles.title: Topological coannihilator
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, with continuous dual $E^*$. The topological coannihilator of a subspace $\Phi$ of
$E^*$ is the subspace of $E$ consisting of the vectors $x$ with $f(x) = 0$ for all
$f \in \Phi$.

articles.title: Banach–Alaoglu–Bourbaki theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real locally convex topological vector
space and let $U$ be a neighbourhood of $0$ in $E$. Then the weak-star polar of $U$ is compact
in the weak dual of $E$, that is, in the space of continuous linear functionals on $E$ with the
weak-star topology.

## Sources

- N. Bourbaki, Espaces vectoriels topologiques; the normed case is L. Alaoglu, Ann. of Math. 41 (1940). Listed as §137 in O. Knill, Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `banach_alaoglu_bourbaki` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Weak-star polar
articles.statement:
For a real topological vector space $E$ and a subset $s \subseteq E$,
the weak-star polar of $s$ is the set of continuous linear functionals $\varphi$ on $E$, viewed
as elements of the weak dual of $E$, such that $|\varphi(x)| \le 1$ for every $x \in s$.

articles.title: Existence of Banach limits
articles.statement:
There is a continuous linear functional $L$ on the real Banach
space $\ell^\infty$ of bounded real sequences with the supremum norm such that $L(f) \ge 0$
whenever $f_n \ge 0$ for every $n$, $L$ maps the constant sequence $1$ to $1$, $L(f) = L(g)$
whenever $g_n = f_{n+1}$ for every $n$, and $L(f) = l$ whenever the sequence $f_n$ converges
to $l$.

## Sources

- S. Banach, Theorie des operations lineaires, 1932, definition of generalised limit; G. Lorentz, Acta Math. 80 (1948) 167-190; Lean formalizes ℓ∞ via `BoundedContinuousFunction ℕ ℝ` and real field `ℝ` with all four classical axioms.

articles.title: Bauer's uniqueness theorem at extreme points
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real Banach space with its Borel
σ-algebra, let $K \subseteq X$ be compact and convex, and let $x$ be an extreme point of $K$. If
$\mu$ is a probability measure on $X$ with $\mu(X \setminus K) = 0$ whose barycenter
$\int y \, d\mu(y)$ (a Bochner integral) equals $x$, then $\mu$ is the Dirac measure at $x$.

## Sources

- H. Bauer, *Minimalstellen von Funktionen und Extremalpunkte*, Arch. Math. 9 (1958), 389–393; see also Phelps, *Lectures on Choquet's Theorem*. Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §88. Problem `bauer_extreme_point_uniqueness` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Choquet representation for compact sets
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a second-countable real Banach space
with its Borel σ-algebra and let $K \subseteq E$ be compact. For every $x \in K$ there is a
probability measure $\mu$ on $E$ such that the set $\operatorname{ext} K$ of extreme points of
$K$ has $\mu(\operatorname{ext} K) = 1$, the identity map $y \mapsto y$ is Bochner integrable
for $\mu$, and $\int_E y \, d\mu(y) = x$.

Neither convexity nor nonemptiness of $K$ is assumed; Choquet's theorem for nonempty compact
convex sets is the special case.

articles.title: Choquet's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a second-countable real Banach space with its Borel σ-algebra
and let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty compact convex set. For every $x \in K$ there is a
probability measure $\mu$ on $E$ such that the set $\operatorname{ext} K$ of extreme points of
$K$ has $\mu(\operatorname{ext} K) = 1$, the identity map $y \mapsto y$ is Bochner integrable
for $\mu$, and $\int_E y \, d\mu(y) = x$.

## Sources

- G. Choquet, Seminaire Bourbaki 1956 and Lectures 1962; Bishop-de Leeuw and Choquet-Bishop-de Leeuw integral representation; Phelps, Lectures on Choquet's Theorem, 1966; Lean states compact-source specialization in second-countable real Banach space with `ProbabilityMeasure` carried by `extremePoints` and Bochner integral barycenter.

articles.title: Choquet's representation theorem in Banach spaces
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real Banach space with its
Borel σ-algebra and let $K \subseteq X$ be compact and convex. For every $x \in K$ there is a
probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that the complement of the set of extreme points of $K$ has
$\mu$-measure $0$ and the barycenter $\int y \, d\mu(y)$ (a Bochner integral) equals $x$.

## Sources

- G. Choquet, *Existence et unicité des représentations intégrales au moyen des points extrémaux dans les cônes convexes*, Séminaire Bourbaki (1956). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §88. Problem `choquet_representation_theorem` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Continuous linear functionals on the space of all real functions
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a set and give
the space $\mathbb{R}^H$ of all real-valued functions on $H$ the topology of pointwise
convergence. Then for every continuous linear functional $f \colon \mathbb{R}^H \to \mathbb{R}$
there are a natural number $n$, points $t_1, \dots, t_n \in H$ and real numbers
$\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$ such that $f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i \, x(t_i)$ for every
$x \in \mathbb{R}^H$.

Continuity is the intended reading of the typescript, whose statement prints no continuity
hypothesis. Without continuity the claim is false: when $H$ is infinite, the algebraic dual of
$\mathbb{R}^H$ is strictly larger than the span of the evaluations.

## Sources

- S. Banach and S. Mazur, Problem 10 of the Scottish Book, stated as a theorem in the Scottish Book typescript.

articles.title: A discontinuous linear functional on an infinite-dimensional normed space
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If $E$ is not finite-dimensional,
then there exists a linear functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ that is not continuous.

articles.title: The algebraic dual is strictly larger than the topological dual
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed
space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If $E$ is not finite-dimensional, then
there is a linear functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ that differs from every continuous
linear functional $g \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$.

articles.title: Every linear functional is continuous if and only if the space is finite-dimensional
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Every linear
functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ is continuous if and only if $E$ is finite-dimensional.

articles.title: Dunford–Pettis weak compactness criterion
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on a measurable
space $\alpha$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a family of integrable real functions on $\alpha$.
The family is uniformly integrable, meaning that it is bounded in $L^1(\mu)$ and that for every
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $\int_s |f_i| \, d\mu \le \varepsilon$ for every $i$
and every measurable set $s$ with $\mu(s) \le \delta$, if and only if the closure of the set of
classes $\{[f_i] : i \in \iota\}$ in the weak topology of $L^1(\mu)$ is weakly compact.

## Sources

- N. Dunford and B. J. Pettis, Linear Operations on Summable Functions, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 47 (1940), 323–392, DOI 10.1090/S0002-9947-1940-0002020-4, criterion for weak compactness in `L¹`; Dunford-Schwartz IV; Lean states finite-measure real `L¹` specialization with weak-space closure characterization.

articles.title: Eberlein–Šmulian theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. A subset of $E$ is compact in the weak topology if and only if it is sequentially
compact in the weak topology, that is, every sequence in it has a subsequence that converges
weakly to a point of the subset.

## Sources

- W. F. Eberlein, Weak Compactness in Banach Spaces, PNAS 33 (1947), 51–53, DOI 10.1073/pnas.33.3.51, and V. Smulian (1947); Dunford-Schwartz, Linear Operators I, 1958, V.5-6; Lean states `RCLike` Banach case with `IsCompact ↔ IsSeqCompact` in `WeakSpace`.

articles.title: Nearest points in reflexive Banach spaces
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a reflexive complex Banach space, that
is, the canonical embedding of $X$ into its double dual is surjective, and let $C \subseteq X$ be a
nonempty closed convex set. Then for every $x_0 \in X$ there is $y_0 \in C$ such that
$\|x_0 - y_0\| = \inf_{y \in C} \|x_0 - y\|$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Functional analysis; Normed linear spaces and Banach spaces; Banach lattices), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_64`.

articles.title: Spaces of type (B)
articles.statement:
A real vector space $E$ with a topology is of type (B) when there is
a function $\|\cdot\| : E \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|x\| \ge 0$, with $\|x\| = 0$ exactly when
$x = 0$, with $\|x + y\| \le \|x\| + \|y\|$ and with $\|a x\| = |a| \, \|x\|$ for all
$x, y \in E$ and $a \in \mathbb{R}$, such that a set $U \subseteq E$ is open exactly when every
$x \in U$ has an $\varepsilon > 0$ with $y \in U$ whenever $\|y - x\| < \varepsilon$, and such
that every Cauchy sequence for $\|\cdot\|$ converges in $E$ for $\|\cdot\|$.

articles.title: Negative answer to Scottish Book Problem 15.1
articles.statement:
The Mazur–Orlicz claim of Problem 15.1 is
false: there is a real vector space $E$ with a topology that is of type (F) and contains a
bounded sphere, but is not of type (B).

## Sources

- S. Mazur and W. Orlicz, Problem 15.1 of the Scottish Book; the typescript itself records the negative answer (Ad 15.1, Mazur, May 1 1937) with the spaces `ℓ ^ p` and `L ^ p` for `0 < p < 1`, with quasi-norm given by the sum (respectively integral) of `|·| ^ p`, as counterexamples: they are of type (F), possess a bounded sphere, and are not normable, hence not of type (B).

articles.title: Mazur and Orlicz's Problem 26 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
The claim of Scottish Book Problem 26
is false: there are a real vector space $E$ with a topology, of type $\{F_o\}$, and a sequence
$(F_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of linear functionals $E \to \mathbb{R}$ that converges to $0$ uniformly on
every bounded subset of $E$ but does not converge to $0$ uniformly on any open set containing
$0$.

## Sources

- S. Mazur and W. Orlicz, Problem 26 of the Scottish Book (prize: one small beer); the typescript itself records the answer on the same page: "Ad 26, The answer is negative. M. Eidelheit, June 4, 1938."

articles.title: Bounded sets in Scottish Book Problem 26
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real vector space with a topology.
A set $R \subseteq E$ is bounded if for every sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of points of $R$ and
every real sequence $(t_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $t_n \to 0$, we have $t_n x_n \to 0$ in $E$.

This sequential definition is the one printed in the problem statement.

articles.title: Sequentially bounded sets
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real vector space with a topology. A set
$R \subseteq E$ is bounded when for every sequence $(x_n)$ of points of $R$ and every sequence
$(t_n)$ of real numbers with $t_n \to 0$, the sequence $(t_n x_n)$ tends to $0$ in $E$.

This is the definition of boundedness as printed in the statement of Scottish Book
Problem 15.1.

articles.title: Spheres in the ray sense
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real vector space. A set $K \subseteq E$ is a
sphere when $0 \notin K$ and for every $x \ne 0$ in $E$ there is exactly one real $t > 0$ with
$t x \in K$; that is, every open ray from the origin meets $K$ exactly once.

articles.title: Spaces of type (F) in Scottish Book Problem 26
articles.statement:
A real vector space $E$ with a topology
is of type (F) if there is a metric $d$ on $E$ that induces its topology, is translation
invariant, $d(x + z, y + z) = d(x, y)$ for all $x, y, z \in E$, and is complete, and if
addition $E \times E \to E$ and scalar multiplication $\mathbb{R} \times E \to E$ are
continuous.

articles.title: Spaces of type (F)
articles.statement:
A real vector space $E$ with a topology is of type (F) when addition
$E \times E \to E$ and scalar multiplication $\mathbb{R} \times E \to E$ are continuous and there
is a metric $d$ on $E$ that is translation invariant, $d(x + z, y + z) = d(x, y)$ for all
$x, y, z \in E$, that induces the topology of $E$, and that is complete: every Cauchy sequence
for $d$ converges for $d$.

articles.title: Spaces of type $\{F_o\}$
articles.statement:
A real vector space $E$ with a topology is of type $\{F_o\}$ if
it is of type (F) and, for every sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ in $E$ with $x_n \to 0$ and every
real sequence $(t_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $\sum_n |t_n| < \infty$, the series $\sum_n t_n x_n$
converges in $E$.

articles.title: Scottish Book Problem 15.1
articles.statement:
The claim of Mazur and Orlicz that every real vector space $E$
with a topology that is of type (F) and contains a bounded sphere is of type (B).

articles.title: Scottish Book Problem 26 (Mazur and Orlicz's claim)
articles.statement:
The claim that for every real vector
space $E$ with a topology that is of type $\{F_o\}$ and every sequence $(F_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of
linear functionals $E \to \mathbb{R}$, if $F_n \to 0$ uniformly on every bounded set
$R \subseteq E$, then there is an open set $U \subseteq E$ containing $0$ on which
$F_n \to 0$ uniformly.

Here $F_n \to 0$ uniformly on a set $S$ means that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$
with $|F_n(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$ and all $x \in S$. The $F_n$ are only assumed
linear, not continuous.

articles.title: Goldstine's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$,
let $E^{**}$ be its bidual and let $J : E \to E^{**}$ be the canonical embedding. In the
weak-star topology of $E^{**}$, the closure of the image under $J$ of the closed unit ball of $E$
is exactly the closed unit ball of $E^{**}$.

## Sources

- H. H. Goldstine, Weakly complete Banach spaces, Duke Math. J. 4 (1938), DOI 10.1215/S0012-7094-38-00410-7; Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed.; Lean states `RCLike` field case with metric closedBall formulation.

articles.title: Separation of convex bodies at positive distance
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real Banach space and let
$A, B \subseteq E$ be convex bodies, that is, convex, closed and bounded sets with nonempty
interior. If there is $\varepsilon > 0$ with $\operatorname{dist}(a, b) \ge \varepsilon$ for all
$a \in A$ and $b \in B$, then there are a nonzero continuous linear functional
$F : E \to \mathbb{R}$ and a constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$ with $F(a) \le c$ for all $a \in A$
and $c \le F(b)$ for all $b \in B$.

## Sources

- S. Mazur, Problem 64 of the Scottish Book; the theorem is true, as recorded in the typescript Ad 64 (Eidelheit, January 11, 1936), which gives the stronger statement that separation holds even for non-disjoint bodies with no common interior points. The positive-distance case follows from standard Hahn–Banach separation.

articles.title: Hahn–Banach distance formula, attainment form
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of
$E$, not necessarily closed, and let $x \in E$. Then there is a continuous linear functional
$f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ with $\|f\| \le 1$ that vanishes on $S$ and satisfies
$f(x) = d(x, S)$, where $d(x, S) = \inf_{s \in S} \|x - s\|$ is the distance from $x$ to $S$.

articles.title: Norm-one annihilating functional at positive distance
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of
$E$, and let $x \in E$ have positive distance $d(x, S) = \inf_{s \in S} \|x - s\| > 0$ from $S$.
Then there is a continuous linear functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ with $\|f\| = 1$ that
vanishes on $S$ and satisfies $f(x) = d(x, S)$.

A functional with $\|f\| \le 1$ that vanishes on $S$ and satisfies $f(x) = d(x, S)$ has norm
exactly $1$: for $s \in S$ we have $d(x, S) = |f(x - s)| \le \|f\| \, \|x - s\|$, and $s$ can be
chosen with $\|x - s\|$ arbitrarily close to $d(x, S) > 0$.

articles.title: Norm-one annihilating functional outside a closed subspace
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space
over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a closed linear
subspace of $E$ and let $x \in E$ with $x \notin S$. Then there is a continuous linear functional
$f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ with $\|f\| = 1$ that vanishes on $S$ and satisfies
$f(x) = d(x, S)$, where $d(x, S) = \inf_{s \in S} \|x - s\|$ is the distance from $x$ to $S$.

Since $S$ is closed and $x \notin S$, the distance $d(x, S)$ is positive.

articles.title: One-step Hahn–Banach extension
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a seminormed space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $M$ be a subspace of $E$, let $C \ge 0$ be a real
number, and let $f \colon M \to \mathbb{K}$ be a continuous linear functional with
$\|f(m)\| \le C\|m\|$ for all $m \in M$. If $x_0 \in E$ does not lie in $M$, then $M$ is strictly
contained in $M' = M + \mathbb{K} x_0$, and there is a continuous linear functional
$g \colon M' \to \mathbb{K}$ that agrees with $f$ on $M$ and satisfies $\|g(v)\| \le C\|v\|$ for all
$v \in M'$.

articles.title: Hahn–Banach distance formula
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, where
$\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of $E$, not
necessarily closed, and let $x \in E$. Then the distance $d(x, S) = \inf_{s \in S} \|x - s\|$
from $x$ to $S$ equals the supremum of $|f(x)|$ over all continuous linear functionals
$f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ with $\|f\| \le 1$ that vanish on $S$.

The supremum is attained, by the attainment form of the distance formula.

articles.title: Quotient seminorm equals distance to the subspace
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of
$E$, and give $E/S$ the quotient seminorm. Then for every $x \in E$ the class $q(x)$ of $x$ under
the quotient map $q \colon E \to E/S$ satisfies $\|q(x)\| = d(x, S)$, where
$d(x, S) = \inf_{s \in S} \|x - s\|$ is the distance from $x$ to $S$.

articles.title: The quotient map has norm at most one
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$,
where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of $E$, and give
$E/S$ the quotient seminorm. Then the quotient map $q \colon E \to E/S$, a continuous linear map,
has operator norm $\|q\| \le 1$.

articles.title: A Banach space with a countable Hamel basis is finite-dimensional
articles.statement:
If `E` is a complete normed space over `𝕜 = ℝ, ℂ` admitting a Hamel basis
indexed by a countable type, then `E` is finite-dimensional. Completeness
is essential: it is what the Baire category argument uses.

articles.title: An infinite-dimensional Banach space has no countable Hamel basis
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complete
normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If $E$ is not finite-dimensional,
then no Hamel basis of $E$ is indexed by a countable set.

articles.title: Finite-coordinate Goldstine theorem
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real normed space, write $X^*$ for
its dual space of continuous linear functionals and $X^{**}$ for the dual of $X^*$, and let
$T \in X^{**}$ with $\|T\| \le 1$. Then for every finite set $s \subseteq X^*$ and every real
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is $x \in X$ with $\|x\| \le 1$ such that $|z(x) - T(z)| < \varepsilon$
for every $z \in s$.

articles.title: James' reflexivity theorem
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $E$ be a
Banach space over $\mathbb{K}$. The canonical embedding of $E$ into its bidual $E^{**}$ is
surjective if and only if every continuous linear functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ attains
its norm on the closed unit ball, that is, there is $x \in E$ with $\|x\| \le 1$ and
$|f(x)| = \|f\|$.

Proof: The reverse implication uses the general real James convex-block argument, with Goldstine
approximation and weak-star cluster hulls. Restriction of scalars transfers the result from real
scalars to $\mathbb{K}$.

## Sources

- R. C. James, Reflexivity and the Supremum of Linear Functionals, Ann. of Math. 66 (1957), DOI 10.2307/1970122; Bourbaki form; Lean states `RCLike` Banach case with norm-attainment equivalence for reflexivity.

articles.title: Josefson–Nissenzweig theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Then there is a sequence $(\varphi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$
of continuous linear functionals on $E$ with $\|\varphi_n\| = 1$ for every $n$ such that
$\varphi_n(x) \to 0$ for every $x \in E$; that is, the unit sphere of the dual of $E$ contains a
weak-star null sequence.

Proof: We apply Rosenthal's `ℓ¹` dichotomy to a separated dual sequence, then use the stable-block
and Banach-limit/Rademacher route of Hagler--Johnson (1977) and Behrends (1995).

## Sources

- B. Josefson, Weak sequential convergence in the dual of a Banach space does not imply norm convergence, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 81 (1975), 166–168, DOI 10.1090/S0002-9904-1975-13691-3; and A. Nissenzweig, w* sequential convergence, Israel J.
