## Sources

- Bañuelos and Janakiraman, *Lp-bounds for the Beurling--Ahlfors transform*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 360 (2008): `‖B‖ₚ ≤ 1.575 (p* - 1)` for all `1 < p`. Stated as the actual finite exponential bound (an admissible `L^p` bound constant), not as an inequality for the totalized infimum; combined with `beurlingNorm_le_of_isBound` (and `0 ≤ 1.575 * (pstar p - 1)`, from `two_le_pstar`) it yields `beurlingNorm p ≤ 1.575 * (pstar p - 1)`.

articles.title: Beurling–Ahlfors constant
articles.statement:
The Beurling–Ahlfors constant is the supremum, over real
numbers $p > 1$, of $\|B\|_p / (p^* - 1)$, where $B$ is the Beurling–Ahlfors transform,
$\|B\|_p$ is the infimum of the real numbers $C \ge 0$ that are admissible $L^p$ bound
constants for $B$ (and $0$ if there is no such $C$), and $p^* = \max(p, p/(p-1))$. The
supremum is taken in $\mathbb{R}$, so it is $0$ when these ratios are not bounded above.

articles.title: Nonnegative admissible bounds bound the Beurling–Ahlfors norm
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $C$ be real
numbers with $C \ge 0$, and let $\|B\|_p$ be the infimum of the nonnegative admissible $L^p$
bound constants for the Beurling–Ahlfors transform $B$ ($0$ if there are none). If $C$ is an
admissible $L^p$ bound constant for $B$, then $\|B\|_p \le C$.

articles.title: Norm of the Beurling–Ahlfors transform
articles.statement:
For a real number $p$, the norm $\|B\|_p$ of the
Beurling–Ahlfors transform $B$ is the infimum of the real numbers $C \ge 0$ that are admissible
$L^p$ bound constants for $B$, and is $0$ when there is no such $C$. In particular an upper
bound on $\|B\|_p$ alone does not imply that $B$ is bounded on $L^p$.

articles.title: Beurling–Ahlfors transform
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ and $z \in \mathbb{C}$,
$Bf(z)$ is the limit as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$ of the truncated Beurling–Ahlfors integrals
$-\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{|w - z| > \varepsilon} \frac{f(w)}{(z - w)^2} \, dw$ (each taken to be $0$
when its integrand is not integrable). Where this limit does not exist, $Bf(z)$ is an
unspecified complex number.

For $f \in L^p$ with $1 < p < \infty$ the limit exists almost everywhere.

articles.title: Truncated Beurling–Ahlfors integral
articles.statement:
For a real number $\varepsilon$, a function
$f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ and $z \in \mathbb{C}$, the truncated Beurling–Ahlfors integral
at cutoff $\varepsilon$ is
$-\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{|w - z| > \varepsilon} \frac{f(w)}{(z - w)^2} \, dw$, the integral being
with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{C}$ and taken to be $0$ when the integrand is not
integrable.

articles.title: Admissible bounds for the Beurling–Ahlfors transform
articles.statement:
For real numbers $p$ and $C$, $C$
is an admissible $L^p$ bound constant for the Beurling–Ahlfors transform $B$ when
$\|Bf\|_q \le \max(C, 0) \, \|f\|_q$ for every almost everywhere strongly measurable function
$f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$, where $q = \max(p, 0)$ and $\|\cdot\|_q$ is the extended
$L^q$ norm with respect to Lebesgue measure (identically $0$ when $q = 0$), with values in
$[0, \infty]$ and the convention $0 \cdot \infty = 0$.

articles.title: Iwaniec's conjecture
articles.statement:
For every real number $p > 1$, the $L^p$ norm of the
Beurling–Ahlfors transform $B$ satisfies $\|B\|_p = p^* - 1$, where $p^* = \max(p, p/(p-1))$.

Given Lehto's lower bound $\|B\|_p \ge p^* - 1$, this is equivalent to the Beurling–Ahlfors
constant being equal to $1$.

articles.title: The Beurling–Ahlfors transform has $L^2$ norm $1$
articles.statement:
For a function
$f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ let $Bf(z)$ be the limit as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$ of
$-\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{|w - z| > \varepsilon} \frac{f(w)}{(z - w)^2} \, dA(w)$, where $dA$ is
Lebesgue area measure (a junk value where the limit does not exist). The infimum $\|B\|_2$ of the
constants $C \ge 0$ such that $\|Bf\|_{L^2} \le C\,\|f\|_{L^2}$ in $[0, \infty]$ for every almost
everywhere strongly measurable $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ (taken to be $0$ when there is no
such $C$) equals $1$.

## Sources

- the `L²` isometry recorded in Bañuelos--Janakiraman (2008), introduction: `‖B‖₂ = 1`.

articles.title: Lehto's lower bound for the Beurling–Ahlfors transform
articles.statement:
For a function
$f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ let $Bf(z)$ be the limit as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$ of
$-\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{|w - z| > \varepsilon} \frac{f(w)}{(z - w)^2} \, dA(w)$, where $dA$ is
Lebesgue area measure (a junk value where the limit does not exist). For real $p > 1$ let
$p^* = \max(p, p/(p - 1))$ and let $\|B\|_p$ be the infimum of the constants $C \ge 0$ such that
$\|Bf\|_{L^p} \le C\,\|f\|_{L^p}$ in $[0, \infty]$ for every almost everywhere strongly
measurable $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$, taken to be $0$ when there is no such $C$. Then
$p^* - 1 \le \|B\|_p$ for every real $p > 1$.

Because $\|B\|_p$ is $0$ when no such $C$ exists, this also asserts that $B$ has an admissible
$L^p$ bound for every $p > 1$.

## Sources

- Lehto (1965): `‖B‖ₚ ≥ p* - 1` for all `1 < p`.

articles.title: Larger of an exponent and its conjugate
articles.statement:
For a real number $p$,
$p^* = \max(p, p/(p-1))$, with division by zero taken to be $0$ (so $p^* = 1$ at $p = 1$). For
$p > 1$ this is the larger of $p$ and its conjugate exponent $p/(p-1)$.

articles.title: Convolution of two square-integrable functions is continuous and vanishes at infinity
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f, g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be square-integrable.
Then the convolution $(f \ast g)(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y) \, g(y) \, dy$ is a continuous
function of $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and $(f \ast g)(x) \to 0$ as $|x| \to \infty$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Functional analysis; Linear function spaces and their duals), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_17`.

articles.title: Convolution theorem
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be a continuous additive character from $\mathbb{R}$ to the
unit circle, and let $\mu$ be a σ-finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$ that is preserved by every
translation $x \mapsto a + x$. For $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ write
$\hat\varphi(w) = \int e(-xw)\,\varphi(x)\,d\mu(x)$ for its Fourier transform with respect to
$e$ and $\mu$, and for $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ write
$(f * g)(x) = \int f(t)\,g(x - t)\,d\mu(t)$ for their convolution. If $f$ and $g$ are
$\mu$-integrable, then $\widehat{f * g}(w) = \hat f(w)\,\hat g(w)$ for every $w \in \mathbb{R}$.

Proof: Integrability of the convolution integrand, Fubini's theorem, translation invariance of
$\mu$ and multiplicativity of $e$, following Stein--Shakarchi, Ch. 5, Prop. 1.11.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolution_theorem.

articles.title: Hausdorff–Young inequality for Schwartz functions
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let
$\mathcal{F}$ be the Fourier transform on $\mathbb{R}^n$,
$\mathcal{F}f(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x) e^{-2\pi i \langle x, \xi \rangle}\, dx$. There is a
constant $C > 0$ such that for all $p, p' \in [0, \infty]$ with $1 \le p \le 2$ and
$\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p'} = 1$ (so $p' = \infty$ when $p = 1$) and every complex-valued
Schwartz function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\|\mathcal{F}f\|_{L^{p'}} \le C \|f\|_{L^p}$, where the
$L^p$ norms are taken with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_84`.

articles.title: Cohn–Kumar–Miller–Radchenko–Viazovska Fourier interpolation theorem
articles.statement:
Let
$(n, k_0)$ be $(8, 1)$ or $(24, 2)$. For a complex-valued Schwartz function $f$ on
$\mathbb{R}^n$, let $\hat f(\xi) = \int f(x) e^{-2\pi i \langle x, \xi \rangle}\,dx$ be its
Fourier transform, let $e_1$ be the first standard basis vector and let $r_k = \sqrt{2k}$.
The sampling map sends $f$ to the four complex sequences indexed by the integers $k \ge k_0$
whose $k$-th terms are $f(r_k e_1)$, $\hat f(r_k e_1)$ and the derivatives at $r = r_k$ of
$r \mapsto f(r e_1)$ and of $r \mapsto \hat f(r e_1)$. Call $f$ radial if $f(x) = f(y)$
whenever $|x| = |y|$, and call a sequence $(a_k)_{k \ge k_0}$ rapidly decreasing if
$k^m |a_k| \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$ for every natural number $m$. Then the sampling map is a
bijection from the radial Schwartz functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$ onto the quadruples of rapidly
decreasing sequences indexed by $k \ge k_0$. So sampling starts at radius $\sqrt 2$ in
dimension $8$ and at radius $2$ in dimension $24$.

## Sources

- H. Cohn, A. Kumar, S. D. Miller, D. Radchenko, and M. Viazovska, 'Universal optimality of the E8 and Leech lattices and interpolation formulas', Ann. of Math. 196 (2022), 983-1082, Theorem 1.9, https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2022.196.3.3. Problem `ckmrv_fourier_interpolation` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Radial Fourier interpolation property
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and $k_0 \ge 0$ be integers. For a
complex-valued Schwartz function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, let
$\hat f(\xi) = \int f(x) e^{-2\pi i \langle x, \xi \rangle}\,dx$ be its Fourier transform, let
$e_1$ be the first standard basis vector and let $r_k = \sqrt{2k}$. The sampling map from index
$k_0$ sends $f$ to the four complex sequences indexed by the integers $k \ge k_0$ whose $k$-th
terms are $f(r_k e_1)$, $\hat f(r_k e_1)$ and the derivatives at $r = r_k$ of
$r \mapsto f(r e_1)$ and of $r \mapsto \hat f(r e_1)$. Call $f$ radial if $f(x) = f(y)$ whenever
$|x| = |y|$, and call a sequence $(a_k)_{k \ge k_0}$ rapidly decreasing if $k^m |a_k| \to 0$ as
$k \to \infty$ for every natural number $m$. The property $\mathrm{CKMRV}(n, k_0)$ holds when
the sampling map from index $k_0$ is a bijection from the radial Schwartz functions on
$\mathbb{R}^n$ onto the quadruples of rapidly decreasing sequences indexed by $k \ge k_0$.

The bijection is required to be the sampling map itself, so no interpolation basis is hidden
in the definition.

articles.title: Fourier sample sequences
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and $k_0 \ge 0$ be integers, let $f$ be a
complex-valued Schwartz function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with Fourier transform
$\hat f(\xi) = \int f(x) e^{-2\pi i \langle x, \xi \rangle}\,dx$, let $e_1$ be the first
standard basis vector and let $r_k = \sqrt{2k}$. The samples of $f$ are the four complex
sequences indexed by the integers $k \ge k_0$ whose $k$-th terms are, in this order,
$f(r_k e_1)$, $\hat f(r_k e_1)$, the derivative at $r = r_k$ of $r \mapsto f(r e_1)$, and the
derivative at $r = r_k$ of $r \mapsto \hat f(r e_1)$.

articles.title: Radial Schwartz functions
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, this is the set of complex-valued
Schwartz functions $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ that are radial: $f(x) = f(y)$ whenever $|x| = |y|$.

articles.title: Radial function
articles.statement: A function is radial if it takes the same value at points with the same norm.

articles.title: Rapidly decreasing sample data
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k_0$, this is the set of families
$(a_{k,j})$ of complex numbers indexed by the integers $k \ge k_0$ and $j \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$
whose four sequences $(a_{k,j})_{k \ge k_0}$ are all rapidly decreasing: $k^m |a_{k,j}| \to 0$
as $k \to \infty$ for every $j$ and every natural number $m$.

articles.title: Rapidly decreasing sample quadruples
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k_0$, a family $(a_{k,j})$
of complex numbers indexed by the integers $k \ge k_0$ and $j \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ is a rapidly
decreasing quadruple if each of its four sequences $(a_{k,j})_{k \ge k_0}$ is rapidly
decreasing, that is, $k^m |a_{k,j}| \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$ for every $j$ and every natural
number $m$.

articles.title: Rapidly decreasing sequences
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k_0$, a complex sequence
$(a_k)_{k \ge k_0}$ indexed by the integers $k \ge k_0$ is rapidly decreasing if
$k^m |a_k| \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$ for every natural number $m$.

articles.title: Embedding of the first coordinate axis
articles.statement:
For a positive integer $n$, this is the map
$\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ sending $r$ to $(r, 0, \dots, 0)$, whose image is the first
coordinate axis.

articles.title: The Fourier–Laplace transform of an integrable compactly supported function is entire
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ be integrable with compact support. Then its Fourier–Laplace
transform $z \mapsto \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x) \, e^{-2\pi i x z} \, dx$ is complex differentiable
at every $z \in \mathbb{C}$, that is, it is entire.

articles.title: Fourier–Laplace transform on the real axis
articles.statement:
For every $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$
and every real $r$, the Fourier–Laplace transform of $f$ at the complex number $r$, namely
$\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x) \, e^{-2\pi i x r} \, dx$, equals the Fourier transform of $f$ at $r$
with the $2\pi$ normalization, $\hat f(r) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-2\pi i x r} f(x) \, dx$.

articles.title: Fourier–Laplace transform
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ and $z \in \mathbb{C}$,
the Fourier–Laplace transform of $f$ at $z$ is the Lebesgue integral
$\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x) \, e^{-2\pi i x z} \, dx$, taken to be $0$ when the integrand is not
integrable.

articles.title: Derivative of the Fourier–Laplace transform
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ be
integrable with compact support, and let $F(z) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x) \, e^{-2\pi i x z} \, dx$
be its Fourier–Laplace transform. Then at every $z \in \mathbb{C}$, $F$ is complex differentiable
with derivative $F'(z) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x) \, (-2\pi i x) \, e^{-2\pi i x z} \, dx$.

articles.title: Fourier transform of a dilated Schwartz function
articles.statement:
Write
$\hat g(y) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-2\pi i x y} g(x)\,dx$ for the Fourier transform of a
function $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$. For every Schwartz function
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$, every real $a > 0$ and every real $y$, the Fourier transform of
$x \mapsto f(ax)$ at $y$ equals $a^{-1} \hat f(y/a)$.

articles.title: Fourier transform of a dilation by a positive factor
articles.statement:
Write
$\hat g(y) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-2\pi i x y} g(x)\,dx$ for the Fourier transform of a
function $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$. For every $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$, every real
$a > 0$ and every real $y$, the Fourier transform of $x \mapsto f(ax)$ at $y$ equals
$a^{-1} \hat f(y/a)$.

No integrability hypothesis is needed because Mathlib's Bochner integral is
totalized, so the identity also uses that convention for nonintegrable
functions.

articles.title: Fourier transform of a dilation
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex normed space, and write
$\hat g(y) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-2\pi i x y} g(x)\,dx$ for the Fourier transform of a
function $g : \mathbb{R} \to E$. For every $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$, every real $a \ne 0$ and
every real $y$, the Fourier transform of $x \mapsto f(ax)$ at $y$ equals $|a|^{-1} \hat f(y/a)$.

No integrability hypothesis is needed because Mathlib's Bochner integral is
totalized, so the identity also uses that convention for nonintegrable
functions.

articles.title: Closed cubes in Euclidean space
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number. For real numbers $a$ and $b$,
the cube $[a,b]^d$ is the set of points $x$ of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ with
$a \le x_i \le b$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Porosity on balls
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number and let $\nu$, $\alpha_0$ and $\alpha_1$ be
real numbers. A set $X$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ is $\nu$-porous on balls from scales
$\alpha_0$ to $\alpha_1$ if for every $y \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and every $R$ with
$\alpha_0 < R < \alpha_1$, the closed ball of radius $R/2$ about $y$ contains a point $x$ such that
the closed ball of radius $\nu R$ about $x$ is disjoint from $X$.

articles.title: Porosity on lines
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number and let $\nu$, $\alpha_0$ and $\alpha_1$ be
real numbers. A set $X$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ is $\nu$-porous on lines from scales
$\alpha_0$ to $\alpha_1$ if for every $R$ with $\alpha_0 < R < \alpha_1$ and all points
$y_1, y_2 \in \mathbb{R}^d$ at distance $R$, the closed segment from $y_1$ to $y_2$ contains a point
$x$ such that the closed ball of radius $\nu R$ about $x$ is disjoint from $X$.

articles.title: Cohen's fractal uncertainty principle for line-porous sets
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number and
$\nu > 0$. Then there are real numbers $\beta > 0$ and $C > 0$ such that for every $h$ with
$0 < h < 1/100$ and all measurable sets $X, Y$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ the following
holds: if $X \subseteq [-1,1]^d$ is $\nu$-porous on balls from scales $h$ to $1$ and
$Y \subseteq [-h^{-1},h^{-1}]^d$ is $\nu$-porous on lines from scales $1$ to $h^{-1}$, then every
$f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ whose Fourier transform $\mathcal{F}f$ vanishes almost everywhere outside
$Y$ satisfies $\|\mathbf{1}_X f\|_2 \le C h^{\beta} \|f\|_2$. Thus $\beta$ and $C$ depend only on
$\nu$ and $d$.

Here $\mathcal{F}$ is the Fourier transform on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, extended by continuity from
$\mathcal{F}f(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-2\pi i \langle x, \xi \rangle} f(x)\,dx$ on Schwartz
functions.

We require $X$ and $Y$ to be measurable to make the statement more natural.

## Sources

- A. Cohen, `Fractal uncertainty in higher dimensions`, Annals of Math, 202 (1) 2025. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_fractal_uncertainty` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Heisenberg uncertainty inequality with shifted moments
articles.statement:
For a complex-valued Schwartz
function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$, write
$\hat{f}(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x) e^{-2\pi i x \xi}\, dx$ for its Fourier transform. There is
a constant $C > 0$ such that for all real numbers $c$ and $d$ and every complex-valued Schwartz
function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$,

$$
\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} |f(x)|^2\, dx\right)^2 \le C
\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} (x - c)^2 |f(x)|^2\, dx\right)
\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} (\xi - d)^2 |\hat{f}(\xi)|^2\, d\xi\right).
$$

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Functional analysis; Distributions, generalized functions, distribution spaces), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_46`.

articles.title: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
articles.statement:
**Heisenberg's uncertainty principle** with the position factor centered: for
`μ = (∫ y * ‖f y‖²) / (∫ ‖f x‖²)`, the position second moment about `μ` satisfies
the same bound. For positive L2 mass, `μ` is the mean position. Zero L2 mass occurs
only for `f = 0`, where `μ = 0 / 0 = 0` by Lean's convention.
Only the position factor is centered.

articles.title: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
articles.statement:
**Heisenberg's uncertainty principle** for complex-valued Schwartz functions:
`(∫ ‖f x‖²)² ≤ 4 * (∫ x² * ‖f x‖²) * (∫ ‖f' x‖²)`.

articles.title: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
articles.statement:
**Heisenberg's uncertainty principle** in Fourier form: with Mathlib's
Fourier normalization, the Fourier second moment about zero is `∫ ξ² * ‖𝓕 f ξ‖²`, and
`(∫ ‖f x‖²)² ≤ 16 * π² * (∫ x² * ‖f x‖²) * (∫ ξ² * ‖𝓕 f ξ‖²)`.

articles.title: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
articles.statement:
**Heisenberg's uncertainty principle** for real-valued Schwartz functions:
`(∫ (f x)²)² ≤ 4 * (∫ x² * (f x)²) * (∫ (f' x)²)`.

articles.title: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
articles.statement:
**Heisenberg's uncertainty principle** about an arbitrary center `a`:
the position second moment is measured about `a`; the derivative factor is unchanged.

articles.title: Weighted $L^2$ inequality for real Schwartz functions
articles.statement:
For every real-valued Schwartz
function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,

$$
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x)^2 \, dx \le 2 \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}} x^2 f(x)^2 \, dx \right)^{1/2}
\left( \int_{\mathbb{R}} f'(x)^2 \, dx \right)^{1/2},
$$

that is, $\|f\|_{L^2}^2 \le 2 \, \|x f\|_{L^2} \, \|f'\|_{L^2}$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Real functions; Inequalities in real analysis), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_40`.

articles.title: Heisenberg uncertainty principle
articles.statement:
Denote by $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$ the Schwartz space on $\mathbb{R}$ consisting of all
complex-valued $C^\infty$ functions $f(x)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} |x|^k \left|\frac{d^\ell f}{dx^\ell}(x)\right| < \infty
\quad\text{for all } k,\ell\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}.
\]
Suppose $\psi(x)\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$ satisfies
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\psi(x)|^2\,dx=1.
\]
Denote by $\hat{\psi}(\xi)$ the Fourier transform of $\psi(x)$ defined by
\[
\hat{\psi}(\xi)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx.
\]
The normalized Fourier Heisenberg corollary then gives
\[
\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2|\psi(x)|^2\,dx\right)
\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \xi^2|\hat{\psi}(\xi)|^2\,d\xi\right)
\ge \frac{1}{16\pi^2}.
\]

Lean variant: the Fourier transform is Mathlib's `𝓕`, which has the source's normalization `∫ ψ(x)
e^{-2πixξ} dx`, instead of the source's helper definition.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Functional analysis; Distributions, generalized functions, distribution spaces), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_57`, with the change above.

articles.title: Integration-by-parts identity for Heisenberg's inequality
articles.statement:
The integration-by-parts identity underlying Heisenberg's inequality:
for real-valued Schwartz `f`, `∫ (f x)² = -2 * ∫ x * f x * f' x`.

articles.title: Besicovitch's Kakeya set of measure zero
articles.statement:
There is a compact set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$
of Lebesgue measure zero that contains a unit segment in every direction: $K$ is measurable,
and for every unit vector $v \in \mathbb{R}^2$ there is a point $a \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with
$a + t v \in K$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$.

The proof here follows T. W. Körner, "Besicovitch via Baire", Studia Math. 158 (2003): a
Baire-category argument in the Hausdorff metric space of compact sets, not a Perron-tree
construction.

## Sources

- A. S. Besicovitch, Math. Z. 27 (1928) 312–320 and S. Kakeya, Tohoku Rep. 6 (1917); Perron-tree gives compact measure-zero Kakeya set; Lean states compact Lebesgue-null oriented version in ℝ² with segments `a+t•v`, `t∈[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Kakeya set
articles.statement:
A Kakeya set is a compact subset $K$ of three-dimensional Euclidean space
that contains a unit line segment in every direction: for every unit vector $v$ there is a
point $x$ with $x + t v \in K$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: Three-dimensional Euclidean space
articles.statement:
The space $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the Euclidean inner
product.

articles.title: Wang–Zahl theorem: the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions
articles.statement:
Every Kakeya set in
three-dimensional Euclidean space has Hausdorff dimension $3$.

## Sources

- H. Wang and J. Zahl, 'Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions', Theorem 1.1, arXiv:2502.17655 (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17655. The proof builds on their 'Sticky Kakeya sets and the sticky Kakeya conjecture', arXiv:2210.09581, and 'The Assouad dimension of Kakeya sets in R^3', arXiv:2401.12337. Problem `wang_zahl_kakeya_dimH` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: A four-function case of the HRT conjecture holds
articles.statement:
For every function
$g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ that is not zero almost everywhere, the four
functions $g(x)$, $g(x - 1)$, $g(x - \sqrt{2})$ and $e^{2\pi i x} g(x)$ are linearly independent:
whenever $c_0, c_1, c_2, c_3 \in \mathbb{C}$ satisfy
$c_0 g(x) + c_1 g(x - 1) + c_2 g(x - \sqrt{2}) + c_3 e^{2\pi i x} g(x) = 0$ for almost every
$x \in \mathbb{R}$, then $c_0 = c_1 = c_2 = c_3 = 0$.

This case was proved by Demeter (Theorem 1.4(b)); Liu (Theorem 1.1(b)) states it for the
time-frequency configuration $\{(0,0),(a,0),(b,0),(0,1)\}$ with $a = 1$ and $b = \sqrt{2}$.

## Sources

- Ciprian Demeter, Linear independence of time frequency translates for special configurations, Math. Res. Lett. 17 (2010) 761-779, arXiv:1006.0732, https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.0732; Wencai Liu, Proof of the HRT conjecture for almost every (1,3) configuration, J. Fourier Anal. Appl. (2019), arXiv:1609.08230, https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.08230.

articles.title: A four-function case of the HRT conjecture
articles.statement:
For every function
$g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ that is not zero almost everywhere, the four
functions $g(x)$, $g(x - 1)$, $g(x - \sqrt{2})$ and $e^{2\pi i x} g(x)$ are linearly independent:
whenever $c_0, c_1, c_2, c_3 \in \mathbb{C}$ satisfy
$c_0 g(x) + c_1 g(x - 1) + c_2 g(x - \sqrt{2}) + c_3 e^{2\pi i x} g(x) = 0$ for almost every
$x \in \mathbb{R}$, we have $c_0 = c_1 = c_2 = c_3 = 0$.

articles.title: Frequency-one modulation factor
articles.statement:
The function $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ given by
$x \mapsto e^{2\pi i x}$; multiplying a function by it modulates that function by frequency one.

articles.title: Fourier support in the Nyquist band
articles.statement:
A Schwartz function
$f \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ has Fourier support in the Nyquist band when its Fourier
transform $\hat f(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x)\, e^{-2\pi i x \xi}\, dx$ vanishes at every real
$\xi$ outside the closed interval $[-\frac12, \frac12]$.

articles.title: Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem (Whittaker–Shannon interpolation formula)
articles.statement:
Let
$\operatorname{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}$ for real $x \neq 0$ and $\operatorname{sinc}(0) = 1$,
and let $f \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ be a Schwartz function whose Fourier transform
$\hat f(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x)\, e^{-2\pi i x \xi}\, dx$ vanishes at every real $\xi$
outside $[-\frac12, \frac12]$. Then for every real $t$ the series
$\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f(n) \operatorname{sinc}(\pi(n - t))$ is summable over $\mathbb{Z}$
(unconditionally convergent) and

$$
f(t) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f(n) \operatorname{sinc}(\pi(n - t)).
$$

## Sources

- C. E. Shannon, *Communication in the presence of noise*, Proc. IRE 37 (1949); H. Nyquist (1928); E. T. Whittaker (1915). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §179. Problem `nyquist_shannon_sampling` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Unnormalised cardinal sine
articles.statement:
The function $\operatorname{sinc} \colon \mathbb{R} \to
\mathbb{C}$ is defined by $\operatorname{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}$ for $x \neq 0$ and
$\operatorname{sinc}(0) = 1$, the value that removes the singularity at $0$. Its values are real.

The Whittaker–Shannon interpolation formula evaluates $\operatorname{sinc}$ at $0$ at the integer
sample points, so the value at $0$ is part of the definition.

articles.title: Unit cube of the Hausdorff moment problem
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the closed unit cube
$I^d = [0,1]^d$ is the set of points $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $0 \le x_i \le 1$ for every
coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Closed unit cube
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the closed unit cube $I^d = [0,1]^d$ is the
set of points $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $0 \le x_i \le 1$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Iterated backward difference
articles.statement:
For a real sequence $a$ indexed by $\mathbb{N}^d$ and
multi-indices $k, n \in \mathbb{N}^d$, the iterated backward difference of $a$ is the real number

$$(\Delta^k a)_n = \sum_{j \le k} (-1)^{|k| - |j|} \binom{k}{j} a_{n - j},$$

where $j$ ranges over the multi-indices with $j \le k$ coordinatewise, $|j| = \sum_i j_i$,
$\binom{k}{j} = \prod_i \binom{k_i}{j_i}$, and $n - j$ is computed coordinatewise in $\mathbb{N}$,
with $n_i - j_i = 0$ when $j_i > n_i$.

For $k \le n$ no truncation occurs, and $\Delta^k a$ is the iterate of the backward partial
differences $(\Delta_i a)_n = a_{n - e_i} - a_n$, applied $k_i$ times in each coordinate $i$,
where $e_i \in \mathbb{N}^d$ is the $i$-th unit multi-index.

articles.title: Iterated backward difference of a multi-sequence
articles.statement:
For a function
$a : \mathbb{N}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ and multi-indices $k, n \in \mathbb{N}^d$,

$$(\Delta^k a)_n = \sum_{j \le k} (-1)^{|k| - |j|} \binom{k}{j} \, a_{n - j},$$

where $j$ runs over the multi-indices with $j_i \le k_i$ for every $i$, $|k| = \sum_i k_i$,
$\binom{k}{j} = \prod_i \binom{k_i}{j_i}$ is the multi-index binomial coefficient, and $n - j$
is taken coordinatewise, with $n_i - j_i$ replaced by $0$ when $j_i > n_i$.

When $k \le n$ coordinatewise, $\Delta^k$ is the composite of $k_i$ applications of
$(\Delta_i a)_n = a_{n - e_i} - a_n$ in each coordinate $i$, where $e_i$ is the $i$-th unit
multi-index.

articles.title: Hausdorff's absolute continuity criterion
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
$\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\mu(\mathbb{R}^d \setminus I^d) = 0$, where $I^d = [0,1]^d$ is the closed
unit cube, and let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $I^d$. For a measure $\rho$ write
$m_\rho(n) = \int_{I^d} x^n \, d\rho(x)$ for its moments, indexed by multi-indices
$n \in \mathbb{N}^d$. Then $\mu$ is uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to $\lambda$ if
and only if there is a real constant $C$ such that
$(\Delta^k m_\mu)_n \le C \, (\Delta^k m_\lambda)_n$ for all multi-indices $k \le n$
(coordinatewise), where $\Delta^k$ is the iterated backward difference.

## Sources

- F. Hausdorff (1921–1923); see Shohat–Tamarkin, *The Problem of Moments*. Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §115. Problem `hausdorff_absolute_continuity` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Hausdorff-bounded sequences
articles.statement:
A real sequence $a$ indexed by $\mathbb{N}^d$ is Hausdorff
bounded if there is a real constant $M$ such that for every multi-index $n \in \mathbb{N}^d$,

$$\sum_{k \le n} \left| \binom{n}{k} (\Delta^k a)_n \right| \le M,$$

where $k$ ranges over the multi-indices with $k \le n$ coordinatewise,
$\binom{n}{k} = \prod_i \binom{n_i}{k_i}$ is the multi-index binomial coefficient, and
$\Delta^k a$ is the iterated backward difference of $a$.

articles.title: Hausdorff–Hildebrandt–Schoenberg moment theorem
articles.statement:
A real sequence $a$ indexed by
$\mathbb{N}^d$ is a moment configuration, that is, there are finite measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ on
$\mathbb{R}^d$ with $a_n = \int_{[0,1]^d} x^n \, d\mu(x) - \int_{[0,1]^d} x^n \, d\nu(x)$ for every
multi-index $n \in \mathbb{N}^d$, where $x^n = \prod_i x_i^{n_i}$, if and only if $a$ is Hausdorff
bounded.

## Sources

- F. Hausdorff (1921, 1923); T. H. Hildebrandt and I. J. Schoenberg, *On linear functional operations and the moment problem for a finite interval in one or several dimensions*, Ann. of Math. 34 (1933). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §115. Problem `hausdorff_hildebrandt_schoenberg` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Hausdorff positivity criterion
articles.statement:
A real sequence $a$ indexed by $\mathbb{N}^d$ is a positive
moment configuration, that is, there is a finite measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with
$a_n = \int_{[0,1]^d} x^n \, d\mu(x)$ for every multi-index $n \in \mathbb{N}^d$, where
$x^n = \prod_i x_i^{n_i}$, if and only if $(\Delta^k a)_n \ge 0$ for all multi-indices $k, n$ with
$k \le n$ coordinatewise, where $\Delta^k a$ is the iterated backward difference of $a$.

## Sources

- F. Hausdorff, *Summationsmethoden und Momentfolgen I, II*, Math. Z. 9 (1921). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §115. Problem `hausdorff_positivity_criterion` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Moment sequences of signed measures on the cube
articles.statement:
A real sequence $a$ indexed by
$\mathbb{N}^d$ is a moment configuration if there are finite measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ on
$\mathbb{R}^d$ such that for every multi-index $n \in \mathbb{N}^d$,

$$a_n = \int_{[0,1]^d} x^n \, d\mu(x) - \int_{[0,1]^d} x^n \, d\nu(x),$$

where $x^n = \prod_i x_i^{n_i}$.

This encodes a signed measure of bounded variation on the cube by its Jordan decomposition
$\mu - \nu$.

articles.title: Moment sequences of positive measures on the cube
articles.statement:
A real sequence $a$ indexed by
$\mathbb{N}^d$ is a positive moment configuration if there is a finite measure $\mu$ on
$\mathbb{R}^d$ such that $a_n = \int_{[0,1]^d} x^n \, d\mu(x)$ for every multi-index
$n \in \mathbb{N}^d$, where $x^n = \prod_i x_i^{n_i}$.

articles.title: Moments on the unit cube
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ and a multi-index
$n \in \mathbb{N}^d$, the $n$-th moment of $\mu$ on the unit cube is the real number
$\int_{[0,1]^d} x^n \, d\mu(x)$, where $x^n = \prod_i x_i^{n_i}$.

When $x^n$ is not $\mu$-integrable on $[0,1]^d$, this integral is taken to be $0$.

articles.title: Moments of a measure on the unit cube
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ and a
multi-index $n \in \mathbb{N}^d$, the $n$-th moment of $\mu$ is the real number
$\int_{I^d} x^n \, d\mu(x)$, the integral over the closed unit cube $I^d = [0,1]^d$ of the
monomial $x^n = \prod_{i=1}^{d} x_i^{n_i}$, taken to be $0$ when the monomial is not
$\mu$-integrable on $I^d$.

articles.title: Multi-index monomial
articles.statement:
For a multi-index $n \in \mathbb{N}^d$, the monomial $x^n$ is the
real function on $\mathbb{R}^d$ given by $x^n = \prod_i x_i^{n_i}$.

articles.title: Multivariate monomial
articles.statement:
For a multi-index $n = (n_1, \dots, n_d) \in \mathbb{N}^d$ and a
point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the monomial $x^n$ is the real number $\prod_{i=1}^{d} x_i^{n_i}$.

articles.title: Multi-index binomial coefficient
articles.statement:
For multi-indices $n, k \in \mathbb{N}^d$, the binomial
coefficient $\binom{n}{k}$ is the natural number $\prod_i \binom{n_i}{k_i}$.

articles.title: Multi-index binomial coefficient
articles.statement:
For multi-indices $n, k \in \mathbb{N}^d$, the
binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}$ is the natural number $\prod_{i=1}^{d} \binom{n_i}{k_i}$.

articles.title: Uniformly absolutely continuous measures
articles.statement:
A measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is uniformly
absolutely continuous with respect to a measure $\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ if there is a real
constant $C \ge 0$ with $\mu(S) \le C \, \nu(S)$ for every measurable set $S$.

When $\nu$ is $\sigma$-finite, this says that $\mu$ has an essentially bounded Radon–Nikodym
density with respect to $\nu$.

articles.title: Holomorphy of the Laplace transform under exponential growth
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex
Banach space, $a \in \mathbb{R}$, and $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ locally integrable on $[0, \infty)$
with $\|f(t)\| = O(e^{a t})$ as $t \to \infty$. Then the Laplace transform
$s \mapsto \int_{(0, \infty)} e^{-st} f(t)\,dt$ is complex differentiable at every point of the
half-plane $\{s \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} s > a\}$.

Local integrability on $[0, \infty)$, not only on $(0, \infty)$, is what makes the Laplace
integral converge on this half-plane: $f(t) = 1/t$ is continuous on $(0, \infty)$ and bounded at
infinity, but not integrable near $0$, so its Laplace integral diverges for every $s$.

## Sources

- ATLAS NumberTheoryI N320 (Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Lecture 16); a corrected, strengthened-premise formalization of the intended holomorphy claim, since the source's piecewise continuity on the open ray does not give integrability near 0. This is not a literal proof of the under-specified source wording.

articles.title: Holomorphy of the Laplace transform under an exponential bound
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex
Banach space, $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ almost everywhere strongly measurable on $(0, \infty)$, and
$a, C \in \mathbb{R}$ with $C \ge 0$ such that $\|f(t)\| \le C e^{a t}$ for all $t \ge 0$. Then the
Laplace transform $s \mapsto \int_{(0, \infty)} e^{-st} f(t)\,dt$ is complex differentiable at
every point of the half-plane $\{s \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} s > a\}$.

articles.title: Laplace transform with a given value
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex normed space,
$f : \mathbb{R} \to E$, $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and $v \in E$. Then $f$ has Laplace transform $v$ at
$s$ when the Laplace transform of $f$ converges at $s$, that is, $t \mapsto e^{-st} f(t)$ is
integrable on $(0, \infty)$, and the Bochner integral $\int_{(0, \infty)} e^{-st} f(t)\,dt$
equals $v$; as usual this integral is taken to be $0$ when $E$ is not complete.

articles.title: Convergence of the Laplace transform under exponential growth
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex
normed space, $a \in \mathbb{R}$, and $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ locally integrable on $[0, \infty)$
with $\|f(t)\| = O(e^{a t})$ as $t \to \infty$. Then for every $s \in \mathbb{C}$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > a$ the Laplace transform of $f$ converges at $s$, that is,
$t \mapsto e^{-st} f(t)$ is integrable on $(0, \infty)$.

Local integrability on $[0, \infty)$, not only on $(0, \infty)$, is needed: $f(t) = 1/t$ is
continuous on $(0, \infty)$ and bounded at infinity, but not integrable near $0$.

## Sources

- ATLAS NumberTheoryI N320 (Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Lecture 16); a corrected, strengthened-premise formalization of the intended convergence claim, since the source's piecewise continuity on the open ray does not give integrability near 0. This is not a literal proof of the under-specified source wording.

articles.title: Convergence of the Laplace transform under an exponential bound
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex
normed space, $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ almost everywhere strongly measurable on $(0, \infty)$, and
$a, C \in \mathbb{R}$ with $C \ge 0$ such that $\|f(t)\| \le C e^{a t}$ for all $t \ge 0$. Then for
every $s \in \mathbb{C}$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > a$ the Laplace transform of $f$ converges at
$s$, that is, $t \mapsto e^{-st} f(t)$ is integrable on $(0, \infty)$.

articles.title: Convergence of the Laplace transform
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex normed space,
$f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ and $s \in \mathbb{C}$. The Laplace transform of $f$ converges at $s$
when the function $t \mapsto e^{-st} f(t)$ is integrable on $(0, \infty)$ with respect to
Lebesgue measure.

Integrability here is absolute (Bochner) integrability, so conditionally convergent Laplace
integrals are not covered.

## Sources

- ATLAS NumberTheoryI Definition 16.9 introduces the Laplace transform for real-valued functions; here functions are complex-valued (or valued in a complex normed space), and the source's real-valued case is covered by coercion.

articles.title: The one-sided Laplace transform
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex normed space,
$f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ and $s \in \mathbb{C}$. The Laplace transform of $f$ at $s$ is the Bochner
integral $\int_{(0, \infty)} e^{-st} f(t)\,dt \in E$.

It is defined for every $s$, with no convergence hypothesis: where $t \mapsto e^{-st} f(t)$ is not
integrable on $(0, \infty)$, or when $E$ is not complete, the integral is $0$ by convention.
Convergence of the Laplace transform is a separate notion.

articles.title: One-dimensional Fourier transform
articles.statement:
For $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ and
$k \in \mathbb{R}$, the Fourier transform of $g$ at $k$ is

$$\hat g(k) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-2\pi i p k} \, g(p) \, dp,$$

where the integral is taken to be $0$ when the integrand is not integrable.

articles.title: Two-dimensional Fourier transform
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{C}$ and
$k = (k_1, k_2) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, the Fourier transform of $f$ at $k$ is

$$\hat f(k) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-2\pi i (x_1 k_1 + x_2 k_2)} \, f(x) \, dx,$$

where $dx$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the integral is taken to be $0$ when the
integrand is not integrable.

articles.title: Fourier slice theorem and injectivity of the Radon transform on Schwartz functions
articles.statement:
Write $R$ for the Radon transform, $\hat g$ for the one-dimensional Fourier transform of
$g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ and $\hat f$ for the two-dimensional Fourier transform of
$f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{C}$. For every Schwartz function
$\varphi : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{C}$ and all $\theta, k \in \mathbb{R}$, the Fourier transform
of $p \mapsto R\varphi(p, \theta)$ at $k$ equals $\hat\varphi(k\cos\theta, k\sin\theta)$.
Moreover, there is a map $S$ sending functions $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{C}$ to functions
$\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{C}$ such that $S(R\varphi) = \varphi$ for every Schwartz function
$\varphi$.

The second part says only that $R$ is injective on Schwartz functions; no formula, linearity or
continuity is asserted for the left inverse $S$.

## Sources

- J. Radon (1917); R. N. Bracewell (Fourier slice theorem, 1956). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §100. Problem `radon_transform_inversion` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Radon transform on the plane
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{C}$ and
$p, \theta \in \mathbb{R}$, the Radon transform of $f$ at $(p, \theta)$ is the integral of $f$
along the line $x \cos\theta + y \sin\theta = p$ with respect to arc length,

$$Rf(p, \theta) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(p\cos\theta - t\sin\theta, p\sin\theta + t\cos\theta)\,dt,$$

where the integral is taken to be $0$ when the integrand is not integrable.

articles.title: Ramanujan's master theorem
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers with $0 < a < b$, and let
$s$ be a complex number with $a < \operatorname{Re} s < b$. Let $\varphi$ be a function from
$\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{C}$ that is analytic on the half-plane $\operatorname{Re} z > -b$, and
suppose there are real constants $C > 0$ and $P < \pi$ such that
$|\varphi(u + iv)| \le C e^{P|v|}$ for all real $u$ and $v$ with $u > -b$. Let $F$ be a function
from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{C}$ such that for every real $x > 0$ the series
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \varphi(k)\,(-x)^k / k!$ converges unconditionally to $F(x)$, and suppose
that $x \mapsto x^{s-1} F(x)$ is Lebesgue integrable on $(0, \infty)$, where
$x^{s-1} = e^{(s-1)\log x}$. Then

$$\int_0^\infty x^{s-1} F(x)\,dx = \Gamma(s)\,\varphi(-s).$$

This is a specialization of the theorem: the growth bound on $\varphi$ is uniform in
$\operatorname{Re} z$, and integrability of $x^{s-1} F(x)$ is assumed rather than derived.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%27s_master_theorem (Raw: `int_0^infty x^{s-1} sum_k phi(k)(-x)^k/k! dx = Gamma(s) phi(-s)`.)

articles.title: Carleman's criterion for the Stieltjes moment problem
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure
on $\mathbb{R}$ with $\mu((-\infty, 0)) = 0$ such that $\int |x|^k \, d\mu(x) < \infty$ for every
integer $k \ge 1$, and write $m_k = \int x^k \, d\mu(x)$. If
$\sum_{k \ge 1} m_k^{-1/(2k)} = \infty$, where the terms are taken in $[0, \infty]$ (so a term
with $m_k = 0$ equals $\infty$), then $\mu$ is Stieltjes moment determinate.

Proof: Symmetrize through the square-root map, apply Denjoy--Carleman quasi-analytic
uniqueness to the difference of characteristic functions, then push forward by squaring.

## Sources

- Gwo Dong Lin, "Recent Developments on the Moment Problem" (2017), Theorem 2, (s6) implies (s7). Source spans: definition lines 57-75, criterion lines 297-321; JIS application lines 152-177.

articles.title: Stieltjes moment determinacy
articles.statement:
A measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is Stieltjes moment
determinate when every probability measure $\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ such that $\nu((-\infty, 0)) = 0$,
$\int |x|^k \, d\nu(x) < \infty$ for every integer $k \ge 1$, and
$\int x^k \, d\nu(x) = \int x^k \, d\mu(x)$ for every integer $k \ge 1$ is equal to $\mu$.

The moments of $\mu$ are Bochner integrals, which are $0$ when $x^k$ is not $\mu$-integrable, and
the definition places no condition on $\mu$ itself.

## Sources

- Gwo Dong Lin, "Recent Developments on the Moment Problem", Journal of Statistical Distributions and Applications (2017), DOI 10.1186/s40488-017-0059-2, arXiv:1703.01027v3. Definition lines 57-75, criterion lines 297-321. JIS application, lines 152-177.

articles.title: Carleman's inequality, summability form
articles.statement:
If $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is a summable sequence of
nonnegative real numbers, then the sequence of geometric means $(a_0 a_1 \cdots a_n)^{1/(n+1)}$,
$n \ge 0$, is summable.

articles.title: Derivative of the squared distance to a point applied to a vector
articles.statement: The `fderiv` of the squared distance to a point, applied to a vector.

articles.title: Second derivative of the squared norm
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real inner product space.
For all $p, u, v \in E$, the second Fréchet derivative of $x \mapsto \|x\|^2$ at $p$,
applied to $u$ and then to $v$, equals $2 \langle u, v \rangle$.

articles.title: Derivative of the norm in a real space applied to a vector
articles.statement: The `fderiv` of the norm in a real inner product space, applied to a vector.

articles.title: Derivative of the norm applied to a vector
articles.statement: The `fderiv` of the norm at a nonzero point, applied to a vector.

articles.title: Formula for the derivative of the norm
articles.statement: The `fderiv` of the norm at a nonzero point.

articles.title: Fréchet derivative of the norm at a nonzero point
articles.statement: The non-strict form of `hasStrictFDerivAt_norm`.

articles.title: Strict derivative of the squared distance to a point
articles.statement: The gradient of the squared distance to a point `a` is `2 • reInnerSL K (x - a)`.

articles.title: Strict derivative of the squared distance to a subspace
articles.statement:
The gradient of the squared distance to a subspace `S` is twice the real
inner product with the residual `x - S.starProjection x`.

articles.title: Strict derivative of the norm in a real inner product space
articles.statement: The Fréchet derivative of the norm in a real inner product space.

articles.title: Strict derivative of the squared norm
articles.statement: The derivative of the squared norm is twice the real inner product with `x`.

articles.title: Strict Fréchet derivative of the norm at a nonzero point
articles.statement:
The Fréchet derivative of the norm at a nonzero point `x` is the norming
functional `y ↦ re ⟪x, y⟫ / ‖x‖`.

articles.title: Strict derivative of the squared projection residual
articles.statement:
The gradient of the squared residual `‖y - S.starProjection y‖ ^ 2` is
`2 • reInnerSL K (x - S.starProjection x)`, using that the residual operator
`1 - S.starProjection` is self-adjoint and idempotent.

articles.title: Distance to a subspace as the norm of the projection residual
articles.statement:
The distance from `y` to a subspace with an orthogonal projection is the
norm of the residual `y - S.starProjection y`.

articles.title: Chain rule for the Fréchet derivative of a norm
articles.statement: Chain rule: the non-strict derivative of the norm of a differentiable map.

articles.title: Derivative of the norm along a curve
articles.statement:
The derivative of the norm along a curve is the normalized real inner product
of the position with the velocity.

articles.title: Derivative of the norm has operator norm one
articles.statement:
The Fréchet derivative of the norm at a nonzero point has operator norm `1`:
the norming functional is a norming functional. This statement needs the inner
product structure, so `K` is an explicit argument.

articles.title: Operator norm of the real inner product functional
articles.statement:
The norming functional `reInnerSL K x` has operator norm `‖x‖` (it attains
`‖x‖` at `‖x‖⁻¹ • x`).

articles.title: Chain rule for the strict derivative of a norm
articles.statement: Chain rule: the derivative of the norm of a differentiable map.

articles.title: Curves on the unit sphere have velocity orthogonal to position
articles.statement:
A differentiable curve lying on the unit sphere has velocity orthogonal to
its position (in the real-inner-product sense).

articles.title: Over the reals the norming functional is the inner product
articles.statement: Over `ℝ`, the norming functional is just `innerSL ℝ x`.

articles.title: Real part of the inner product as a real-linear functional
articles.statement:
The real-linear functional `y ↦ re ⟪x, y⟫`, the unnormalized gradient of
the norm at `x`. The scalar field `K` is an explicit argument because the
type `E →L[ℝ] ℝ` does not determine it.

articles.title: Canonical dual frame
articles.statement:
Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$ finite, be a frame with
bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let
$S^{-1}$ be the inverse of its frame operator. The canonical dual frame is the family
$(S^{-1} f_i)_{i \in \iota}$.

articles.title: Frame operator formula
articles.statement:
For a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in an inner product
space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, the frame operator $S$ of the family
satisfies $S x = \sum_{i \in \iota} \langle f_i, x \rangle f_i$ for every $x \in E$, where the
inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument.

articles.title: The inverse frame operator is a right inverse
articles.statement:
Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$
finite, be a frame with bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, with frame operator $S$ and inverse frame operator $S^{-1}$. Then
$S \circ S^{-1}$ is the identity operator on $E$.

articles.title: Frame operator of the canonical dual frame
articles.statement:
Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$
finite, be a frame with bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, and let $S^{-1}$ be the inverse of its frame operator. Then the frame operator of
the canonical dual frame $(S^{-1} f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is $S^{-1}$.

articles.title: Tight frames have scalar frame operator
articles.statement:
Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$
finite, be a frame in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ whose lower
and upper frame bounds are both equal to $A$. Then its frame operator is $S = A \cdot I$, where $I$
is the identity operator on $E$.

articles.title: The inverse frame operator is a left inverse
articles.statement:
Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$
finite, be a frame with bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, with frame operator $S$ and inverse frame operator $S^{-1}$. Then
$S^{-1} \circ S$ is the identity operator on $E$.

articles.title: Inverse frame operator
articles.statement:
Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$ finite, be a frame with
bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Its frame
operator $S$ is invertible in the algebra of bounded linear operators on $E$, and the inverse
frame operator $S^{-1}$ is its inverse there.

articles.title: Frame operator
articles.statement:
For a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in an inner product space $E$
over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, the frame operator is the bounded linear operator
$S \colon E \to E$ given by $S x = \sum_{i \in \iota} \langle f_i, x \rangle f_i$, the sum of the
rank-one operators $x \mapsto \langle f_i, x \rangle f_i$. The inner product is conjugate-linear
in its first argument.

articles.title: Frame reconstruction formula
articles.statement:
Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$ finite, be a frame
with bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and
let $S^{-1}$ be the inverse of its frame operator. Then every $x \in E$ satisfies
$x = \sum_{i \in \iota} \langle f_i, S^{-1} x \rangle f_i$.

articles.title: Quadratic form of the frame operator
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be the frame operator of a finite family
$(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in an inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
For every $x \in E$,
$\langle S x, x \rangle = \sum_{i \in \iota} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2$; the right side is a
real number, viewed as an element of $\mathbb{K}$.

articles.title: Inner product against the frame operator
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an inner product space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with inner product conjugate-linear in the first
argument, and let $S$ be the frame operator of a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in $E$. Then
$\langle S x, y \rangle = \sum_{i \in \iota} \overline{\langle f_i, x \rangle} \,
\langle f_i, y \rangle$ for all $x, y \in E$.

articles.title: The canonical dual frame is a frame
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$
with frame bounds $A$ and $B$ and frame operator $S$. Then the canonical dual frame
$(S^{-1} f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is a frame with lower frame bound $1/B$ and upper frame bound $1/A$.

articles.title: Finite frame
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. A finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in $E$ is a frame with frame bounds
$A, B \in \mathbb{R}$ if $A > 0$, $B > 0$ and, for every $x \in E$,
$A \|x\|^2 \le \sum_{i \in \iota} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2 \le B \|x\|^2$.

articles.title: The inverse frame operator is self-adjoint
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$
with frame bounds $A$ and $B$. Then the inverse $S^{-1}$ of its frame operator $S$ is
self-adjoint.

articles.title: The frame operator is self-adjoint
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For every finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in $E$,
not necessarily a frame, the frame operator of $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is self-adjoint.

articles.title: The frame operator of a frame is invertible
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$
with frame bounds $A$ and $B$. Then its frame operator $S$ is a unit in the algebra of bounded
linear operators on $E$, that is, $S$ has a bounded linear two-sided inverse.

The operator $S$ is bounded below and self-adjoint, so it is injective with closed range whose
orthogonal complement is trivial.

articles.title: The frame operator is bounded below
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an inner product space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$
with frame bounds $A$ and $B$ and frame operator $S$. Then $A \|x\| \le \|S x\|$ for every
$x \in E$.

articles.title: Lower frame inequality
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$
or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$ with frame bounds $A$ and
$B$. Then $A \|x\|^2 \le \sum_{i \in \iota} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2$ for every $x \in E$.

articles.title: The frame operator has norm at most the upper frame bound
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an inner product
space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite
frame in $E$ with frame bounds $A$ and $B$ and frame operator $S$. Then the operator norm of $S$
satisfies $\|S\| \le B$.

articles.title: The lower frame bound is positive
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an inner product space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in $E$ is a
frame with frame bounds $A$ and $B$, then $A > 0$.

articles.title: The upper frame bound is positive
articles.statement:
If a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in an inner
product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$) is a frame with frame bounds $A$
and $B$, then $0 < B$.

articles.title: Real part of the frame quadratic form
articles.statement:
Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite family in an
inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$), with frame operator $S$.
For every $x \in E$,
$\operatorname{Re} \langle S x, x \rangle = \sum_{i} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2$.

articles.title: Cauchy–Schwarz bound for the frame operator
articles.statement:
Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite family in
an inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$), with frame operator
$S$. For all $x, y \in E$,

$$
|\langle S x, y \rangle|^2 \le \Big(\sum_{i} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2\Big)
\Big(\sum_{i} |\langle f_i, y \rangle|^2\Big).
$$

articles.title: Upper frame inequality
articles.statement:
If a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in an inner product space
$E$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$) is a frame with frame bounds $A$ and $B$, then
$\sum_{i} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2 \le B \|x\|^2$ for every $x \in E$.

articles.title: Nearest points coincide with the convex projection
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex
subset of a real inner product space $F$, let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$, and
let $x \in F$. If $p \in K$ satisfies $\|x - p\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$, then $P_K(x) = p$.

articles.title: The convex projection fixes the points of the set
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex
subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$.
Then $P_K(x) = x$ for every $x \in K$.

articles.title: Firm nonexpansiveness of the convex projection
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex
subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$.
For all $x, y \in F$,
$\|P_K(x) - P_K(y)\|^2 + \|(x - P_K(x)) - (y - P_K(y))\|^2 \le \|x - y\|^2$.

articles.title: Idempotence of the convex projection
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a
real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. Then
$P_K(P_K(x)) = P_K(x)$ for every $x \in F$.

articles.title: The convex projection lies in the set
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a
real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. Then
$P_K(x) \in K$ for every $x \in F$.

articles.title: The convex projection minimizes the distance to the set
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty complete
convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection
onto $K$. Then $\|x - P_K(x)\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$ for every $x \in F$.

articles.title: Defining property of the convex projection
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset
of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. For
every $x \in F$, $P_K(x) \in K$ and $\|x - P_K(x)\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$.

articles.title: Variational inequality for the convex projection
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex
subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$.
For every $x \in F$ and every $w \in K$, $\langle x - P_K(x), w - P_K(x) \rangle \le 0$.

articles.title: Nearest-point projection onto a convex set
articles.statement:
For a subset $K$ of a real inner product space
$F$ and a point $x \in F$, the nearest-point projection $P_K(x)$ is a chosen point of $F$ such
that, whenever $K$ is nonempty, complete and convex, $P_K(x) \in K$ and
$\|x - P_K(x)\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$; it is then the unique point of $K$ nearest to $x$.
When $K$ fails one of these hypotheses, the value of $P_K(x)$ is unspecified.

articles.title: Totalized existence of the convex projection
articles.statement:
For every subset $K$ of a real inner product
space $F$ and every $x \in F$, there is a point $p \in F$ such that, if $K$ is nonempty, complete
and convex, then $p \in K$ and $\|x - p\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$.

articles.title: Existence and uniqueness of the nearest point
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex
subset of a real inner product space $F$. For every $x \in F$ there is exactly one $p \in K$
with $\|x - p\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$, that is, exactly one point of $K$ nearest to $x$.

articles.title: The convex projection is $1$-Lipschitz
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a
real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. Then
$\|P_K x - P_K y\| \le \|x - y\|$ for all $x, y \in F$, that is, $P_K$ is $1$-Lipschitz.

articles.title: Nonexpansiveness of nearest-point selection
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a convex subset of a real inner
product space $F$, let $x, y \in F$, and let $p, q \in K$ satisfy
$\|x - p\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$ and $\|y - q\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|y - w\|$, so that $p$
is a point of $K$ nearest to $x$ and $q$ is a point of $K$ nearest to $y$. Then
$\|p - q\| \le \|x - y\|$.

articles.title: Firm nonexpansiveness of nearest-point selection
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a convex subset of a real
inner product space $F$, let $x, y \in F$, and let $p, q \in K$ satisfy
$\|x - p\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$ and $\|y - q\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|y - w\|$, so that $p$
is a point of $K$ nearest to $x$ and $q$ is a point of $K$ nearest to $y$. Then
$\|p - q\|^2 + \|(x - p) - (y - q)\|^2 \le \|x - y\|^2$.

articles.title: Kirszbraun extension theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real inner product space (not necessarily
complete), let $F$ be a complete real inner product space, let $s \subseteq E$ and let $K \ge 0$.
Every map $f : E \to F$ that is $K$-Lipschitz on $s$ agrees on $s$ with some map
$g : E \to F$ that is $K$-Lipschitz on all of $E$.

## Sources

- M. Kirszbraun, Fund. Math. 22 (1934) 77-108 thesis; Valentine 1945 extension to Hilbert; Federer, Geometric Measure Theory, 2.10.43; the Lean theorem takes a real inner-product-space domain `E` and a complete real inner-product-space target `F`, with the same Lipschitz constant `LipschitzWith K`.

articles.title: Kirszbraun extension theorem for Hilbert spaces
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be real Hilbert spaces,
let $s \subseteq E$ and let $K \ge 0$. Every map $f : E \to F$ that is $K$-Lipschitz on $s$
agrees on $s$ with some map $g : E \to F$ that is $K$-Lipschitz on all of $E$.

Completeness of $E$ is not used: this is a special case of the Kirszbraun extension theorem for
an arbitrary real inner product space domain.

articles.title: Weakly convergent sequences are norm-bounded
articles.statement:
A weakly convergent sequence is norm-bounded (Banach–Steinhaus applied
to the evaluation maps on the dual space).

articles.title: Opial's property, squared-norm form
articles.statement:
If `u n ⇀ x` weakly and
`y ≠ x`, then `liminf ‖u n - x‖² < liminf ‖u n - y‖²`.

articles.title: Opial's property
articles.statement:
If `u n ⇀ x` weakly and `y ≠ x`, then
`liminf ‖u n - x‖ < liminf ‖u n - y‖`.

articles.title: Cross term vanishes under weak convergence
articles.statement:
The cross term in the squared-norm identity tends to `0` under weak
convergence, via the Fréchet–Riesz representation of the functional
`z ↦ ⟪x - y, z⟫`.

articles.title: Hilbert basis of orthogonal polynomials on $(-1, 1)$
articles.statement:
Let $L^2([-1, 1])$ be the real
Hilbert space of square-integrable real-valued functions on $[-1, 1]$ with respect to
Lebesgue measure. There is a Hilbert basis $(b_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of $L^2([-1, 1])$ such
that for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ there is a real polynomial $q_n$ of degree exactly $n$ (for
$n = 0$, a constant polynomial) with $b_n(x) = q_n(x)$ for almost every $x \in [-1, 1]$.

The normalized Legendre polynomials form such a basis.

## Sources

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §18.3, Table 18.3.1 (Legendre polynomials: weight `1` on `(-1, 1)`, `∫ P_n ^ 2 = 2 / (2n + 1)`).
- E. Kreyszig, *Introductory Functional Analysis with Applications*, Wiley, 1978, §3.6 ("Total Orthonormal Sets and Sequences") and §3.7 ("Legendre, Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials": the normalized Legendre polynomials are a total orthonormal sequence in `L²[-1, 1]`).
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_polynomials#Orthogonality_and_completeness

articles.title: Banach's Scottish Book Problem 86 fails
articles.statement:
The Scottish Book Problem 86 claim is false: there
are a real $M > 0$ and a sequence $(\varphi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of functions
$\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, almost everywhere measurable on $[0, 1]$, orthonormal in
$L^2[0, 1]$ and with $|\varphi_n(t)| \le M$ for all $n$ and all $t \in [0, 1]$, such that there
is no sequence $(\psi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of functions $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, almost
everywhere measurable on $[0, 1]$, orthonormal in $L^2[0, 1]$ and with $|\psi_n(t)| \le M$ for
all $n$ and all $t \in [0, 1]$, that has every $\varphi_n$ as one of its terms and is complete:
every $g \in L^2[0, 1]$ with $\int_0^1 \psi_n g \, dt = 0$ for all $n$ vanishes almost
everywhere on $[0, 1]$.

## Sources

- S. Banach, Problem 86 of the Scottish Book; negative answer via A. Plichko and A. Razenkov, "On three problems from the Scottish Book connected with orthogonal systems", Colloq. Math. 70 (1996), 227–234, Proposition 3, which constructs a bounded orthogonal sequence in a Banach space densely and non-compactly embedded in a Hilbert space that admits no extension to a fundamental orthogonal sequence using elements of the Banach space. Earlier work on the problem includes S. Kaczmarz (1936) and K. S. Kazarian ("On a problem of S. Banach from the Scottish Book", Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 110 (1990), 881–887).

articles.title: Banach's Problem 186: a complete orthonormal system with divergent Fourier series
articles.statement:
There is a
sequence $(\varphi_i)_{i \ge 0}$ of square-integrable real functions on $[0, 1]$, with respect to
Lebesgue measure, that is orthonormal, $\int_0^1 \varphi_i \varphi_j \, dx = \delta_{ij}$ for
all $i, j$, and complete, in the sense that every square-integrable $g$ on $[0, 1]$ with
$\int_0^1 g \varphi_i \, dx = 0$ for all $i$ vanishes almost everywhere on $[0, 1]$, such that
the following holds: for every continuous $f \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is not
identically zero on $[0, 1]$, with Fourier coefficients $c_i = \int_0^1 f \varphi_i \, dx$, the
partial sums $\sum_{i < N} c_i \varphi_i(t)$ are unbounded in $N$ for almost every
$t \in [0, 1]$.

The $\varphi_i$ are not assumed continuous: the source imposes continuity only on $f$, and
continuity of the $\varphi_i$ would make the claim false (taking $f = \varphi_0$ would give
Fourier coefficients $\delta_{0i}$ and bounded partial sums).

## Sources

- S. Banach, Problem 186 of the Scottish Book; answered by A. M. Olevskii, "Fourier series with respect to general orthogonal systems" (1975). See the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Countability of orthogonal systems of functions
articles.statement:
Let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure on
$[0, 1]$. This is the statement that every set $S$ of functions $[0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ with the
following three properties is at most countable: no member of $S$ is $\lambda$-almost everywhere
equal to $0$; any two members of $S$ that are equal $\lambda$-almost everywhere are equal; and
any two members $f, g$ of $S$ that are not equal $\lambda$-almost everywhere are measurable, have
$\lambda$-integrable product $fg$, and satisfy $\int_{[0, 1]} f g \, d\lambda = 0$.

No square-integrability is assumed. Without the second property, uncountably many
almost-everywhere-equal copies of one function would satisfy the orthogonality condition
vacuously. The first property excludes the indicator functions of single points, each of which
is zero almost everywhere.

articles.title: Orthogonal systems need not be countable
articles.statement:
Both of the following statements are false.
(a) Every set $S$ of real sequences $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in which no member is the zero
sequence, and in which for any two distinct $f, g \in S$ the series $\sum_n f_n g_n$ converges
absolutely with sum $0$, is at most countable. (b) Let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure on
$[0, 1]$. Every set $S$ of functions $[0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ in which no member is
$\lambda$-almost everywhere equal to $0$, no two distinct members are equal $\lambda$-almost
everywhere, and any two members $f, g$ that are not equal $\lambda$-almost everywhere are
measurable with $fg$ $\lambda$-integrable and $\int_{[0, 1]} f g \, d\lambda = 0$, is at most
countable.

This answers both parts of Mazur's Problem 51 of the Scottish Book in the negative: Plichko and
Razenkov construct a continuum-sized pairwise-orthogonal family of sequences, and from it an
uncountable orthogonal system of functions on an interval. No square-integrability is assumed;
in $\ell^2$ or $L^2$ an orthogonal family is at most countable, since those spaces are
separable Hilbert spaces.

## Sources

- S. Mazur, Problem 51 of the Scottish Book; A. M. Plichko and V. Razenkov, On three problems from the Scottish Book connected with orthogonal systems, Colloq. Math. 70 (1996), 227-234, Section 3; see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Lebesgue measure on the unit interval (Scottish Book Problem 86)
articles.statement:
Lebesgue measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ restricted to the unit interval $[0, 1]$, the ambient measure for Problem 86.

articles.title: Scottish Book Problem 86 (Banach)
articles.statement:
The claim that for every real $M > 0$ and every
sequence $(\varphi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of functions $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that are
almost everywhere measurable on $[0, 1]$, orthonormal in $L^2[0, 1]$ (that is,
$\int_0^1 \varphi_n \varphi_m \, dt$ is $1$ if $n = m$ and $0$ otherwise) and satisfy
$|\varphi_n(t)| \le M$ for all $n$ and all $t \in [0, 1]$, there is a sequence
$(\psi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of functions $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, almost everywhere
measurable on $[0, 1]$, orthonormal in the same sense and with $|\psi_n(t)| \le M$ for all $n$
and all $t \in [0, 1]$, such that every $\varphi_n$ equals some $\psi_m$ and $(\psi_n)$ is
complete: every $g \in L^2[0, 1]$ with $\int_0^1 \psi_n g \, dt = 0$ for all $n$ vanishes
almost everywhere on $[0, 1]$.

The case of interest in the original problem is when infinitely many functions are necessary
for the completion.

articles.title: Countability of orthogonal systems of sequences
articles.statement:
This is the statement that every set $S$
of real sequences $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with the following two properties is at most
countable: no member of $S$ is the zero sequence; and for any two distinct $f, g \in S$ the series
$\sum_{n} f_n g_n$ converges absolutely and its sum is $0$.

The zero sequence is excluded because it is orthogonal to everything, so without this it
would be a trivial member of every family.

articles.title: Radon–Riesz characterization of norm convergence
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be an inner product space
over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, not necessarily complete, let
$(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $H$ and let $x \in H$. Then $u_n \to x$ in norm if
and only if $\langle u_n, y \rangle \to \langle x, y \rangle$ for every $y \in H$ and
$\|u_n\| \to \|x\|$.

articles.title: Radon–Riesz theorem, dual-functionals form
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be an inner product space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, not necessarily complete, let
$(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $H$ and let $x \in H$. If $f(u_n) \to f(x)$ for
every continuous linear functional $f : H \to \mathbb{K}$ and $\|u_n\| \to \|x\|$, then
$u_n \to x$ in norm.

articles.title: Radon–Riesz theorem, inner-product form
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be an inner product space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, not necessarily complete, let
$(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $H$ and let $x \in H$. If
$\langle u_n, y \rangle \to \langle x, y \rangle$ for every $y \in H$ and $\|u_n\| \to \|x\|$,
then $u_n \to x$ in norm.

articles.title: Radon–Riesz theorem, weak-topology form
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be an inner product space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, not necessarily complete, let
$(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $H$ and let $x \in H$. If $u_n \to x$ in the weak
topology of $H$ (the coarsest topology making every continuous linear functional
$H \to \mathbb{K}$ continuous) and $\|u_n\| \to \|x\|$, then $u_n \to x$ in norm.

articles.title: Kernel ridge fit is the unique minimizer
articles.statement: The kernel ridge fit is the unique minimizer for `λ > 0`.

articles.title: The representer theorem
articles.statement:
**The representer theorem** (Schölkopf, Herbrich and Smola, Theorem 1): for a
finite-dimensional output space `V` (for instance a scalar kernel, `V = 𝕜`) and `Ω` strictly
increasing on `[0, ∞)`, every global minimizer of `L (f x₁, …, f xₙ) + Ω ‖f‖` is a kernel
expansion `∑ i, kerFun H (x i) (c i)`.

articles.title: Existence of a minimizer
articles.statement:
For finite-dimensional `V`, a continuous loss bounded below,
and a continuous regularizer that is monotone on `[0, ∞)` and tends to `∞`, the regularized risk
has a global minimizer, and it can be taken to be a kernel expansion.

articles.title: Projection onto Riesz representers with Pythagorean residual
articles.statement:
Orthogonal projection onto the span of the Riesz representers preserves
the values of the functionals, and the Pythagorean identity holds for the
residual.

articles.title: Projection onto Riesz representers does not increase the norm
articles.statement:
Orthogonal projection onto the span of the Riesz representers does not
increase the norm.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the minimizer
articles.statement:
**Uniqueness of the minimizer** (real scalars): for a convex loss `L` and a regularizer `Ω`
that is strictly convex and monotone on `[0, ∞)` (for instance `Ω t = λ t²` with `λ > 0`), the
regularized risk has at most one global minimizer.

articles.title: Values of a kernel expansion at the sample points
articles.statement: The values of a kernel expansion at the sample points are `K c`.

articles.title: Kernel expansion map centered at the sample points
articles.statement:
The kernel expansion map `c ↦ ∑ i, kerFun H (x i) (c i)`. Its range is the span of the
kernel functions at the sample points `x i`.

articles.title: Kernel Gram matrix
articles.statement:
The Gram matrix `K i j = k(x i, x j)` of a real scalar kernel at the sample points, where
`k(x, y) = kernel H x y 1`.

articles.title: Fitted values of kernel ridge regression
articles.statement: The fitted values of kernel ridge regression are `K (K + λ I)⁻¹ y`.

articles.title: Kernel ridge regression fit
articles.statement: The kernel ridge fit: the kernel expansion with coefficients `(K + λ I)⁻¹ y`.

articles.title: Kernel ridge objective as a regularized risk
articles.statement:
The kernel ridge objective is the regularized risk with the squared loss and
`Ω t = λ t²`.

articles.title: Kernel ridge regression
articles.statement:
**Kernel ridge regression** (Kimeldorf and Wahba): for `λ > 0` the kernel ridge fit
minimizes `∑ i, (y i - f (x i))² + λ ‖f‖²` over the whole RKHS.

articles.title: Kernel ridge regression objective
articles.statement: The kernel ridge objective `∑ i, (y i - f (x i))² + λ ‖f‖²`.

articles.title: Representer theorem
articles.statement:
Any minimizer of a ridge-regularized problem
`F (fun i => L i g) + Λ * ‖g‖ ^ 2` with `Λ > 0` lies in the span of the
Riesz representers of the functionals `L i`.

articles.title: The representer theorem
articles.statement:
**The representer theorem** (closed-span form): if `Ω` is strictly increasing on `[0, ∞)`,
every global minimizer of the regularized risk lies in the closure of the span of the kernel
functions at the sample points.

articles.title: Kernel Gram matrix is positive semidefinite
articles.statement: The kernel Gram matrix is positive semidefinite.

articles.title: Regularized risk in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space
articles.statement: The regularized risk `L (f x₁, …, f xₙ) + Ω ‖f‖` of `f` in the RKHS `H`.

articles.title: Riesz bases have dense span
articles.statement: A Riesz basis has dense span.

articles.title: Biorthogonal dual of a Riesz basis
articles.statement:
A Riesz basis admits a biorthogonal dual family with a reconstruction
formula: there is `g : ι → E` with `⟪f i, g j⟫ = if i = j then 1 else 0` and
`x = ∑' i, ⟪g i, x⟫ • f i` for every `x`. The dual is `g j = (T⁻¹)† (b j)`
for the operator `T` witnessing that `f` is a Riesz basis.

articles.title: Paley–Wiener stability theorem
articles.statement:
If `b` is a Hilbert basis and
`∑' i, ‖f i - b i‖ ^ 2 < 1`, then `f` is a Riesz basis.

articles.title: Riesz basis of a Hilbert space
articles.statement:
A family `f : ι → E` is a **Riesz basis** (with respect to the Hilbert basis
`b`) if it is the image of `b` under a bounded invertible operator.

articles.title: Riesz bases are linearly independent
articles.statement: A Riesz basis is linearly independent.

articles.title: $\ell^2$ norm of the norm sequence
articles.statement:
The `ℓ²` norm of the norms of a coefficient sequence is the norm of the
sequence.

articles.title: Norm sequence of an $\ell^2$ coefficient sequence
articles.statement:
The sequence of norms of an `ℓ²` coefficient sequence, as an element of
`ℓ²(ι, ℝ)`.

articles.title: Norm sequence of a square-summable family
articles.statement:
The sequence of norms of a square-summable family, as an element of
`ℓ²(ι, ℝ)`.

articles.title: Operator norm bound for the synthesis operator
articles.statement:
The operator norm of the synthesis operator is at most
`√(∑' i, ‖d i‖ ^ 2)`.

articles.title: Norm bound for a synthesis series
articles.statement: Norm bound for a synthesis series, by Cauchy–Schwarz for `ℓ²`.

articles.title: Absolute summability of a synthesis series
articles.statement:
The norms of the terms of a synthesis series are summable when the
coefficient sequence is in `ℓ²` and the synthesized family is square-summable:
this is Cauchy–Schwarz for `ℓ²`, via `lp.tsum_mul_le_mul_norm` applied to the
two real `ℓ²` sequences of norms.

articles.title: Summability of a synthesis series
articles.statement:
The terms of a synthesis series are summable when the coefficient sequence
is in `ℓ²` and the synthesized family is square-summable.

articles.title: Synthesis operator on a basis vector
articles.statement:
The synthesis operator at a basis vector picks out one term of the
family.

articles.title: Synthesis operator of a square-summable family
articles.statement:
The **synthesis operator**: for a square-summable family `d : ι → E`, the
bounded operator `ℓ²(ι, 𝕜) →L[𝕜] E` sending `c` to `∑' i, c i • d i`.

articles.title: Linear map underlying the synthesis operator
articles.statement: The linear map underlying the synthesis operator.

articles.title: An orthonormal family in a separable space is countable
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a separable inner
product space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If $(v_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is an orthonormal family
in $H$, then the index set $\iota$ is countable.

Distinct orthonormal vectors are at distance $\sqrt{2}$, so the open balls of radius $1/2$ around
them are pairwise disjoint.

articles.title: A separable Hilbert space admits a countable Hilbert basis
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a separable Hilbert
space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Then $H$ has a Hilbert basis $(e_i)_{i \in \iota}$ (an
