articles.title: Invertibility of a direct sum operator
articles.statement: A direct sum is a unit iff both summands are units.

articles.title: Kernel of a direct sum operator
articles.statement: The kernel of a direct sum is the product of the kernels.

articles.title: Operator norm of a direct sum is the maximum of the norms
articles.statement: The operator norm of a direct sum is the maximum of the operator norms.

articles.title: Composition of direct sum operators is componentwise
articles.statement: Composing direct sums is componentwise.

articles.title: Direct sum of identity operators is the identity
articles.statement: The identity direct sum is the identity.

articles.title: Scalar multiplication of a direct sum operator
articles.statement: Scaling a direct sum scales both summands by the same factor.

articles.title: Direct sum of zero operators is zero
articles.statement: The zero direct sum is zero.

articles.title: Range of a direct sum operator
articles.statement: The range of a direct sum is the product of the ranges.

articles.title: Resolvent set of a direct sum operator
articles.statement: The resolvent set of a direct sum is the intersection of the resolvent sets.

articles.title: Spectrum of a direct sum operator is the union of spectra
articles.statement: The spectrum of a direct sum is the union of the spectra.

articles.title: Douglas factor gives a preimage under B
articles.statement: The canonical factor is a preimage: `B (C x) = A x`.

articles.title: Continuity of the Douglas factor via the closed graph theorem
articles.statement:
The canonical factor is continuous, by the (sequential) closed graph theorem:
if `u n → x` and `C (u n) → y`, then `y ∈ (ker B)ᗮ` (the orthogonal complement
is closed) and `B y = A x` (continuity of `A` and `B`), so `y = C x` by
uniqueness of the preimage in `(ker B)ᗮ`.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the Douglas factor
articles.statement: The canonical factor is the unique operator with the two defining properties.

articles.title: Defining properties of the Douglas preimage
articles.statement: The defining properties of the chosen preimage.

articles.title: Underlying function of the Douglas factor
articles.statement:
The underlying function of the canonical factor: the chosen preimage of `A x`
in `(ker B)ᗮ`.

articles.title: Douglas factor as a linear map
articles.statement: The canonical factor as a linear map.

articles.title: Douglas factor takes values in the kernel's orthogonal complement
articles.statement: The canonical factor lands in `(ker B)ᗮ`.

articles.title: Canonical factor in Douglas' lemma
articles.statement:
The canonical factor in Douglas' lemma: for `x : E`, the unique element of
`(ker B)ᗮ` mapped by `B` to `A x`.

articles.title: Douglas factor factors A through B
articles.statement: The canonical factor factors `A` through `B`.

articles.title: Injectivity of an operator on the orthogonal complement of its kernel
articles.statement:
Two points of `(ker B)ᗮ` with the same image under `B` are equal, since
their difference lies in `ker B ∩ (ker B)ᗮ`.

articles.title: Douglas' lemma: majorization gives a norm-bounded factor
articles.statement:
Douglas' lemma, factorization form with a norm bound: majorization with
constant `c` yields a factor `C` with `A = B ∘L C` and `‖C‖ ≤ c`.

articles.title: Preimages in the orthogonal complement of the kernel under range inclusion
articles.statement: If `A.range ≤ B.range`, every `A x` has a preimage under `B` in `(ker B)ᗮ`.

articles.title: Douglas' lemma: majorization iff factorization
articles.statement:
Douglas' lemma, majorization form: majorization holds iff `A` factors
through `B`.

articles.title: Factorization implies majorization
articles.statement: If `A = B ∘L C`, then majorization holds with constant `‖C‖`.

articles.title: Adjoint preserves the operator norm
articles.statement: Adjoints preserve operator norm.

articles.title: Douglas' lemma: range inclusion iff factorization
articles.statement:
Douglas' lemma, range form: `A.range ≤ B.range` iff `A = B ∘L C` for some
bounded `C`.

articles.title: Douglas' lemma: range inclusion iff majorization
articles.statement:
Douglas' lemma, range/majorization form: `A.range ≤ B.range` iff
majorization holds.

articles.title: A symmetric linear map from a Banach space to its dual is bounded
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real
Banach space with dual space $E^*$ of continuous linear functionals, and let $T : E \to E^*$ be
a linear map that is symmetric: $(Tx)(y) = (Ty)(x)$ for all $x, y \in E$. Then $T$ is bounded:
there is a constant $C \ge 0$ such that $\|Tx\| \le C \|x\|$ for all $x \in E$, where $\|Tx\|$
is the operator norm of the functional $Tx$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_22`.

articles.title: Hypercyclicity criterion
articles.statement:
The *hypercyclicity criterion*: along a sequence `n_k → ∞`, suppose
`T^(n_k) x → 0` on the dense set `X₀`, `S k y → 0` on the dense set `Y₀`,
and `T^(n_k) (S k y) → y` on `Y₀`. Then `T` is hypercyclic.
The Baire proof combines all three eventual estimates and uses cofinality
to meet each rational ball after every prescribed time threshold.
This includes the full-iterate, exact-inverse special case by taking
`n_k = id` and converting the exact identities to constant convergence.

articles.title: Hypercyclic operator
articles.statement:
A bounded operator `T` is *hypercyclic* if some vector has a dense
orbit under iteration of `T`.

articles.title: Lomonosov's invariant subspace theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an infinite-dimensional complex Banach
space, let $K$ be a nonzero compact operator on $E$, and let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on
$E$ with $TK = KT$. Then there is a closed linear subspace $M$ of $E$ with $M \ne \{0\}$ and
$M \ne E$ that is invariant under $T$: $T x \in M$ for every $x \in M$.

## Sources

- V. Lomonosov, Functional Anal. Appl. 7 (1973) and J. Hilden elementary proof, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.; Aronszajn-Smith 1954 precursor; Radjavi-Rosenthal invariant subspace book, 1973; Lean states complex Banach infinite-dimensional case `K≠0` compact commuting with `T` yields nontrivial closed invariant subspace.

articles.title: Centered state vector of an observable
articles.statement:
The centered vector subtracts the normalized real expectation times the state.
Its squared norm divided by the squared state norm is `variance`.

articles.title: Commutator of commuting operators vanishes
articles.statement: The commutator of commuting operators vanishes.

articles.title: Commutator expectation of self-adjoint operators is purely imaginary
articles.statement:
The commutator expectation of two self-adjoint operators is purely
imaginary: its real part vanishes.

articles.title: Commutator expectation as the skew part of the centered inner product
articles.statement:
The commutator expectation is the skew part of the inner product of
the centered vectors.

articles.title: Inner product of two centered vectors
articles.statement:
The inner product of two centered vectors, for self-adjoint
operators at a unit vector: the uncentered inner product minus the
product of the mean values.

articles.title: Flipped expectation inner product of a self-adjoint operator
articles.statement: The flipped expectation has the same necessary squared-state-norm factor.

articles.title: Expectation inner product of a self-adjoint operator
articles.statement:
For a self-adjoint operator, the expectation inner product is the normalized
mean multiplied by the squared state norm. The norm factor is required off the unit sphere.

articles.title: Normalized expectation on a unit vector
articles.statement: On a unit vector, normalized expectation equals the original quadratic mean.

articles.title: Normalized expectation value of an observable
articles.statement:
The normalized real expectation is Mathlib's canonical Rayleigh quotient.
For a nonzero state and self-adjoint observable it is the physical expectation.
At zero this total definition is zero; zero is not a physical state.

articles.title: Norm of the commutator expectation
articles.statement:
The commutator expectation has norm twice the absolute imaginary
part of the centered inner product.

articles.title: Squared norm of the commutator expectation
articles.statement:
The squared norm of the commutator expectation is four times the
squared imaginary part of the centered inner product.

articles.title: Robertson's uncertainty principle
articles.statement:
The product of the variances
is at least a quarter of the squared norm of the commutator
expectation.

articles.title: Robertson–Schrödinger uncertainty principle
articles.statement:
The **Robertson–Schrödinger uncertainty principle**: the product of
the variances is at least the squared covariance plus a quarter of the
squared norm of the commutator expectation.

articles.title: Variance as second moment minus squared mean
articles.statement: The variance is the second moment minus the squared mean.

articles.title: Normalized variance on the unit sphere
articles.statement: On the unit sphere, normalized variance is the centered squared norm.

articles.title: Normalized variance is invariant under nonzero scaling
articles.statement: Nonzero scalar multiplication does not change normalized variance.

articles.title: Normalized variance of an observable
articles.statement:
Normalized variance is the centered squared norm divided by the squared state norm.
For a nonzero state and self-adjoint observable it is the physical variance.
The totalized value at zero is zero. Off the unit sphere this corrects the raw
quadratic quantities; agreement with the original formulas is asserted only for unit states.

articles.title: Strong operator convergence characterized by weak operator convergence
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a real
or complex Hilbert space with inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$, let
$(T_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of bounded linear operators on $H$, let $T$ be a bounded
linear operator on $H$, and write $S^*$ for the adjoint of an operator $S$. Then $T_n \to T$ in
the strong operator topology, that is, $T_n x \to T x$ for every $x \in H$, if and only if both
$T_n \to T$ in the weak operator topology, that is, $\langle y, T_n x \rangle \to
\langle y, T x \rangle$ for all $x, y \in H$, and $T_n^* T_n \to T^* T$ in the weak operator
topology, that is, $\langle y, T_n^* T_n x \rangle \to \langle y, T^* T x \rangle$ for all
$x, y \in H$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_59`.

articles.title: Weakly bounded sets of operators are bounded
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $H$ and $K$ be Hilbert spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, and let $Q$ be a set of
bounded linear operators from $H$ to $K$. Suppose $Q$ is weakly bounded: for every $f \in H$
and $g \in K$ there is a real number $\alpha$ such that $|\langle A f, g \rangle| \le \alpha$
for all $A \in Q$. Then $Q$ is bounded in operator norm: there is a real number $M$ such that
$\|A\| \le M$ for all $A \in Q$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_60`.

articles.title: Pointwise convergent operators converge along convergent sequences
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be real
Banach spaces, let $(T_n)$ be a sequence of bounded linear operators from $E$ to $F$, and suppose
that for every $x \in E$ the sequence $(T_n x)$ converges to a limit $T x$. Then for every
sequence $x_n \to x$ in $E$ we have $T_n x_n \to T x$ in $F$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_68`.

articles.title: One-step Wold splitting into wandering vector plus range
articles.statement:
One step of the Wold decomposition: every vector splits as a wandering
vector plus a vector in the range.

articles.title: Finite Wold decomposition
articles.statement:
Finite Wold decomposition: every vector is a finite sum of pushed-forward
wandering vectors plus a remainder in the range of `V ^ n`. The wandering
coefficients vanish at and beyond `n`.

articles.title: Powers of an isometry preserve inner products
articles.statement: Pulling inner products back along powers of an isometry.

articles.title: Orthogonality of pushed-forward wandering vectors, symmetric form
articles.statement: The symmetric form of `inner_pow_wandering`.

articles.title: Orthogonality of pushed-forward wandering vectors
articles.statement:
A wandering vector, pushed forward `k` times, is orthogonal to any vector
pushed forward strictly more times.

articles.title: Residual subspace is orthogonal to the wandering part
articles.statement:
The residual subspace is orthogonal to every pushed-forward wandering
vector: the wandering part and the residual part of Wold's decomposition are
orthogonal.

articles.title: Isometry restricted to the residual subspace preserves inner products
articles.statement:
The restriction of an isometry to its residual subspace preserves inner
products.

articles.title: Wandering subspace and range are complementary
articles.statement: The ambient space splits as the wandering subspace plus the range.

articles.title: An isometry maps its residual subspace into itself
articles.statement: The isometry maps its residual subspace into itself.

articles.title: Positive powers of an isometry land in its range
articles.statement: A positive power of an isometry lands in the range of the isometry.

articles.title: Residual subspace of an isometry
articles.statement:
The **residual subspace** of an isometry: vectors in the range of every
power of `V`.

articles.title: Isometry restricted to the residual subspace is bijective
articles.statement: The restriction of an isometry to its residual subspace is bijective.

articles.title: Wandering subspace of an isometry
articles.statement:
The **wandering subspace** of an isometry `V`: the orthogonal complement of
its range. Vectors here are orthogonal to every vector in the range of `V`.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the finite Wold decomposition
articles.statement:
Uniqueness of the Wold decomposition at level `n`: the remainder and the
finite wandering sum are uniquely determined.

articles.title: Pythagorean identity for the Wold decomposition
articles.statement:
Pythagoras for a Wold decomposition: the squared norm of a vector is the sum
of the squared norms of its wandering coefficients plus the squared norm of
the remainder.

articles.title: Action of the residual unitary of an isometry
articles.statement:
Applying the residual unitary is the same as applying `V` and viewing the
result in the ambient space.

articles.title: Unitary part of an isometry on its residual subspace
articles.statement:
The isometry restricts to a unitary operator (a linear isometric
equivalence) on its residual subspace.

articles.title: Restriction to the orthogonal complement of the kernel is injective
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$
be inner product spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$,
and let $T : E \to F$ be a bounded linear operator. Then the restriction of $T$ to the
orthogonal complement $(\ker T)^\perp$ of its kernel is injective: a vector lying in both
$\ker T$ and $(\ker T)^\perp$ is zero.

articles.title: Closed range theorem for adjoints
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be Hilbert spaces over $\mathbb{K}$,
where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $T : E \to F$ be a bounded linear
operator with adjoint $T^\dagger$. Then the range of $T$ is closed in $F$ if and only if the
range of $T^\dagger$ is closed in $E$.

The reverse direction is the forward direction applied to $T^\dagger$, using
$T^{\dagger\dagger} = T$.

articles.title: Closed range passes to the Hilbert space adjoint
articles.statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be complex Hilbert spaces
and let $A : X \to Y$ be a bounded linear operator with Hilbert space adjoint $A^* : Y \to X$. If
the range of $A$ is closed in $Y$, then the range of $A^*$ is closed in $X$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_85`.

articles.title: Closed range passes to the adjoint
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be Hilbert spaces over $\mathbb{K}$,
where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $T : E \to F$ be a bounded linear
operator with adjoint $T^\dagger$. If the range of $T$ is closed in $F$, then the range of
$T^\dagger$ is closed in $E$.

Proof sketch: if the range of $T$ is closed, then $T$ is bounded below on $(\ker T)^\perp$
(the anti-Lipschitz criterion for its injective restriction), say $\|x\| \le C \|T x\|$ there.
Every $y \in (\ker T^\dagger)^\perp$ lies in the range of $T$, because
$(\operatorname{ran} T)^\perp = \ker T^\dagger$ and the range is closed. Writing $y = T x$ with
$x \in (\ker T)^\perp$ gives
$\|y\|^2 = \operatorname{Re} \langle x, T^\dagger y \rangle \le \|x\| \|T^\dagger y\| \le
C \|y\| \|T^\dagger y\|$; cancelling $\|y\|$ shows that $T^\dagger$ is bounded below on
$(\ker T^\dagger)^\perp$, so its range, which is the range of its restriction to
$(\ker T^\dagger)^\perp$, is closed.

articles.title: Closed range from a Fredholm $T^*T$
articles.statement:
**Closed range from a Fredholm $T^*T$.** Let $X$ and $Y$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let
$T : X \to Y$ be a bounded linear operator with Hilbert space adjoint $T^* : Y \to X$. If
$T^*T : X \to X$ is a Fredholm operator, then the range of $T$ is closed in $Y$.

Here a Fredholm operator is a bounded linear operator that is open onto its range, whose range is
closed and of finite codimension, and whose kernel is finite-dimensional and has a closed
complement. The source asks only for a finite-dimensional kernel and a range of finite
codimension; between Hilbert spaces the two agree, since a finite-codimensional range of a bounded
operator is closed.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_23`, with the change above.

articles.title: Restriction to the orthogonal complement of the kernel keeps the range
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
Hilbert space and $F$ an inner product space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $T : E \to F$ be a bounded linear operator. Then the
restriction of $T$ to the orthogonal complement $(\ker T)^\perp$ of its kernel has the same
range as $T$: every value $T x$ is attained at the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto
$(\ker T)^\perp$, since the difference lies in $\ker T$.

articles.title: The range of a bounded operator as a set
articles.statement:
Let $E'$ and $F'$ be Hilbert spaces over
$\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $S : E' \to F'$ be a
bounded linear operator. The set of values of $S$ equals the underlying set of the range of $S$
regarded as a linear subspace of $F'$.

This lets closedness of the range pass between the anti-Lipschitz criterion, stated for the
set of values, and the adjoint orthogonality identities, stated for the linear subspace.

articles.title: Compact operators send weakly null sequences to norm null sequences
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$
be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ and $F$ be normed spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, and let
$T : E \to F$ be a compact continuous linear operator. If a sequence $(u_n)$ in $E$ converges
weakly to $0$, that is, $f(u_n) \to 0$ for every continuous linear functional
$f : E \to \mathbb{K}$, then $T u_n \to 0$ in norm.

articles.title: Complete continuity of compact operators, weak-topology form
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ and $F$ be normed spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, and let
$T : E \to F$ be a compact continuous linear operator. If a sequence $(u_n)$ in $E$ converges
to $x \in E$ in the weak topology of $E$, then $T u_n \to T x$ in norm.

articles.title: Complete continuity of compact operators
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ and $F$ be normed spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, and let $T : E \to F$ be a
compact continuous linear operator. If a sequence $(u_n)$ in $E$ converges weakly to $x \in E$,
that is, $f(u_n) \to f(x)$ for every continuous linear functional $f : E \to \mathbb{K}$, then
$T u_n \to T x$ in norm.

The proof is the standard subsequence argument: if $T u_n$ did not converge in norm to $T x$,
some subsequence would stay $\varepsilon$-away from $T x$; the sequence $(u_n)$ is norm-bounded
by uniform boundedness, so compactness gives a further subsequence of $(T u_n)$ converging in
norm to some $a$; but $T$ preserves weak convergence, so $a = T x$ by uniqueness of scalar
limits and the fact that the dual separates points, contradicting the
$\varepsilon$-separation.

articles.title: Finite-rank approximation of compact operators
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be an inner product space over
$\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ ($H$ need not be complete),
and let $T$ be a compact bounded linear operator on $H$. For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there
is a bounded linear operator $F$ on $H$ with finite-dimensional range such that
$\|T - F\| \le \varepsilon$.

The approximant is the composition of $T$ with the orthogonal projection onto the span of a
finite $\varepsilon$-net for the image of the closed unit ball.

articles.title: Compact operators are norm limits of finite-rank operators
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be an inner product
space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ ($H$ need not be
complete), and let $T$ be a compact bounded linear operator on $H$. Then there is a sequence
$(F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of bounded linear operators on $H$, each with finite-dimensional
range, such that $\|T - F_n\| \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Fredholm alternative for compact self-adjoint operators
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a compact self-adjoint bounded operator on
$H$, let $I$ be the identity of $H$, and let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\mu \neq 0$. Then the range
of $\mu I - T$ equals the orthogonal complement $(\ker(\mu I - T))^\perp$ of its kernel, and either
$\mu I - T$ is bijective, or its kernel is nonzero and finite-dimensional.

articles.title: Fredholm alternative for compact self-adjoint operators, operator-minus-scalar form
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a compact
self-adjoint bounded operator on $H$, let $I$ be the identity of $H$, and let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$
with $\mu \neq 0$. Then the range of $T - \mu I$ equals the orthogonal complement
$(\ker(T - \mu I))^\perp$ of its kernel, and either $T - \mu I$ is bijective, or its kernel is
nonzero and finite-dimensional.

This differs from the $\mu I - T$ form of the Fredholm alternative only by a sign.

articles.title: Closed range for compact self-adjoint perturbations of nonzero scalars
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a
Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a compact self-adjoint
bounded operator on $H$, let $I$ be the identity of $H$, and let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with
$\mu \neq 0$. Then the range of $\mu I - T$ is a closed subset of $H$.

articles.title: The kernel of a scalar minus an operator is an eigenspace
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be an inner product
space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on $H$,
let $I$ be the identity of $H$, and let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$. Then the kernel of $\mu I - T$
equals the eigenspace $\{x \in H : T x = \mu x\}$ of $T$ for $\mu$.

articles.title: Adjoint of a Hilbert–Schmidt operator
articles.statement:
The adjoint of a Hilbert–Schmidt operator is the Hilbert–Schmidt operator
of the conjugate-transpose matrix.

articles.title: Canonical Hilbert–Schmidt norm equals the matrix norm
articles.statement:
In the standard `ℓ²` basis, the existing extended operator squared norm
equals the finite matrix squared norm. This bridge is specialized to real
scalars because the canonical operator norm API is real-only.

articles.title: Canonical Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the constructed operator
articles.statement:
The constructed real Hilbert–Schmidt operator has the canonical extended
squared norm given by the finite squared norm of its matrix.

articles.title: Operator with Hilbert–Schmidt matrix is the operator of its matrix
articles.statement:
A bounded operator whose matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt is the Hilbert–Schmidt
operator of its matrix.

articles.title: The Hilbert–Schmidt norm of a finite-rank operator is controlled by its operator norm
articles.statement:
There is a function $C$ from the natural numbers to the positive reals with the following
property. Let $H$ be an infinite-dimensional separable real Hilbert space, let
$(u_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a Hilbert basis of $H$, and let $T : H \to H$ be a bounded linear
operator such that the quotient $H/\ker T$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension $n$. Then the
Hilbert–Schmidt norm of $T$ computed in the basis $(u_i)$, taken in $[0,\infty]$, satisfies

$$\Big(\sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \|Tu_i\|^2\Big)^{1/2} \le C(n)\,\|T\|,$$

where $\|T\|$ is the operator norm of $T$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_98`.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt coordinates as inner products with rows
articles.statement: The coordinate series is the inner product with the row vector.

articles.title: Diagonal infinite matrix
articles.statement: The diagonal matrix with diagonal `d`.

articles.title: Extended Hilbert–Schmidt norm in a family
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a real inner product space, let
$T : H \to H$ be a continuous linear operator and let $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in
$H$. The Hilbert–Schmidt norm of $T$ in the family $(u_n)$ is the square root, taken in
$[0, \infty]$ with $\sqrt{\infty} = \infty$, of the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \|T u_n\|^2 \in [0, \infty]$.

In particular it is $\infty$, not $0$, when the series $\sum_n \|T u_n\|^2$ diverges, for example
for the identity operator when $(u_n)$ is an orthonormal basis of $H$ indexed by $\mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the Hilbert–Schmidt linear map
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the Hilbert–Schmidt linear map.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt operator as a linear map
articles.statement: The Hilbert–Schmidt operator of a matrix, as a linear map.

articles.title: Matrix of the Hilbert–Schmidt operator of a matrix
articles.statement: The matrix of a Hilbert–Schmidt operator is the matrix itself.

articles.title: Matrix of a bounded operator on $\ell^2$
articles.statement:
The matrix of a bounded operator on `ℓ²(ℕ, 𝕜)`: entry `(i, j)` is the `i`-th
coordinate of the image of the `j`-th standard basis vector.

articles.title: Squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm in a family
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a real inner product space, let
$T : H \to H$ be a continuous linear operator and let $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in
$H$. The squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of $T$ in the family $(u_n)$ is the extended nonnegative
real $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \|T u_n\|^2$, the sum being taken in $[0, \infty]$. It is $\infty$
exactly when the real series $\sum_n \|T u_n\|^2$ diverges.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt norm of a diagonal matrix
articles.statement:
The squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of a diagonal matrix is the sum of the squared
diagonal entries.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt norm of a rank-one matrix
articles.statement: The squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of a rank-one matrix is `‖u‖² * ‖v‖²`.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the truncation error as a tail sum
articles.statement: The squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the truncation error is the tail sum.

articles.title: Squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of a matrix
articles.statement:
The finite squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm: the sum of the squared entry norms.
The witness restricts this real quantity to summable matrices, avoiding the
zero default of a nonsummable real `tsum`. Divergent operators are handled
by the existing extended-valued operator norm.

articles.title: Additivity of the Hilbert–Schmidt operator
articles.statement: The Hilbert–Schmidt operator of a sum is the sum of the operators.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the Hilbert–Schmidt operator
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the Hilbert–Schmidt operator.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt operator is independent of the summability proof
articles.statement: The Hilbert–Schmidt operator depends only on the matrix, not on the summability proof.

articles.title: Diagonal Hilbert–Schmidt operator acts by pointwise multiplication
articles.statement: A diagonal Hilbert–Schmidt operator acts by pointwise multiplication by the diagonal.

articles.title: Action of a rank-one Hilbert–Schmidt operator
articles.statement: A rank-one Hilbert–Schmidt operator acts as the inner product with `v` times `u`.

articles.title: Truncated Hilbert–Schmidt operator as a sum of rank-one operators
articles.statement: A truncated Hilbert–Schmidt operator is a finite sum of rank-one operators.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt operator of a scalar multiple of a matrix
articles.statement: The Hilbert–Schmidt operator of a scalar multiple is the scalar multiple of the operator.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt operator of a difference of matrices
articles.statement: The Hilbert–Schmidt operator of a difference is the difference of the operators.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt operator of the zero matrix is zero
articles.statement: The Hilbert–Schmidt operator of the zero matrix is zero.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt operator on ℓ²
articles.statement: The Hilbert–Schmidt operator of a matrix, as a bounded operator on `ℓ²(ℕ, 𝕜)`.

articles.title: Rank-one infinite matrix
articles.statement: The rank-one matrix `u i * star (v j)`.

articles.title: Row vector of a Hilbert–Schmidt matrix
articles.statement: The row vector of a Hilbert–Schmidt matrix, as an `ℓ²` element (conjugated).

articles.title: Conjugate transpose of an infinite matrix
articles.statement: The conjugate transpose of a matrix: `(aᵀ*) i j = star (a j i)`.

articles.title: Truncation of a matrix to its top-left block
articles.statement: The truncation of a matrix to the top-left `N × N` block.

articles.title: Truncated Hilbert–Schmidt operators are compact
articles.statement: A truncated Hilbert–Schmidt operator is compact.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt operators on $\ell^2$ are compact
articles.statement: Every Hilbert–Schmidt operator on `ℓ²(ℕ, 𝕜)` is compact.

articles.title: Bounded operator with Hilbert–Schmidt matrix is compact
articles.statement: A bounded operator whose matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt is compact.

articles.title: Rank-one operators on $\ell^2$ are compact
articles.statement: A rank-one operator on `ℓ²` is compact: it factors through the one-dimensional space `𝕜`.

articles.title: Sum of Hilbert–Schmidt matrices is Hilbert–Schmidt
articles.statement: The sum of Hilbert–Schmidt matrices is Hilbert–Schmidt.

articles.title: Diagonal matrix with square-summable diagonal is Hilbert–Schmidt
articles.statement: A diagonal matrix with square-summable diagonal is Hilbert–Schmidt.

articles.title: Rank-one matrix of $\ell^2$ vectors is Hilbert–Schmidt
articles.statement: A rank-one matrix with `ℓ²` vectors is Hilbert–Schmidt.

articles.title: Truncated matrices are Hilbert–Schmidt
articles.statement: A truncation of any matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt: it is supported on a finite set.

articles.title: Negation preserves the Hilbert–Schmidt property
articles.statement: The negative of a Hilbert–Schmidt matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt.

articles.title: Scalar multiple of a Hilbert–Schmidt matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt
articles.statement: A scalar multiple of a Hilbert–Schmidt matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt.

articles.title: Difference of Hilbert–Schmidt matrices is Hilbert–Schmidt
articles.statement: The difference of Hilbert–Schmidt matrices is Hilbert–Schmidt.

articles.title: Conjugate transpose of a Hilbert–Schmidt matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt
articles.statement: The conjugate transpose of a Hilbert–Schmidt matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt.

articles.title: Zero matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt
articles.statement: The zero matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt matrix
articles.statement: A matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt if the squared norms of its entries are summable.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt matrix maps ℓ² vectors into ℓ²
articles.statement: The coordinate series of a Hilbert–Schmidt matrix applied to an `ℓ²` vector is in `ℓ²`.

articles.title: Square-summable sequences lie in ℓ²
articles.statement: `Memℓp` at `2` from summability of squared norms.

articles.title: The Hilbert–Schmidt norm bounds an operator on unit vectors
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, let $T : H \to H$ be a bounded linear operator, and let $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be an
orthonormal basis of $H$ indexed by the natural numbers. Let
$\|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}} = \bigl(\sum_{n} \|T u_n\|^2\bigr)^{1/2} \in [0, \infty]$ be the
Hilbert–Schmidt norm of $T$ computed in this basis; it is $\infty$ when the series diverges.
Then $\|Tx\| \le \|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$ for every $x \in H$ with $\|x\| = 1$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; Special classes of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_68`.

articles.title: Norm bound for the Hilbert–Schmidt linear map
articles.statement: The Hilbert–Schmidt operator is bounded by the square root of `hsNormSq`.

articles.title: Operator norm is at most the Hilbert–Schmidt norm
articles.statement: The operator norm of a Hilbert–Schmidt operator is at most its Hilbert–Schmidt norm.

articles.title: Operator norm bounded by the Hilbert–Schmidt norm
articles.statement:
A bounded operator whose matrix is Hilbert–Schmidt has norm at most its
Hilbert–Schmidt norm.

articles.title: Squared ℓ² norm as a sum of squared coordinates
articles.statement: Norm squared of an `ℓ²(ℕ, 𝕜)` vector is the sum of the squared coordinate norms.

articles.title: Scaled rank-one operator on standard basis vectors
articles.statement: The action of a scaled rank-one operator on standard basis vectors, pointwise.

articles.title: Summability of the Hilbert–Schmidt coordinate series
articles.statement: The coordinate series defining the Hilbert–Schmidt operator is summable.

articles.title: Rows of a diagonal matrix are square-summable
articles.statement: A row of a diagonal matrix is square-summable.

articles.title: Entries of a rank-one matrix are square-summable
articles.statement: The squared norms of the entries of a rank-one matrix are summable over the product.

articles.title: Square-summability of a Hilbert–Schmidt image
articles.statement: The squared norms of the coordinates of a Hilbert–Schmidt image are summable.

articles.title: Square-summability of coordinates of an ℓ² vector
articles.statement: Summability of squared coordinate norms from `Memℓp`.

articles.title: Rows of a Hilbert–Schmidt matrix are square-summable
articles.statement: Fiber summability: each row of a Hilbert–Schmidt matrix is square-summable.

articles.title: Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the truncation error tends to zero
articles.statement: The squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the truncation error tends to zero.

articles.title: Truncated operators converge in norm to the Hilbert–Schmidt operator
articles.statement: The truncated operators converge in norm to the Hilbert–Schmidt operator.

articles.title: Square partial sums converge to the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm
articles.statement: The partial sums of the squared norms over expanding squares converge to `hsNormSq`.

articles.title: Squared row norm of a diagonal matrix
articles.statement: The squared norms in a row of a diagonal matrix sum to the squared diagonal entry.

articles.title: Rank-one operators have finite range
articles.statement: A rank-one operator has finite range.

articles.title: Finite-rank perturbation preserves the Fredholm index
articles.statement:
Adding a finite-rank operator does not change the Fredholm index.
The proof follows the segment `T + t • F`, `t ∈ [0, 1]`, which is a
continuous path of Fredholm operators.

articles.title: Fredholm index is constant along a path continuous on (0, 1)
articles.statement:
The Fredholm index is constant along a continuous path of Fredholm
operators on `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Fredholm index is constant along a globally continuous path
articles.statement:
The Fredholm index is constant along a globally continuous path of
Fredholm operators on `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Fredholm index is constant on preconnected families
articles.statement:
The Fredholm index is constant along a continuous family of Fredholm
operators indexed by a preconnected set, because the index is locally
constant (Mathlib) and takes values in the discrete space `ℤ`.

articles.title: Left finite-rank perturbation preserves the Fredholm index
articles.statement:
Adding a finite-rank operator on the left does not change the
Fredholm index.

articles.title: Subtracting a finite-rank operator preserves the Fredholm index
articles.statement:
Subtracting a finite-rank operator does not change the Fredholm
index.

articles.title: The kernel of a compact operator on a nonseparable Hilbert space is nonseparable
articles.statement:
Let
$H$ be a complex Hilbert space that is not separable and let $A : H \to H$ be a compact operator.
Then the kernel $\ker A$ is not separable.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; Special classes of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_42`.

articles.title: Adjoint of a shifted operator
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on $E$ with
adjoint $T^*$, let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ and let $I$ be the identity operator on $E$. Then
$(\mu I - T)^* = \overline{\mu} I - T^*$, where $\overline{\mu}$ is the complex conjugate of
$\mu$ (so $\overline{\mu} = \mu$ when $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$).

articles.title: Continuous projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space
over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $K$ be a finite-dimensional subspace of $E$. Then
there is a continuous linear map $P : E \to E$ such that $P x = x$ for every $x \in K$ and
$P x \in K$ for every $x \in E$.

The projection is built from a basis of $K$, with the coordinate functionals extended to all
of $E$ by Hahn–Banach.

articles.title: Riesz–Schauder theorem, kernel part
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $T : E \to E$ be a compact bounded linear operator, let $\mu \neq 0$ be a
scalar and let $I$ be the identity of $E$. Then the kernel of $\mu I - T$ is
finite-dimensional.

The proof is the standard restriction trick: $T$ maps the kernel of $\mu I - T$ into itself and
agrees with $\mu I$ there, so the identity of the kernel is a compact operator.

articles.title: Fredholm alternative, Riesz–Schauder form
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{R}$
or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T : E \to E$ be a compact bounded linear operator, let $\mu \neq 0$ be a
scalar and let $I$ be the identity of $E$. Then either $\mu I - T$ is bijective, or the kernel
of $\mu I - T$ is nonzero and finite-dimensional and the range of $\mu I - T$ is closed.

articles.title: Riesz–Schauder theorem, range part
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $T : E \to E$ be a compact bounded linear operator, let $\mu \neq 0$ be a
scalar and let $I$ be the identity of $E$. Then the range of $\mu I - T$ is closed in $E$.

The proof restricts $\mu I - T$ to a closed complement of its kernel, where a sequence argument
using compactness of $T$ shows that it is bounded below, hence has closed range.

articles.title: Riesz–Schauder theorem on a Hilbert space
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a compact operator on $E$, let
$\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\mu \ne 0$, and let $I$ be the identity operator on $E$. Then the range
of $\mu I - T$ is the orthogonal complement of the kernel of its adjoint:
$\operatorname{ran}(\mu I - T) = \ker\big((\mu I - T)^*\big)^\perp$.

For self-adjoint $T$ this gives $\operatorname{ran}(\mu I - T) = \ker(\mu I - T)^\perp$.

articles.title: Riesz–Schauder theorem on a Hilbert space, adjoint form
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a compact operator on $E$ with adjoint $T^*$,
let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\mu \ne 0$, and let $I$ be the identity operator on $E$. Then the
range of $\mu I - T$ is the orthogonal complement of the kernel of $\overline{\mu} I - T^*$,
where $\overline{\mu}$ is the complex conjugate of $\mu$:
$\operatorname{ran}(\mu I - T) = \ker(\overline{\mu} I - T^*)^\perp$.

articles.title: Schauder's theorem, iff form
articles.statement:
A bounded operator between Hilbert
spaces is compact if and only if its adjoint is compact.

articles.title: The adjoint of a finite-rank operator is compact
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be Hilbert spaces over
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If a bounded linear operator $T : E \to F$ has finite-dimensional
range, then its adjoint $T^* : F \to E$ is a compact operator.

The proof factors $T$ through its range $R$ as $T = i \circ \pi$, where $\pi : E \to R$ is $T$
with its codomain restricted to $R$ and $i : R \to F$ is the inclusion. Then
$T^* = \pi^* \circ i^*$, and $\pi^*$ is compact because its domain $R$ is finite-dimensional,
hence locally compact.

articles.title: Schauder's theorem
articles.statement:
The adjoint of a compact operator between
Hilbert spaces is compact.

articles.title: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are not in the span of earlier ones
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a bounded linear operator
on $E$, let $(\lambda_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be pairwise distinct scalars in $\mathbb{K}$, and let
$(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be nonzero vectors in $E$ with $T u_n = \lambda_n u_n$ for every $n$.
Then for every $n$, the vector $u_n$ does not lie in the linear span of $\{u_i : i < n\}$.

This is the non-orthogonal replacement for the orthogonality of eigenspaces used in the
self-adjoint case: it follows from the fact that the eigenspaces of a linear operator form an
independent family.

articles.title: Riesz separation for nested spans
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be vectors in $E$, and
for each $n$ let $V_n$ be the linear span of $\{u_i : i < n\}$. Suppose $u_n \notin V_n$ for
every $n$. Then for every $n$ there is a vector $y \in V_{n+1}$ with $\|y\| = 1$ and
$\|y - z\| \ge 1/2$ for every $z \in V_n$.

This is Riesz's lemma for the finite-dimensional, hence closed, subspace $V_n$: one takes $y$ to be
the normalization of $u_n - z$ for a $z \in V_n$ almost realizing the distance $d > 0$ from
$u_n$ to $V_n$.

articles.title: Finiteness of eigenvalues of a compact operator bounded away from zero
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed
space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a compact bounded linear operator
on $E$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$ be real. Then the set of eigenvalues $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ of $T$
with $|\mu| \ge \varepsilon$ is finite.

If it were infinite, distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_n$ with eigenvectors $u_n$ would give, by Riesz
separation for the spans of the $u_n$, unit vectors $y_n$ whose images $T y_n$ are pairwise at
distance at least $\varepsilon / 2$, contradicting compactness of $T$. No self-adjointness, inner
product or completeness is needed.

articles.title: Invariance of spans of eigenvectors
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a normed space over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on $E$, and let
$(\lambda_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\mathbb{K}$ and $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $E$ satisfy
$T u_n = \lambda_n u_n$ for every $n$. Then for every $n$ and every $y$ in the linear span of
$\{u_i : i \le n\}$, the vector $T y$ also lies in that span.

articles.title: A compact operator on an infinite-dimensional Banach space is not bijective
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an
infinite-dimensional Banach space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $T$ be a
compact bounded linear operator on $E$. Then $T$ is not bijective.

By the bounded inverse theorem, a bijective bounded operator on a Banach space has a bounded
inverse, so this follows from the fact that a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space
has no bounded two-sided inverse.

articles.title: A compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is not a unit
articles.statement:
If `T` is compact and `E` is infinite-dimensional, then `T` has no
two-sided inverse among bounded operators. (Completeness of `E` is not
needed for this statement.)

articles.title: An operator acts as a scalar on a span of eigenvectors modulo a smaller span
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a bounded linear operator
on $E$, let $(\lambda_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\mathbb{K}$ and $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $E$
satisfy $T u_n = \lambda_n u_n$ for every $n$, and for each $n$ let $V_n$ be the linear span of
$\{u_i : i < n\}$. Then for every $n$ and every $y \in V_{n+1}$, we have
$T y - \lambda_n y \in V_n$.

The proof is induction on the span: each generator $u_i$ with $i < n$ contributes
$(\lambda_i - \lambda_n) u_i$ and the generator $u_n$ contributes $0$.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a compact operator tend to zero along any injective sequence
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $T$ be a compact bounded linear
operator on $E$. If $(\lambda_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of pairwise distinct eigenvalues
of $T$, then $\lambda_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

Otherwise some $\varepsilon > 0$ would satisfy $|\lambda_n| \ge \varepsilon$ for infinitely many
$n$, giving infinitely many eigenvalues of modulus at least $\varepsilon$, which contradicts the
finiteness of eigenvalues of a compact operator bounded away from zero.

articles.title: Zero lies in the spectrum of a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be
an infinite-dimensional normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $T$ be
a compact bounded linear operator on $E$. Then $0$ lies in the spectrum of $T$ in the algebra of
bounded linear operators on $E$; that is, $T$ has no bounded two-sided inverse.

articles.title: Attained form of the Bauer–Fike theorem
articles.statement:
The attained form of Bauer–Fike: some eigenvalue-like point of the
spectrum of `A` is within `‖E‖` of `μ`.

articles.title: Hausdorff distance between spectra of self-adjoint perturbations
articles.statement:
For self-adjoint `A` and `A + E`, the Hausdorff distance of the two
spectra is at most `‖E‖`.

articles.title: Bauer–Fike theorem
articles.statement:
The Bauer–Fike theorem: every point of the spectrum of `A + E` lies
within `‖E‖` of the spectrum of a normal operator `A`.

articles.title: Resolvent norm bound for a normal operator
articles.statement:
The resolvent norm bound for a normal operator: if `z` lies outside the
spectrum of a normal `A`, then `‖(z • 1 - A)⁻¹‖ ≤ 1 / dist z (spectrum ℂ A)`.

articles.title: Cauchy interlacing
articles.statement:
For a codimension-one subspace `S`, the
eigenvalues `μₖ` of the compression of a self-adjoint operator `T`
interlace the eigenvalues `λₖ` of `T`:
`λₖ₊₁ ≤ μₖ ≤ λₖ`.

articles.title: Action of the compression of an operator
articles.statement: The compression acts by projecting the image back onto the subspace.

articles.title: Compression of a symmetric operator is symmetric
articles.statement: The compression of a symmetric operator is symmetric.

articles.title: Rayleigh form of a compression
articles.statement:
The Rayleigh form of the compression at `y` equals the Rayleigh form
of the original operator at the underlying vector `(y : E)`.

articles.title: Compression of an operator to a subspace
articles.statement:
The compression of an operator `T` to a subspace `S`: project `T x`
orthogonally back onto `S`.

articles.title: Cauchy interlacing, upper half
articles.statement:
The `k`-th eigenvalue of the
compression to a codimension-one subspace is at most the `k`-th
eigenvalue of the original operator.

articles.title: Cauchy interlacing, lower half
articles.statement:
The `k`-th eigenvalue of the
compression to a codimension-one subspace is at least the `(k+1)`-st
eigenvalue of the original operator.

articles.title: Subspaces of every smaller dimension inside a given subspace
articles.statement:
A subspace of dimension `m` can be thinned to a subspace of any
smaller dimension.

articles.title: The k-th eigenvector attains the Rayleigh bound on the head
articles.statement:
The `k`-th eigenvector lies in the head span, is a unit vector, and
attains the Rayleigh value `λₖ`.

articles.title: The k-th eigenvector attains the Rayleigh bound on the tail
articles.statement:
The `k`-th eigenvector lies in the tail span, is a unit vector, and
attains the Rayleigh value `λₖ`.

articles.title: Courant–Fischer max–min, extremal subspace form
articles.statement:
There is a
subspace `U` of dimension `k + 1` on which every unit vector has Rayleigh
quotient at least `λₖ`, and the bound is attained.

articles.title: Courant–Fischer min–max, extremal subspace form
articles.statement:
There is a
subspace `W` of dimension `n - k` on which every unit vector has Rayleigh
quotient at most `λₖ`, and the bound is attained.

articles.title: Courant–Fischer min–max, lower-bound form
articles.statement:
Every subspace of
dimension `n - k` contains a unit vector with Rayleigh quotient at
least `λₖ`.

articles.title: Courant–Fischer max–min, lower-bound form
articles.statement:
Every subspace of
dimension `k + 1` contains a unit vector with Rayleigh quotient at
most `λₖ`.

articles.title: Dimension of the span of the eigenbasis head
articles.statement: The span of the head of the eigenbasis has dimension `k + 1`.

articles.title: Dimension of the span of the eigenbasis tail
articles.statement: The span of the tail of the eigenbasis has dimension `n - k`.

articles.title: Linear independence of the eigenbasis head
articles.statement:
The head family is linearly independent, as a restriction of the
orthonormal eigenbasis.

articles.title: Head of an orthonormal eigenbasis
articles.statement:
The head of the eigenbasis: the eigenvectors with index `≤ k`,
as a family indexed by `Fin (k + 1)`.

articles.title: Span of some eigenvectors is orthogonal to the remaining ones
articles.statement:
A vector in the span of some of the eigenvectors is orthogonal to the
remaining eigenvectors.

articles.title: Eigenbasis expansion of the quadratic form of a self-adjoint operator
articles.statement:
Expansion of `⟪x, T x⟫` in the orthonormal eigenbasis: a weighted sum
of the eigenvalues with weights `‖⟪eᵢ, x⟫‖²`.

articles.title: Eigenbasis expansion of the Rayleigh form
articles.statement: The Rayleigh form expanded in the orthonormal eigenbasis.

articles.title: Lower bound for the Rayleigh form on the eigenbasis head
articles.statement:
On the span of the head of the eigenbasis, the Rayleigh form is at
least `λₖ * ‖x‖²`.

articles.title: Upper bound for the Rayleigh form on the eigenbasis tail
articles.statement:
On the span of the tail of the eigenbasis, the Rayleigh form is at
most `λₖ * ‖x‖²`.

articles.title: Rayleigh form scales quadratically
articles.statement:
Scaling a vector by a real scalar scales the Rayleigh form by the
square of the scalar.

articles.title: Rayleigh form of an operator
articles.statement:
The Rayleigh form of a vector for an operator `T`: `re ⟪T x, x⟫`.
On unit vectors this is the Rayleigh quotient.

articles.title: Linear independence of the eigenbasis tail
articles.statement:
The tail family is linearly independent, as a restriction of the
orthonormal eigenbasis.

articles.title: Tail of an orthonormal eigenbasis
articles.statement:
The tail of the eigenbasis: the eigenvectors with index `≥ k`,
as a family indexed by `Fin (n - k)`.

articles.title: Eckart–Young theorem in operator norm
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be finite-dimensional inner product
spaces over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T : E \to F$ be a linear map and let
$k \ge 0$ be an integer. The infimum of the operator norms $\|T - S\|$ over all linear maps
$S : E \to F$ whose range has dimension at most $k$ equals $\sigma_k(T)$, where
$\sigma_0(T) \ge \sigma_1(T) \ge \cdots$ are the singular values of $T$ listed with multiplicity
and indexed from $0$, and $\sigma_j(T) = 0$ for $j \ge \dim E$.

## Sources

- C. Eckart and G. Young, The Approximation of One Matrix by Another of Lower Rank, Psychometrika 1 (1936), 211-218, DOI 10.1007/BF02288367; unitary-invariant extension L. Mirsky, QJM 11 (1960), DOI 10.1093/qmath/11.1.50.

articles.title: Prefix sum of a finite real sequence
articles.statement:
For real numbers $\lambda_0, \dots, \lambda_{n-1}$
and a natural number $k \le n$, the prefix sum of length $k$ is $\sum_{i < k} \lambda_i$, the
sum of the first $k$ entries. Applied to the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix, listed in
decreasing order, it is the sum of the $k$ largest ones.

articles.title: Ky Fan inequality for sums of largest eigenvalues
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be Hermitian $n \times n$
complex matrices and let $k \le n$. Then the sum of the $k$ largest eigenvalues of $A + B$ is at
most the sum of the $k$ largest eigenvalues of $A$ plus the sum of the $k$ largest eigenvalues
of $B$, where eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity.

## Sources

- Ky Fan, On a theorem of Weyl, PNAS 35 (1949), 652-655, DOI 10.1073/pnas.35.11.652.

articles.title: Convex differentiable functions lie above their tangent lines
articles.statement:
The first-order (tangent-line) characterization of a convex
differentiable function: the graph lies above every tangent line.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a positive semidefinite operator are nonnegative
articles.statement:
Eigenvalues of a positive semidefinite symmetric operator are
nonnegative: an eigenvalue is the Rayleigh quotient at a unit
eigenvector.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a positive definite operator are positive
articles.statement: Eigenvalues of a positive definite symmetric operator are positive.

articles.title: Entropy tangent bound in an arbitrary orthonormal basis
articles.statement:
The entropy tangent bound in an arbitrary orthonormal basis. Its diagonal entries
need not align with the eigenvalues of `S`; `klein_entropy` supplies the aligned
quantum-relative-entropy form.

articles.title: Klein's entropy inequality
articles.statement:
Klein's entropy inequality in the eigenbasis of `S`. The eigenvalue at index `i`
is paired with its eigenvector, so this is the quantum-relative-entropy form up to
the trace terms. In particular, its tangent correction vanishes when `T = S`.

articles.title: Klein's inequality
articles.statement:
**Klein's inequality** (sum form): for a convex function `f`
differentiable at the eigenvalues of `S`, the tangent-line sum at the
eigenvalues of `S` evaluated on the diagonal of `T` is at most the sum
of `f` over the eigenvalues of `T`.

articles.title: Klein's inequality for the square function
articles.statement: Klein's inequality for `f x = x ^ 2`.

articles.title: Peierls' inequality for the exponential
articles.statement: Peierls' inequality for the exponential function.

articles.title: Peierls' inequality
articles.statement:
The diagonal of a self-adjoint operator in
any orthonormal basis is majorized by its eigenvalues, as measured by
any convex function.

articles.title: Schur's theorem on diagonals of self-adjoint operators
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex inner product
space of finite dimension $n$, let $T : E \to E$ be a linear operator that is symmetric, that is,
$\langle T x, y \rangle = \langle x, T y \rangle$ for all $x, y \in E$, let
$\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ be the eigenvalues of $T$ listed with multiplicity, and let
$b_1, \dots, b_n$ be an orthonormal basis of $E$. Then there is a doubly stochastic real
$n \times n$ matrix $D$ such that $\operatorname{Re} \langle b_i, T b_i \rangle =
\sum_{j=1}^n D_{ij} \lambda_j$ for every $i$.

## Sources

- I. Schur, 1923, Über eine Klasse von Mittelbildungen mit Anwendungen auf die Determinantentheorie; A. Horn, Doubly Stochastic Matrices and the Diagonal of a Rotation Matrix, Amer. J. Math. 76 (1954), 620–630, DOI 10.2307/2372705.

articles.title: Weyl's inequality (upper bound), matrix form
articles.statement:
For Hermitian matrices
`A, B`, `λ_{a+b}(A + B) ≤ λ_a(A) + λ_b(B)` whenever `a + b < n`.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of equal Hermitian matrices agree
articles.statement:
Eigenvalues are unchanged when the matrix is replaced by an equal
matrix (useful to transport eigenvalue computations along identities such
as `diagonal d₁ + diagonal d₂ = diagonal (d₁ + d₂)`).

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix with decreasing entries
articles.statement:
The eigenvalues of a diagonal Hermitian matrix whose diagonal entries
are already in decreasing order are exactly those entries.

articles.title: Weyl's inequality (lower bound), matrix form
articles.statement:
For Hermitian matrices
`A, B`, `λ_a(A) + λ_b(B) ≤ λ_{a+b-(n-1)}(A + B)` whenever `n - 1 ≤ a + b`.

articles.title: Weyl's inequality (lower bound)
articles.statement:
For self-adjoint operators `T, S`,
`λ_a(T) + λ_b(S) ≤ λ_{a+b-(n-1)}(T + S)` whenever `n - 1 ≤ a + b`.

articles.title: Weyl's inequality (upper bound)
articles.statement:
For self-adjoint operators `T, S`,
`λ_{a+b}(T + S) ≤ λ_a(T) + λ_b(S)` whenever `a + b < n`.

articles.title: Weyl's perturbation inequality
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be Hermitian $n \times n$ complex matrices,
and let $\lambda_1(A) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(A)$ and $\lambda_1(B) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(B)$ be
their eigenvalues, listed with multiplicity in decreasing order. Then
$|\lambda_i(A) - \lambda_i(B)| \le \|A - B\|$ for every $i$, where $\|A - B\|$ is the operator
norm of $A - B$ acting on $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the Euclidean norm.

## Sources

- H. Weyl, Math. Ann. 71 (1912), DOI 10.1007/BF01456804.

articles.title: Adjoint of the Cesàro operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and
let $C$ be the Cesàro operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by
$(Cx)_n = (x_0 + \dots + x_n)/(n + 1)$. For every $y \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and
every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the adjoint $C^*$ of $C$ satisfies

$$(C^* y)_n = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{y_{n+k}}{n + k + 1}.$$

articles.title: The adjoint of the Cesàro operator fixes the first basis vector
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $C$ be the Cesàro operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$,
and let $e_0 = (1, 0, 0, \dots)$ be the first standard basis vector. Then $C^* e_0 = e_0$, where
$C^*$ is the adjoint of $C$.

articles.title: Formula for the Cesàro operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let
$C$ be the Cesàro operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$(Cx)_n = \bigl(\sum_{k=0}^{n} x_k\bigr)/(n + 1)$.

articles.title: Second coordinate of the Cesàro operator at the first basis vector
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $C$ be the Cesàro operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$,
and let $e_0 = (1, 0, 0, \dots)$ be the first standard basis vector. With coordinates indexed
from $0$, $(C e_0)_1 = 1/2$.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator agrees with the Cesàro linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$
or $\mathbb{C}$. For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the Cesàro operator, as a
continuous linear map on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, takes the same value at $x$ as the
Cesàro linear map, the same averaging map considered only as a linear map.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator is injective
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The
Cesàro operator $C$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by
$(Cx)_n = (x_0 + \dots + x_n)/(n + 1)$, is injective.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator on standard basis vectors
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $C$ be the Cesàro operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, and for
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $e_n$ be the standard basis vector with $1$ in coordinate $n$ and $0$
elsewhere. For all $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$, $(C e_n)_k = 1/(k + 1)$ if $n \le k$, and
$(C e_n)_k = 0$ if $k < n$.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator on a test vector, past its support
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $C$ be the Cesàro operator on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For $N \in \mathbb{N}$ let $t_N$ be the test vector whose
first $N$ coordinates equal $(\sqrt{N})^{-1}$ and whose other coordinates are $0$. For all
$N, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $N \le n$, $(C t_N)_n = N (\sqrt{N})^{-1}/(n + 1)$, where
$(\sqrt{0})^{-1}$ is read as $0$.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator on a test vector, within its support
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $C$ be the Cesàro operator on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For $N \in \mathbb{N}$ let $t_N$ be the test vector whose
first $N$ coordinates equal $1/\sqrt{N}$ and whose other coordinates are $0$. For all
$n, N \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n < N$, $(C t_N)_n = 1/\sqrt{N}$.

articles.title: Cesàro operator on square-summable sequences
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. The Cesàro operator $C$ is the continuous linear map from
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ to itself that sends a sequence $x$ to its sequence of
averages, $(Cx)_n = (x_0 + x_1 + \dots + x_n)/(n + 1)$. It is obtained from the Cesàro linear
map with the bound $\|Cx\| \le 2 \|x\|$.

articles.title: The Cesàro denominator $n + 1$ is nonzero
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
For every natural number $n$, the element $n + 1$ of $\mathbb{K}$ is nonzero.

articles.title: Coordinates of the first standard basis vector of $\ell^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $e_0 \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ be the first standard
basis vector. For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $e_0(n) = 1$ if $n = 0$ and $e_0(n) = 0$ otherwise.

articles.title: The first standard basis vector of $\ell^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. The vector $e_0 \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ is the sequence with $e_0(0) = 1$
and $e_0(n) = 0$ for every $n \ge 1$.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator as a linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The Cesàro operator is the $\mathbb{K}$-linear map $C$ from $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ to
itself that sends a sequence $x$ to its sequence of Cesàro means,
$(Cx)(n) = \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} x(k)$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

That $Cx$ is again square-summable follows from Hardy's inequality.

articles.title: Cesàro means of a sequence
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For a
sequence $x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th Cesàro mean of $x$ is
the average of its first $n + 1$ terms, $\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} x(k)$.

articles.title: Coordinates of the alternating harmonic sequence in $\ell^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $y$ be the alternating harmonic sequence, viewed as an
element of $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$y(n) = (-1)^n / (n + 1)$.

articles.title: The alternating harmonic sequence in $\ell^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. The sequence $y$ with $y(n) = (-1)^n / (n + 1)$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ is
square-summable, and it is regarded as an element of $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: One step of inverting the Cesàro operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, and let $C$ be the Cesàro operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$x(n+1) = (n+2)\,(Cx)(n+1) - (n+1)\,(Cx)(n)$.

articles.title: The sequence space $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$
articles.statement:
For $\mathbb{K}$ equal to $\mathbb{R}$
or $\mathbb{C}$, this is the space $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of square-summable sequences
$x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$, with the norm $\|x\| = \left(\sum_{n} |x(n)|^2\right)^{1/2}$.

articles.title: Partial sums from Cesàro means
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let
$C$ be the Cesàro operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$\sum_{k=0}^{n} x(k) = (n+1)\,(Cx)(n)$.

articles.title: Coordinates of the Cesàro test vectors
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$
and let $N$ and $j$ be natural numbers. The $j$-th coordinate of the Cesàro test vector
$t_N \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ is $1/\sqrt{N}$ if $j < N$, and $0$ if $j \ge N$.

articles.title: Cesàro test vectors
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $e_i$ be the
$i$-th standard basis vector of $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For a natural number $N$, the
test vector $t_N = \sum_{i < N} \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} e_i$ has coordinate $1/\sqrt{N}$ at each
$j < N$ and $0$ at each $j \ge N$; in particular $t_0 = 0$.

These vectors are used to show that the Cesàro operator is not compact.

articles.title: Lower bound for the Cesàro operator on the test vectors
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$
or $\mathbb{C}$, let $C$ be the Cesàro operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and let $t_N$
be the $N$-th Cesàro test vector. For every natural number $N \ge 1$, $\|C t_N\|^2 \ge 5/4$.

The first $N$ coordinates of $C t_N$ contribute $1$ to $\|C t_N\|^2$, and the next $N$
contribute at least $1/4$.

articles.title: Cesàro means preserve square-summability
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
If $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, then the sequence of its Cesàro means
$n \mapsto \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} x_k$ also lies in $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator has norm at most 2
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The Cesàro operator $C$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by
$(Cx)_n = \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} x_k$, has operator norm $\|C\| \le 2$.

articles.title: Norm of the Cesàro denominator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For every
natural number $n$, the element $n + 1$ of $\mathbb{K}$ (the denominator of the $n$-th Cesàro
mean) has norm equal to the real number $n + 1$.

articles.title: The first basis vector is a unit vector
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The first standard basis vector $e_0 = (1, 0, 0, \dots)$ of $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$
has norm $\|e_0\| = 1$.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator is bounded by 2
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and
let $C$ be the Cesàro operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, viewed as a linear map, given
by $(Cx)_n = \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} x_k$. For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$,
$\|Cx\| \le 2 \|x\|$.

articles.title: A Cesàro mean is bounded by the mean of the norms
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be any sequence and let $n$ be a natural
number. Then $\|\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} x_k\| \le \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} \|x_k\|$.

articles.title: Norm of the Cesàro test-vector coefficient
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. For every natural number $N$, the norm of $(\sqrt{N})^{-1}$, computed in
$\mathbb{K}$, equals the real number $(\sqrt{N})^{-1}$; for $N = 0$ both sides are $0$, with the
convention $0^{-1} = 0$.

articles.title: The Cesàro test vectors are unit vectors
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. For every natural number $N \ge 1$, the test vector
$t_N \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, equal to $1/\sqrt{N}$ at the coordinates
$0, \dots, N - 1$ and to $0$ elsewhere, has norm $\|t_N\| = 1$.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator is not compact
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The
Cesàro operator $C$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by
$(Cx)_n = (x_0 + x_1 + \dots + x_n)/(n + 1)$, is not a compact operator.

For $N \ge 1$ let $t_N$ be the unit vector equal to $1/\sqrt{N}$ at the coordinates
$0, \dots, N - 1$ and to $0$ elsewhere. Then $\|C t_N\|^2 \ge 5/4$ for every $N$, while each
coordinate of $C t_N$ tends to $0$ as $N \to \infty$, so no subsequence of $(C t_N)$ converges
in norm.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator is not self-adjoint
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The Cesàro operator $C$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by
$(Cx)_n = (x_0 + x_1 + \dots + x_n)/(n + 1)$, is not self-adjoint.

Indeed, its adjoint fixes the first basis vector $e_0$, while $(C e_0)_1 = 1/2$.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator is not surjective
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The sequence $y \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ with $y_n = (-1)^n/(n + 1)$ is not in the
range of the Cesàro operator $C$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by
$(Cx)_n = (x_0 + x_1 + \dots + x_n)/(n + 1)$. In particular $C$ is not surjective.

A preimage $x$ would have to satisfy $x_{n+1} = -2(-1)^n$ for all $n$, so it would not be
square-summable.

articles.title: The Cesàro operator has norm at least one
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The Cesàro operator $C$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by
$(Cx)_n = (x_0 + x_1 + \dots + x_n)/(n + 1)$, has operator norm $\|C\| \ge 1$.

This is seen on the first basis vector $e_0$, for which $\|e_0\| = 1$ and $(C e_0)_0 = 1$.

articles.title: Cesàro means of square-summable sequences are square-summable
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the Cesàro means
$\sigma_n = (x_0 + x_1 + \dots + x_n)/(n + 1)$ satisfy: the series $\sum_n |\sigma_n|^2$ converges.

This follows from Hardy's inequality at $p = 2$.

articles.title: The Cesàro images of the test vectors tend to zero coordinatewise
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $C$ be the Cesàro operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$,
$(Cx)_n = (x_0 + x_1 + \dots + x_n)/(n + 1)$, and for $N \ge 1$ let $t_N$ be the vector equal to
$1/\sqrt{N}$ at the coordinates $0, \dots, N - 1$ and to $0$ elsewhere. Then for every fixed
coordinate $n$, $(C t_{N+1})_n \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$.

articles.title: Adjoint of a diagonal operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let
$\iota$ be a type and let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded sequence. The adjoint of the
diagonal operator $D_a$ on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ with coefficients $a$ is the diagonal
operator with the conjugate coefficients $i \mapsto \overline{a_i}$.

articles.title: Coordinates of a diagonal operator on ℓ²
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $\iota$ be a type, let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded sequence and let
$D_a$ be the diagonal operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ with coefficients $a$. For every
$x \in \ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ and every $i \in \iota$, the $i$-th coordinate of $D_a x$ is
$a_i x_i$.

articles.title: Composition of diagonal operators
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let
$\iota$ be a type, and for a bounded sequence $c : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ let $D_c$ be the diagonal
operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ with coefficients $c$. For bounded sequences
$a, b : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$, we have $D_b \circ D_a = D_{ba}$, where $ba$ is the pointwise
product $i \mapsto b_i a_i$.

articles.title: The diagonal operator with all coefficients one is the identity
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $\iota$ be a type. The diagonal operator on
$\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ whose coefficients all equal $1$ is the identity operator.

articles.title: Diagonal operators on standard basis vectors
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $\iota$ be a type, let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded sequence and let
$D_a$ be the diagonal operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ with coefficients $a$. For
$i \in \iota$ let $e_i \in \ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ be the sequence equal to $1$ at $i$ and $0$
elsewhere. Then for every $i \in \iota$ and every $c \in \mathbb{K}$ we have
$D_a(c\,e_i) = a_i \, (c\,e_i)$.

articles.title: Difference of diagonal operators
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let
$\iota$ be a type, and for a bounded sequence $c : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ let $D_c$ be the diagonal
operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ with coefficients $c$. For bounded sequences
$a, b : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$, we have $D_a - D_b = D_{a - b}$, where $a - b$ is the sequence
$i \mapsto a_i - b_i$.

articles.title: Diagonal operator on ℓ²
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $\iota$ be
a type and let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded sequence, that is, $\|a_i\| \le C$ for some
real $C$ and all $i \in \iota$. The diagonal operator $D_a$ with coefficients $a$ is the bounded
linear operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ that sends $x$ to the sequence
$(a_i x_i)_{i \in \iota}$.

It is defined as the Hilbert-basis diagonal operator for the standard Hilbert basis of
$\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$, using the bound $\max(C, 0)$ for a chosen bound $C$, so that empty
index types also admit a nonnegative bound.

articles.title: Coordinates of the diagonal linear map on ℓ²
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $\iota$ be a type and let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded sequence. For
every $x \in \ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ and every $i \in \iota$, the diagonal operator with
coefficients $a$, regarded as a linear map, sends $x$ to a sequence whose $i$-th coordinate is
$a_i x_i$.

articles.title: Diagonal operator on ℓ² as a linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $\iota$ be a type and let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded sequence. This
is the diagonal operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ with coefficients $a$, regarded as a
$\mathbb{K}$-linear map $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K}) \to \ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ by forgetting
its continuity.

articles.title: Action of a diagonal operator on the basis
articles.statement:
Let $(b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a Hilbert
basis of an inner product space $H$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$), let
$a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ satisfy $|a_i| \le C$ for all $i$, and let $D$ be the diagonal
operator with coefficients $a$. Then $D b_j = a_j b_j$ for every $j \in \iota$.

articles.title: Series formula for a diagonal operator
articles.statement:
Let $(b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a Hilbert basis of an
inner product space $H$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$), with inner product
$\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ conjugate-linear in the first argument, and let
$a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ satisfy $|a_i| \le C$ for all $i$. The diagonal operator $D$ with
coefficients $a$ satisfies, for every $x \in H$,

$$
D x = \sum_{i \in \iota} a_i \langle b_i, x \rangle \, b_i,
$$

where the sum is the unconditional sum over $\iota$ (taken to be $0$ if the family is not
summable).

articles.title: Square of a diagonal operator
articles.statement:
Let $(b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a Hilbert basis of an
inner product space $H$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$), and let
$a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ satisfy $|a_i| \le C$ for all $i$. Let $D_a$ be the diagonal
operator with coefficients $a$, and let $D_{a^2}$ be the diagonal operator with coefficients
$a_i^2$, which satisfy $|a_i^2| \le C^2$. Then $D_a(D_a x) = D_{a^2} x$ for every
$x \in H$.

articles.title: Bounded diagonal operator on a Hilbert basis
articles.statement:
The bounded diagonal continuous linear map with coefficients `a` in the
Hilbert basis `b`. Its uniform coefficient bound is part of the constructor.

articles.title: Compact diagonal operators on ℓ²
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let
$\iota$ be a type and let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded sequence. The diagonal operator
on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ with coefficients $a$ is compact if and only if $a$ tends to $0$
along the cofinite filter on $\iota$, that is, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ only finitely many
$i \in \iota$ satisfy $\|a_i\| \ge \varepsilon$.

articles.title: Self-adjoint diagonal operators on $\ell^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be bounded, and let $D_a$ be the diagonal operator
$x \mapsto (a_i x_i)_{i \in \iota}$ on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$. Then $D_a$ is self-adjoint if
and only if $\overline{a_i} = a_i$, that is, $a_i$ is real, for every $i \in \iota$.

articles.title: Invertibility of a shifted diagonal operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded family of coefficients, let $D_a$ be the
diagonal operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ given by $(D_a x)_i = a_i x_i$, and let $I$ be
the identity operator. If $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ does not lie in the closure of
$\{a_i : i \in \iota\}$, then $\mu I - D_a$ is invertible in the algebra of bounded operators on
$\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: Scalar multiplication on $\ell^2$ is pointwise
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. For every $c \in \mathbb{K}$, every $x \in \ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ and every
$i \in \iota$, the $i$-th coordinate of $c x$ is $(c x)_i = c \, x_i$.

articles.title: Bounded multipliers preserve $\ell^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If
$a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ is bounded, that is, $|a_i| \le C$ for some real $C$ and all $i$, then
for every $x \in \ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ the sequence $(a_i x_i)_{i \in \iota}$ lies in
