$\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$, that is, the family $(|a_i x_i|^2)_{i \in \iota}$ is summable.

articles.title: Operator norm bound for diagonal operators
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be bounded, and let $D_a$ be the diagonal operator
$x \mapsto (a_i x_i)_{i \in \iota}$ on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$. If $C \ge 0$ and $|a_i| \le C$
for every $i \in \iota$, then the operator norm satisfies $\|D_a\| \le C$.

articles.title: Operator norm of a diagonal operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let
$a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be bounded, and let $D_a$ be the diagonal operator
$x \mapsto (a_i x_i)_{i \in \iota}$ on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$. Then the operator norm of $D_a$
is $\|D_a\| = \sup_{i \in \iota} |a_i|$, where the supremum is taken to be $0$ when $\iota$ is
empty.

articles.title: Pointwise bound for diagonal operators
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$,
let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be bounded, and let $D_a$ be the diagonal operator
$x \mapsto (a_i x_i)_{i \in \iota}$ on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$, viewed as a linear map. If
$C \ge 0$ and $|a_i| \le C$ for every $i \in \iota$, then $\|D_a x\| \le C \|x\|$ for every
$x \in \ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: Points off the closure of the coefficients are not in the spectrum
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded family of coefficients,
and let $D_a$ be the diagonal operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ given by
$(D_a x)_i = a_i x_i$. If $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ does not lie in the closure of
$\{a_i : i \in \iota\}$, then $\mu$ is not in the spectrum of $D_a$ over $\mathbb{K}$, that is,
$\mu I - D_a$ is invertible as a bounded operator, where $I$ is the identity operator.

articles.title: Every coefficient of a diagonal operator lies in its spectrum
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded family of coefficients,
and let $D_a$ be the diagonal operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ given by
$(D_a x)_i = a_i x_i$. Then every $a_j$ with $j \in \iota$ lies in the spectrum of $D_a$ over
$\mathbb{K}$, the set of $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ for which $\mu I - D_a$ is not invertible as a
bounded operator, where $I$ is the identity operator.

For each $j \in \iota$, the $j$-th coordinate vector lies in the kernel of $a_j I - D_a$.

articles.title: Coordinates of a diagonal operator
articles.statement:
Let $(b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a Hilbert basis of an inner
product space $H$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$), with inner product
$\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ conjugate-linear in the first argument, let
$a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ satisfy $|a_i| \le C$ for all $i$, and let $D$ be the diagonal operator
with coefficients $a$. For every $x \in H$ and $i \in \iota$, the $i$-th coordinate of $D x$ in
$\ell^2(\iota)$ with respect to the basis $(b_i)$ is $a_i \langle b_i, x \rangle$.

articles.title: Rank-one term of the finite-support decomposition on $\ell^2$
articles.statement: A rank-one term of the finite-support decomposition, evaluated pointwise.

articles.title: Shifting a diagonal operator by a scalar
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded family of coefficients, let $D_a$ be the
diagonal operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ given by $(D_a x)_i = a_i x_i$, and let $I$ be
the identity operator. For every $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$, $\mu I - D_a = D_{\mu - a}$, the diagonal
operator with coefficients $\mu - a_i$.

articles.title: Spectrum of a diagonal operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let
$a : \iota \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded family of coefficients, and let $D_a$ be the diagonal
operator on $\ell^2(\iota, \mathbb{K})$ given by $(D_a x)_i = a_i x_i$. The spectrum of $D_a$ over
$\mathbb{K}$, the set of $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ for which $\mu I - D_a$ is not invertible as a
bounded operator ($I$ the identity operator), is the closure of $\{a_i : i \in \iota\}$.

articles.title: An $L^p$ bound for Hilbert's integral operator
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a real number with
$p > 1$ and let $T$ be the operator on functions $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by

$$Tg(x) = \int_0^\infty \frac{g(y)}{x+y}\,dy \qquad (x \in \mathbb{R}).$$

Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[0,\infty)$, compactly supported and zero
outside $[0,\infty)$, and put

$$C_p = \int_0^\infty \frac{dx}{x^{1/p}(1+x)}.$$

Then

$$\|Tf\|_{L^p([0,\infty))} \le C_p \, \|f\|_{L^p([0,\infty))},$$

where both norms are taken in $[0,\infty]$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; Integral, integro-differential, and pseudodifferential operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_29`.

articles.title: Integral operators with an $L^p$ kernel map $L^q$ to $L^p$
articles.statement:
Let $1 < p < \infty$ and let
$q \ge 1$ be the dual exponent, $p^{-1} + q^{-1} = 1$. Let $K : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ lie
in $L^p((0,1)^2)$, where $L^p((0,1)^2)$, $L^p(0,1)$ and $L^q(0,1)$ are spaces of real functions
for Lebesgue measure. Then for every $f \in L^q(0,1)$ the function $y \mapsto K(x,y)f(y)$ is
integrable on $(0,1)$ for almost every $x \in (0,1)$, and there is a bounded linear operator
$A : L^q(0,1) \to L^p(0,1)$ such that for every $f \in L^q(0,1)$,

$$(Af)(x) = \int_0^1 K(x,y) f(y)\,dy \quad \text{for almost every } x \in (0,1).$$

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; Integral, integro-differential, and pseudodifferential operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_87`.

articles.title: Joint continuity of the kernel integrand
articles.statement:
Let $\pi(t) = \max(0, \min(1, t))$ clamp a
real number $t$ to $[0, 1]$. For every continuous kernel $k$ on $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ and every
bounded continuous function $f$ on $[0, 1]$, the kernel integrand
$(x, t) \mapsto k(x, \pi(t)) \, f(\pi(t))$ is jointly continuous on $[0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Separable kernels give finite-rank integral operators
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a finite set of indices
and, for $i \in s$, let $\varphi_i$ and $\psi_i$ be bounded continuous functions on $[0, 1]$. If a
continuous kernel $k$ on $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ satisfies
$k(x, y) = \sum_{i \in s} \varphi_i(x) \psi_i(y)$ for all $x, y \in [0, 1]$, then the range of the
integral operator $K$ on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$, given by
$(Kf)(x) = \int_0^1 k(x, t) f(t) \, dt$, is a finite-dimensional real vector space.

The proof shows that the range lies in the span of the functions $\varphi_i$, $i \in s$.

articles.title: Integral operators with continuous kernels are compact
articles.statement:
For every continuous kernel $k$ on
$[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, the integral operator $K$ on the space of bounded continuous real functions
on $[0, 1]$, given by $(Kf)(x) = \int_0^1 k(x, t) f(t) \, dt$, is a compact operator.

The proof uses Arzelà–Ascoli: the image of the unit ball is equicontinuous by uniform continuity
of the kernel.

articles.title: The clamped extension agrees with the function on $(0, 1)$
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a bounded continuous
function on $[0, 1]$ and let $\tilde f(s) = f(\max(0, \min(1, s)))$ for real $s$ be its clamped
extension. Then $\tilde f(t) = f(t)$ for every $t \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: Continuity of the clamped extension
articles.statement:
For every bounded continuous function $f$ on
$[0, 1]$, the clamped extension $t \mapsto f(\max(0, \min(1, t)))$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Clamped extension
articles.statement:
For a bounded continuous function $f$ on $[0, 1]$, its clamped extension
is the function $\tilde f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by
$\tilde f(t) = f(\max(0, \min(1, t)))$. Thus $\tilde f(t) = f(0)$ for $t < 0$,
$\tilde f(t) = f(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$, and $\tilde f(t) = f(1)$ for $t > 1$.

articles.title: Continuity of the kernel integrand in $t$
articles.statement:
Let $\pi(t) = \max(0, \min(1, t))$ clamp a real
number $t$ to $[0, 1]$. For every continuous kernel $k$ on $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, every bounded
continuous function $f$ on $[0, 1]$ and every $x \in [0, 1]$, the function
$t \mapsto k(x, \pi(t)) \, f(\pi(t))$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Kernel integrand
articles.statement:
Let $\pi(t) = \max(0, \min(1, t))$ clamp a real number $t$ to $[0, 1]$.
For a continuous kernel $k$ on $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, a bounded continuous function $f$ on
$[0, 1]$ and a point $x \in [0, 1]$, the kernel integrand is the function
$\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $t \mapsto k(x, \pi(t)) \, f(\pi(t))$.

articles.title: Sup-norm bound for the integral operator with continuous kernel
articles.statement:
Write $\|\cdot\|$ for the
sup norm. For every continuous kernel $k$ on $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ and every bounded continuous
function $f$ on $[0, 1]$, the function $Kf$ given by $(Kf)(x) = \int_0^1 k(x, t) f(t) \, dt$
satisfies $\|Kf\| \le \|k\| \, \|f\|$.

articles.title: The integral operator with continuous kernel, as a linear map
articles.statement:
For a continuous kernel $k$
on $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, this is the $\mathbb{R}$-linear map $K$ from the space of bounded
continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$ to itself given by $(Kf)(x) = \int_0^1 k(x, t) f(t) \, dt$
for $x \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: The integral operator is additive in the kernel
articles.statement:
For a continuous kernel $k$ on
$[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, write $T_k$ for the integral operator with kernel $k$ on
$C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$. For all continuous kernels $k_1$ and $k_2$, the operator with the
pointwise sum kernel is the sum of the operators: $T_{k_1 + k_2} = T_{k_1} + T_{k_2}$.

articles.title: Evaluation formula for the integral operator
articles.statement:
Let $\pi(t) = \max(0, \min(1, t))$ be the
projection of $\mathbb{R}$ onto $[0, 1]$. For a continuous kernel $k$ on $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$,
write $T_k$ for the integral operator with kernel $k$ on $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$. For every
$f \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ and every $x \in [0, 1]$,

$$(T_k f)(x) = \int_0^1 k(x, \pi(t))\, f(\pi(t))\, dt,$$

the integral over $[0, 1]$ of the kernel integrand. Since $\pi(t) = t$ for $t \in [0, 1]$, this
is $\int_0^1 k(x, t)\, f(t)\, dt$.

articles.title: The integral operator is homogeneous in the kernel
articles.statement:
For a continuous kernel $k$ on
$[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, write $T_k$ for the integral operator with kernel $k$ on
$C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$. For every real number $c$ and every continuous kernel $k$,
$T_{c k} = c\, T_k$.

articles.title: The zero kernel gives the zero operator
articles.statement:
The integral operator on
$C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ whose kernel is the zero function on $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ is the
zero operator.

articles.title: Integral operator with a continuous kernel
articles.statement:
For a continuous kernel $k$ on
$[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, the integral operator $T_k$ with kernel $k$ is the continuous linear
operator on $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ given, for $f \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ and $x \in [0, 1]$, by
$(T_k f)(x) = \int_0^1 k(x, t)\, f(t)\, dt$.

articles.title: Continuous functions on the unit interval
articles.statement:
$C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ denotes the space of
bounded continuous functions $[0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$, with the supremum norm
$\|f\| = \sup_{x \in [0, 1]} |f(x)|$.

articles.title: Continuous kernels on the unit square
articles.statement:
A continuous kernel is a bounded continuous
function $k : [0, 1] \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$. These kernels form a normed space under the
supremum norm $\|k\| = \sup_{x, y \in [0, 1]} |k(x, y)|$.

articles.title: Continuity of the kernel value
articles.statement:
For every continuous kernel $k$ on
$[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ and every $f \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$, the kernel value of $k$ and
$f$, the function $x \mapsto \int_0^1 k(x, t)\, f(t)\, dt$ on $[0, 1]$, is continuous.

articles.title: Kernel value
articles.statement:
Let $\pi(t) = \max(0, \min(1, t))$ be the projection of $\mathbb{R}$ onto
$[0, 1]$. For a continuous kernel $k$ on $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, a function
$f \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ and a point $x \in [0, 1]$, the kernel value is the real number

$$\int_0^1 k(x, \pi(t))\, f(\pi(t))\, dt.$$

Since $\pi(t) = t$ for $t \in [0, 1]$, it equals $\int_0^1 k(x, t)\, f(t)\, dt$, the value at
$x$ of the integral operator with kernel $k$ applied to $f$.

articles.title: The clamped extension is bounded by the supremum norm
articles.statement:
Let
$\pi(t) = \max(0, \min(1, t))$ be the projection of $\mathbb{R}$ onto $[0, 1]$. For every
$f \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ and every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, the clamped extension
$f \circ \pi$ of $f$ satisfies $|f(\pi(t))| \le \|f\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the supremum norm.

articles.title: Difference bound for the values of a kernel operator
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a continuous kernel on
$[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, let $K$ be the integral operator with kernel $k$ on $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$,
let $f \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$, and let $x, x' \in [0, 1]$ and $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$. If
$|k(x, y) - k(x', y)| \le \delta$ for every $y \in [0, 1]$, then
$|(Kf)(x) - (Kf)(x')| \le \delta \, \|f\|_\infty$.

articles.title: Norm bound for a kernel integral operator
articles.statement:
For every continuous kernel $k$ on
$[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, the integral operator $K$ with kernel $k$ on $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ has
operator norm $\|K\| \le \|k\|_\infty$.

articles.title: Pointwise bound for a kernel integral
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a continuous kernel on
$[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ and let $f \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$. For every $x \in [0, 1]$, the integral
$\int_0^1 k(x, t) \, f(t) \, dt$ has absolute value at most $\|k\|_\infty \, \|f\|_\infty$.

articles.title: The Laplace transform is bounded on $L^p((0,\infty))$ exactly when $p = 2$
articles.statement:
For a real
function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ let

$$Lf(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-xs} f(x)\,dx \qquad (s \in \mathbb{R}).$$

Let $p \in [1,\infty]$. Then $p = 2$ if and only if there is a constant $C$ with $0 < C < \infty$
such that every real function $f \in L^p([0,\infty))$ satisfies $Lf \in L^p([0,\infty))$ and
$\|Lf\|_{L^p([0,\infty))} \le C\,\|f\|_{L^p([0,\infty))}$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; Integral, integro-differential, and pseudodifferential operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_31`.

articles.title: Pointwise bound by the essential supremum norm
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable
space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$, that is,
$\mu$-almost everywhere strongly measurable and essentially bounded. Then
$|\varphi(x)| \le \|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}$ for $\mu$-almost every $x \in \alpha$.

articles.title: Shifting a multiplication operator by a scalar
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable
space $\alpha$, let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$, let
$z \in \mathbb{C}$, and suppose the function $x \mapsto z - \varphi(x)$ is also in
$L^\infty(\mu)$. For $\psi \in L^\infty(\mu)$ write $M_\psi$ for the multiplication operator
$f \mapsto \psi f$ on $L^2(\mu)$. Then $z I - M_\varphi = M_{z - \varphi}$, where $I$ is the
identity operator on $L^2(\mu)$.

articles.title: Multiplication by $x$ on $L^2((1,2))$ is bounded, bijective and self-adjoint
articles.statement:
Let
$L^2([1,2])$ be the real Hilbert space of square-integrable real functions for Lebesgue measure
on $[1,2]$, with inner product $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_1^2 f(x)g(x)\,dx$. Let
$T : L^2([1,2]) \to L^2([1,2])$ be a linear map such that for every $f$, $(Tf)(x) = x f(x)$ for
almost every $x \in [1,2]$. Then $T$ is continuous and bijective, and $T = T^*$, where $T^*$ is
the Hilbert space adjoint of $T$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_26`.

articles.title: The essential range is invariant under almost-everywhere equality
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi, \psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$. If
$\varphi = \psi$ $\mu$-almost everywhere, then $\varphi$ and $\psi$ have the same essential range
with respect to $\mu$.

articles.title: Essential range of a constant function
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space
$\alpha$ with $\mu(\alpha) \neq 0$, and let $c \in \mathbb{C}$. Then the essential range of the
constant function $x \mapsto c$ with respect to $\mu$ is $\{c\}$.

articles.title: Essential range for counting measure on a finite type
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite type
with a measurable structure in which singletons are measurable, and let
$\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$. Then the essential range of $\varphi$ with respect to counting
measure on $\alpha$ is the range $\varphi(\alpha)$.

articles.title: Essential range
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let
$\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$. The essential range of $\varphi$ with respect to $\mu$ is the
set of $z \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $\mu(\{x \in \alpha : |\varphi(x) - z| < \varepsilon\}) > 0$
for every $\varepsilon > 0$.

articles.title: Multiplication by $t$ is bounded on $L^2((0,1))$
articles.statement:
Let $L^2([0,1])$ be the space of real
square-integrable functions for Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$. There is a bounded linear operator
$T : L^2([0,1]) \to L^2([0,1])$ such that for every $f \in L^2([0,1])$, $(Tf)(t) = t f(t)$ for
almost every $t \in [0,1]$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_31`.

articles.title: Measurable representatives of essentially bounded functions
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a
measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$, that
is, $\mu$-almost everywhere strongly measurable and essentially bounded. Then there is a measurable
$\psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ such that $\varphi = \psi$ $\mu$-almost everywhere and $\psi$ is in
$L^\infty(\mu)$.

In particular $\varphi$ and $\psi$ define the same multiplication operator on $L^2(\mu)$.

articles.title: Normalized indicator of a set of finite positive measure
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a
measurable space $\alpha$ and let $t \subseteq \alpha$ be a measurable set with
$0 < \mu(t) < \infty$. Then there is $u \in L^2(\mu)$ (complex valued) with $\|u\| = 1$ such that
$u(x) = \mu(t)^{-1/2}$ for $\mu$-almost every $x \in t$ and $u(x) = 0$ for $\mu$-almost every
$x \notin t$.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a multiplication operator on $L^2$, measurable multiplier
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
$\sigma$-finite measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be
measurable and in $L^\infty(\mu)$, and let $M_\varphi$ be the multiplication operator
$f \mapsto \varphi f$ on $L^2(\mu)$. Then $z \in \mathbb{C}$ is an eigenvalue of $M_\varphi$ if and
only if $\mu(\{x \in \alpha : \varphi(x) = z\}) > 0$.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a multiplication operator on $L^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure
on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$, and let
$M_\varphi$ be the multiplication operator $f \mapsto \varphi f$ on $L^2(\mu)$. Then
$z \in \mathbb{C}$ is an eigenvalue of $M_\varphi$ if and only if
$\mu(\{x \in \alpha : \varphi(x) = z\}) > 0$.

articles.title: The space $L^2((1,2))$
articles.statement:
$L^2([1,2])$ is the space of real-valued functions on
$\mathbb{R}$ that are square-integrable for Lebesgue measure restricted to $[1,2]$, taken modulo
equality almost everywhere on $[1,2]$.

articles.title: Lower bound for the norm of a multiplication operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a
measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be an essentially
bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable function, and let $M_\varphi$ be the
multiplication operator $f \mapsto \varphi f$ on $L^2(\mu)$. If $C \ge 0$ is a real number and
$f \in L^2(\mu)$ satisfies $\|f\| = 1$ and $C\,|f(x)| \le |\varphi(x)|\,|f(x)|$ for
$\mu$-almost every $x$, then $C \le \|M_\varphi\|$.

articles.title: Multiplication operators with almost everywhere equal multipliers coincide
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be
a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi, \psi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be
essentially bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable functions. If $\varphi = \psi$
$\mu$-almost everywhere, then the multiplication operators $M_\varphi$ and $M_\psi$ on
$L^2(\mu)$ are equal.

articles.title: Multiplication by a constant function on $L^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable
space $\alpha$ and let $c \in \mathbb{C}$. The multiplication operator on $L^2(\mu)$ by the
constant function $x \mapsto c$ sends every $f \in L^2(\mu)$ to the scalar multiple $c f$.

articles.title: Product of multiplication operators
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space
$\alpha$ and, for an essentially bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable function
$\chi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$, let $M_\chi$ be the multiplication operator
$f \mapsto \chi f$ on $L^2(\mu)$. Let $\varphi, \psi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be essentially
bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable functions such that the pointwise product
$\varphi\psi \colon x \mapsto \varphi(x)\psi(x)$ is also essentially bounded and almost
everywhere strongly measurable. Then $M_{\varphi\psi} = M_\varphi M_\psi$, where the right side
is the composition of operators.

articles.title: Multiplication by one is the identity
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space
$\alpha$. The multiplication operator on $L^2(\mu)$ by the constant function $1$ is the
identity operator.

articles.title: Multiplication operator on $L^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$
and let $\varphi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be an essentially bounded, almost everywhere
strongly measurable function. The multiplication operator $M_\varphi$ is the continuous
$\mathbb{C}$-linear operator on $L^2(\mu)$ that sends $f$ to the class of the pointwise product
$x \mapsto \varphi(x) f(x)$.

articles.title: Constant functions are essentially bounded
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space
$\alpha$ and let $c \in \mathbb{C}$. The constant function $x \mapsto c$ belongs to
$\mathcal{L}^\infty(\mu)$: it is almost everywhere strongly measurable and essentially
bounded.

articles.title: An essentially bounded multiple of an $L^2$ function is in $L^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure
on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be an essentially
bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable function, and let $f \in L^2(\mu)$. Then the
pointwise product $x \mapsto \varphi(x) f(x)$, formed with a representative of $f$, belongs
to $\mathcal{L}^2(\mu)$: it is almost everywhere strongly measurable and square integrable.

articles.title: Almost everywhere bound for a multiplication operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a
measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be an essentially
bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable function, and let $M_\varphi$ be the
multiplication operator on $L^2(\mu)$. If $C$ is a real number with $|\varphi(x)| \le C$ for
$\mu$-almost every $x$, then $\|M_\varphi f\| \le C \|f\|$ for every $f \in L^2(\mu)$.

articles.title: Bound for a multiplication operator on the support of a vector
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure
on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $\varphi \colon \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be an essentially
bounded, almost everywhere strongly measurable function, and let $M_\varphi$ be the
multiplication operator on $L^2(\mu)$. If $C$ is a real number and $f \in L^2(\mu)$ is such
that, for $\mu$-almost every $x$, either $|\varphi(x)| \le C$ or $f(x) = 0$, then
$\|M_\varphi f\| \le C \|f\|$.

articles.title: Norm bound for multiplication operators on L²
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable
space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$, with essential
supremum norm $\|\varphi\|_\infty$. Then the multiplication operator $M_\varphi$ on the complex
space $L^2(\mu)$ has operator norm $\|M_\varphi\| \le \|\varphi\|_\infty$.

articles.title: Norm of an L² multiplication operator with measurable multiplier
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
$\sigma$-finite measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$
be a measurable function in $L^\infty(\mu)$, with essential supremum norm $\|\varphi\|_\infty$.
Then the multiplication operator $M_\varphi$ on the complex space $L^2(\mu)$ has operator norm
$\|M_\varphi\| = \|\varphi\|_\infty$.

articles.title: Norm of a multiplication operator on L²
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure on a
measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$, with
essential supremum norm $\|\varphi\|_\infty$. Then the multiplication operator $M_\varphi$ on the
complex space $L^2(\mu)$ has operator norm $\|M_\varphi\| = \|\varphi\|_\infty$.

articles.title: Points outside the essential range
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$,
let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ and let $z \in \mathbb{C}$. Then $z$ is not in the essential
range of $\varphi$ with respect to $\mu$ if and only if there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that the
preimage under $\varphi$ of the open ball
$B(z, \varepsilon) = \{w \in \mathbb{C} : |w - z| < \varepsilon\}$ has $\mu$-measure zero.

articles.title: Spectrum of an L² multiplication operator with measurable multiplier
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
$\sigma$-finite measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$
be a measurable function in $L^\infty(\mu)$. Then the spectrum of the multiplication operator
$M_\varphi$, as an element of the complex algebra of bounded operators on $L^2(\mu)$, equals the
essential range of $\varphi$ with respect to $\mu$.

articles.title: Spectrum of a multiplication operator on L²
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure on a
measurable space $\alpha$ and let $\varphi : \alpha \to \mathbb{C}$ be in $L^\infty(\mu)$. Then the
spectrum of the multiplication operator $M_\varphi$, as an element of the complex algebra of
bounded operators on $L^2(\mu)$, equals the essential range of $\varphi$ with respect to $\mu$.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a multiplication operator
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space, let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $\varphi \in C(X, \mathbb{K})$ and let
$\mu \in \mathbb{K}$. Then $\mu$ is an eigenvalue of the multiplication operator
$M_\varphi f = \varphi f$ on $C(X, \mathbb{K})$ if and only if the level set
$\varphi^{-1}(\{\mu\})$ has nonempty interior.

articles.title: Invertibility of a multiplication operator
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a compact topological space, let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $\varphi \in C(X, \mathbb{K})$. The
multiplication operator $M_\varphi f = \varphi f$ is invertible in the algebra of bounded linear
operators on $C(X, \mathbb{K})$ if and only if $\varphi(x) \neq 0$ for every $x \in X$.

articles.title: Multiplication by a constant on continuous functions
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a compact topological
space, let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$. The
multiplication operator on $C(X, \mathbb{K})$ by the constant function with value $\mu$ equals
$\mu$ times the identity operator.

articles.title: The multiplication operator on continuous functions
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a compact topological
space, let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $C(X, \mathbb{K})$ be the Banach
algebra of continuous functions $X \to \mathbb{K}$ with the supremum norm. For
$\varphi \in C(X, \mathbb{K})$, the multiplication operator $M_\varphi$ is the bounded linear
operator on $C(X, \mathbb{K})$ given by $M_\varphi f = \varphi f$.

articles.title: Spectrum of a multiplication operator
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a compact topological space, let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $\varphi \in C(X, \mathbb{K})$. The spectrum
of the multiplication operator $M_\varphi f = \varphi f$, as an element of the algebra of bounded
linear operators on $C(X, \mathbb{K})$, is the range $\varphi(X)$ of $\varphi$.

articles.title: Schur's test, adjoint form
articles.statement:
The adjoint of a Schur operator is the
Schur operator of the conjugate-transpose matrix.

articles.title: Coordinates of a Schur image lie in $\ell^2$
articles.statement: The coordinates of a Schur image are in `ℓ²`.

articles.title: Schur's test for the $L^2$ operator norm of a matrix
articles.statement: Schur's test for the actual scoped L2 operator norm of a matrix.

articles.title: Norm bound for the Schur linear map
articles.statement: The Schur operator is bounded by `√(R * C)`.

articles.title: Schur's test with a single row and column bound
articles.statement:
The single-bound form: if all row and column sums are at most `B`,
then the operator norm is at most `B`.

articles.title: Schur's test
articles.statement: The operator norm is at most `√(R * C)`.

articles.title: Schur's test for square Euclidean continuous linear maps
articles.statement: Schur's test for Mathlib's square Euclidean continuous linear map.

articles.title: Schur's test for rectangular Euclidean matrix operators
articles.statement: Schur's test for the canonical rectangular Euclidean matrix operator.

articles.title: Norm estimate in Schur's test
articles.statement: The unsquared estimate in Schur's test: `‖A x‖ ≤ √(R * C) * ‖x‖`.

articles.title: Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz for one row of a Schur matrix
articles.statement: Finite weighted Cauchy–Schwarz for one row.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the Schur linear map
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the Schur linear map.

articles.title: Schur operator of an infinite matrix as a linear map
articles.statement: The Schur operator of a matrix, as a linear map.

articles.title: Row bound of a Schur matrix is nonnegative
articles.statement: A single row bound: the row bound `R` is nonnegative.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the Schur operator
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the Schur operator.

articles.title: Schur operator depends only on the matrix
articles.statement: The Schur operator depends only on the matrix, not on the bounds or proofs.

articles.title: Schur operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N})$
articles.statement: The Schur operator of a matrix, as a bounded operator on `ℓ²(ℕ, 𝕜)`.

articles.title: Per-row estimate in Schur's test on $\ell^2$
articles.statement: The per-row estimate: `‖(T x) i‖² ≤ R * ∑' j, ‖a i j‖ * ‖x j‖²`.

articles.title: Entries of a Schur matrix are bounded by the row bound
articles.statement: A single entry of a Schur matrix is bounded by the row bound.

articles.title: Column bounds for the conjugate-transpose matrix in Schur's test
articles.statement: Column bounds for the conjugate-transpose matrix.

articles.title: Row bounds for the conjugate-transpose Schur matrix
articles.statement: Row bounds for the conjugate-transpose matrix.

articles.title: Bound on the double weighted series in Schur's test
articles.statement: The double weighted series is bounded by `C * ‖x‖²`, via the `tsum` interchange.

articles.title: Squared-norm estimate in Schur's test
articles.statement:
The squared-norm estimate in Schur's test: `‖A x‖² ≤ R * C * ‖x‖²`
when every row sum of `‖A i j‖` is at most `R` and every column sum is at
most `C`.

articles.title: Per-row estimate in Schur's test
articles.statement:
The per-row estimate in Schur's test: the `i`-th coordinate of `A x`
satisfies `‖(A x) i‖² ≤ R * ∑ j, ‖A i j‖ * ‖x j‖²` when every row sum of
`‖A i j‖` is at most `R`.

articles.title: Weighted partial sums grouped by the first index
articles.statement: A finite partial sum of the weighted series, grouped by the first index.

articles.title: Weighted partial sums grouped by the second index
articles.statement: A finite partial sum of the weighted series, grouped by the second index.

articles.title: Partial sums of the weighted row series in Schur's test
articles.statement: A finite partial sum of the weighted series is bounded by `R * ‖x‖²`.

articles.title: Squared coordinates of a Schur image are summable
articles.statement: Summability of the squared coordinates of a Schur image.

articles.title: Summability of the row series defining a Schur coordinate
articles.statement: Summability of the row series defining one coordinate of the operator.

articles.title: Absolute summability of rows of a Schur matrix
articles.statement: Summability of the row series of absolute values.

articles.title: Product summability for the Schur bilinear form
articles.statement: Product summability for the bilinear form of a Schur matrix.

articles.statement: Column summability for the conjugate-transpose matrix.

articles.statement: Summability of the double weighted series `∑' i, ∑' j, ‖a i j‖ * ‖x j‖²`.

articles.title: Summability of the weighted row series in Schur's test

articles.title: The Volterra-form sub-conjecture of Scottish Book Problem 124 holds
articles.statement:
For every continuous
function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(0) \ne 0$ and every function
$y : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is Lebesgue integrable on $[0, 1]$, if
$\int_0^x y(t) f(x - t)\,dt = 0$ for every $x \in [0, 1]$, then $y = 0$ almost everywhere on
$[0, 1]$.

## Sources

- Józef Marcinkiewicz, Problem 124 of the Scottish Book; typescript PDF p.58, printed p.55. TYPESCRIPT TYPO, CORRECTED (Phase 5): the typescript prints the equation as `∫₀¹ y(t) f(x-t) dt = 0`, but the intended upper limit is `x` (Volterra form). The literal `∫₀¹` reading is false: `f ≡ 1`, `y(t) = t - 1/2` is a nonzero solution. Only the Volterra `∫₀ˣ` reading is filed here. Positive by the local Titchmarsh convolution theorem: E. C. Titchmarsh, "The zeros of certain integral functions", Proc. London Math. Soc. s2-25 (1926), 283–302, DOI 10.1112/plms/s2-25.1.283. Sketch: Titchmarsh gives `λ, μ ≥ 0` with `λ + μ ≥ 1` such that `y = 0` a.e. on `(0, λ)` and `f = 0` a.e. on `(0, μ)`. Continuity of `f` at `0` with `f 0 ≠ 0` forces `μ = 0` (otherwise `f` would be a.e. zero on a positive-measure initial interval while being nonzero near `0`), so `λ ≥ 1` and `y = 0` a.e. on `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: The Volterra-form sub-conjecture of Scottish Book Problem 124
articles.statement:
The statement that for every
continuous function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(0) \ne 0$ and every function
$y : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is Lebesgue integrable on $[0, 1]$, if
$\int_0^x y(t) f(x - t)\,dt = 0$ for every $x \in [0, 1]$, then $y = 0$ almost everywhere on
$[0, 1]$.

The Scottish Book typescript prints the upper limit of the integral as $1$, but the entry's own
arguments show that the intended upper limit is $x$ (Volterra form); with upper limit $1$ the
claim is false, since $f \equiv 1$ and $y(t) = t - 1/2$ give a nonzero solution. The typescript
does not specify a function class for $y$; integrability on $[0, 1]$ is motivated by the $L^2$
context of the entry.

articles.title: Clamping to the unit interval
articles.statement:
For a real number $t$, its clamp to the unit interval is
$\max(0, \min(t, 1))$, regarded as a point of $[0, 1]$.

articles.title: The clamped extension is bounded by the sup norm
articles.statement:
For every bounded continuous real
function $f$ on $[0, 1]$ and every real $t$, the extension of $f$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by clamping
satisfies $|f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))| \le \|f\|_\infty$, where
$\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in [0, 1]} |f(x)|$ is the sup norm of $f$.

articles.title: The Volterra operator has norm at most one
articles.statement:
The Volterra operator $V$,
$(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$, acting on the space of bounded continuous real functions on
$[0, 1]$ with the sup norm, has operator norm $\|V\| \le 1$.

articles.title: Factorial bound for powers of the Volterra operator
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be the Volterra operator
$(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$
with the sup norm. For every natural number $n$, the operator norm of $V^n$ satisfies
$\|V^n\| \le 1/n!$.

articles.title: The Volterra operator is not invertible
articles.statement:
The Volterra operator $V$,
$(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$, on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$ is
not a unit in the algebra of bounded linear operators on that space.

The reason is that $(Vf)(0) = 0$ for every $f$, so $V$ is not surjective.

articles.title: Pointwise factorial bound for powers of the Volterra operator
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be the Volterra
operator $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ on the space of bounded continuous real functions on
$[0, 1]$. For every natural number $n$, every such function $f$ and every $x \in [0, 1]$,
$|(V^n f)(x)| \le \frac{x^n}{n!} \|f\|_\infty$, where $\|f\|_\infty$ is the sup norm of $f$.

articles.title: The spectral radius of the Volterra operator is zero
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be the Volterra operator
$(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$.
Its spectral radius over the real scalars, the supremum of $|z|$ over real $z$ in the spectrum
of $V$, is $0$.

articles.title: The clamped extension agrees with the original function on the unit interval
articles.statement:
For
every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$ and every real $t$ with $0 \le t \le 1$,
the extension $s \mapsto f(\max(0, \min(s, 1)))$ of $f$ to $\mathbb{R}$ takes the value
$f(t)$ at $t$.

articles.title: The clamped extension is continuous
articles.statement:
For every bounded continuous real function $f$ on
$[0, 1]$, its extension $t \mapsto f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by clamping is
continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Extension by clamping
articles.statement:
For a bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$, its
extension to $\mathbb{R}$ is the function $t \mapsto f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))$.

This continuous extension is used to write $(Vf)(x)$, for $V$ the Volterra operator, as an
interval integral over $\mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Sup-norm bound for the Volterra linear map
articles.statement:
For every bounded continuous real function
$f$ on $[0, 1]$, the Volterra linear map $V$ satisfies $\|Vf\| \le 1 \cdot \|f\|$, where
$\|\cdot\|$ is the sup norm.

articles.title: The Volterra operator as a linear map
articles.statement:
The real-linear map $V$ on the space of bounded
continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$ given by $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ for
$x \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: Volterra integrals vanish at the left endpoint
articles.statement:
For every bounded continuous real function
$f$ on $[0, 1]$, the Volterra operator $V$ satisfies $(Vf)(0) = 0$.

articles.title: Evaluation formula for the Volterra operator
articles.statement:
For every bounded continuous real function
$f$ on $[0, 1]$ and every $x \in [0, 1]$, the Volterra operator $V$ satisfies
$(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x \tilde f(t)\,dt$, where $\tilde f(t) = f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))$ is the
extension of $f$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by clamping the argument into $[0, 1]$.

articles.title: Nonzero reals lie in the resolvent set of the Volterra operator
articles.statement:
For every nonzero real
$z$, $z$ lies in the real resolvent set of the Volterra operator $V$: the bounded operator
$z - V$ is invertible.

The operator $z - V$ is bijective, with inverse given by the Neumann series
$g \mapsto \sum_{n \ge 0} z^{-(n+1)} V^n g$.

articles.title: The spectrum of the Volterra operator is `{0}`
articles.statement: **The spectrum of the Volterra operator is `{0}`.**

articles.title: The Volterra operator
articles.statement:
The bounded real-linear operator $V$ on the space of bounded
continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$ (equivalently $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ with the sup norm)
given by $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ for $x \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: Continuity of the Volterra primitive
articles.statement:
For every bounded continuous real function $f$ on
$[0, 1]$, the function $x \mapsto \int_0^x \tilde f(t)\,dt$ on $[0, 1]$ is continuous, where
$\tilde f(t) = f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))$ is the extension of $f$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by clamping the
argument into $[0, 1]$.

articles.title: Sup-norm bound for the Volterra primitive
articles.statement:
For every bounded continuous real function $f$
on $[0, 1]$ and every $x \in [0, 1]$, $\left|\int_0^x \tilde f(t)\,dt\right| \le \|f\|$, where
$\|f\|$ is the sup norm of $f$ and $\tilde f(t) = f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))$ is the extension of
$f$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by clamping the argument into $[0, 1]$.

articles.title: The domain of the Volterra operator
articles.statement:
The space on which the Volterra operator acts is the
space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$, with the sup norm.

articles.title: Expansion of $(XV)^n$ in Bessel numbers
articles.statement:
Let $X$ and $V$ be the operators on functions
$\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $(Xg)(y) = y \, g(y)$ and $(Vg)(y) = \int_0^y g(t) \, dt$,
write $(XV)^n$ and $V^m$ for iterated composition, and let $a(m, k)$ be the coefficient of $x^k$
in the Bessel polynomial $y_m$. For every natural number $n \ge 1$, every continuous function
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and every real number $x$,

$$(XV)^n f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (-1)^k \, a(n-1, k) \, x^{n-k} \, (V^{n+k} f)(x).$$

## Sources

- Abdelhay Benmoussa, *On the Expansion of `(XV)^n` and Bessel Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.5, Theorem 1 (`jis-2026-26.3.5-thm-1`).

articles.title: Applying $\mu I - T$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$, let
$\mu \in \mathbb{K}$, and let $\mu I$ be the image of $\mu$ under the algebra map from $\mathbb{K}$
to the bounded operators on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$, that is, $\mu$ times the identity.
Then for every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$, $(\mu I - T)x = \mu x - Tx$.

articles.title: Truncated approximate eigenfunction of the bilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$, and write
$\bar{\mu}$ for the complex conjugate of $\mu$. This is the function
$f_{\mu,N} : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{K}$ with $f_{\mu,N}(n) = \bar{\mu}^{\,n}$ for
$-N \le n \le N$ and $f_{\mu,N}(n) = 0$ otherwise (negative powers are inverses, with the
convention $0^{n} = 0$ for $n < 0$).

It is used for $\mu$ on the unit circle, where it gives approximate eigenvectors of the
bilateral shift.

articles.title: Truncated approximate eigenvector of the bilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$, and write
$\bar{\mu}$ for the complex conjugate of $\mu$. This is the vector
$v_{\mu,N} \in \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ whose $n$-th coordinate is the truncated
approximate eigenfunction $f_{\mu,N}(n)$, that is, $\bar{\mu}^{\,n}$ for $-N \le n \le N$ and
$0$ otherwise; it lies in $\ell^2$ because it has finite support.

It is used for $\mu$ on the unit circle, where it is an approximate eigenvector of the
bilateral shift.

articles.title: Bilateral backward shift operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and
let $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ be the Hilbert space of square-summable functions
$\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{K}$. The bilateral backward shift is the bounded $\mathbb{K}$-linear
operator $B$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ given by $(Bx)(n) = x(n + 1)$ for all
$n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Bilateral backward shift of a sequence
articles.statement:
For a function $x : \mathbb{Z} \to K$ with values
in any set $K$, the bilateral backward shift of $x$ is the function $Bx : \mathbb{Z} \to K$
given by $(Bx)(n) = x(n + 1)$.

articles.title: Bilateral backward shift as a linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$
and let $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ be the space of square-summable functions
$\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{K}$. The bilateral backward shift is the $\mathbb{K}$-linear map
$B : \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K}) \to \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ given by
$(Bx)(n) = x(n + 1)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Bilateral shift operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let
$\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ be the Hilbert space of square-summable functions
$\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{K}$. The bilateral shift is the bounded $\mathbb{K}$-linear operator $S$
on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ given by $(Sx)(n) = x(n - 1)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Bilateral shift of a sequence
articles.statement:
For a function $x : \mathbb{Z} \to K$ with values in any
set $K$, the bilateral (forward) shift of $x$ is the function $Sx : \mathbb{Z} \to K$ given by
$(Sx)(n) = x(n - 1)$.

articles.title: Bilateral shift as a linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let
$\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ be the space of square-summable functions
$\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{K}$. The bilateral shift is the $\mathbb{K}$-linear map
$S : \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K}) \to \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ given by
$(Sx)(n) = x(n - 1)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Every point of the unit circle lies in the spectrum of the bilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $S$ be the bilateral shift on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$. Every $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $|\mu| = 1$ lies in the
spectrum of $S$ in the algebra of bounded operators on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$, that
is, $\mu I - S$ is not invertible there, where $\mu I$ is $\mu$ times the identity operator.

If $\mu I - S$ were invertible it would be bounded below, but the truncated approximate
eigenvectors $v_{\mu,N}$ satisfy $\|v_{\mu,N}\| = \sqrt{2N + 1}$ and
$\|(\mu I - S)v_{\mu,N}\| = \sqrt{2}$ for every $N \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: A unit scalar times its conjugate is one
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. If $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ satisfies $|\mu| = 1$, then $\mu \bar{\mu} = 1$, where
$\bar{\mu}$ is the complex conjugate of $\mu$.

articles.title: Multiplying a power of the conjugate by a unit scalar
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$
or $\mathbb{C}$, and write $\bar{\mu}$ for the complex conjugate of $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$. If
$|\mu| = 1$, then for every integer $n$, $\mu \bar{\mu}^{\,n} = \bar{\mu}^{\,n-1}$.

articles.title: Norm of the truncated approximate eigenvector
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $|\mu| = 1$, and let $N \in \mathbb{N}$. The
truncated approximate eigenvector $v_{\mu,N} \in \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$, whose $n$-th
coordinate is $\bar{\mu}^{\,n}$ for $-N \le n \le N$ and $0$ otherwise ($\bar{\mu}$ the complex
conjugate of $\mu$), satisfies $\|v_{\mu,N}\|^2 = 2N + 1$.

articles.title: Residual of the truncated approximate eigenvector
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be the bilateral shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$, let
$\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $|\mu| = 1$, and let $N \in \mathbb{N}$. The truncated approximate
eigenvector $v_{\mu,N}$ satisfies $\|(\mu I - S)v_{\mu,N}\|^2 = 2$, where $\mu I$ is $\mu$ times
the identity operator.

The only nonzero coordinates of $(\mu I - S)v_{\mu,N}$ are those at $n = -N$ and $n = N + 1$,
each of absolute value $1$.

articles.title: Coordinates of the residual of the truncated approximate eigenvector
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be the bilateral shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$,
and let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$, $N \in \mathbb{N}$ and $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Let $f_{\mu,N}$ be the
truncated approximate eigenfunction and $v_{\mu,N} \in \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ the
corresponding truncated approximate eigenvector. Then the $n$-th coordinate of
$(\mu I - S)v_{\mu,N}$ is $\mu f_{\mu,N}(n) - f_{\mu,N}(n - 1)$, where $\mu I$ is $\mu$ times
the identity operator.

articles.title: Spectrum of the bilateral backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$ and let $B$ be the bilateral backward shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$.
The spectrum of $B$ in the algebra of bounded operators on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$ is
the unit circle $\{\mu \in \mathbb{K} : |\mu| = 1\}$.

articles.title: Spectrum of the bilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The
spectrum of the bilateral shift, as a bounded operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{K})$, is the
set of scalars $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $|\mu| = 1$; for $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{C}$ this is the
unit circle.

articles.title: Conjugates of unimodular scalars are nonzero
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. If $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ satisfies $|\mu| = 1$, then its conjugate $\bar{\mu}$ is
nonzero.

articles.title: Adjoint of a composition operator is the fiber-sum operator
articles.statement:
The adjoint of the composition operator is the fiber-sum operator:
`((C_ψ)† y) m` is the sum of `y` over the fiber of `m`.

articles.title: Adjoint of a composition operator with a permutation symbol
articles.statement:
The adjoint of the composition operator for a permutation symbol is the
composition operator of the inverse permutation.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the bounded composition operator
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the composition operator.

articles.title: Composition of composition operators
articles.statement:
Composition of composition operators is composition of symbols in the
reversed order: `C_φ ∘L C_ψ = C_{ψ ∘ φ}`.

articles.title: Composition operator of a pointwise identity symbol
articles.statement: If `ψ` is pointwise the identity, `C_ψ` is the identity operator.

articles.title: Composition operator of the identity is the identity
articles.statement: `C_id` is the identity operator.

articles.title: Permutation composition operators are unitary
articles.statement: A permutation symbol gives a unitary composition operator.

articles.title: Bounded composition operator on $\ell^2$
articles.statement: The composition operator as a bounded operator on `ℓ²(ℕ, 𝕜)`.

articles.title: Precomposition of a sequence with a map
articles.statement: The composition function: precompose a sequence with `ψ`.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the composition linear map
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the composition linear map.

articles.title: Composition operator as a linear map
articles.statement: The composition operator as a linear map.

articles.title: Fiber count agrees with set cardinality
articles.statement: On its finite domain, the fiber count agrees with the standard natural cardinality.

articles.title: Fiber cardinality of a map
articles.statement: The number of preimages of `m` under `ψ`, defined for a finite fiber.

articles.title: Fiber supremum as a supremum of cardinalities
articles.statement:
On its bounded finite domain, the fiber supremum agrees with the supremum of natural
cardinalities. Its value is independent of the chosen bound and evidence.

articles.title: Fiber supremum is nonnegative
articles.statement: `fiberSup ψ hψ` is nonnegative.

articles.title: Supremum of the fiber counts of a map
articles.statement:
The real supremum of the fiber counts of `ψ`, defined for uniformly bounded finite
fibers. The bound in `hψ` ensures that the real-valued family is bounded above.

articles.title: Bounded fibers are preserved under composition
articles.statement:
Fiber bounds compose: the fibers of `ψ ∘ φ` are bounded by the product
of the bounds.

articles.title: Halving map has fibers of size at most two
articles.statement: Halving pairs: the map `n ↦ n / 2` has fibers of size at most two.

articles.title: Permutations have fibers of size one
articles.statement: A permutation symbol has fibers of size one.

articles.title: Injective maps have fibers of size at most one
articles.statement: An injective symbol has fibers of size at most one.

articles.title: Uniformly bounded fibers of a map on the naturals
articles.statement:
The fibers of `ψ` are finite and uniformly bounded by `M`: every value
is taken at most `M` times. This is the boundedness hypothesis for the
composition operator.

articles.title: Composition operator is injective iff its symbol is surjective
articles.statement:
`C_ψ` is injective iff `ψ` is surjective: a missing value gives a
basis vector in the kernel, and a surjective symbol lets every coordinate
be read off from the image.

articles.title: Precomposition preserves square-summability
articles.statement:
The composed sequence of an `ℓ²` sequence is in `ℓ²`, under the bounded
fibers hypothesis.

articles.title: Vectorwise norm bound for the composition operator
articles.statement: The composition operator is bounded by `√(fiberSup ψ hψ)` on every vector.

articles.title: Operator-norm bound for the composition operator
articles.statement: The operator norm of `C_ψ` is at most `√(fiberSup ψ hψ)`.

articles.title: Norm of the composition operator on a basis vector
articles.statement:
The norm of `C_ψ` applied to a standard basis vector is the square root
of the corresponding fiber count.

articles.title: Operator norm of a composition operator
articles.statement:
The operator norm of the composition operator:
`‖C_ψ‖ = √(fiberSup ψ hψ)`, the square root of the largest fiber count.

articles.title: Norm bound for the composition linear map
articles.statement: The composition operator is bounded by `√(fiberSup ψ hψ)`.

articles.title: Squared-norm bound for the composition linear map
articles.statement: The squared norm of `C_ψ x` is at most `fiberSup ψ hψ * ‖x‖²`.

articles.title: Composition operators on $\ell^2$ are never compact
articles.statement:
A composition operator on `ℓ²(ℕ, 𝕜)` is never compact: the images of
the basis vectors indexed by the (necessarily infinite) range of `ψ` are
pairwise orthogonal and bounded below in norm, so they have no Cauchy
subsequence.

articles.title: Composition operator is surjective iff its symbol is injective
articles.statement:
`C_ψ` is surjective iff `ψ` is injective: if `ψ a = ψ b` with
`a ≠ b`, the `a`-th and `b`-th coordinates of every vector in the range
agree, so `e_a` is not in the range; if `ψ` is injective, the preimage of
`y` is obtained by applying the adjoint and reading off the fiber sums.

articles.title: Squared-norm sum bound for a precomposed sequence
articles.statement:
The squared-norm sum of the composed sequence is at most `fiberSup ψ hψ`
times the squared-norm sum of the original sequence.

articles.title: Adjoint of a Hankel operator
articles.statement:
Adjoint of a Hankel operator: `(Hₐ)† = H_{star a}`, by passing the
adjoint through the finite partial sums and taking the limit.

articles.title: Anti-diagonal slice operator is self-adjoint
articles.statement: A slice is self-adjoint.

articles.title: Hankel operator as the sum of its slices
articles.statement: The Hankel operator is the sum of its slices.

articles.title: Partial sums of the Hankel slice series are compact
articles.statement:
A finite partial sum of the slice series has finite-dimensional range,
hence is a compact operator.

articles.title: Anti-diagonal slice of an ℓ² sequence lies in ℓ²
articles.statement: The slice of an `ℓ²` sequence is in `ℓ²`.

articles.title: Matrix entries of the Hankel operator
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the Hankel operator: `(Hₐ x) i = ∑' j, a (i + j) * x j`.

articles.title: Hankel operator with zero symbol is zero
articles.statement: The zero symbol gives the zero operator.

articles.title: Hankel operator with absolutely summable symbol
articles.statement:
The Hankel operator with symbol `a`. Defined as the norm-convergent
series `∑' k, a k • hankelSlice k` over the anti-diagonal slices.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the anti-diagonal slice operator
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the slice operator.

articles.title: Anti-diagonal slice of a sequence
articles.statement:
The `k`-th anti-diagonal slice function: reverse the first `k + 1`
coordinates, kill the rest.

articles.title: Anti-diagonal slice is symmetric
articles.statement:
A slice is symmetric for the inner product: the anti-diagonal symmetry
is a finite-sum reflection.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the anti-diagonal slice map
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the slice linear map.

articles.title: Anti-diagonal slice as a linear map
articles.statement: The `k`-th anti-diagonal slice as a linear map.

articles.title: Anti-diagonal slice operator
articles.statement: The `k`-th anti-diagonal slice as a bounded operator.

articles.title: Summability of weighted anti-diagonal slices
articles.statement:
The slice operators weighted by `a` are summable in operator norm when
`a` is absolutely summable.

articles.title: Anti-diagonal slice does not increase the sum of squared norms
articles.statement:
The (squared) norms of a sliced sequence sum to at most the squared
norms of the original sequence: only the first `k + 1` coordinates survive,
in reverse order.

articles.title: Hankel operator with absolutely summable symbol is compact
articles.statement:
A Hankel operator with an absolutely summable symbol is compact:
it is the norm limit of its finite partial sums, each of which has
finite-dimensional range.

articles.title: Hankel operator with real symbol is self-adjoint
articles.statement:
A Hankel operator with a real-valued (`star`-fixed) symbol is
self-adjoint.

articles.title: Norm bound for the Hankel operator
articles.statement: Operator-norm bound: `‖Hₐ‖ ≤ ∑' k, ‖a k‖`.

articles.title: Anti-diagonal slice operator has norm at most one
articles.statement: The operator norm of a slice is at most `1`.

articles.title: Anti-diagonal slice map does not increase norms
articles.statement: A slice does not increase norms.

articles.title: Backward shift annihilates truncations after $N$ steps
articles.statement: Applying the backward shift `N` times to a truncation gives `0`.

articles.title: Periodic points of $\mu B$ are dense iff $|\mu| > 1$
articles.statement: The periodic points of `μ • B` are dense if and only if `‖μ‖ > 1`.

articles.title: Dense periodic points of the Rolewicz operator for $|\mu| > 1$
articles.statement: The periodic points of `μ • B` are dense when `‖μ‖ > 1`.

articles.title: Finitely supported vectors are dense in $\ell^2(\mathbb{N})$
articles.statement:
The span of the single-coordinate vectors is dense in `ℓ²(ℕ, 𝕜)`:
every vector is the sum of its canonical series.

articles.title: No nonzero periodic points of $\mu B$ when $|\mu| \le 1$
articles.statement: The only periodic point of `μ • B` is `0` when `‖μ‖ ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Vectors in the span of coordinate vectors have finite support
articles.statement:
Every vector in the span of the single-coordinate vectors is
eventually zero: it has finite support.

articles.title: Rolewicz's theorem
articles.statement:
The scalar multiple `μ • B` of the backward
shift on `ℓ²(ℕ, 𝕜)` is hypercyclic if and only if `‖μ‖ > 1`.

articles.title: Zero is a periodic point of every operator
articles.statement: `0` is a periodic point of every period for every operator.

articles.title: Powers of the backward shift do not increase norms
articles.statement: Powers of the backward shift do not increase norms.

articles.title: Powers of the forward shift preserve norms
articles.statement: Powers of the forward shift preserve norms.

articles.title: Geometric ratio of the periodic approximant is below 1
articles.statement: The geometric ratio `‖μ⁻¹ ^ N‖` is `< 1` when `‖μ‖ > 1` and `N > 0`.

articles.title: Distance from the periodic approximant to the truncation
articles.statement:
The distance from the periodic approximant to the truncation is at
most the geometric tail `(r / (1 - r)) * ‖y‖`, where `r = ‖μ‖⁻¹ ^ N`.

articles.title: Norm of a term of the periodic approximant
articles.statement: The norm of a term of the periodic approximant.

articles.title: Periodic approximant is a periodic point
articles.statement: The periodic approximant is periodic of period `N` when `‖μ‖ > 1`.

articles.title: Action of the scaled backward shift power on approximant terms
articles.statement:
How `(μ • B) ^ N` acts on a term of the periodic approximant:
the `m = 0` term is killed, and every later term shifts down by one.

articles.title: First term of the periodic approximant is the truncation
articles.statement: The `m = 0` term of the periodic approximant is the truncation.

articles.title: Periodic approximant of a truncated sequence
articles.statement:
The periodic extension of the truncation of `y` to its first `N`
coordinates: the geometric series over forward shifts by blocks of
length `N`, with coefficients `(μ⁻¹ ^ N) ^ m`.

articles.title: Coordinate recurrence for periodic points of $\mu B$
articles.statement:
If `x` is periodic for `μ • B`, its coordinates satisfy
`x k = μ ^ (n * m) * x (k + n * m)` for all `m`.

articles.title: Coordinates of powers of a scaled backward shift
articles.statement: Coordinate form of a power of a scalar multiple of the backward shift.

articles.title: Powers of a scaled backward shift as operators
articles.statement: A power of a scalar multiple of the backward shift, as an operator.

articles.title: Powers of a scalar multiple of the backward shift
articles.statement: Powers of a scalar multiple of the backward shift, applied pointwise.

articles.title: Summability of the geometric bound for periodic approximants
articles.statement: The geometric series bounding the periodic approximant terms is summable.

articles.title: Summability of the shifted periodic approximant terms
articles.statement:
Summability of the terms of the periodic approximant after applying
`(μ • B) ^ N`.

articles.title: Summability of the periodic approximant terms
articles.statement: Summability of the terms of the periodic approximant.

articles.title: Coordinates of an $\ell^2$ vector tend to zero
articles.statement: The coordinates of an `ℓ²` vector tend to `0`.

articles.title: Mazur's Scottish Book Problem 88 fails
articles.statement:
The Scottish Book Problem 88 claim is false: there is
a real sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ such that for every real sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with
$|x_n| \le 1$ for all $n$, each series $\sum_n a_{m+n} x_n$ with $m \ge 0$ converges, as the
limit of its partial sums, to some $L_m$, and $\sum_m |L_m| < \infty$, but $\sum_n n |a_n|$
diverges.

## Sources

- S. Mazur, Problem 88 of the Scottish Book; negative solution as an immediate consequence of Peller (1982), J. Operator Theory 7, 341-372, §5, via V. V. Peller, "On S. Mazur's Problems 8 and 88 from the Scottish Book", arXiv:math/0703716: a Hankel matrix in the injective tensor product need not have finite sum of moduli of its entries.

articles.title: Scottish Book Problem 88 (Mazur)
articles.statement:
The claim that every real sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$
with the following property satisfies $\sum_n n |a_n| < \infty$: for every real sequence
$(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $|x_n| \le 1$ for all $n$, each series $\sum_n a_{m+n} x_n$ with $m \ge 0$
converges, as the limit of its partial sums, to some $L_m$, and $\sum_m |L_m| < \infty$.

The inner series is required to converge as a limit of partial sums, not absolutely, as in
Mazur's original question.

articles.title: Adjoint of a Toeplitz operator
articles.statement: Adjoint of a Toeplitz operator: `(Tₐ)† = T_{a*}`.

articles.title: Adjoint of a diagonal slice is the opposite slice
articles.statement: A slice is adjoint to the slice at the negated index.

articles.title: A Toeplitz operator is compact iff its symbol is zero
articles.statement: A Toeplitz operator is compact iff its symbol is zero.

articles.title: Characterization of self-adjoint Toeplitz operators
articles.statement:
Self-adjointness of a Toeplitz operator iff the symbol satisfies
`star (a (-k)) = a k` for all `k`.

articles.title: Toeplitz operators with self-adjoint symbol are self-adjoint
articles.statement: A Toeplitz operator with a `star`-fixed adjoint symbol is self-adjoint.

articles.title: Operator norm of a Toeplitz operator with delta symbol
articles.statement: The operator norm of a Toeplitz operator with a delta symbol is `‖c‖`.

articles.title: Operator norm bound for a Toeplitz operator
articles.statement: Operator-norm bound: `‖Tₐ‖ ≤ ∑' k, ‖a k‖`.

articles.title: Operator norm of a diagonal slice is at most one
articles.statement: The operator norm of a slice is at most `1`.

articles.title: Diagonal slices do not increase norms
articles.statement: A slice does not increase norms.

articles.title: Toeplitz operators with nonzero symbol are not compact
articles.statement:
A Toeplitz operator with a nonzero symbol is not compact: the images
of the standard basis vectors converge coordinatewise to `0` but keep a
nonzero coordinate.

articles.title: Absolute summability of the adjoint symbol
articles.statement:
The adjoint symbol of an absolutely summable symbol is absolutely
summable.

articles.title: Absolute summability of a delta symbol
articles.statement: A delta symbol is absolutely summable.

articles.title: Adjoint symbol of a Toeplitz operator
articles.statement: The adjoint symbol: `a* k = star (a (-k))`.

articles.title: Delta symbol for Toeplitz operators
articles.statement: The delta symbol at `m` with value `c`.

articles.title: Toeplitz operator as the sum of its diagonal slices
articles.statement: The Toeplitz operator is the sum of its slices.

articles.title: Diagonal slices preserve square-summability
articles.statement: The slice of an `ℓ²` sequence is in `ℓ²`.

articles.title: Toeplitz operator applied to a standard basis vector
articles.statement: The Toeplitz operator applied to a standard basis vector.

articles.title: Pointwise action of a Toeplitz operator
articles.statement:
Pointwise action of the Toeplitz operator:
`(Tₐ x) i = ∑' j, a (i - j) * x j`.

articles.title: Toeplitz operator of a delta symbol is a scaled slice
articles.statement:
A Toeplitz operator with a delta symbol is the corresponding scalar
multiple of its diagonal slice.

articles.title: Toeplitz operator of the zero symbol
articles.statement: The zero symbol gives the zero operator.

articles.title: Toeplitz operator with absolutely summable symbol
articles.statement:
The Toeplitz operator with symbol `a`. Defined as the norm-convergent
series `∑' k, a k • toeplitzSlice k` over the diagonal slices.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the diagonal slice operator
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the slice operator.

articles.title: Diagonal slices are powers of the forward or backward shift
articles.statement:
Every nonnegative Toeplitz slice is the corresponding power of the
canonical unilateral shift, and every negative slice is the corresponding
power of the canonical backward shift.

articles.title: Diagonal slice function of a Toeplitz matrix
articles.statement:
The `k`-th diagonal slice function: shift coordinates by `k`, killing
the coordinates that fall off the end. For `k ≥ 0` this is the `k`-fold
forward shift; for `k < 0` it is the `(-k)`-fold backward shift.

articles.title: Inner product symmetry of opposite diagonal slices
articles.statement:
A slice is adjoint to the slice at the negated index: the diagonal
symmetry exchanges the two sides of the inner product.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the diagonal slice linear map
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the slice linear map.

articles.title: Diagonal slice as a linear map
articles.statement: The `k`-th diagonal slice as a linear map.

articles.title: Diagonal slice as a bounded operator
articles.statement: The `k`-th diagonal slice as a bounded operator.

articles.title: Summability of weighted diagonal slices
articles.statement:
The slice operators weighted by `a` are summable in operator norm when
`a` is absolutely summable.

articles.title: $\ell^1$ norm of a delta symbol
articles.statement: The `ℓ¹` norm of a delta symbol is `‖c‖`.

articles.title: Adjoint of the unilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The
adjoint of the unilateral shift $S$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ is the backward shift
$B$: $S^* = B$.

articles.title: Applying a scalar operator minus an operator on ℓ²(ℕ)
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$
or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, let
$\mu \in \mathbb{K}$, and let $\mu I$ be the image of $\mu$ under the algebra map from $\mathbb{K}$
into the bounded operators, i.e. $\mu$ times the identity $I$. Then $(\mu I - T)x = \mu x - Tx$
for every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: Backward shift power inverts the shift power modulo finite rank
articles.statement:
The quasi-inverse relation `B ^ n ∘L S ^ n = 1` holds exactly,
hence also modulo finite-rank operators.

articles.title: Truncated geometric sequence
articles.statement: The truncated geometric sequence `(1, μ̄, μ̄², …, μ̄ᴺ, 0, …)`.

articles.title: Shift power inverts the backward shift power modulo finite rank
articles.statement:
The defect `S ^ n ∘L B ^ n - 1` has finite rank: its range lies in
the finite-dimensional kernel of `B ^ n`, since applying `B ^ n`
after it gives `0`.

articles.title: Truncated geometric vector in $\ell^2$
articles.statement: The truncated geometric sequence as an `ℓ²` vector.

articles.title: Coordinates of the backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For
every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and every $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the $i$-th coordinate
of the backward shift $Bx$ is the $i$-th term of the backward shift of the sequence $x$,
that is, $(Bx)_i = x_{i+1}$.

articles.title: Backward shift of the geometric vector
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$
and let $c \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\|c\| < 1$. Let $v = (1, c, c^2, \dots)$ be the geometric vector
of $c$ in $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and let $B$ be the backward shift on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. Then $Bv = c\,v$.

articles.title: Pointwise action of a power of the backward shift
articles.statement: Pointwise action of `B ^ n`: it drops the first `n` coordinates.

articles.title: Powers of the backward shift as iterates of the backward map
articles.statement: The coercion of `B ^ n` is the `n`-fold iterate of `backwardFun`.

articles.title: Backward shift power is a left inverse of the shift power
articles.statement:
`B ^ n` is a left inverse of `S ^ n`: shifting up then down
recovers the original sequence.

articles.title: Backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The backward shift is the
bounded linear operator $B$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ given by $(Bx)_n = x_{n+1}$ for
all $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Left inverse of the unilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The backward shift $B$ is a left inverse of the unilateral shift $S$ on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$: $BS = I$, where $I$ is the identity operator.

articles.title: Iterated backward shift drops leading coordinates
articles.statement:
Iterating the backward-shift function `n` times drops the first
`n` coordinates.

articles.title: Backward shift of a sequence
articles.statement:
For any type $K$, the backward shift of a sequence
$x \colon \mathbb{N} \to K$ is the sequence $n \mapsto x_{n+1}$: it drops the coordinate $x_0$
and shifts every other coordinate down by one.

articles.title: Coordinates of the backward-shift linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and every $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the
$i$-th coordinate of the image of $x$ under the backward-shift linear map $B$ is the $i$-th term
of the backward shift of the sequence $x$, that is, $(Bx)_i = x_{i+1}$.

articles.title: Backward shift as a linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The
backward-shift linear map is the $\mathbb{K}$-linear map $B$ from $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$
to itself given by $(Bx)_n = x_{n+1}$ for all $x$ and all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Essential spectrum of the unilateral shift is the unit circle
articles.statement:
The essential spectrum of the unilateral shift is the unit circle:
`S - μ • 1` is Fredholm exactly off the circle.

articles.title: Essential spectrum of a bounded operator
articles.statement:
The **essential spectrum** of a bounded operator `T`: the set of
scalars `μ` for which `T - μ • 1` is not a Fredholm operator.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the extension-by-zero map
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the extension-by-zero map.

articles.title: Kernel vectors of a backward shift power are zero-extended tuples
articles.statement:
A vector in the kernel of `B ^ n` is determined by its first `n`
coordinates: extending those coordinates by zeroes recovers it.

articles.title: Extension of a finite tuple by zeroes
articles.statement: The extension of a tuple of `n` coordinates by zeroes.

articles.title: Linear extension-by-zero map into $\ell^2$
articles.statement: The linear extension-by-zero map `(Fin n → 𝕜) →ₗ[𝕜] ℓ²(ℕ, 𝕜)`.

articles.title: Finite-dimensionality of the kernel of a backward shift power
articles.statement: The kernel of `B ^ n` is finite-dimensional.

articles.title: Dimension of the kernel of a backward shift power
articles.statement: The kernel of `B ^ n` has dimension `n`.

articles.title: Dimension of the cokernel of a unilateral shift power
articles.statement:
The cokernel of `S ^ n` has dimension `n`: the quotient of `ℓ²`
by the range of `S ^ n` is equivalent to `Fin n → 𝕜` via the first
`n` coordinates.

articles.title: First coordinates of a zero extension recover the tuple
articles.statement: Taking first coordinates after extension by zeroes is the identity.

articles.title: First-coordinates map on square-summable sequences
articles.statement: The map taking a sequence to its first `n` coordinates.

articles.title: Pointwise action of the geometric vector
articles.statement: Pointwise action of the geometric vector.

articles.title: Geometric unit vector attached to a point of the disc
articles.statement:
The geometric vector attached to `u`: the `ℓ²` sequence with
coordinates `√(1 - ‖u‖²) * u ^ n`.

articles.title: Coordinates of the geometric vector
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and
let $c \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\|c\| < 1$. For every $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the $i$-th coordinate of
the geometric vector of $c$ in $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ is $c^i$.

articles.title: The geometric vector is nonzero
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let
$c \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\|c\| < 1$. The geometric vector $(1, c, c^2, \dots)$ in
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ is nonzero, since its $0$-th coordinate is $1$.

articles.title: Geometric vector
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let
$c \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\|c\| < 1$. The geometric vector of $c$ is the sequence
$(1, c, c^2, \dots)$, that is $i \mapsto c^i$, regarded as an element of the Hilbert space
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of square-summable sequences.

articles.title: Fredholm index of a backward shift power is $n$
articles.statement:
The Fredholm index of `B ^ n` is `n`: the backward shift power is
surjective, and its kernel has dimension `n`.

articles.title: Fredholm index of the backward shift is $1$
articles.statement: The Fredholm index of the backward shift is `1`.

articles.title: Fredholm index of a unilateral shift power is $-n$
articles.statement:
The Fredholm index of `S ^ n` is `-n`: the shift power is
injective, and its cokernel has dimension `n`.

articles.title: Fredholm index of the unilateral shift is $-1$
articles.statement: The Fredholm index of the unilateral shift is `-1`.

articles.title: Shift composed with backward shift has Fredholm index zero
articles.statement:
`S ∘L B` has Fredholm index `0`, as index additivity under
composition demands: `(-1) + 1 = 0`.

articles.title: Shifted unilateral shift has index $-1$ inside the unit disk
articles.statement:
The index of `S - μ • 1` is `-1` for `‖μ‖ < 1`: the canonical
homotopy theorem makes the index constant along `S - (t μ) • 1`,
`t ∈ [0, 1]`, and the canonical shift has index `-1` at `t = 0`.

articles.title: Shifted unilateral shift has index zero outside the unit disk
articles.statement: For `‖μ‖ > 1`, `S - μ • 1` has index `0`: a unit is bijective.

articles.title: Injectivity of powers of the unilateral shift
articles.statement: The unilateral shift power is injective.

articles.title: The unilateral shift is injective
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The
unilateral shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ is injective.

articles.title: Shifted unilateral shift has trivial kernel
articles.statement:
`S - μ • 1` has trivial kernel for every `μ`: the coordinate
equations force every coordinate to vanish.

articles.title: Powers of the backward shift are Fredholm
articles.statement:
Every power of the backward shift is a Fredholm operator: `S ^ n`
is a quasi-inverse.

articles.title: Invertible operators are Fredholm
articles.statement:
A unit operator is Fredholm, via `IsHomeomorph` and
`IsInvertible.isFredholm`.

articles.title: One minus a small multiple of the backward shift is Fredholm
articles.statement: `1 - μ • B` is Fredholm when `‖μ‖ < 1`.

articles.title: Powers of the unilateral shift are Fredholm
articles.statement:
Every power of the unilateral shift is a Fredholm operator: `B ^ n`
is a quasi-inverse.

articles.title: Shift composed with backward shift is Fredholm
articles.statement: `S ∘L B` is Fredholm: it is the composite of two Fredholm operators.

articles.title: Shifted unilateral shift is Fredholm inside the unit disk
articles.statement:
For `‖μ‖ < 1`, `S - μ • 1` is Fredholm: it is the Fredholm
operator `S (1 - μ B)` plus the finite-rank operator `μ (S B - 1)`.

articles.title: Shifted unilateral shift is Fredholm outside the unit disk
articles.statement: For `‖μ‖ > 1`, `S - μ • 1` is Fredholm, as it is a unit.

articles.title: Isometric characterization of the unilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a separable complex
Hilbert space, and call a bounded linear operator $T : H \to H$ a shift if there is an
orthonormal basis $(e_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of $H$ with $T e_n = e_{n+1}$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then a bounded linear operator $T : H \to H$ is a shift if and only if the
following three conditions hold: $T$ is an isometry, that is,
