$\langle T x, T y \rangle = \langle x, y \rangle$ for all $x, y \in H$; the ranges of the powers
of $T$ satisfy $\bigcap_{n \ge 1} \mathrm{Ran}(T^n) = \{0\}$; and the orthogonal complement
$(\mathrm{Ran}\, T)^\perp$ of the range of $T$ has dimension $1$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; Special classes of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_33`.

articles.title: Unilateral shift operator
articles.statement:
A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex inner product
space $H$ is a unilateral shift if there is a Hilbert basis $(b_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of $H$
such that $T b_n = b_{n+1}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: One minus a small multiple of the backward shift is invertible
articles.statement:
`1 - μ • B` is a unit when `‖μ‖ < 1`, by the Neumann-series
criterion `isUnit_one_sub_of_norm_lt_one`.

articles.title: Shifted unilateral shift is invertible outside the unit disk
articles.statement:
For `‖μ‖ > 1`, `S - μ • 1` is a unit: it equals
`(algebraMap (-μ)) * (1 - μ⁻¹ • S)`, a product of units.

articles.title: The unilateral shift preserves distances
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. The unilateral shift $S$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ is an isometry:
$\|Sx - Sy\| = \|x - y\|$ for all $x, y \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: Kernel of the backward shift power as a space of finite tuples
articles.statement:
The kernel of `B ^ n` is linearly equivalent to `Fin n → 𝕜`: a
vector in the kernel is exactly its first `n` coordinates.

articles.title: Kernel of the first-coordinates map is the range of the shift power
articles.statement:
The kernel of the first-`n`-coordinates map is the range of
`S ^ n`: both consist of the sequences whose first `n` coordinates
vanish.

articles.title: Membership in the essential spectrum of the unilateral shift
articles.statement:
Membership form: `μ` is in the essential spectrum of the shift
iff `‖μ‖ = 1`.

articles.title: Kernel of a power of the backward shift
articles.statement:
A vector is in the kernel of `B ^ n` iff its coordinates from `n`
onwards all vanish.

articles.title: Open unit disc lies in the backward shift's numerical range
articles.statement:
Every `w` with `‖w‖ < 1` lies in the numerical range of the backward
shift, witnessed by the geometric vector attached to `conj w`.

articles.title: Open unit disc lies in the forward shift's numerical range
articles.statement:
Every `u` with `‖u‖ < 1` lies in the numerical range of the forward
shift, witnessed by the geometric vector attached to `u`.

articles.title: Truncated geometric sequence is square-summable
articles.statement: The truncated geometric sequence is in `ℓ²`: it has finite support.

articles.title: The backward shift of an $\ell^2$ sequence is in $\ell^2$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the backward
shift $n \mapsto x_{n+1}$ of the sequence $x$ is square-summable, that is, it lies in
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

Its squared absolute values are a tail of the squared absolute values of $x$.

articles.title: Zero-extended finite tuples are square-summable
articles.statement: A finitely supported sequence is in `ℓ²`.

articles.title: Square-summability of the scaled geometric sequence
articles.statement:
The geometric sequence attached to `u`, with coordinates
`√(1 - ‖u‖²) * u ^ n`, is in `ℓ²`. When `‖u‖ ≥ 1` the square root is `0`
and the sequence is identically `0`; the interesting case is `‖u‖ < 1`.

articles.title: Geometric sequences with ratio of norm less than one are square-summable
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $c \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\|c\| < 1$. Then
the sequence $(c^i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ lies in $\ell^2$, that is,
$\sum_{i} \|c^i\|^2 < \infty$.

articles.title: The forward shift of a square-summable sequence is square-summable
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For every square-summable sequence $x = (x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots)$ in
$\mathbb{K}$, the forward-shifted sequence $(0, x_0, x_1, \dots)$ is also square-summable, that is,
it belongs to $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: Range of a power of the unilateral shift
articles.statement:
A vector is in the range of `S ^ n` iff its first `n` coordinates
vanish.

articles.title: The open unit ball lies in the spectrum of the backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $B$ be the backward shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.
Every $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\|\mu\| < 1$ lies in the spectrum of $B$ in the algebra of
bounded operators on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

Indeed, writing $I$ for the identity operator, the geometric vector $(1, \mu, \mu^2, \dots)$ lies
in the kernel of $\mu I - B$, so $\mu I - B$ is not injective, hence not invertible.

articles.title: The open unit ball lies in the spectrum of the unilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $S$ be the unilateral shift on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. Every $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\|\mu\| < 1$ lies in the
spectrum of $S$ in the algebra of bounded operators on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

Indeed, write $I$ for the identity operator. If $\mu I - S$ were invertible it would be
surjective, so $(\mu I - S)x = v$ for some $x$, where $v = (1, \bar\mu, \bar\mu^2, \dots)$ is the
geometric vector of the conjugate $\bar\mu$. Since the adjoint of $S$ is the backward shift $B$
and $Bv = \bar\mu v$, pairing $(\mu I - S)x = v$ with $v$ gives $\|v\|^2 = 0$, contradicting
$v \neq 0$.

articles.title: The backward shift has operator norm at most one
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, and let $B$ be the backward shift on the Hilbert space
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of square-summable sequences in $\mathbb{K}$, given by
$(Bx)_n = x_{n+1}$. Then the operator norm of $B$ satisfies $\|B\| \le 1$.

articles.title: The backward shift linear map does not increase norms
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, and let $B$ be the backward shift on the space $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of
square-summable sequences in $\mathbb{K}$, viewed as a linear map and given by
$(Bx)_n = x_{n+1}$. Then $\|Bx\| \le \|x\|$ for every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: Geometric vector of a point in the open disc is a unit vector
articles.statement: The geometric vector attached to `u` with `‖u‖ < 1` is a unit vector.

articles.title: Backward shift's numerical range lies in the open unit disc
articles.statement:
Every point of the numerical range of the backward shift has norm
strictly less than `1`, by the AM–GM strict bound.

articles.title: Forward shift's numerical range lies in the open unit disc
articles.statement:
Every point of the numerical range of the forward shift has norm
strictly less than `1`, by the AM–GM strict bound.

articles.title: The identity on ℓ²(ℕ) has norm at most one
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. The operator norm of the identity operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ is
at most $1$.

articles.title: The unilateral shift preserves norms
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and
let $S$ be the unilateral shift on the Hilbert space $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of
square-summable sequences in $\mathbb{K}$, given by $S(x_0, x_1, \dots) = (0, x_0, x_1, \dots)$.
Then $\|Sx\| = \|x\|$ for every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: The unilateral shift has operator norm one
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, and let $S$ be the unilateral shift on the Hilbert space
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of square-summable sequences in $\mathbb{K}$, given by
$S(x_0, x_1, \dots) = (0, x_0, x_1, \dots)$. Then the operator norm of $S$ is $\|S\| = 1$.

articles.title: The forward shift linear map preserves norms
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, and let $S$ be the forward shift on the space $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of
square-summable sequences in $\mathbb{K}$, viewed as a linear map and given by
$S(x_0, x_1, \dots) = (0, x_0, x_1, \dots)$. Then $\|Sx\| = \|x\|$ for every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: Squared norm of the truncated geometric vector
articles.statement:
The squared norm of the truncated geometric vector is `N + 1`,
when `‖μ‖ = 1`.

articles.title: Squared norm of the shifted shift on the truncated geometric vector
articles.statement:
The squared norm of `(S - μ • 1)` applied to the truncated
geometric vector is `2`, when `‖μ‖ = 1`.

articles.title: Shifted unilateral shift is not Fredholm on the unit circle
articles.statement:
For `‖μ‖ = 1`, `S - μ • 1` is not Fredholm: it has trivial kernel
and closed range would make it bounded below, contradicting the
approximate eigenvectors.

articles.title: The unilateral shift is not surjective
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$,
and let $S$ be the unilateral shift on the Hilbert space $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of
square-summable sequences in $\mathbb{K}$, given by $S(x_0, x_1, \dots) = (0, x_0, x_1, \dots)$.
Then $S$ is not surjective.

The first standard basis vector $e_0 = (1, 0, 0, \dots)$ is not in the range of $S$, since every
vector in the range has $0$ in coordinate $0$.

articles.title: Numerical range of the backward shift is the open unit disc
articles.statement:
The numerical range of the backward shift on `ℓ²(ℕ, ℂ)` is the
open unit disc.

articles.title: Numerical range of the unilateral shift is the open unit disc
articles.statement:
The numerical range of the unilateral shift on `ℓ²(ℕ, ℂ)` is the
open unit disc.

articles.title: Pointwise action of one minus a scaled backward shift
articles.statement: Pointwise action of `1 - μ • B`.

articles.title: Backward shift quadratic form at a geometric vector
articles.statement:
The quadratic form of the backward shift at the geometric vector
attached to `u` is `conj u`.

articles.title: Quadratic form of the backward shift as a series
articles.statement:
The quadratic form of the backward shift as a series over consecutive
coordinates: `⟪B x, x⟫ = ∑' n, conj (x (n + 1)) * x n`.

articles.title: Forward shift quadratic form at a geometric vector
articles.statement:
The quadratic form of the forward shift at the geometric vector
attached to `u` is `u` itself.

articles.title: Quadratic form of the forward shift as a series
articles.statement:
The quadratic form of the forward shift as a series over consecutive
coordinates: `⟪S x, x⟫ = ∑' n, conj (x n) * x (n + 1)`.

articles.title: Coordinates of the unilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and
let $S$ be the unilateral shift on the Hilbert space $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of
square-summable sequences in $\mathbb{K}$. For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and
every $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the coordinate $(Sx)_i$ is the $i$-th term of the forward shift of $x$:
$(Sx)_0 = 0$ and $(Sx)_{n+1} = x_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Pointwise action of a power of the unilateral shift
articles.statement: Pointwise action of `S ^ n`: it inserts `n` zeroes in front.

articles.title: Powers of the unilateral shift as iterates of the shift map
articles.statement: The coercion of `S ^ n` is the `n`-fold iterate of `shiftFun`.

articles.title: The unilateral shift operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The
unilateral shift is the bounded linear operator $S$ on the Hilbert space
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of square-summable sequences in $\mathbb{K}$ given by
$S(x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots) = (0, x_0, x_1, \dots)$. It is bounded because $\|Sx\| = \|x\|$ for every
$x$.

articles.title: Coordinates of the unilateral shift after the backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and on the Hilbert space $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ of
square-summable sequences in $\mathbb{K}$ let $S$ be the unilateral shift,
$S(x_0, x_1, \dots) = (0, x_0, x_1, \dots)$, and $B$ the backward shift, $(Bx)_n = x_{n+1}$.
Then for every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and every $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the coordinate
$(SBx)_i$ is $0$ if $i = 0$ and is $x_i$ if $i \ne 0$.

articles.title: The unilateral shift composed with the backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be the unilateral (forward) shift and $B$ the
backward shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, and let $e_0$ be the first standard
basis vector. Then $S \circ B = 1 - P$, where $P$ is the rank-one operator
$P x = \langle e_0, x \rangle e_0 = x_0 e_0$.

Thus $S \circ B$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\{e_0\}^\perp$.

articles.title: Iterated forward shift inserts leading zeroes
articles.statement:
Iterating the forward-shift function `n` times inserts `n` zeroes
in front of the sequence.

articles.title: Forward shift of a sequence
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The
forward shift of a sequence $x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ is the sequence $S x$ with
$(S x)_0 = 0$ and $(S x)_{n+1} = x_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Coordinates of the forward-shift linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and every $i \in \mathbb{N}$,
the $i$-th coordinate of the forward-shift linear map applied to $x$ equals the $i$-th term
of the forward shift of the sequence $x$, namely $0$ for $i = 0$ and $x_{i-1}$ for
$i \ge 1$.

articles.title: Forward shift as a linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The
forward shift is the $\mathbb{K}$-linear map
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K}) \to \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ sending $x$ to the forward
shift of the sequence $x$, that is, to $(0, x_0, x_1, \dots)$, which is again
square-summable.

articles.title: Factorization of the shifted unilateral shift
articles.statement: The key factorization: `S - μ = S (1 - μ B) + μ (S B - 1)`.

articles.title: Spectrum of the backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The
spectrum of the backward shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, in the algebra of bounded
operators, is the closed unit ball $\{\mu \in \mathbb{K} : \|\mu\| \le 1\}$: the closed unit
disc when $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{C}$ and the interval $[-1, 1]$ when $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Spectrum of the unilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The spectrum over $\mathbb{K}$ of the unilateral shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$
is the closed unit ball $\{\mu \in \mathbb{K} : |\mu| \le 1\}$ of $\mathbb{K}$.

articles.title: Shifted unilateral shift on the truncated geometric vector
articles.statement:
The coordinates of `(S - μ • 1)` applied to the truncated
geometric vector: `-μ` at `0`, `(star μ)^N` at `N + 1`, and `0`
elsewhere, when `‖μ‖ = 1`.

articles.title: Strict AM-GM bound on consecutive coordinates of a unit vector
articles.statement:
For a unit vector `x`, the sum of the products of consecutive
coordinate norms is strictly less than `1`: termwise AM–GM gives a
bound of `(1 + (1 - ‖x 0‖²)) / 2 ≤ 1`, and the AM–GM inequality is
strict at the coordinate supplied by `exists_norm_ne_norm_succ`.

articles.title: Surjectivity of powers of the backward shift
articles.statement: The backward shift power is surjective.

articles.title: Square sum of the backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the backward shift $(x_1, x_2, \dots)$ of
$x$ satisfies $\sum_{i=0}^{\infty} |x_{i+1}|^2 \le \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} |x_i|^2$: the left
side is a tail of the right side.

articles.title: Square sum of the forward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the forward shift $S x = (0, x_0, x_1, \dots)$
of $x$ satisfies $\sum_{i=0}^{\infty} |(S x)_i|^2 = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} |x_i|^2$.

articles.title: Adjoint of the weighted shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let
$(w_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $\mathbb{K}$. The adjoint of the weighted
forward shift $S_w$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by $(S_w x)_0 = 0$ and
$(S_w x)_{n+1} = w_n x_n$, is the weighted backward shift $B_w$, given by
$(B_w x)_i = \overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1}$; that is, $S_w^* = B_w$.

articles.title: The weighted backward shift after the forward shift is diagonal
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $(w_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $\mathbb{K}$,
and on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ let $S_w$ be the weighted forward shift,
$(S_w x)_0 = 0$ and $(S_w x)_{n+1} = w_n x_n$, and $B_w$ the weighted backward shift,
$(B_w x)_i = \overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1}$. Then $(B_w S_w x)_i = |w_i|^2 x_i$ for every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and every $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: The weighted backward shift is a left inverse for unimodular weights
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(w_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $\mathbb{K}$ with
$|w_n| = 1$ for every $n$. On $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ let $S_w$ be the weighted forward
shift, $(S_w x)_0 = 0$ and $(S_w x)_{n+1} = w_n x_n$, and $B_w$ the weighted backward shift,
$(B_w x)_i = \overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1}$. Then $B_w S_w$ is the identity operator.

articles.title: Differences of bounded sequences are bounded
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, and let $w, v : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be bounded sequences, that is, there are
constants $C$ and $D$ with $|w_n| \le C$ and $|v_n| \le D$ for all $n$. Then $w - v$ is bounded:
there is a constant $E$ with $|w_n - v_n| \le E$ for all $n$.

articles.title: Truncated weights are bounded
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let
$w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be bounded, that is, $|w_n| \le C$ for all $n$ for some constant
$C$, and let $N \in \mathbb{N}$. Then the truncation $w^{(N)}$ of $w$ after $N$ coordinates, given
by $w^{(N)}_n = w_n$ for $n < N$ and $w^{(N)}_n = 0$ for $n \ge N$, is bounded as well.

articles.title: Weighted shifts with nonzero weights are injective
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$ and let $(w_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $\mathbb{K}$ with
$w_n \neq 0$ for every $n$. Then the weighted forward shift $S_w$ on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by $(S_w x)_0 = 0$ and $(S_w x)_{n+1} = w_n x_n$, is
injective.

The coordinates of $x$ are recovered from $S_w x$ one by one: $x_n = (S_w x)_{n+1} / w_n$.

articles.title: Compactness criterion for weighted shifts
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$
and let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded sequence of weights, that is, $|w_n| \le C$
for all $n$ for some constant $C$. The weighted forward shift $S_w$ on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, which sends $x$ to $(0, w_0 x_0, w_1 x_1, \dots)$, is a compact
operator if and only if $w_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Weighted shifts with eventually vanishing weights are compact
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded sequence of weights,
and suppose there is $N \in \mathbb{N}$ with $w_n = 0$ for all $n \ge N$. Then the weighted forward
shift $S_w$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, which sends $x$ to $(0, w_0 x_0, w_1 x_1, \dots)$,
is a compact operator.

articles.title: Isometric weighted shifts
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let
$(w_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $\mathbb{K}$. The weighted forward shift
$S_w$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by $(S_w x)_0 = 0$ and
$(S_w x)_{n+1} = w_n x_n$, is an isometry if and only if $|w_n| = 1$ for every $n$.

articles.title: Weighted backward shifts preserve square-summability
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$ and let $(w_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $\mathbb{K}$. For every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the sequence $(\overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1})_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$
is square-summable.

articles.title: Weighted forward shifts preserve square-summability
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$ and let $(w_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $\mathbb{K}$. For every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the sequence $y$ with $y_0 = 0$ and
$y_{n+1} = w_n x_n$ is square-summable.

articles.title: Norm of the weighted backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and
let $(w_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $\mathbb{K}$. The weighted backward shift
$B_w$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by $(B_w x)_i = \overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1}$, has
operator norm $\|B_w\| = \sup_n |w_n|$.

articles.title: Norm bound for the weighted backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$ and let $(w_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $\mathbb{K}$, and let
$B_w$ be the weighted backward shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by
$(B_w x)_i = \overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1}$. Then $\|B_w x\| \le (\sup_n |w_n|)\, \|x\|$ for every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: Weighted shifts with unimodular weights preserve norms
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$ and let $(w_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $\mathbb{K}$ with $|w_n| = 1$ for
every $n$. Then the weighted forward shift $S_w$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, given by
$(S_w x)_0 = 0$ and $(S_w x)_{n+1} = w_n x_n$, satisfies $\|S_w x\| = \|x\|$ for every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: Uniform weight bounds bound the weighted shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with bounded moduli, and let $S_w$ be
the weighted forward shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. If $C$ is a real number with
$|w_n| \le C$ for every $n$, then the operator norm of $S_w$ is at most $C$.

articles.title: Operator norm of a weighted shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and
let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with bounded moduli. The weighted forward shift
$S_w$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ has operator norm $\|S_w\| = \sup_n |w_n|$.

articles.title: Norm bound for weighted shift images
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and
let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with bounded moduli. For every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the weighted forward shift $S_w$, viewed as a linear map,
satisfies $\|S_w x\| \le \left(\sup_n |w_n|\right) \|x\|$.

articles.title: A vanishing weight makes the weighted shift non-injective
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with bounded
moduli. If $w_n = 0$ for some $n$, then the weighted forward shift $S_w$ on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ is not injective.

Indeed, $S_w$ sends the $n$-th standard basis vector to $0$.

articles.title: Forward-after-backward weighted shift is diagonal
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with bounded moduli, and let $S_w$ and
$B_w$ be the weighted forward and backward shifts on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the composite $S_w B_w$ satisfies $(S_w B_w x)_0 = 0$ and
$(S_w B_w x)_i = |w_{i-1}|^2 x_i$ for every $i \ge 1$.

articles.title: Weighted shifts with truncated weights converge in operator norm
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be a bounded sequence with
$w_n \to 0$. For $N \in \mathbb{N}$ let $w^{(N)}$ be the truncation of $w$ after $N$ coordinates,
with $w^{(N)}_n = w_n$ for $n < N$ and $w^{(N)}_n = 0$ for $n \ge N$, and for bounded weights $u$
let $S_u$ be the weighted forward shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, sending $x$ to
$(0, u_0 x_0, u_1 x_1, \dots)$. Then $S_{w^{(N)}} \to S_w$ in operator norm as $N \to \infty$.

articles.title: Truncated weights vanish from the cutoff on
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$, and let $N, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge N$.
Then the truncation $w^{(N)}$ of $w$ after $N$ coordinates (equal to $w_k$ for $k < N$ and to $0$
for $k \ge N$) satisfies $w^{(N)}_n = 0$.

articles.title: Truncated weights agree with the weights below the cutoff
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$, and let $N, n \in \mathbb{N}$
with $n < N$. Then the truncation $w^{(N)}$ of $w$ after $N$ coordinates (equal to $w_k$ for
$k < N$ and to $0$ for $k \ge N$) satisfies $w^{(N)}_n = w_n$.

articles.title: Truncated weights
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For a sequence
$w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the truncation of $w$ after $N$ coordinates
is the sequence $w^{(N)}$ with $w^{(N)}_n = w_n$ for $n < N$ and $w^{(N)}_n = 0$ for $n \ge N$.

articles.title: Coordinates of the weighted backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with bounded moduli, and let $B_w$ be
the weighted backward shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For every
$x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and every $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the $i$-th coordinate of
$B_w x$ is the weighted backward-shift function of $w$ applied to $x$ at $i$, that is,
$(B_w x)_i = \overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1}$.

articles.title: Unit weights give the plain backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. With every weight equal to $1$, the weighted backward shift on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ is the canonical backward shift.

articles.title: Weighted backward shift on basis vectors
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with bounded moduli, and write $e_n$
for the $n$-th standard basis vector of $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For every $n$, the
weighted backward shift $B_w$ satisfies $B_w e_{n+1} = \overline{w_n}\, e_n$.

articles.title: Weighted backward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let
$w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with bounded moduli. The weighted backward shift $B_w$
is the bounded operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ obtained by applying the backward shift
$(x_0, x_1, \dots) \mapsto (x_1, x_2, \dots)$ and then multiplying coordinate $i$ by
$\overline{w_i}$; thus $(B_w x)_i = \overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1}$.

articles.title: Coordinates of the weighted backward-shift function
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. For weights $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$, a sequence
$x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ and $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the weighted backward-shift function of
$w$ applied to $x$ takes the value $\overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1}$ at $i$.

articles.title: Weighted backward shift of a sequence
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
For weights $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ and a sequence $x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$, the
weighted backward shift of $x$ is the sequence whose term at index $i$ is
$\overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1}$.

The weights are conjugated so that the resulting operator on $\ell^2$ is the adjoint of the
weighted forward shift.

articles.title: The weighted backward shift linear map agrees with the shift of sequences
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with
$\sup_n |w_n| < \infty$. For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the image of $x$ under
the weighted backward shift with weights $w$, regarded as a linear map on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, is as a sequence the weighted backward shift of $x$: its term
at index $i$ is $\overline{w_i}\, x_{i+1}$ for every $i$.

articles.title: Weighted backward shift as a linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$
and let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with $\sup_n |w_n| < \infty$. The weighted
backward shift linear map with weights $w$ is the bounded weighted backward shift operator on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ with weights $w$, regarded as a $\mathbb{K}$-linear map from
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ to itself (forgetting continuity).

articles.title: The weighted forward shift agrees with the shift of sequences
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with
$\sup_n |w_n| < \infty$. For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the image of $x$ under
the weighted forward shift operator with weights $w$ is as a sequence the weighted forward
shift of $x$: its term at index $0$ is $0$ and its term at index $n + 1$ is $w_n x_n$ for
every $n$.

articles.title: Coordinates of the weighted forward shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with $\sup_n |w_n| < \infty$, and let
$S_w$ be the weighted forward shift operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ with weights $w$.
For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ and every $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the coordinate
$(S_w x)_i$ is the term at index $i$ of the weighted forward shift of the sequence $x$; that is,
$(S_w x)_0 = 0$ and $(S_w x)_{n+1} = w_n x_n$.

articles.title: The weighted forward shift with unit weights is the unilateral shift
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The weighted forward shift operator on
$\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ whose weights are all equal to $1$ is the unilateral forward
shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$.

articles.title: The weighted forward shift on basis vectors
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with $\sup_n |w_n| < \infty$, and let
$(e_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be the standard basis vectors of $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$. For
every $n$, the weighted forward shift operator with weights $w$ sends $e_n$ to $w_n e_{n+1}$.

articles.title: Weighted shift of a difference of weights
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, and let $w, v : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be sequences such that $w$, $v$ and $w - v$
are bounded. Writing $S_u$ for the weighted forward shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ with
bounded weights $u$, sending $x$ to $(0, u_0 x_0, u_1 x_1, \dots)$, we have
$S_{w - v} = S_w - S_v$.

articles.title: Weighted forward shift operator
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let
$w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be weights with $\sup_n |w_n| < \infty$. The weighted forward
shift with weights $w$ is the bounded operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ obtained by
first applying the diagonal operator $x \mapsto (w_n x_n)_{n}$ and then the unilateral forward
shift $(x_0, x_1, \dots) \mapsto (0, x_0, x_1, \dots)$.

articles.title: Weighted forward shift at a successor index
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. For weights $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$, a sequence
$x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the term at index $n + 1$ of the weighted
forward shift of $x$ is $w_n x_n$.

articles.title: Weighted forward shift at index zero
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
For all weights $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ and every sequence $x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$,
the term at index $0$ of the weighted forward shift of $x$ is $0$.

articles.title: Weighted forward shift of a sequence
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. For a weight sequence $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ and a sequence
$x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$, the weighted forward shift of $x$ is the sequence $y$ with
$y_0 = 0$ and $y_{n+1} = w_n x_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Coordinates of the weighted forward shift linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be a weight sequence
whose norms $\|w_n\|$ are bounded above. For every $x \in \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$, the
image of $x$ under the weighted forward shift linear map, viewed as a sequence, is the weighted
forward shift of $x$: its coordinate $0$ is $0$ and its coordinate $n + 1$ is $w_n x_n$ for
every $n$.

articles.title: Weighted forward shift as a linear map
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, and let $w : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{K}$ be a weight sequence whose norms
$\|w_n\|$ are bounded above. The weighted forward shift linear map is the $\mathbb{K}$-linear
map $\ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K}) \to \ell^2(\mathbb{N}, \mathbb{K})$ underlying the bounded
weighted forward shift operator (multiplication by $w$ followed by the forward shift), which
sends $x$ to the sequence $y$ with $y_0 = 0$ and $y_{n+1} = w_n x_n$.

articles.title: The sequence space $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$
articles.statement:
We write $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ for the Hilbert
space of square-summable sequences $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of complex numbers.

articles.title: Almost Mathieu operator
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$, $\lambda$ and $\theta$ be real numbers. A bounded
complex-linear operator $H$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ is an almost Mathieu operator with frequency
$\alpha$, coupling $\lambda$ and phase $\theta$ when, for every $u \in \ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ and
every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$,

$$(Hu)(n) = u(n+1) + u(n-1) + 2\lambda \cos(2\pi(\theta + n\alpha))\, u(n).$$

articles.title: Ten Martini theorem (Avila–Jitomirskaya)
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$, $\lambda$ and $\theta$ be real
numbers with $\alpha$ irrational and $\lambda \neq 0$. Then there is an almost Mathieu operator $H$
on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ with frequency $\alpha$, coupling $\lambda$ and phase $\theta$, and the
spectrum of $H$ is nonempty, compact, perfect and totally disconnected, that is, a Cantor set.

## Sources

- A. Avila and S. Jitomirskaya, 'The Ten Martini Problem', Ann. of Math. 170 (2009), 303-342, https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2009.170.303. Problem `ten_martini_problem` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Normal operator with trivial kernel has dense range
articles.statement:
A normal operator with trivial kernel has dense range: the residual
spectrum of a normal operator is empty.

articles.title: Epsilon characterization of approximate eigenvalues
articles.statement: The `∀ ε > 0` characterization of approximate eigenvalues.

articles.title: Eigenvalues are approximate eigenvalues
articles.statement: Exact eigenvalues are approximate eigenvalues.

articles.title: Spectral values of a normal operator are approximate eigenvalues
articles.statement: Every spectral value of a normal operator is an approximate eigenvalue.

articles.title: Approximate eigenvalue of an operator
articles.statement:
`μ` is an **approximate eigenvalue** of `T` if there is a sequence of
unit vectors `xₙ` with `(μ • 1 - T) xₙ → 0`.

articles.title: Scalar shifts of a normal operator are normal
articles.statement: Shifting by a scalar preserves normality.

articles.title: Weyl's criterion for self-adjoint operators
articles.statement:
Weyl's criterion: for a self-adjoint operator, the spectrum is exactly
the approximate point spectrum.

articles.title: Spectrum of a normal operator equals its approximate point spectrum
articles.statement:
For a normal operator, the spectrum is exactly the approximate point
spectrum.

articles.title: Approximate eigenvalues lie in the spectrum
articles.statement: Every approximate eigenvalue is a spectral value (no normality needed).

articles.title: Resolvent factorization for the Cayley transform
articles.statement:
The resolvent-type factorization behind the spectral mapping: for
`μ ≠ 1` and `λ = i * (1 + μ) / (1 - μ)`,
`μ • 1 - U = ((μ - 1) • (A - λ • 1)) * (A + i • 1)⁻¹`.

articles.title: Cayley transform of an operator
articles.statement:
The Cayley transform of an operator `A`: `(A - i) * (A + i)⁻¹`. The
factor `A + i • 1` is a unit when `A` is self-adjoint on a complete Hilbert space (see
`isUnit_add_I_smul_one_of_isSelfAdjoint` below), in which case the ring
inverse here is the genuine operator inverse.

articles.title: Factors of the Cayley transform commute
articles.statement: The two factors of the Cayley transform commute.

articles.title: Inverse Cayley formula
articles.statement: The inverse Cayley formula: `A = i • (1 + U) * (1 - U)⁻¹`.

articles.title: Spectral mapping for the Cayley transform, preimage direction
articles.statement:
The preimage direction of the spectral mapping: every point of the
spectrum of `U` is `(w - i) / (w + i)` for some `w` in the spectrum of `A`.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of the Cayley transform
articles.statement:
The eigenvalue correspondence: for `μ ≠ 1`, `μ` is an eigenvalue of the
Cayley transform `U` iff `i * (1 + μ) / (1 - μ)` is an eigenvalue of `A`.

articles.title: Self-adjoint operator plus $i$ is invertible
articles.statement: For a self-adjoint operator, `A + i • 1` is a unit.

articles.title: Cayley transform of a self-adjoint operator is invertible
articles.statement: The Cayley transform of a self-adjoint operator is a unit.

articles.title: One minus the Cayley transform is invertible
articles.statement:
`1 - U` is a unit for the Cayley transform of a self-adjoint operator:
`1` is never in the spectrum of `U`.

articles.title: Inverse of a self-adjoint operator plus $i$ is a unit
articles.statement: The inverse of `A + i • 1` is a unit for self-adjoint `A`.

articles.title: Nonzero scalar operators are units
articles.statement: A nonzero scalar operator is a unit.

articles.title: Self-adjoint operator minus $i$ is invertible
articles.statement: For a self-adjoint operator, `A - i • 1` is a unit.

articles.title: Self-adjoint operator minus a non-real scalar is invertible
articles.statement:
For a self-adjoint operator, `A - w • 1` is a unit whenever `w` has
nonzero imaginary part. The proof is the norm estimate
`‖(A - w • 1) x‖ ≥ |w.im| * ‖x‖`, read off from the imaginary part of
`⟪(A - w • 1) x, x⟫`.

articles.title: Spectral mapping for the Cayley transform, image direction
articles.statement:
The image direction of the spectral mapping: if `w` is in the spectrum
of `A`, then `(w - i) / (w + i)` is in the spectrum of `U`.

articles.title: Cayley transform of a self-adjoint operator is unitary
articles.statement: The Cayley transform of a self-adjoint operator is unitary.

articles.title: Adjoint of the Cayley transform is a right inverse
articles.statement: The Cayley transform of a self-adjoint operator satisfies `U * U† = 1`.

articles.title: Cayley transform preserves norms of vectors
articles.statement: The Cayley transform of a self-adjoint operator is an isometry.

articles.title: Operator norm of the Cayley transform is one
articles.statement: On a nontrivial space, the Cayley transform has operator norm `1`.

articles.title: Spectrum of the Cayley transform lies on the unit circle
articles.statement: Points of the spectrum of the Cayley transform lie on the unit circle.

articles.title: Formula for one plus the Cayley transform
articles.statement: `1 + U` is `2 • A` times the inverse of `A + i • 1`.

articles.title: One is not in the spectrum of the Cayley transform
articles.statement: `1` is never in the spectrum of the Cayley transform.

articles.title: Formula for one minus the Cayley transform
articles.statement: `1 - U` is `2 • (i • 1)` times the inverse of `A + i • 1`.

articles.title: Inverse of a scalar operator
articles.statement:
The ring inverse of a scalar operator is the scalar operator of the
inverse scalar.

articles.title: Spectrum of the Cayley transform
articles.statement:
The spectrum of the Cayley transform is the image of the spectrum of `A`
under the Möbius map `λ ↦ (λ - i) / (λ + i)`.

articles.title: Adjoint of the Cayley transform
articles.statement: The adjoint of the Cayley transform.

articles.title: Adjoint of the Cayley transform is a left inverse
articles.statement: The Cayley transform of a self-adjoint operator satisfies `U† * U = 1`.

articles.title: Spectral theorem for compact normal operators
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex Hilbert space and $T$
a compact normal operator on $E$. Then there are a Hilbert basis $(b_i)_{i \in I}$ of $E$
and complex numbers $(\mu_i)_{i \in I}$ such that $T b_i = \mu_i b_i$ for every $i$, and the
eigenvalues vanish at infinity: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ the set of $i$ with
$|\mu_i| \ge \varepsilon$ is finite.

## Sources

- Compact normal spectral theorem, Hilbert-Schmidt and Riesz 1910s; Reed-Simon I; Rudin Functional Analysis; Lean states complex Hilbert compact `IsStarNormal` case with same finite-level-set vanishing condition and same-universe index.

articles.title: Scattering length
articles.statement:
Let $v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ be a potential. If there is a
radial scattering solution $w$ to the scattering equation with potential $v$, the scattering
length of $v$ is $a(v) = (8\pi)^{-1} \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} v(x)\,(1 - w(x))\,dx$, where $w$ is
one such solution, chosen arbitrarily; if there is no radial scattering solution, $a(v) = 0$.

This is Equation (3.5) of Fournais–Solovej. Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.2 the radial
scattering solution exists and is unique, so the choice does not matter there.

articles.title: The box $((0,L)^3)^N$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$ and a real number $L$, the box
$([0,L]^3)^N$ is the set of configurations $(x_1, \dots, x_N)$ of $N$ points of $\mathbb{R}^3$
such that every coordinate of every point $x_i$ lies in the closed interval $[0, L]$.

articles.title: Smooth functions supported inside the box
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$ and a real number
$L$, $C_0^\infty(([0,L]^3)^N) \setminus \{0\}$ consists of the functions
$\Psi : (\mathbb{R}^3)^N \to \mathbb{R}$ that are smooth on the box $([0,L]^3)^N$, whose closed
support is contained in the interior of the box, and that are not identically zero.

The functions are defined on all of $(\mathbb{R}^3)^N$ rather than on the box only.

articles.title: Radial functions
articles.statement:
A function $v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ is radial if
$v(x) = v(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\|x\| = \|y\|$.

articles.title: Scattering solutions
articles.statement:
Let $v, w : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$. The function $w$ is a
scattering solution for the potential $v$ if $w$ and $v\,(1 - w)$ are locally integrable,
$w(x) \to 0$ as $\|x\| \to \infty$, and $w$ solves the scattering equation
$-\Delta w = \frac{1}{2} v\,(1 - w)$ (Equation (3.4) of Fournais–Solovej) in the weak sense:
for every smooth, compactly supported $\varphi : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$,

$$-\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} w\,\Delta\varphi = \frac{1}{2} \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} v\,(1 - w)\,\varphi.$$

articles.title: Lee–Huang–Yang lower bound for dilute Bose gases
articles.statement:
There are a real number $\eta$ and a
function $\mathcal{C}$ of two real variables such that the following holds. Let
$v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ be a non-negative, radial, integrable potential that is not
almost everywhere zero, and let $R > 0$ be such that the closed support of $v$ lies in the open
ball $B(0, R)$. Let $a$ be the scattering length of $v$, let $\mathcal{R}(v) = \int v/(8\pi a)$,
and let $e(\rho, v)$ be the ground state energy density at density $\rho$: the limit, as
$L \to \infty$ and $N/L^3 \to \rho$, of $L^{-3}$ times the infimum, over
$\Psi \in C_0^\infty(([0,L]^3)^N) \setminus \{0\}$, of
$\langle \Psi, H_N \Psi \rangle / \|\Psi\|^2$, where the inner product and norm are those of
$L^2(([0,L]^3)^N)$ and, writing points of $(\mathbb{R}^3)^N$ as $(x_1, \dots, x_N)$ and
$\Delta_{x_i}$ for the Laplacian in the variable $x_i$,
$H_N = \sum_{i=1}^{N} -\Delta_{x_i} + \sum_{1 \le i < j \le N} v(x_i - x_j)$. Then
$\eta > 0$, and for all sufficiently small $\rho > 0$,

$$
e(\rho, v) \ge 4\pi\rho^2 a \left(1 + \frac{128}{15\sqrt{\pi}}\sqrt{\rho a^3} -
\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{R}(v), R/a)\,(\rho a^3)^{1/2 + \eta}\right).
$$

The source takes the limit $\rho a^3 \to 0^+$; for fixed $v$ this is the same as $\rho \to 0^+$.
Although the wording of Theorem 1.2 in the source suggests that $\eta$ may depend on
$\mathcal{R}(v)$ and $R/a$, Theorem 6.8 there shows that $\eta$ is a universal constant.

## Sources

- S. Fournais and J. P. Solovej, `The energy of dilute Bose gases`, Annals of Math, 192 (3) 2020. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_bose_gases` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Lee–Huang–Yang error exponent
articles.statement:
$\eta$ is a real constant, not given explicitly, that
serves as the exponent in the error term $(\rho a^3)^{1/2 + \eta}$ of the Lee–Huang–Yang lower
bound (Theorem 1.2), where $\rho$ is the density and $a$ the scattering length of the
potential; that theorem asserts $\eta > 0$.

## Sources

- S. Fournais and J. P. Solovej, `The energy of dilute Bose gases`, Annals of Math, 192 (3) 2020. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_bose_gases` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Lee–Huang–Yang error constant
articles.statement:
$\mathcal{C}$ is a real-valued function of two real
variables, not given explicitly. Let $v$ be a potential with scattering length $a$ whose closed
support lies in the open ball $B(0, R)$, and let $\mathcal{R}(v) = \int v/(8\pi a)$. In the
Lee–Huang–Yang lower bound (Theorem 1.2) for $v$ at density $\rho$, the error term is
$\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{R}(v), R/a)\,(\rho a^3)^{1/2 + \eta}$, where $\eta$ is the Lee–Huang–Yang
error exponent, so its constant depends only on $\mathcal{R}(v)$ and $R/a$.

## Sources

- S. Fournais and J. P. Solovej, `The energy of dilute Bose gases`, Annals of Math, 192 (3) 2020. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_bose_gases` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: The ratio $\mathcal{R}(v)$
articles.statement:
For a potential $v : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ with
scattering length $a(v)$, let $\mathcal{R}(v) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} v(x)/(8\pi a(v))\,dx$. When
$a(v) \neq 0$ this is the ratio of $(8\pi)^{-1} \int v$ to $a(v)$.

articles.title: Krein–Rutman theorem for $C(K)$
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff space and let $T$ be a compact
bounded linear operator on the real Banach space $C(K, \mathbb{R})$ of continuous real functions
on $K$ that is positive: $Tf \ge 0$ pointwise whenever $f \ge 0$ pointwise. Let $r(T)$ be the
spectral radius of $T$, the supremum of $|\lambda|$ over the real spectrum of $T$. If $r(T) > 0$,
then there is a nonzero $f \in C(K, \mathbb{R})$ with $f \ge 0$ pointwise and $Tf = r(T) f$.

## Sources

- M. G. Krein and M. A. Rutman, Linear operators leaving invariant a cone in a Banach space, Uspekhi Mat. Nauk 3 (1948), 1–95, positive compact operator principal eigenvalue; Deimling, Nonlinear Functional Analysis; Lean states `C(K, ℝ)` compact positive case with spectralRadius eigenvector and nonnegativity.

articles.title: Numerical radius bounds the normalized imaginary part of the quadratic form
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be
a bounded linear operator on a complex inner product space $H$, with numerical radius $w(T)$. For
every $x \in H$, $|\operatorname{Im} \langle Tx, x\rangle| / \|x\|^2 \le w(T)$, where division by
zero is taken to be $0$, so the case $x = 0$ is trivial.

articles.title: Numerical radius bounds the Rayleigh quotient
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on a
complex inner product space $H$, with numerical radius $w(T)$. For every $x \in H$, the Rayleigh
quotient $R_T(x) = \operatorname{Re} \langle Tx, x\rangle / \|x\|^2$, taken to be $0$ at $x = 0$,
satisfies $|R_T(x)| \le w(T)$.

articles.title: Numerical radius bounds the normalized real part of the quadratic form
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a
bounded linear operator on a complex inner product space $H$, with numerical radius $w(T)$. For
every $x \in H$, $|\operatorname{Re} \langle Tx, x\rangle| / \|x\|^2 \le w(T)$, where division by
zero is taken to be $0$, so the case $x = 0$ is trivial.

articles.title: The numerical-radius family is bounded above
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on a
complex inner product space $H$. The set $\{|\langle Tx, x\rangle| : x \in H,\ \|x\| = 1\}$ is
bounded above.

The proof shows that $\|T\|$ is an upper bound, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

articles.title: Cartesian decomposition
articles.statement:
Every bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space
satisfies $T = A + iB$, where $A = (T + T^*)/2$ and $B = (T - T^*)/(2i)$ are the real and
imaginary Cartesian parts of $T$ and $T^*$ is the adjoint of $T$.

articles.title: Imaginary Cartesian part of an operator
articles.statement:
For a bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex
Hilbert space with adjoint $T^*$, the imaginary Cartesian part of $T$ is the bounded linear
operator $(T - T^*)/(2i)$.

articles.title: Real Cartesian part of an operator
articles.statement:
For a bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert
space with adjoint $T^*$, the real Cartesian part of $T$ is the bounded linear operator
$(T + T^*)/2$.

articles.title: Conjugates of spectral values lie in the closed numerical range
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a bounded
linear operator on a complex Hilbert space $E$, whose inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$
is conjugate-linear in its first argument and linear in its second, and let
$W(A) = \{\langle A x, x \rangle : x \in E,\ \|x\| = 1\}$ be the numerical range of $A$. If $z$
is in the spectrum of $A$, then the complex conjugate $\overline{z}$ lies in the closure of
$W(A)$.

articles.title: Conjugates of eigenvalues lie in the numerical range
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a bounded linear operator
on a complex inner product space $E$, whose inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is
conjugate-linear in its first argument and linear in its second, let
$W(A) = \{\langle A x, x \rangle : x \in E,\ \|x\| = 1\}$ be the numerical range of $A$ and let
$z \in \mathbb{C}$. If there is a vector $x \in E$ with $\|x\| = 1$ and $A x = z x$, then the
complex conjugate $\overline{z}$ lies in $W(A)$ itself, not just in its closure.

Indeed $\langle A x, x \rangle = \overline{z}$ for such a unit eigenvector $x$.

articles.title: Lower bound from the numerical range
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner
product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$, conjugate-linear in the first argument and linear in the
second, and let $T : H \to H$ be a bounded linear operator. Let
$N(T) = \{\langle \psi, T\psi \rangle : \psi \in H,\ \|\psi\| = 1\} \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be the
numerical range of $T$, and for $z \in \mathbb{C}$ let $d(z, N(T))$ be the infimum of the
distances from $z$ to the points of $N(T)$, taken to be $0$ when $N(T)$ is empty. Then for every
$\psi \in H$ and every $z \in \mathbb{C}$, $\|(T - zI)\psi\| \ge d(z, N(T))\,\|\psi\|$, where $I$
is the identity operator on $H$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Operator theory; General theory of linear operators), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_55`.

articles.title: Unit vectors give points of the numerical range
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a bounded linear operator on a
complex inner product space $E$. For every $x \in E$ with $\|x\| = 1$, the number
$\langle A x, x \rangle$ lies in the numerical range $W(A)$.

articles.title: The imaginary Cartesian part is symmetric
articles.statement:
For every bounded linear operator $T$ on a
complex Hilbert space $H$ with adjoint $T^*$, the imaginary Cartesian part $B = (T - T^*)/(2i)$ is
symmetric: $\langle Bx, y\rangle = \langle x, By\rangle$ for all $x, y \in H$.

articles.title: The real Cartesian part is symmetric
articles.statement:
For every bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex
Hilbert space $H$ with adjoint $T^*$, the real Cartesian part $A = (T + T^*)/2$ is symmetric:
$\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle$ for all $x, y \in H$.

articles.title: Conjugate shifts off the closed numerical range are invertible
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a bounded
linear operator on a complex Hilbert space $E$, whose inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$
is conjugate-linear in its first argument and linear in its second, let
$W(A) = \{\langle A x, x \rangle : x \in E,\ \|x\| = 1\}$ be the numerical range of $A$ and let
$\mu \in \mathbb{C}$. If $\mu$ is not in the closure of $W(A)$, then $A - \overline{\mu}\, I$,
where $\overline{\mu}$ is the complex conjugate of $\mu$ and $I$ is the identity operator, is
invertible in the algebra of bounded linear operators on $E$.

Both this operator and its adjoint are bounded below, so it is injective with closed range, and
its range has trivial orthogonal complement, hence it is surjective.

articles.title: The numerical radius bounds the quadratic form on unit vectors
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded
linear operator on a complex inner product space $H$, with numerical radius $w(T)$. For every
$x \in H$ with $\|x\| = 1$, $|\langle Tx, x\rangle| \le w(T)$.

articles.title: Membership in the numerical range
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a bounded linear operator on a complex inner
product space $E$. A complex number $c$ lies in the numerical range $W(A)$ if and only if there is
a vector $x \in E$ with $\|x\| = 1$ and $\langle A x, x \rangle = c$.

articles.title: Norm of the imaginary part is at most the numerical radius
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a
bounded operator on a complex Hilbert space, with adjoint $T^*$, and let $B = (T - T^*)/(2i)$ be
its imaginary Cartesian part. Then $\|B\| \le w(T)$, where $\|B\|$ is the operator norm of $B$
and $w(T)$ is the numerical radius of $T$.

articles.title: Norm of the real part is at most the numerical radius
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded
operator on a complex Hilbert space, with adjoint $T^*$, and let $A = (T + T^*)/2$ be its real
Cartesian part. Then $\|A\| \le w(T)$, where $\|A\|$ is the operator norm of $A$ and $w(T)$ is
the numerical radius of $T$.

articles.title: Operator norm at most twice the numerical radius
articles.statement:
For every bounded operator $T$ on a
complex Hilbert space, $\|T\| \le 2\,w(T)$, where $\|T\|$ is the operator norm and $w(T)$ is the
numerical radius of $T$.

articles.title: Normalizing a nonzero vector gives a unit vector
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a nonzero vector in a
complex inner product space. Then the vector $\|x\|^{-1} x$ has norm $1$.

articles.title: The quadratic form of the adjoint has the same modulus
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded operator
on a complex Hilbert space $H$, with adjoint $T^*$. For every $x \in H$,
$|\langle T^* x, x\rangle| = |\langle T x, x\rangle|$, since $\langle T^* x, x\rangle$ is the
complex conjugate of $\langle T x, x\rangle$.

articles.title: Numerical radius of the adjoint
articles.statement:
For every bounded operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert
space, the numerical radius of its adjoint $T^*$ equals the numerical radius of $T$:
$w(T^*) = w(T)$.

articles.title: Numerical radius of a self-adjoint operator
articles.statement:
If $T$ is a self-adjoint bounded operator
on a complex Hilbert space, then its numerical radius equals its operator norm:
$w(T) = \|T\|$.

articles.title: Numerical radius at most the operator norm
articles.statement:
For every bounded operator $T$ on a complex
inner product space, the numerical radius $w(T)$ is at most the operator norm: $w(T) \le \|T\|$.

The proof is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

articles.title: Bounding the numerical radius from above
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded operator on a complex
inner product space $H$ and let $c \ge 0$ be a real number. If $|\langle T x, x\rangle| \le c$
for every unit vector $x \in H$, then the numerical radius of $T$ satisfies $w(T) \le c$.

The hypothesis $c \ge 0$ matters only when $H = 0$: there are no unit vectors, and $w(T) = 0$.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the numerical radius
articles.statement:
For every bounded operator $T$ on a complex inner
product space, the numerical radius $w(T)$ of $T$ satisfies $w(T) \ge 0$.

articles.title: Numerical radius
articles.statement:
The numerical radius of a bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex
Hilbert space $H$ is the real number
$w(T) = \sup \{ |\langle T x, x \rangle| : x \in H,\ \|x\| = 1 \}$, the supremum of the moduli of
the values $\langle T x, x \rangle$ over the unit vectors of $H$ (taken to be $0$ when $H = 0$).

articles.title: The numerical range is bounded by the operator norm
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a bounded linear operator
on a complex inner product space $E$. Then every point of the numerical range $W(A)$ has absolute
value at most the operator norm $\|A\|$: $W(A)$ lies in the closed disc of radius $\|A\|$ centred
at $0$.

articles.title: Numerical range
articles.statement:
For a bounded linear operator $A$ on a complex inner product space $E$,
the numerical range of $A$ is the set
$W(A) = \{\langle A x, x \rangle : x \in E,\ \|x\| = 1\} \subseteq \mathbb{C}$, where the inner
product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ of $E$ is conjugate-linear in its first argument and linear
in its second.

articles.title: Quadratic form of the imaginary Cartesian part
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded operator on a complex
Hilbert space $H$, whose inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is conjugate-linear in its
first argument, and let $B = (T - T^*)/(2i)$ be the imaginary Cartesian part of $T$. Then for
every $x \in H$ one has $\langle B x, x \rangle = -\operatorname{Im} \langle T x, x \rangle$.

The sign comes from the convention on the inner product: writing $T = A + iB$ with
$A = (T + T^*)/2$, one has
$\langle T x, x \rangle = \langle A x, x \rangle - i \langle B x, x \rangle$.

articles.title: Quadratic form of the real Cartesian part
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded operator on a complex
Hilbert space $H$ and let $A = (T + T^*)/2$ be the real Cartesian part of $T$. Then for every
$x \in H$ one has $\langle A x, x \rangle = \operatorname{Re} \langle T x, x \rangle$.

articles.title: Quadratic form at the normalized vector
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded operator on a complex inner
product space $H$. For every $x \in H$,
$\langle T(\|x\|^{-1} x), \|x\|^{-1} x \rangle = \|x\|^{-2} \langle T x, x \rangle$,
where $0^{-1}$ is read as $0$, so that for $x = 0$ both sides vanish.

articles.title: The spectrum lies in the conjugate of the closed numerical range
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a bounded
linear operator on a complex Hilbert space $E$, whose inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$
is conjugate-linear in its first argument and linear in its second, and let
$W(A) = \{\langle A x, x \rangle : x \in E,\ \|x\| = 1\}$ be the numerical range of $A$. Then
every point of the spectrum of $A$ is the complex conjugate $\overline{w}$ of some point $w$ of
the closure of $W(A)$.

articles.title: Complex conjugate of one half
articles.statement:
The complex conjugate of $1/2 \in \mathbb{C}$ is $1/2$, that
is, $\overline{1/2} = 1/2$.

articles.title: Complex conjugate of minus half the imaginary unit
articles.statement:
The complex conjugate of
$-i/2 \in \mathbb{C}$ is $i/2$, that is, $\overline{-i/2} = i/2$.

articles.title: Toeplitz–Hausdorff theorem without completeness
articles.statement:
The numerical range of a bounded linear
operator on a complex inner product space is convex. Completeness of the space is not needed.

articles.title: Toeplitz–Hausdorff theorem
articles.statement:
The numerical range of a bounded linear operator on a complex
Hilbert space is convex.

## Sources

- O. Toeplitz, Das algebraische Analogon zu einem Satze von Fejer, Math. Z. 2 (1918), 187-197, DOI 10.1007/BF01212904; F. Hausdorff, Der Wertvorrat einer Bilinearform, Math. Z. 3 (1919), 314-316, DOI 10.1007/BF01292610. It follows from `toeplitz_hausdorff_general`; the hypothesis `CompleteSpace E` is unused and keeps the source's shape.

articles.title: Spectral theorem for bounded self-adjoint operators, multiplication form
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
complex Hilbert space and $T$ a bounded self-adjoint operator on $E$. Then there are a measure
space $(X, \mu)$, a measurable function $\varphi : X \to \mathbb{R}$ and a linear isometric
isomorphism $U$ of $E$ onto $L^2(X, \mu; \mathbb{C})$ such that for every $x \in E$,
$U(Tx)(a) = \varphi(a)\,(Ux)(a)$ for $\mu$-almost every $a \in X$.

Proof: Scalar measures from the continuous functional calculus identify each cyclic subspace with an
$L^2$ space. A maximal orthogonal family of cyclic subspaces is then assembled over a disjoint-union
measure, where the spectral coordinate acts by multiplication.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Ch. 12.

articles.title: Scalar spectral measure of a vector
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complex Hilbert space, $T$ a bounded
self-adjoint operator on $E$ and $v \in E$. There is a finite regular measure $\mu$ on the
spectrum $\sigma(T) \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ of $T$ such that for every continuous function
$f : \sigma(T) \to \mathbb{R}$,
$\int_{\sigma(T)} f \, d\mu = \operatorname{Re} \langle f(T) v, v \rangle$, where $f(T)$ is the
continuous functional calculus of $T$ applied to $f$ viewed as a complex-valued function.

The measure lives on the complex spectrum. Its support is real because the spectrum of a
self-adjoint operator is real.

articles.title: Maximum principle for compact self-adjoint operators in finite dimension
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a
finite-dimensional Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $T$ be a
compact self-adjoint operator on $H$. Then there are $N \in \mathbb{N}$, nonzero real numbers
$s_0, \dots, s_{N-1}$ and an orthonormal family $u_0, \dots, u_{N-1}$ in $H$ such that
$T u_i = s_i u_i$ for every $i < N$, $|s_0| \ge |s_1| \ge \dots \ge |s_{N-1}|$, and for every
$i < N$ every unit vector $x \in H$ orthogonal to $u_0, \dots, u_{i-1}$ satisfies
$|\langle T x, x \rangle| \le |s_i|$, while $|\langle T u_i, u_i \rangle| = |s_i|$. Moreover
$T x = 0$ for every $x \in H$ orthogonal to all of $u_0, \dots, u_{N-1}$.

articles.title: Finite-rank approximation of compact self-adjoint operators
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a compact
self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space $H$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For every
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is a bounded self-adjoint operator $F$ on $H$ with finite-dimensional
range such that $\|T - F\| \le \varepsilon$.

articles.title: A nonzero compact self-adjoint operator has an eigenvalue of modulus equal to its norm
articles.statement:
Let $T \neq 0$ be a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space $H$ over
$\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Then $T$ has an eigenvalue $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with
$\mu \neq 0$ and $|\mu| = \|T\|$, where $\|T\|$ is the operator norm of $T$.

articles.title: Next eigenvalue after a finite family of eigenvectors
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a compact self-adjoint
operator on a Hilbert space $H$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $u_1, \dots, u_n \in H$ and
scalars $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n$ satisfy $T u_i = \mu_i u_i$ for every $i$, and let $S$ be the
orthogonal complement of the span of $u_1, \dots, u_n$. If $Tz \neq 0$ for some $z \in S$, then
there are a real number $r$ and a unit vector $v$ with $\langle v, u_i \rangle = 0$ for every $i$,
$Tv = rv$ and $\langle Tv, v \rangle = r$, such that $|\langle Tx, x \rangle| \le |r|$ for
every unit vector $x \in S$. In particular $v \in S$, so $|r|$ is the maximum of
$|\langle Tx, x \rangle|$ over unit vectors $x \in S$.

The vectors $u_i$ need not be orthonormal, or even nonzero.

articles.title: Deflation step
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space $H$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $S$ be a linear subspace of $H$ that admits an orthogonal
projection $P : H \to H$ onto $S$ and satisfies $T(S) \subseteq S$, and let $T_1 = PTP$ be the
compression of $T$ to $S$. If $T_1 \neq 0$, then there are a real number $r$ and a unit vector
$v \in S$ with $Tv = rv$, $|r| = \|T_1\|$ and $|r| \le \|T\|$.

articles.title: Maximum principle for compact self-adjoint operators
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a compact self-adjoint
operator on a Hilbert space $H$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Then one of the
following two alternatives holds.

Either there are $N \in \mathbb{N}$ (possibly $N = 0$, as for $T = 0$), nonzero real numbers
$s_0, \dots, s_{N-1}$ and an orthonormal family $u_0, \dots, u_{N-1}$ in $H$ such that
$T u_i = s_i u_i$ for every $i < N$, $|s_0| \ge |s_1| \ge \dots \ge |s_{N-1}|$, for every $i < N$
every unit vector $x \in H$ orthogonal to $u_0, \dots, u_{i-1}$ satisfies
$|\langle T x, x \rangle| \le |s_i|$ while $|\langle T u_i, u_i \rangle| = |s_i|$, and $T x = 0$
for every $x \in H$ orthogonal to all of $u_0, \dots, u_{N-1}$.

Or there are nonzero real numbers $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$ and an orthonormal sequence
$u_0, u_1, u_2, \dots$ in $H$ such that $T u_n = s_n u_n$ for every $n$, the sequence $|s_n|$ is
nonincreasing and tends to $0$ as $n \to \infty$, for every $n$ every unit vector $x \in H$
orthogonal to $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$ satisfies $|\langle T x, x \rangle| \le |s_n|$ while
$|\langle T u_n, u_n \rangle| = |s_n|$, and $T x = 0$ for every $x \in H$ orthogonal to every
$u_n$.

articles.title: Maximum principle as a sequence in infinite dimension
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a compact self-adjoint
operator on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space $H$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$. Then there are real numbers $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$ and an orthonormal sequence
$u_0, u_1, u_2, \dots$ in $H$ such that $T u_n = s_n u_n$ and $|s_{n+1}| \le |s_n|$ for every
$n$, $|s_n| \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, and for every $n$ every unit vector $x \in H$ orthogonal to
$u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$ satisfies $|\langle T x, x \rangle| \le |s_n|$, while
$|\langle T u_n, u_n \rangle| = |s_n|$.

Unlike the maximum principle for compact self-adjoint operators, the $s_n$ are not required to be
nonzero, and no claim is made that $T$ vanishes on the vectors orthogonal to every $u_n$.

articles.title: A nonzero compact self-adjoint operator has a real eigenvalue of modulus equal to its norm, with a unit eigenvector
articles.statement:
**A nonzero compact self-adjoint operator has a real eigenvalue of modulus equal to its norm,
with a unit eigenvector.** Let $T \neq 0$ be a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space
$H$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Then there are a real number $r$ and a unit
vector $u \in H$ with $T u = r u$ and $|r| = \|T\|$, where $\|T\|$ is the operator norm of $T$.

articles.title: Finiteness of large eigenvalues of a compact self-adjoint operator
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a compact
self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the set of eigenvalues $\mu$ of $T$ with $\varepsilon \le |\mu|$ is finite.

articles.title: Eigenvalues are bounded by the operator norm
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on an
inner product space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Every eigenvalue $\mu$ of $T$ satisfies
$|\mu| \le \|T\|$.

Indeed, if $Tx = \mu x$ with $x \neq 0$, then $|\mu| \, \|x\| = \|Tx\| \le \|T\| \, \|x\|$.

articles.title: Orthogonal complement of the nonzero-eigenvalue eigenspaces
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Hilbert space
over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $T : H \to H$ be a compact self-adjoint
bounded linear operator. Then the orthogonal complement of the subspace spanned by the
eigenspaces $\ker(T - \mu I)$ for all nonzero $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ equals the kernel of $T$.

articles.title: Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators (range decomposition form)
articles.statement:
**Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators (range
decomposition form).** Let $H$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$
and let $T : H \to H$ be a compact self-adjoint bounded linear operator. Then:
(1) the closure of the subspace spanned by the eigenspaces $\ker(T - \mu I)$ for all
nonzero $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ equals the closure of the range of $T$;
(2) the closure of the range of $T$ and the kernel of $T$ are complementary subspaces: their
intersection is $\{0\}$ and their sum is $H$; and
(3) the eigenspaces $\ker(T - \mu I)$, $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$, are pairwise orthogonal for distinct
values of $\mu$.

articles.title: Eigenvectors for nonzero eigenvalues lie in the range
articles.statement:
An eigenvector for a nonzero eigenvalue lies in the range: if
`T v = μ • v` with `μ ≠ 0`, then `v = T (μ⁻¹ • v)`.

articles.title: Independent eigenvectors for distinct nonzero eigenvalues
articles.statement:
Choose one eigenvector for each nonzero eigenvalue of `T`. The chosen
eigenvectors are linearly independent (eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues)
and all lie in the range of `T`.

articles.title: Eigenvalue finiteness for finite-rank operators
articles.statement:
A finite-rank
operator has only finitely many distinct nonzero eigenvalues.

articles.title: Spectrum of a finite-rank operator is finite
articles.statement: The spectrum of a finite-rank operator is finite.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a finite-rank operator lie in its spectrum
articles.statement: Every eigenvalue of a finite-rank operator lies in its spectrum.

articles.title: Finite-rank operators are compact
articles.statement:
A finite-rank operator is compact: it factors through its
finite-dimensional range, and every continuous linear map out of a
finite-dimensional (hence locally compact) space is compact.

articles.title: Eigenvalue-count bound for finite-rank operators
articles.statement:
There are at most
`finrank (range T)` distinct nonzero eigenvalues.

articles.title: Bound on the size of the spectrum of a finite-rank operator
articles.statement:
The spectrum of a finite-rank operator has at most
`finrank (range T) + 1` points.

articles.title: Spectrum of a finite-rank operator on an infinite-dimensional space
articles.statement: The spectrum is exactly `{0} ∪ {eigenvalues}`.

articles.title: Nonzero spectral values of a finite-rank operator are eigenvalues
articles.statement:
The spectrum of a finite-rank operator is contained in
`{0} ∪ {eigenvalues}`: every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue, by
the Fredholm alternative for compact operators.

articles.title: $f(y)$ is an eigenvalue of $x \mapsto f(x)\,y$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, let $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ be a
continuous linear functional, and let $y \in E$ with $y \neq 0$. Then $f(y)$ is an eigenvalue of
the linear operator $T x = f(x)\,y$ on $E$.

An eigenvector is $y$ itself, since $T y = f(y)\,y$.

articles.title: $0$ is an eigenvalue of $x \mapsto f(x)\,y$ when $f$ has a nontrivial kernel
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, let
$f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ be a continuous linear functional, and let $y \in E$. If some
$w \in E$ with $w \neq 0$ satisfies $f(w) = 0$, then $0$ is an eigenvalue of the linear operator
$T x = f(x)\,y$ on $E$.

An eigenvector is $w$ itself, since $T w = f(w)\,y = 0$.

articles.title: $0$ lies in the spectrum of $x \mapsto f(x)\,y$ when $f$ has a nontrivial kernel
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{K}$, let
$f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ be a continuous linear functional, and let $y \in E$. If some
$w \in E$ with $w \neq 0$ satisfies $f(w) = 0$, then $0$ lies in the spectrum of the bounded
operator $T x = f(x)\,y$ on $E$.

articles.title: $f(y)$ lies in the spectrum of $x \mapsto f(x)\,y$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{K}$, let $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ be a
continuous linear functional, and let $y \in E$ with $y \neq 0$. Then $f(y)$ lies in the spectrum
of the bounded operator $T x = f(x)\,y$ on $E$.

articles.title: The spectrum of $x \mapsto f(x)\,y$ lies in $\{0, f(y)\}$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, let
$f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ be a continuous linear functional, let $y \in E$, and let $T$ be the
bounded operator on $E$ given by $T x = f(x)\,y$. If $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ satisfies $\mu \neq 0$
and $\mu \neq f(y)$, then $\mu$ is not in the spectrum of $T$ in the algebra of bounded operators
on $E$.

Explicitly, the inverse of $\mu I - T$, where $I$ is the identity operator, is
$\mu^{-1} I + \mu^{-1} (\mu - f(y))^{-1}\,T$.

articles.title: Square of the operator $x \mapsto f(x)\,y$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$, let $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ be a
continuous linear functional, let $y \in E$, and let $T$ be the bounded operator on $E$ given by
$T x = f(x)\,y$. Then $T^2 = f(y)\,T$.

articles.title: Spectrum of the operator $z \mapsto \langle y, z \rangle\,x$ on a Hilbert space
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $H$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K}$ whose
inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is linear in the second argument, let $x, y \in H$
with $x \neq 0$, and let $T$ be the bounded operator on $H$ given by
$T z = \langle y, z \rangle\,x$. If some $w \in H$ with $w \neq 0$ satisfies
$\langle y, w \rangle = 0$, then the spectrum of $T$ is $\{0, \langle y, x \rangle\}$.

articles.title: Spectrum of $x \mapsto f(x)\,y$ when $f(y) = 0$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{K}$, let $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ be a
continuous linear functional, and let $y \in E$ with $y \neq 0$ and $f(y) = 0$. Then the
spectrum of the bounded operator $T x = f(x)\,y$ on $E$ is $\{0\}$.

articles.title: Spectrum of the operator $x \mapsto f(x)\,y$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{K}$, let
$f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$ be a continuous linear functional, and let $y \in E$ with $y \neq 0$.
If some $w \in E$ with $w \neq 0$ satisfies $f(w) = 0$, then the spectrum of the bounded
operator $T x = f(x)\,y$ on $E$ is exactly $\{0, f(y)\}$.

Here $y$ is an eigenvector for $f(y)$ and $w$ is an eigenvector for $0$; the zero functional is
allowed. Without the kernel hypothesis this fails: on a one-dimensional space a nonzero operator
of this form is a nonzero multiple of the identity, whose spectrum is a single point.

articles.title: Positivity iff spectrum nonnegative
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a self-adjoint bounded linear operator on a
nonzero Hilbert space $H$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Then
$\operatorname{Re}\langle Tu, u\rangle \ge 0$ for every $u \in H$ if and only if every element
$\mu$ of the spectrum of $T$ satisfies $\operatorname{Re}\mu \ge 0$.

articles.title: Rayleigh quotient of a shifted operator
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on an inner
product space $H$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $I$ be the identity operator on $H$, and
write $R_S(x) = \operatorname{Re}\langle Sx, x\rangle / \|x\|^2$ for the Rayleigh quotient of an
operator $S$. Then for every real number $t$ and every nonzero $x \in H$,
$R_{tI - T}(x) = t - R_T(x)$.

articles.title: Spectrum bounds over nonzero vectors
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a self-adjoint bounded linear operator on
a nonzero Hilbert space $H$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with Rayleigh quotient
$R_T(x) = \operatorname{Re}\langle Tx, x\rangle / \|x\|^2$. Then every $\mu$ in the spectrum of
$T$ satisfies $\inf_{x \ne 0} R_T(x) \le \operatorname{Re}\mu \le \sup_{x \ne 0} R_T(x)$, where
the infimum and supremum range over the nonzero vectors $x \in H$.

articles.title: Spectrum bounds over all vectors
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a self-adjoint bounded linear operator on a
nonzero Hilbert space $H$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with Rayleigh quotient
$R_T(x) = \operatorname{Re}\langle Tx, x\rangle / \|x\|^2$ for $x \ne 0$ and $R_T(0) = 0$. Then
every $\mu$ in the spectrum of $T$ satisfies
$\inf_{x \in H} R_T(x) \le \operatorname{Re}\mu \le \sup_{x \in H} R_T(x)$.

Unlike the bounds over nonzero vectors, these extrema also take into account the value $0$ of the
quotient at $x = 0$.

articles.title: Spectrum of an accretive operator has nonnegative real part
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a bounded linear
operator on a Hilbert space $H$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If
$\operatorname{Re}\langle Tu, u\rangle \ge 0$ for every $u \in H$, then every element $\mu$ of
the spectrum of $T$ satisfies $\operatorname{Re}\mu \ge 0$.

articles.title: Comparison principle for the Dirichlet problem on $(0, 1)$
articles.statement:
Let $J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$
be an open set containing $[0, 1]$, and let $u, v : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be functions
that are differentiable at every point of $J$ and whose derivatives $u'$ and $v'$ are
differentiable at every point of $J$. If $-u''(x) \le -v''(x)$ for every $x \in (0, 1)$,
$u(0) \le v(0)$ and $u(1) \le v(1)$, then $u(x) \le v(x)$ for every $x \in [0, 1]$.

## Sources

- Standard maximum-principle argument; Protter-Weinberger. Problem `bvp_comparison` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Cauchy–Peano existence theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space and let
$f : \mathbb{R} \times E \to E$ be continuous. Then for every $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ and
$x_0 \in E$ there are $\varepsilon > 0$ and a function $x : \mathbb{R} \to E$ with
$x(t_0) = x_0$ such that, for every $t \in (t_0 - \varepsilon, t_0 + \varepsilon)$, $x$ is
differentiable at $t$ with $x'(t) = f(t, x(t))$.

## Sources

- G. Peano, Math. Ann. 37 (1890), 182-228, DOI 10.1007/BF01200235.

articles.title: Decay rate of solutions of $y' = -y^3$
articles.statement:
Let $y : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be
differentiable at every $t > 0$ with $y'(t) = -y(t)^3$, continuous at $0$ within $[0, \infty)$,
and such that $y(0) = 1$. Then $y(t) \sqrt{t} \to 1/\sqrt{2}$ as $t \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Standard ODE textbook exercise. Problem `cubic_decay_asymptotic` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Dirichlet eigenvalues of $-y'' = \lambda y$ on $(0, \pi)$
articles.statement:
For every real number
$\lambda$, the following are equivalent:
(i) there are a function $y : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and an open set $J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$
