Problem 17.1 is false: the answer is negative. Source: S. Ulam, Problem 17.1
of the Scottish Book; Z. Zahorski gave a negative answer by constructing a
`C ^ ∞` function that agrees with every real-analytic function on at most
finitely many points, so no nonempty perfect set `C` can work for it: Z.
Zahorski, "Sur l'ensemble des points singuliers d'une fonction d'une
variable reelle admettant les derivees de tous les ordres", Fund. Math. 34
(1947), 183-245. The 2026 survey "90+ years of the Scottish Book"
(arXiv:2603.27867) confirms the negative solution.

articles.title: Perfect sets of real numbers
articles.statement:
A set $s \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is perfect if it is closed,
nonempty, and has no isolated points: every $x \in s$ lies in the closure of $s \setminus \{x\}$.

articles.title: Ulam's problem on analytic agreement on a perfect set
articles.statement:
Ulam's Problem 17.1 from the Scottish Book: for every continuous `f` on
`[0, 1]`, do there exist a perfect set `C` in `[0, 1]` and an analytic
function `φ` with `f x = φ x` for every `x ∈ C`? The claim is stated for
`C ^ ∞` functions, which is the case refuted by Zahorski's construction.

articles.title: Steinhaus's periodization problem (Scottish Book Problem 181)
articles.statement:
There is a continuous function
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(x) > 0$ for every real $x$ such that, for every real $x$,
the series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f(x + n)$ converges and its sum is $1$.

## Sources

- H. Steinhaus, Problem 181 of the Scottish Book; the addendum Ad 181 records that the Gaussian `(1 / √π) exp (-x ^ 2)` does not have the property, while Mazur's note gives a construction, taking a positive continuous `g` with finite periodization and dividing `g` by that periodization (e.g. `g(x) = exp (-x ^ 2)`). See the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Midpoint identity for the divide-and-conquer D-node count
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ be the
divide-and-conquer D-node count. Let $k$ and $r$ be natural numbers with $0 < r < 2^k$, put
$n = 2^k + r$, and let $\nu_2(r)$ be the position of the lowest nonzero binary digit of $r$,
counted from $0$ (the exponent of the largest power of $2$ dividing $r$). Then
$\delta(n) = \frac{\delta(n-1) + \delta(n+1)}{2} + 1 - \nu_2(r)$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Corollary 10 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-cor-10`).

articles.title: Level-sum formula for the divide-and-conquer D-node count
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ be the
divide-and-conquer D-node count. For every integer $n > 0$, let $k = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$,
let $\lambda_i(n)$ be the level-$i$ D-node count, and let $n_i$ be the binary digit of $n$ at
$2^i$. Then

$$\delta(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \lambda_i(n),$$

and explicitly

$$\delta(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \left(n_i 2^i + (-1)^{n_i} (n \bmod 2^i)\right).$$

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 11 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-thm-11`).

articles.title: Binary-digit formula for the divide-and-conquer D-node count
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ be the
divide-and-conquer D-node count and let $s_1(m)$ be the number of ones in the binary expansion
of $m$. For every integer $n > 0$, let $k = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ and let $n_j$ be the binary
digit of $n$ at $2^j$. Then

$$\delta(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} 2^i n_i \Big(k - i - 2 \sum_{j=i}^{k} n_j + 4\Big),$$

and also

$$\delta(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} 2^i n_i \Big(k - i - 2\, s_1(\lfloor n / 2^i \rfloor) + 4\Big).$$

The printed inner sum $\sum_{j=i}^k n_i$ is read as $\sum_{j=i}^k n_j$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 22 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-thm-22`).

articles.title: The divide-and-conquer D-node count at one leaf
articles.statement:
The divide-and-conquer D-node count
$\delta$ satisfies $\delta(1) = 0$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 9 (`exp_D_recursive`).

articles.title: Small values of the divide-and-conquer D-node count
articles.statement:
The divide-and-conquer D-node count
$\delta$ satisfies $\delta(2) = 0$, $\delta(3) = 1$, $\delta(4) = 0$, $\delta(5) = 2$,
$\delta(6) = 2$ and $\delta(7) = 2$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 9 (`exp_D_recursive`).

articles.title: Successor formula for the D-node count at even arguments
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ be the
divide-and-conquer D-node count and $s_1(n)$ the number of ones in the binary expansion of $n$.
For every even integer $n > 0$, $\delta(n+1) = \delta(n) + \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor - 2 s_1(n) + 2$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 19 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-19`).

articles.title: Successor formula for the D-node count at odd arguments
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ be the
divide-and-conquer D-node count and $s_1(n)$ the number of ones in the binary expansion of $n$.
For every odd natural number $n$,
$\delta(n+1) = \delta(n) + \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor - 2 s_1(n) + 2$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 20 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-20`).

articles.title: Successor formula for the divide-and-conquer D-node count
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ be the
divide-and-conquer D-node count and $s_1(n)$ the number of ones in the binary expansion of $n$.
For every integer $n > 0$,
$\delta(n+1) = \delta(n) + \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor - 2 s_1(n) + 2$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 21 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-thm-21`).

articles.title: Odd-argument recurrence for the divide-and-conquer D-node count
articles.statement:
For every integer
$m > 0$, the divide-and-conquer D-node count $\delta$ satisfies
$\delta(2m+1) = \delta(m) + \delta(m+1) + 1$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 9 (`exp_D_recursive`).

articles.title: Doubling recurrence for the divide-and-conquer D-node count
articles.statement:
For every integer $m > 0$,
the divide-and-conquer D-node count $\delta$ satisfies $\delta(2m) = 2\delta(m)$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 9 (`exp_D_recursive`).

articles.title: Symmetry of the D-node counts
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$ and $r$ with $r \le 2^k$,
$\delta(2^{k+1} - r) = \delta(2^k + r)$, where $\delta(n)$ denotes the number of D-nodes in the
divide-and-conquer tree on $n$ leaves.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 18 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-18`).

articles.title: Number of D-nodes of the divide-and-conquer tree
articles.statement:
The number $\delta(n)$ of D-nodes in the
divide-and-conquer tree on $n$ leaves (OEIS A296062) is defined by the recurrence the paper
quotes from Coronado et al.: $\delta(1) = 0$, and for every natural number $m \ge 1$,
$\delta(2m) = 2\,\delta(m)$ and $\delta(2m+1) = \delta(m) + \delta(m+1) + 1$. The value at $0$
is the junk value $\delta(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 9 (`exp_D_recursive`).

articles.title: Level count of D-nodes when the binary digit is one
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $i$ be natural numbers
such that the binary digit $n_i$ of $n$ (the coefficient of $2^i$ in the binary expansion of
$n$) equals $1$. Then the level count of D-nodes is $\lambda_i(n) = 2^i - (n \bmod 2^i)$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 11 (`exp_D_closed`).

articles.title: Level count of D-nodes when the binary digit is zero
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $i$ be natural numbers
such that the binary digit $n_i$ of $n$ (the coefficient of $2^i$ in the binary expansion of
$n$) equals $0$. Then the level count of D-nodes is $\lambda_i(n) = n \bmod 2^i$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 11 (`exp_D_closed`).

articles.title: Level counts of D-nodes at consecutive integers
articles.statement:
Let $k$, $r$ and $i$ be natural numbers
with $r$ odd, $r < 2^k$ and $0 < i < k$, and let $n = 2^k + r$. Then the level counts of
D-nodes satisfy $\lambda_i(n) - \lambda_i(n-1) = 1$ if the binary digit $n_i$ of $n$ is $0$,
and $\lambda_i(n) - \lambda_i(n-1) = -1$ if $n_i = 1$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 17 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-17`).

articles.title: Level count of D-nodes on level zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the level count of
D-nodes on level $0$ is $\lambda_0(n) = n \bmod 2$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 11 (`exp_D_closed`).

articles.title: Level counts of D-nodes
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $i$, let $n_i$ be the binary digit
of $n$ at position $i$ (the coefficient of $2^i$ in the binary expansion of $n$). The level count
$\lambda_i(n)$ is $n \bmod 2^i$ if $n_i = 0$, and $2^i - (n \bmod 2^i)$ if $n_i = 1$.

This is the paper's closed form for the number of D-nodes on level $i$ of the
divide-and-conquer tree on $n$ leaves.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 11 (`exp_D_closed`).

articles.title: Normalized form of $n = 2^k + r$
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $k$ and $r$ be natural numbers with $r < 2^k$
and $n = 2^k + r$, and let $x$ be a rational number with $n = 2^k (1 + x)$. Then $x = r / 2^k$
and $1 + x = n / 2^k$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 2 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-2`).

articles.title: Binary digit sum from consecutive D-node counts
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n > 0$, the
sum $s_1(n)$ of the binary digits of $n$ satisfies
$s_1(n) = (\delta(n) - \delta(n+1) + \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor)/2 + 1$ in $\mathbb{Q}$, where
$\delta(m)$ denotes the number of D-nodes in the divide-and-conquer tree on $m$ leaves.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Corollary 23 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-cor-23`).

articles.title: Binary digit sum from consecutive Takagi values
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $r$ be natural numbers
with $r < 2^k$, let $n = 2^k + r$, and let $s_1(n)$ be the sum of the binary digits of $n$.
Writing $\tau(m, k - 1)$ for the Takagi value of the dyadic presentation $m / 2^k$, one has
$s_1(n) = 2^{k-1} \bigl(\tau(r, k - 1) - \tau(r + 1, k - 1)\bigr) + (k + 2)/2$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 28 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-thm-28`).

articles.title: Hamming weight of the predecessor of an odd number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, write
$s_1(m)$ for the sum of the binary digits of $m$ (the number of ones in its binary expansion).
If $n$ is an odd natural number, then $s_1(n - 1) = s_1(n) - 1$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 15 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-15`).

articles.title: Hamming weight of the successor of an even number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, write
$s_1(m)$ for the sum of the binary digits of $m$ (the number of ones in its binary expansion).
If $n$ is an even natural number (including $n = 0$), then $s_1(n + 1) = s_1(n) + 1$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 14 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-14`).

articles.title: Adding a larger power of two raises the Hamming weight by one
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$,
write $s_1(m)$ for the sum of the binary digits of $m$ (the number of ones in its binary
expansion). For all natural numbers $k$ and $r$ with $r < 2^k$, $s_1(2^k + r) = s_1(r) + 1$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 13 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-13`).

articles.title: Hamming weight of a power of two minus an odd number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, write
$s_1(m)$ for the sum of the binary digits of $m$ (the number of ones in its binary expansion).
Let $k$ and $r$ be natural numbers with $r$ odd and $2r < 2^k$, that is, $r < 2^{k-1}$. Then
$s_1(2^k - r) = 1 + k - s_1(r)$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 16 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-16`).

articles.title: The divide-and-conquer condition at the root
articles.statement:
A full binary tree whose root has left
subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ is a divide-and-conquer tree if and only if the numbers of
leaves of $L$ and $R$ differ by at most $1$ and both $L$ and $R$ are divide-and-conquer trees.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition (Divide-and-conquer tree).

articles.title: Divide-and-conquer trees
articles.statement:
A divide-and-conquer tree is a full binary tree in which, at
every interior node, the numbers of leaves of the two subtrees differ by at most $1$. In
particular a single leaf is a divide-and-conquer tree.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition (Divide-and-conquer tree).

articles.title: Cumulative binary digit sums via the Takagi function
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, write
$s_1(m)$ for the sum of the binary digits of $m$ and $S_1(m) = \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} s_1(i)$. Let
$k$ and $r$ be natural numbers with $r < 2^k$, and put $n = 2^k + r$ and $x = r / 2^k$. Write
$\tau(x)$ for the Takagi value of the dyadic presentation $r / 2^k$, and $\delta(n)$ for the
number of $D$-nodes of the divide-and-conquer tree on $n$ leaves, given by $\delta(1) = 0$,
$\delta(2m) = 2 \delta(m)$ and $\delta(2m + 1) = \delta(m) + \delta(m + 1) + 1$ for $m \ge 1$.
Then $S_1(n) = (nk + 2^k (2x - \tau(x)))/2$, $S_1(n) = (nk + 2r - 2^k \tau(x))/2$ and
$S_1(n) = (nk + 2r - \delta(n))/2$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Corollary 31 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-cor-31`).

articles.title: Trollope's formula via the Takagi function
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, write $s_1(m)$ for
the sum of the binary digits of $m$ and $S_1(m) = \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} s_1(i)$. Let $k$ and $r$ be
natural numbers with $r < 2^k$, and put $n = 2^k + r$ and $x = r / 2^k$. Write $\tau(x)$ for
the Takagi value of the dyadic presentation $r / 2^k$. Then

$$S_1(n) = \frac{n \log_2 n}{2} + 2^{k-1} \left(2x - \tau(x) - (1 + x) \log_2 (1 + x)\right).$$

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Corollary 30 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-cor-30`).

articles.title: Formula for the binary digits
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every integer $i$, the
binary digit $n_i$ of $n$ equals $1$ if $i \ge 0$ and the coefficient of $2^i$ in the binary
expansion of $n$ is $1$, and equals $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition.

articles.title: Binary digits at negative positions vanish
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every
integer $i < 0$, the binary digit $n_i$ of $n$ is $0$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition.

articles.title: Binary digits of a natural number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and an integer $i$, the binary
digit $n_i \in \{0, 1\}$ of $n$ is the coefficient of $2^i$ in the binary expansion of $n$ when
$i \ge 0$, and $n_i = 0$ when $i < 0$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7.

articles.title: The Takagi function at dyadic rationals counts D-nodes (Coronado et al.)
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $r$
be natural numbers with $r \le 2^k$. Write $\tau(r / 2^k)$ for the Takagi value of the dyadic
presentation $r / 2^k$, and $\delta(n)$ for the number of $D$-nodes of the divide-and-conquer
tree on $n$ leaves, given by $\delta(1) = 0$, $\delta(2m) = 2 \delta(m)$ and
$\delta(2m + 1) = \delta(m) + \delta(m + 1) + 1$ for $m \ge 1$. Then
$\tau(r / 2^k) = \delta(2^k + r) / 2^k$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 8 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-thm-8`).

articles.title: Midpoint recurrence for the Takagi function at dyadic rationals
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $r$ be
natural numbers with $1 \le r < 2^k$. For a natural number $m$, write $\tau(m / 2^k)$ for the
Takagi value of the dyadic presentation $m / 2^k$, and let $\rho_1$ be the $2$-adic valuation of
$r$, the position (counted from $0$) of the lowest nonzero binary digit of $r$. Then
$\tau(r / 2^k) = (\tau((r - 1) / 2^k) + \tau((r + 1) / 2^k))/2 + (1 - \rho_1)/2^k$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 24 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-thm-24`).

articles.title: Takagi values at dyadic rationals from level $D$-node counts
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $r$ be
natural numbers with $r < 2^k$ and put $n = 2^k + r$. Write $\tau(r, k-1)$ for the Takagi value
of the dyadic presentation $r/2^k$, write $n_i = \lfloor n/2^i \rfloor \bmod 2$ for the binary
digit of $n$ at position $i$, and let $\lambda_i(n)$ be the level-$i$ $D$-node count, which
equals $n \bmod 2^i$ if $n_i = 0$ and $2^i - (n \bmod 2^i)$ if $n_i = 1$. Then

$$\tau(r, k-1) = 2^{-k} \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \lambda_i(n)$$

and

$$\tau(r, k-1) = 2^{-k} \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} (n_i 2^i + (-1)^{n_i} (n \bmod 2^i)).$$

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 25 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-thm-25`).

articles.title: Takagi values at dyadic rationals from binary digits
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $r$ be natural
numbers with $r < 2^k$ and put $n = 2^k + r$. Write $\tau(r, k-1)$ for the Takagi value of the
dyadic presentation $r/2^k$, write $n_j = \lfloor n/2^j \rfloor \bmod 2$ for the binary digit of
$n$ at position $j$, and write $s_1(m)$ for the number of ones in the binary expansion of $m$.
Then

$$\tau(r, k-1) = 2^{-k} \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} 2^i n_i (k - i - 2 \sum_{j=i}^{k} n_j + 4)$$

and

$$\tau(r, k-1) = 2^{-k} \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} 2^i n_i (k - i - 2 s_1(\lfloor n/2^i \rfloor) + 4).$$

The paper prints the inner sum as $\sum_{j=i}^{k} n_i$; it is read here as $\sum_{j=i}^{k} n_j$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 27 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-thm-27`).

articles.title: Consecutive Takagi values at dyadic rationals
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $r$ be natural numbers with
$r < 2^k$ and put $n = 2^k + r$. Write $\tau(m, k-1)$ for the Takagi value of the dyadic
presentation $m/2^k$, and $s_1(n)$ for the number of ones in the binary expansion of $n$. Then
$\tau(r+1, k-1) = \tau(r, k-1) + (k - 2 s_1(n) + 2)/2^k$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 26 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-thm-26`).

articles.title: The first Takagi coefficient vanishes
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every integer $k$,
the Takagi coefficient $\ell_1(n, k)$ is $0$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition.

articles.title: Formula for the Takagi coefficients
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, every integer $k$ and
every natural number $i$, let $s_i = \sum_{j=0}^{i-1} n_{k-j}$, where $n_j$ denotes the binary
digit of $n$ at position $j$. Then the Takagi coefficient $\ell_{i+1}(n, k)$ equals $s_i$ if
$n_{k-i} = 0$, and equals $i - s_i$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition.

articles.title: The Takagi coefficient at index zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every integer $k$,
the Takagi coefficient $\ell_0(n, k)$ is $0$.

The index $0$ is only an auxiliary base value: the Takagi series starts at $\ell_1$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition.

articles.title: Takagi coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and $k$ an integer, and write $n_j$ for
the binary digit of $n$ at position $j$ (so $n_j = 0$ for $j < 0$). The Takagi coefficients
$\ell_i(n, k)$, for natural numbers $i$, are the natural numbers given by $\ell_0(n, k) = 0$ and,
for every natural number $i$, with $s_i = \sum_{j=0}^{i-1} n_{k-j}$, by $\ell_{i+1}(n, k) = s_i$
if $n_{k-i} = 0$ and $\ell_{i+1}(n, k) = i - s_i$ otherwise.

In particular $\ell_1(n, k) = 0$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7.

articles.title: Series for the Takagi value
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every integer $k$, the
Takagi value $\tau(n, k)$ of the dyadic presentation $n / 2^{k+1}$ satisfies
$\tau(n, k) = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \ell_{i+1}(n, k) / 2^{i+1}$, where $\ell_i(n, k)$ denotes the
$i$-th Takagi coefficient of $n$ and $k$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition.

articles.title: Takagi function on dyadic presentations
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and an integer $k$, the
Takagi value $\tau(n, k)$ of the dyadic presentation $n / 2^{k+1}$ is the sum of the real series
$\sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \ell_{i+1}(n, k) / 2^{i+1}$, where $\ell_i(n, k)$ denotes the $i$-th Takagi
coefficient of $n$ and $k$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition.

articles.title: Coronado et al.'s count of $D$-nodes in divide-and-conquer trees
articles.statement:
Every
divide-and-conquer tree with $n$ leaves has exactly $\delta(n)$ $D$-nodes, where $\delta$ is the
function on positive integers given by $\delta(1) = 0$, $\delta(2m) = 2\delta(m)$ and
$\delta(2m+1) = \delta(m) + \delta(m+1) + 1$ for $m \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Theorem 9 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-thm-9`).

articles.title: $D$-nodes and $S$-nodes of a full binary tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a full binary tree with $n$
leaves and let $a$ be the number of $S$-nodes of $t$. Then the number of $D$-nodes of $t$ is
$n - 1 - a$ (subtraction of natural numbers, truncated at $0$).

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 5 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-5`).

articles.title: Recursion for the number of $D$-nodes
articles.statement:
Write $D(t)$ for the number of $D$-nodes of a
full binary tree $t$. If the root of $t$ has left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$, then
$D(t) = \varepsilon + D(l) + D(r)$, where $\varepsilon = 0$ if $l$ and $r$ have the same number
of leaves and $\varepsilon = 1$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition (`S`-nodes and `D`-nodes).

articles.title: Number of $D$-nodes of a full binary tree
articles.statement:
A $D$-node of a full binary tree is an
interior node whose two subtrees have different numbers of leaves. The number of $D$-nodes of a
full binary tree is the number of its interior nodes that are $D$-nodes.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition (`S`-nodes and `D`-nodes).

articles.title: The single-leaf tree
articles.statement:
The full binary tree consisting of a single leaf has no $D$-nodes
and no $S$-nodes, and it is a divide-and-conquer tree.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definitions (`S`-nodes and `D`-nodes; Divide-and-conquer tree).

articles.title: Recursion for the number of $S$-nodes
articles.statement:
Write $S(t)$ for the number of $S$-nodes of a
full binary tree $t$. If the root of $t$ has left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$, then
$S(t) = \varepsilon + S(l) + S(r)$, where $\varepsilon = 1$ if $l$ and $r$ have the same number
of leaves and $\varepsilon = 0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition (`S`-nodes and `D`-nodes).

articles.title: Number of $S$-nodes of a full binary tree
articles.statement:
An $S$-node of a full binary tree is an
interior node whose two subtrees have the same number of leaves. The number of $S$-nodes of a
full binary tree is the number of its interior nodes that are $S$-nodes.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Definition (`S`-nodes and `D`-nodes).

articles.title: Sum of binary digit sums below a power of two
articles.statement:
For a natural number $i$, let $s_1(i)$
denote the sum of the binary digits of $i$. Then for every natural number $m$,
$2 \sum_{i < 2^m} s_1(i) = 2^m m$; that is, the binary expansions of $0, 1, \dots, 2^m - 1$
contain $2^m m / 2$ ones in total.

## Sources

- Laura Monroe, *Takagi Function Identities on Dyadic Rationals*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.7, Lemma 29 (`jis-2024-24.2.7-lem-29`).

articles.title: Continuity of the interval cutoff
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $a$, $b$ and $\delta$, including
$\delta = 0$, the interval cutoff $\chi_{a,b,\delta} \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with
endpoints $a$, $b$ and width $\delta$ is continuous.

articles.title: The interval cutoff equals one on its plateau
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$, $b$, $\delta$ and $x$
with $\delta > 0$ and $a + \delta \le x \le b - \delta$, the interval cutoff $\chi_{a,b,\delta}$
with endpoints $a$, $b$ and width $\delta$ satisfies $\chi_{a,b,\delta}(x) = 1$.

articles.title: The interval cutoff vanishes at the left endpoint
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $a$, $b$ and
$\delta$, the interval cutoff $\chi_{a,b,\delta}$ with endpoints $a$, $b$ and width $\delta$
satisfies $\chi_{a,b,\delta}(a) = 0$.

articles.title: The interval cutoff vanishes right of the interval
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$, $b$, $\delta$
and $x$ with $\delta > 0$ and $b \le x$, the interval cutoff $\chi_{a,b,\delta}$ with endpoints
$a$, $b$ and width $\delta$ satisfies $\chi_{a,b,\delta}(x) = 0$.

articles.title: The interval cutoff vanishes left of the interval
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$, $b$, $\delta$
and $x$ with $\delta > 0$ and $x \le a$, the interval cutoff $\chi_{a,b,\delta}$ with endpoints
$a$, $b$ and width $\delta$ satisfies $\chi_{a,b,\delta}(x) = 0$.

articles.title: The interval cutoff vanishes at the right endpoint
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $a$, $b$ and
$\delta$, the interval cutoff $\chi_{a,b,\delta}$ with endpoints $a$, $b$ and width $\delta$
satisfies $\chi_{a,b,\delta}(b) = 0$.

articles.title: The interval cutoff is at most one
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $a$, $b$, $\delta$ and $x$, the
interval cutoff $\chi_{a,b,\delta}$ with endpoints $a$, $b$ and width $\delta$ satisfies
$\chi_{a,b,\delta}(x) \le 1$.

articles.title: The interval cutoff is nonnegative
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $a$, $b$, $\delta$ and $x$, the
interval cutoff $\chi_{a,b,\delta}$ with endpoints $a$, $b$ and width $\delta$ satisfies
$0 \le \chi_{a,b,\delta}(x)$.

articles.title: The interval cutoff of zero width vanishes
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $a$, $b$ and $x$, the
interval cutoff $\chi_{a,b,0}$ with endpoints $a$, $b$ and width $0$ satisfies
$\chi_{a,b,0}(x) = 0$.

articles.title: Interval cutoff
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$, $b$ and $\delta$, the interval cutoff is the
function $\chi_{a,b,\delta} \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by

$$
\chi_{a,b,\delta}(x) = \max\{0, \min\{1, (x - a)/\delta, (b - x)/\delta\}\},
$$

where division by zero is taken to give $0$.

It vanishes at $a$ and at $b$. For $\delta > 0$ it equals $1$ on $[a + \delta, b - \delta]$, which
is nonempty when $2\delta \le b - a$; for $\delta = 0$ it is identically zero.

articles.title: Continuity of the Weierstrass function
articles.statement:
The Weierstrass function
$W(x) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \cos(160^k x) / 4^k$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

It is a uniform limit of continuous partial sums.

articles.title: Cosine oscillation (scaled form)
articles.statement:
For every real number $c$ and every positive integer
$K$, there is a real number $y$ with $c + \pi / K < y < c + 3\pi / K$ such that
$|\cos(Kc) - \cos(Ky)| \ge 1$.

This is the estimate that drives the slope blow-up in the proof that the Weierstrass function is
nowhere differentiable.

articles.title: Cosine oscillation (phase-shift form)
articles.statement:
For every real number $\theta$ there is a real
number $\varphi$ with $\pi < \varphi < 3\pi$ such that
$|\cos\theta - \cos(\theta + \varphi)| \ge 1$.

The two candidate shifts are $3\pi/2$ and $5\pi/2$, where $\cos(\theta + \varphi)$ equals
$\sin\theta$ and $-\sin\theta$ respectively; at least one of $|\cos\theta - \sin\theta|$ and
$|\cos\theta + \sin\theta|$ is at least $1$, since their squares sum to $2$.

articles.title: Termwise bound for the Weierstrass series
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$ and every real
number $x$, $|\cos(160^k x) / 4^k| \le (1/4)^k$.

The right-hand side is the $k$-th term of a convergent geometric series.

articles.title: Reverse triangle inequality, three terms
articles.statement:
For all real numbers
`a`, `b`, `c`, the absolute value of their sum is at least
`|a| - |b| - |c|`.

articles.title: Absolute convergence of the Weierstrass series
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$, the series
$\sum_{k \ge 0} \cos(160^k x) / 4^k$ defining the Weierstrass function converges absolutely,
that is, $\sum_{k \ge 0} |\cos(160^k x) / 4^k|$ is summable.

articles.title: Summability of the Weierstrass series
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$, the series
$\sum_{k \ge 0} \cos(160^k x) / 4^k$ defining the Weierstrass function is summable, by
comparison with the geometric series $\sum_{k \ge 0} (1/4)^k$.

articles.title: Bound on the Weierstrass function
articles.statement:
The Weierstrass function
$W(x) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \cos(160^k x) / 4^k$ satisfies $|W(x)| \le 4/3$ for every real number $x$.

articles.title: The Weierstrass function is nowhere differentiable
articles.statement:
The Weierstrass function
$W(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \cos(160^k x) / 4^k$ is differentiable at no point of $\mathbb{R}$:
for every real number $c$, $W$ is not differentiable at $c$.

The proof uses the slope blow-up lemma to exhibit a sequence of points approaching $c$ along
which the absolute values of the difference quotients of $W$ tend to infinity, contradicting
the convergence of the slope to a finite derivative.

articles.title: Slope blow-up lemma
articles.statement:
For every real `c` and every natural number
`n`, there exists a point `y ≠ c` with `|y - c| < 3π / 160ⁿ` such that
the difference quotient of the Weierstrass function between `y` and `c`
has absolute value at least `40ⁿ / (117 π)`. Since
`40ⁿ / (117 π) → ∞`, this witnesses that the function cannot have a
finite derivative at `c`.

articles.title: The Weierstrass function
articles.statement:
The Weierstrass function is the function
$W : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $W(x) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \cos(160^k x) / 4^k$, the sum
running over all natural numbers $k$.

articles.title: Borel's lemma
articles.statement:
For every sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of real numbers there is an infinitely
differentiable function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ whose derivatives at $0$ are
$f^{(n)}(0) = a_n$ for every $n \ge 0$.

## Sources

- E. Borel, Ann. Sci. Ec. Norm. Sup. (3) 12 (1895), 9-55, DOI 10.24033/asens.406.

articles.title: Gluing $C^n$ functions on adjacent closed intervals
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed space, let
$n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ and let $a \le b \le c$ be real numbers. Let
$f, g : \mathbb{R} \to E$ be such that $f$ is $C^n$ on $[a, b]$ and $g$ is $C^n$ on $[b, c]$, and
suppose that for every natural number $k \le n$ the $k$-th derivative of $f$ within $[a, b]$ and
the $k$-th derivative of $g$ within $[b, c]$ agree at $b$. Then the function equal to $f$ on
$[a, b]$ and to $g$ elsewhere is $C^n$ on $[a, c]$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piecewise#Continuity_and_differentiability_of_piecewise_functions

articles.title: The derivative of $x^2 \sin(1/x^2)$ exists everywhere but is not integrable
articles.statement:
Let
$F : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be given by $F(x) = x^2 \sin(1/x^2)$ for $x \ne 0$ and $F(0) = 0$.
Then $F$ is differentiable at every real $x$, but its derivative $F'$ is not Lebesgue integrable
on $[-1,1]$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_99`.

articles.title: An even $C^2$ function is a $C^1$ function of $x^2$
articles.statement:
Let $a>0$ and let
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be twice continuously differentiable on $[-a,a]$ with $f(x)=f(-x)$
for all $x\in[-a,a]$. Then there is $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, continuously differentiable on
$[0,a^2]$, with $f(x)=g(x^2)$ for all $x\in[-a,a]$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_11`.

articles.title: A monotone differentiable function with discontinuous derivative
articles.statement:
There is a
nondecreasing function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is differentiable at every point and
whose derivative $f'$ is not continuous.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_92`.

articles.title: A smooth function on the unit interval with some vanishing derivative at each point is a polynomial there
articles.statement:
**A smooth function on the unit interval with some vanishing derivative at each point is a
polynomial there.** Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be infinitely differentiable on $[0, 1]$,
and suppose that for every $x \in [0, 1]$ there is an integer $n \ge 0$ such that the $n$-th
derivative of $f$ within $[0, 1]$ vanishes at $x$ (at the endpoints these derivatives are
one-sided). Then there is a polynomial $p$ with real coefficients such that $f(x) = p(x)$ for
every $x \in [0, 1]$.

Smoothness means infinite differentiability here, not real analyticity: the source's formal
statement assumed real analyticity, which reduces the problem to the identity theorem.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_81`, with the change above.

articles.title: The map $x \mapsto e^{x-1} - e^{1-x}$ has a unique fixed point
articles.statement:
There is exactly one
real number $x$ such that $e^{x-1} - e^{1-x} = x$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_59`.

articles.title: Odd Taylor polynomials of the exponential have exactly one real zero
articles.statement:
For every odd
positive integer $n$, the polynomial $1+x+x^2/2!+\cdots+x^n/n!$ has exactly one real zero.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Polynomials, rational functions in real analysis), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_19`.

articles.title: Interchange of limits and derivatives at interior points
articles.statement:
Let $a < b$ be real numbers,
and let $f_n, f_n' : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
$g, g' : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be functions. Suppose that for every $n$ and every
$x \in [a, b]$, $f_n$ is differentiable at $x$ (two-sided, also at the endpoints) with
derivative $f_n'(x)$; that each $f_n'$ is continuous on $[a, b]$; that $f_n' \to g'$
uniformly on $[a, b]$; and that $f_n(x) \to g(x)$ for every $x \in [a, b]$. Then $g$ is
differentiable at every $x \in (a, b)$ with derivative $g'(x)$.

articles.title: Interchange of limits and derivatives on a closed interval
articles.statement:
Let $a < b$ be real
numbers, and let $f_n, f_n' : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
$g, g' : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be functions. Suppose that for every $n$ and every
$x \in [a, b]$, $f_n$ is differentiable at $x$ (two-sided, also at the endpoints) with
derivative $f_n'(x)$; that each $f_n'$ is continuous on $[a, b]$; that $f_n' \to g'$
uniformly on $[a, b]$; and that $f_n(x) \to g(x)$ for every $x \in [a, b]$. Then for every
$x \in [a, b]$, $g$ has derivative $g'(x)$ at $x$ within $[a, b]$ (a one-sided derivative at
the endpoints), and $g'$ is continuous on $[a, b]$.

articles.title: A strict local maximum is a local maximum
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a function from a
topological space $X$ to a preordered set $Y$. If $f$ has a strict local maximum at $a \in X$,
then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$, that is, $f(x) \le f(a)$ for all $x$ in some neighborhood
of $a$.

articles.title: A strict local minimum is a local minimum
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a function from a
topological space $X$ to a preordered set $Y$. If $f$ has a strict local minimum at $a \in X$,
then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$, that is, $f(a) \le f(x)$ for all $x$ in some neighborhood
of $a$.

articles.title: Strict second-derivative test, maximum version
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and
$x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$. If $f''(x_0) < 0$, $f'(x_0) = 0$, and $f$ is continuous at $x_0$, then $f$
has a strict local maximum at $x_0$.

This is the minimum version applied to $-f$.

articles.title: Strict local maximum
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a function from a topological space
$X$ to a set $Y$ equipped with a relation $<$. Then $f$ has a strict local maximum at a point
$a \in X$ if $f(x) < f(a)$ for all $x \ne a$ in some neighborhood of $a$.

articles.title: Strict second-derivative test, minimum version
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and
$x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$. If $f''(x_0) > 0$, $f'(x_0) = 0$, and $f$ is continuous at $x_0$, then $f$
has a strict local minimum at $x_0$.

articles.title: Strict local minimum
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a function from a topological space
$X$ to a set $Y$ equipped with a relation $<$. Then $f$ has a strict local minimum at a point
$a \in X$ if $f(a) < f(x)$ for all $x \ne a$ in some neighborhood of $a$.

This strengthens the usual (non-strict) notion of local minimum: the inequality is strict and
the point $a$ itself is excluded.

articles.title: Negation turns a strict local maximum into a strict local minimum
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a
topological space and let $Y$ be an additive group with a relation $<$ such that addition on
the left and addition on the right are strictly monotone. If $f \colon X \to Y$ has a strict
local maximum at $a \in X$, then $x \mapsto -f(x)$ has a strict local minimum at $a$.

articles.title: Negation turns a strict local minimum into a strict local maximum
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a
topological space and let $Y$ be an additive group with a relation $<$ such that addition on
the left and addition on the right are strictly monotone. If $f \colon X \to Y$ has a strict
local minimum at $a \in X$, then $x \mapsto -f(x)$ has a strict local maximum at $a$.

articles.title: Unit-window bound for the integral of $\sin(t^2)$
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be
given by $f(x) = \int_x^{x+1} \sin(t^2)\,dt$. Then $|f(x)| < 1/x$ for every real $x > 0$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_29`.

articles.title: Bhandari's arcsine-over-sine integral
articles.statement:
Let $G = \sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n/(2n+1)^2$ be
Catalan's constant, and for $s > 0$ let $S_s = \sum_{n \ge 0} 1/(n + s)^2$. Then the integral
$\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\arcsin(\sin^2 x)}{\sin x}\,dx$ equals
$-2G - \frac{\pi^2}{2\sqrt 2} + \frac{S_{1/8} + S_{3/8}}{8\sqrt 2}$.

The series $S_{1/8}$ and $S_{3/8}$ are the trigamma values $\psi_1(1/8)$ and $\psi_1(3/8)$;
Catalan's constant and these trigamma values are written out as their defining series.

Proof: The route follows Bhandari's reduction to log-tangent integrals, followed by an
Abel-regularized Fourier expansion and residue-class evaluation.

## Sources

- Narendra Bhandari, "Infinite Series Associated with the Ratio and Product of Central Binomial Coefficients", Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), equation (36), lines 307--309, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Bhandari/bhan8.tex>.

articles.title: Recursion for the limiting areas between cosine powers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$,
let $A_n(k) = \int_0^\pi |\cos^n x - \cos^n(kx)|\,dx$. For every natural number $n \ge 3$ there
are real numbers $L$ and $L'$ such that $A_n(k) \to L$ and $A_{n-2}(k) \to L'$ as $k \to \infty$
through the natural numbers, and $L = \frac{n-1}{n} L' + \frac{c}{n^2 \pi}$, where $c = 8$ if $n$
is odd and $c = 16$ if $n$ is even.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Theorem 3 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-thm-3`).

articles.title: The area between cosine powers vanishes at frequency one
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$,
let $A_n(k) = \int_0^\pi |\cos^n x - \cos^n(kx)|\,dx$ be the area between $\cos^n x$ and
$\cos^n(kx)$ on $[0, \pi]$. Then $A_n(1) = 0$ for every natural number $n$, since the two curves
then coincide.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Eq. (1).

articles.title: The area between cosine powers vanishes for exponent zero
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and
$k$, let $A_n(k) = \int_0^\pi |\cos^n x - \cos^n(kx)|\,dx$ be the area between $\cos^n x$ and
$\cos^n(kx)$ on $[0, \pi]$. Then $A_0(k) = 0$ for every natural number $k$, since both curves are
then the constant $1$.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Eq. (1).

articles.title: Area between powers of cosines
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the area between the
curves $y = \cos^n x$ and $y = \cos^n(kx)$ on $[0, \pi]$ is
$A_n(k) = \int_0^\pi |\cos^n x - \cos^n(kx)|\,dx$, where $\cos^n x$ means $(\cos x)^n$.

The paper's $A_n$ is the limit of $A_n(k)$ as $k \to \infty$ (Eq. (1)), with $k$ running over
the natural numbers.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Eq. (1).

articles.title: Double-factorial sums as derivatives of arcsine quotients
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number.
If $n$ is odd, the $n$th derivative at $0$ of $x \mapsto \arcsin x / (1 - x)$ is

$$n! \sum_{j=0}^{(n-1)/2} \frac{(2j-1)!!}{(2j)!!\,(2j+1)},$$

and if $n \ge 2$ is even, the $n$th derivative at $0$ of $x \mapsto (\arcsin x)^2 / (2(1 - x))$ is

$$n! \sum_{j=0}^{(n-2)/2} \frac{(2j)!!}{(2j+1)!!\,(2j+2)},$$

where $(-1)!! = 1$ and $0!! = 1$.

These are the $n$th terms of the exponential generating functions of $\arcsin x / (1 - x)$
(OEIS A296726) and of $(\arcsin x)^2 / (2(1 - x))$ (OEIS A372324).

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Theorem 4 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-thm-4`).

articles.title: Half-step sine sum for even modulus and even multiplier
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a positive even
natural number and $q$ an even natural number. Then $\sum_{\ell=1}^{N/2} \sin(q \ell \pi / N)$
equals $0$ if $q \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ and $\cot(q\pi / (2N))$ if $q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$.

The paper also assumes $q > 0$; that hypothesis is dropped here.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Lemma 7 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-lem-7`).

articles.title: Half-period sine sum for even modulus
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a positive even natural number. For
every natural number $q$, $\sum_{\ell=1}^{N/2} \sin(2\pi q \ell / N)$ equals $0$ if $q$ is even
and $\cot(q\pi / N)$ if $q$ is odd.

The paper also assumes $q > 0$; for $q = 0$ both sides are $0$.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Lemma 5 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-lem-5`).

articles.title: Half-period sine sum for odd modulus
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be an odd natural number. For every
natural number $q$, $\sum_{\ell=1}^{(N-1)/2} \sin(2\pi q \ell / N)$ equals
$-\frac{1}{2} \tan\frac{q\pi}{2N}$ if $q$ is even and $\frac{1}{2} \cot\frac{q\pi}{2N}$ if $q$ is
odd.

The paper also assumes $q > 0$; for $q = 0$ both sides are $0$.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Lemma 6 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-lem-6`).

articles.title: Limiting area between cosine powers via double factorials
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and
$k$, let $A_n(k) = \int_0^\pi |\cos^n x - \cos^n(kx)|\,dx$. As $k \to \infty$ through the natural
numbers: if $n$ is odd, then

$$A_n(k) \to \frac{8 \, n!}{\pi (n!!)^2} \sum_{j=0}^{(n-1)/2} \frac{(2j-1)!!}{(2j)!! (2j+1)},$$

and if $n \ge 2$ is even, then

$$A_n(k) \to \frac{16 \, n!}{\pi (n!!)^2} \sum_{j=0}^{(n-2)/2} \frac{(2j)!!}{(2j+1)!! (2j+2)}.$$

Here $(-1)!! = 1$ and $0!! = 1$.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Theorem 4 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-thm-4`).

articles.title: Limiting area between even cosine powers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, let
$A_n(k) = \int_0^\pi |\cos^n x - \cos^n(kx)|\,dx$. As $k \to \infty$ through the natural numbers:
if $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, then

$$A_n(k) \to \frac{16}{2^n \pi} \sum_{j=0}^{(n-2)/4} \frac{\binom{n}{2j}}{(n/2 - 2j)^2},$$

and if $n \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, then

$$A_n(k) \to \frac{16}{2^n \pi} \sum_{j=0}^{(n-4)/4} \frac{\binom{n}{2j+1}}{(n/2 - 2j - 1)^2}.$$

For $n = 0$ the right-hand side is $0$, as is $A_0(k)$ for every $k$, so no positivity hypothesis
is needed.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Theorem 2 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-thm-2`).

articles.title: Area between $\cos^n x$ and $\cos^n(kx)$ in the limit, odd $n$
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be an odd natural
number. As $k \to \infty$ through the natural numbers, the area
$\int_0^\pi |\cos^n x - \cos^n(kx)|\,dx$ between $\cos^n x$ and $\cos^n(kx)$ on $[0, \pi]$
converges to

$$\frac{8}{2^{n-1}\pi} \sum_{j=0}^{(n-1)/2} \frac{\binom{n}{j}}{(n-2j)^2}.$$

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Theorem 1 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-thm-1`).

articles.title: The cotangent limit $4/x$
articles.statement:
For every nonzero real number $x$, as $k \to \infty$ through the
natural numbers,

$$\left(\frac{1}{k} - 1\right)\cot\frac{x}{k-1} + \left(\frac{1}{k} + 1\right)\cot\frac{x}{k+1}
\to \frac{4}{x}.$$

The paper states this for every real number $x$; the hypothesis $x \neq 0$ is added because at
$x = 0$ the cotangents and $4/x$ are undefined.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Lemma 8 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-lem-8`).

articles.title: Alternating integral sums of $\cos qx - \cos qkx$ for even $q$ and even $k$
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an
even natural number, for each natural number $m$ put $k = 2m$, and let
$f(x) = \cos(qx) - \cos(qkx)$. Then, as $m \to \infty$,

$$\sum_{\ell=1}^{m} \left(\int_{(\ell-1)\pi/(k-1)}^{\ell\pi/(k+1)} f(x)\,dx -
\int_{\ell\pi/(k+1)}^{\ell\pi/(k-1)} f(x)\,dx\right)$$

tends to $0$ if $q \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ and to $16/(q^2\pi)$ if $q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Lemma 12 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-lem-12`).

articles.title: Alternating integral sums of $\cos qx - \cos qkx$ for odd $q$ and even $k$
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an
odd natural number, for each natural number $m$ put $k = 2m$, and let
$f(x) = \cos(qx) - \cos(qkx)$. Then, as $m \to \infty$,

$$\sum_{\ell=1}^{m} \left(\int_{2(\ell-1)\pi/(k-1)}^{2\ell\pi/(k+1)} f(x)\,dx -
\int_{2\ell\pi/(k+1)}^{2\ell\pi/(k-1)} f(x)\,dx\right) \to \frac{8}{q^2\pi}.$$

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Lemma 11 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-lem-11`).

articles.title: Alternating integral sums of $\cos qx - \cos qkx$ for even $q$ and odd $k$
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an
even natural number, for each natural number $m$ put $k = 2m + 1$, and let
$f(x) = \cos(qx) - \cos(qkx)$. Then, as $m \to \infty$,

$$\sum_{\ell=1}^{m} \left(\int_{(\ell-1)\pi/(k-1)}^{\ell\pi/(k+1)} f(x)\,dx -
\int_{\ell\pi/(k+1)}^{\ell\pi/(k-1)} f(x)\,dx\right)$$

tends to $0$ if $q \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ and to $16/(q^2\pi)$ if $q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Lemma 10 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-lem-10`).

articles.title: Integral sums of $\cos qkx - \cos qx$ for odd $q$ and odd $k$
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an odd natural
number, and for each natural number $m$ put $k = 2m + 1$. Then, as $m \to \infty$,

$$\sum_{\ell=1}^{m} \int_{2\pi\ell/(k+1)}^{2\pi\ell/(k-1)} \bigl(\cos(qkx) - \cos(qx)\bigr)\,dx
\to \frac{4}{q^2\pi}.$$

## Sources

- Muhammad Adam Dombrowski and Gregory Dresden, *Areas Between Cosines*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.3, Lemma 9 (`jis-2025-25.2.3-lem-9`).

articles.title: A function continuous on $(0,1)$ with vanishing moments is zero on $(0,1)$
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[0,1]$, and suppose that
$\int_0^1 f(x)\,x^n\,dx = 0$ for every natural number $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$. Then $f(x) = 0$ for
every $x \in [0,1]$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_51`.

articles.title: Conditional convergence of the Dirichlet integral on $(1, \infty)$
articles.statement:
The function
$x \mapsto \sin x / x$ is interval integrable on $[1, b]$ for every real $b \ge 1$, the integrals
$\int_1^b \frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx$ converge to a real limit as $b \to \infty$, and $\sin x / x$ is
not Lebesgue integrable on $(1, \infty)$.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, *Principles of Mathematical Analysis*, 3rd ed., Ch. 11, Exercise 15 (conditional convergence of the sine integral).

articles.title: Comparison test for improper integrals
articles.statement:
Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and let
$f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be interval integrable on $[a, b]$ for every $b \ge a$, with
$0 \le f(x) \le g(x)$ for all $x \ge a$. If $\int_a^b g(x)\,dx$ converges to a real limit as
$b \to \infty$, then $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ also converges to a real limit as $b \to \infty$.

## Sources

- https://mathbooks.unl.edu/Calculus/sec-5-11-comparison.html

articles.title: Limit comparison test for improper integrals
articles.statement:
Let $a, L \in \mathbb{R}$
with $L \ne 0$, and let $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be interval integrable on $[a, b]$ for
every $b \ge a$, with $f(x) > 0$ and $g(x) > 0$ for all $x \ge a$. If $f(x) / g(x) \to L$ as
$x \to \infty$, then $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ converges to a real limit as $b \to \infty$ if and
only if $\int_a^b g(x)\,dx$ converges to a real limit as $b \to \infty$.

## Sources

- T. Apostol, *Mathematical Analysis*, 2nd ed., §10.23 (limit comparison test).

articles.title: Serret's integral
articles.statement:
With $\log$ the natural logarithm,

$$\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+x)}{1+x^2}\,dx = \frac{\pi}{8}\log 2.$$

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_58`.

articles.title: The integral of $x f(x) f'(x)$ equals $-1/2$
articles.statement:
Let $a\lt b$ and let
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuously differentiable on $[a,b]$ with $f(a)=f(b)=0$ and

$$
\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx=1.
$$

Then

$$
\int_a^b x\,f(x)\,f'(x)\,dx=-\frac12.
$$

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_16`.

articles.title: Integral of $1/(a + b\cos\theta)$ over a period
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers with
$a > |b|$. Then

$$\int_0^{2\pi} \frac{d\theta}{a + b\cos\theta} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}.$$

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Functions of a complex variable; General properties of functions of one complex variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_89`.

articles.title: Integral of the squared sinc function over the half-line
articles.statement:
The integral of
$(\sin x / x)^2$ over $(0, \infty)$ is $\pi/2$:

$$\int_0^\infty \left(\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)^2 dx = \frac{\pi}{2}.$$

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_35`.

articles.title: Ramanujan's closed form for $\int_0^x du/(1 + u^{10})$ (Chapter 8, Entry 14)
articles.statement:
Put
$a_\pm = \sqrt{6 \pm 2\sqrt5}$ and $b_\pm = \sqrt{10 \pm 2\sqrt5}$. For every real $x$ with
$0 \le x < 1$,

$$\int_0^x \frac{du}{1 + u^{10}} = \frac{\arctan x}{5} +
\frac{a_+}{20} \arctan \frac{a_+ x}{2(1 - x^2)} + \frac{a_-}{20} \arctan \frac{a_- x}{2(1 - x^2)} +
\frac{b_+}{40} \log \frac{1 + b_+ x/2 + x^2}{1 - b_+ x/2 + x^2} +
\frac{b_-}{40} \log \frac{1 + b_- x/2 + x^2}{1 - b_- x/2 + x^2}.$$

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 8.

articles.title: Ramanujan's closed form for $\int_0^x du/(1 + u^5)$ (Chapter 8, Entry 14(v))
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be
a real number with $-1 < x < 4/(\sqrt5 + 1)$, and put $c_\pm = \sqrt{10 \pm 2\sqrt5}$ and

$$Q(x) = \frac{1 + \tfrac12 x(\sqrt5 - 1) + x^2}{1 - \tfrac12 x(\sqrt5 + 1) + x^2}.$$

Then $u \mapsto 1/(1 + u^5)$ is integrable on the interval between $0$ and $x$,
$(1 + x)^5/(1 + x^5) > 0$, $Q(x) > 0$, $4 + x(\sqrt5 - 1) \ne 0$, $4 - x(\sqrt5 + 1) \ne 0$, and

$$\int_0^x \frac{du}{1 + u^5} = \frac{1}{20} \log \frac{(1 + x)^5}{1 + x^5} +
\frac{1}{4\sqrt5} \log Q(x) + \frac{c_+}{10} \arctan \frac{c_+ x}{4 + x(\sqrt5 - 1)} +
\frac{c_-}{10} \arctan \frac{c_- x}{4 - x(\sqrt5 + 1)}.$$

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 8, Entry 14(v), pp. 189–191.

articles.title: Ramanujan's closed form for $\int_0^x du/(1 + u^6)$ (Chapter 8, Entry 14(vi))
articles.statement:
For every
real number $x$, the function $u \mapsto 1/(1 + u^6)$ is integrable on the interval between $0$
and $x$, $1 + \sqrt3\,x + x^2 > 0$, $1 - \sqrt3\,x + x^2 > 0$, and

$$\int_0^x \frac{du}{1 + u^6} = \frac12 \arctan x + \frac16 \arctan x^3 +
\frac{1}{4\sqrt3} \log \frac{1 + \sqrt3\,x + x^2}{1 - \sqrt3\,x + x^2}.$$

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 8, Entry 14(vi), pp. 189–190.

articles.title: Ramanujan's closed form for $\int_0^x du/(1 + u^8)$ (Chapter 8, Entry 14(vii))
articles.statement:
Put
$s_\pm = \sqrt{2 \pm \sqrt2}$ and, for real $x$,
$R_\pm(x) = \frac{1 + s_\pm x + x^2}{1 - s_\pm x + x^2}$. For every real $x$ with $|x| < 1$, the
function $u \mapsto 1/(1 + u^8)$ is integrable on the interval between $0$ and $x$, $R_+(x) > 0$,
$R_-(x) > 0$, $1 - x^2 \ne 0$, and

$$\int_0^x \frac{du}{1 + u^8} = \frac{s_+}{16} \left( \log R_+(x) +
2 \arctan \frac{s_+ x}{1 - x^2} \right) + \frac{s_-}{16} \left( \log R_-(x) +
2 \arctan \frac{s_- x}{1 - x^2} \right).$$

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 8, Entry 14(vii), pp. 189–190.

articles.title: Ramanujan's integrals of $\cos^n x \sin nx$ (Entry 33)
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and
let $H_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} 1/k$ be the $n$-th harmonic number. Then $x \cos^n x \sin(nx)$ and
$\cos^n x \sin(nx)$ are integrable on $[0, \pi/2]$,
$\int_0^{\pi/2} x \cos^n x \sin(nx)\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2^{n+2}} H_n$ and
$\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^n x \sin(nx)\,dx = \frac{1}{2^{n+1}} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{2^k}{k}$.

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 9.

articles.title: Ramanujan's integrals of $\cos^n x \sin nx$ for every $n \ge 0$
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural
number and let $H_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} 1/k$ be the $n$-th harmonic number. Then
$x \cos^n x \sin(nx)$ and $\cos^n x \sin(nx)$ are integrable on $[0, \pi/2]$,
$\int_0^{\pi/2} x \cos^n x \sin(nx)\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2^{n+2}} H_n$ and
$\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^n x \sin(nx)\,dx = \frac{1}{2^{n+1}} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{2^k}{k}$.

This is Entry 33 without the hypothesis $n > 0$: at $n = 0$ both sides of each identity are $0$.

articles.title: Cauchy's formula for the twice-iterated integral
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real Banach space, let
$\alpha \le \beta$ be real numbers and let $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ be continuous on
$[\alpha, \beta]$. Then for every $s \in [\alpha, \beta]$,

$$\int_\alpha^s \Bigl(\int_\alpha^t f(\tau)\,d\tau\Bigr)\,dt = \int_\alpha^s (s - t)\, f(t)\,dt.$$

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_44`.

articles.title: Endpoints of a partition are ordered
articles.statement:
If $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and the interval $[a, b]$
has a partition, then $a \le b$.

articles.title: Common refinement of two tagged partitions
articles.statement:
Let $a, b$ be real numbers. For any two
tagged partitions $T_1$ and $T_2$ of $[a, b]$, there is a tagged partition $T''$ of $[a, b]$
that is a tagged refinement of both $T_1$ and $T_2$.

The proof takes for $T''$ the partition whose points are the union of the points of $T_1$
and $T_2$, with each tag at the left endpoint of its subinterval.

articles.title: Refinement of a partition
articles.statement:
For partitions $P$ and $Q$ of $[a, b]$, $Q$ is a refinement of
$P$ when every point of $P$ is a point of $Q$, that is, when the point set of $P$ is contained in
the point set of $Q$.

articles.title: Tagged-refinement data
articles.statement:
Let $T$ and $T'$ be tagged partitions of $[a, b]$ with points
$a = x_0 < \dots < x_n = b$ and $a = x'_0 < \dots < x'_{n'} = b$ respectively. Tagged-refinement
data from $T$ to $T'$ consist of a map $\sigma$ assigning to each index $j < n'$ an index
$\sigma(j) < n$ such that $x_{\sigma(j)} \le x'_j$ and $x'_{j+1} \le x_{\sigma(j)+1}$ for every
$j < n'$ (so the $j$-th subinterval of $T'$ lies in the $\sigma(j)$-th subinterval of $T$), and
such that for every $k < n$ the lengths assigned to $k$ add up to its length:
$\sum_{j < n',\ \sigma(j) = k} (x'_{j+1} - x'_j) = x_{k+1} - x_k$. The tags of $T$ and $T'$
play no role.

Such data exist whenever every point of $T$ is a point of $T'$.

articles.title: Subinterval lengths are at most the mesh
articles.statement:
Let $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$ be a
partition of $[a, b]$. Then for every $i$ with $0 \le i < n$, the subinterval length
$x_{i+1} - x_i$ is at most the mesh of the partition.

articles.title: The mesh is positive on a nondegenerate interval
articles.statement:
If $a < b$, then every partition of
$[a, b]$ has strictly positive mesh.

articles.title: Mesh of a partition
articles.statement:
The mesh (also called the norm) of a partition
$a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$ of $[a, b]$ is the maximum subinterval length
$\max_{1 \le k \le n} (x_k - x_{k-1})$ when $n \ge 1$, and $0$ when $n = 0$.

articles.title: A partition of a nondegenerate interval has a subinterval
articles.statement:
If $a < b$, then every
partition $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$ of $[a, b]$ has at least one subinterval, that is,
$n \ge 1$.

articles.title: Refinements carry tagged-refinement data
articles.statement:
Let $T$ and $T'$ be tagged partitions of
$[a, b]$ such that every point of $T$ is a point of $T'$. Then tagged-refinement data from $T$
to $T'$ exist: an assignment of each subinterval of $T'$ to a subinterval of $T$ that contains
it, such that for each subinterval of $T$ the lengths of the subintervals of $T'$ assigned to it
add up to its length.

articles.title: Partition of an interval
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$ and $b$, a partition of the closed interval
$[a, b]$ consists of a natural number $n$, the number of subintervals, together with $n + 1$
points forming a strictly increasing sequence $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$.

articles.title: Points of a partition
articles.statement:
The point set of a partition $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$ of
$[a, b]$ is the set of its points $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n$.

articles.title: Riemann sum of a constant function
articles.statement:
For every real constant $c$ and every tagged partition
of $[a, b]$, the Riemann sum of the constant function $x \mapsto c$ equals $c(b - a)$.

articles.title: Riemann sum regrouped over a refinement
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, let $T$ be
a tagged partition of $[a, b]$ with points $x_0 < \dots < x_n$ and tags
$\xi_0, \dots, \xi_{n-1}$, and let $T'$ be a tagged partition of $[a, b]$ with points
$x'_0 < \dots < x'_{n'}$, together with tagged-refinement data from $T$ to $T'$ assigning to
each $j < n'$ an index $\sigma(j) < n$. Then the Riemann sum $S_f(T)$ of $f$ over $T$ satisfies

$$S_f(T) = \sum_{j=0}^{n'-1} f(\xi_{\sigma(j)}) \, (x'_{j+1} - x'_j).$$

articles.title: Riemann sum over a trivial partition
articles.statement:
For every function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$
and every tagged partition of $[a, b]$ with no subintervals, the Riemann sum of $f$ is $0$, since
it is an empty sum.

articles.title: Riemann sums of two partitions with a common refinement
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$
and let $T_1$, $T_2$ be tagged partitions of $[a, b]$ with meshes $\|T_1\|$ and $\|T_2\|$.
Suppose $\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy, for $i = 1, 2$, $|f(x) - f(y)| \le \omega_i$
for all $x, y \in [a, b]$ with $|x - y| \le \|T_i\|$. Let $T''$ be a tagged partition of
$[a, b]$ together with tagged-refinement data from $T_1$ to $T''$ and from $T_2$ to $T''$.
Writing $S_f(T)$ for the Riemann sum of $f$ over $T$, we have
$|S_f(T_1) - S_f(T_2)| \le (\omega_1 + \omega_2)(b - a)$.

This is Theorem III of the Riemann integral section in oscillation form: explicit bounds
$\omega_i$ replace the modulus of continuity, so $f$ need not be continuous.

articles.title: Riemann sums under refinement
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, let $T$ and $T'$ be
tagged partitions of $[a, b]$ such that every point of $T$ is a point of $T'$, and let
$\omega \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|f(x) - f(y)| \le \omega$ for all $x, y \in [a, b]$ with
$|x - y| \le \|T\|$, where $\|T\|$ is the mesh of $T$. Writing $S_f(T)$ for the Riemann sum of
$f$ over $T$, we have $|S_f(T) - S_f(T')| \le \omega (b - a)$.

This is Theorem II of the Riemann integral section in oscillation form: an explicit bound
$\omega$ replaces the modulus of continuity, so $f$ need not be continuous.

articles.title: Riemann sums under refinement, given refinement data
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
let $T$ and $T'$ be tagged partitions of $[a, b]$ together with tagged-refinement data from $T$
to $T'$, and let $\omega \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|f(x) - f(y)| \le \omega$ for all
$x, y \in [a, b]$ with $|x - y| \le \|T\|$, where $\|T\|$ is the mesh of $T$. Writing $S_f(T)$
for the Riemann sum of $f$ over $T$, we have $|S_f(T) - S_f(T')| \le \omega (b - a)$.

articles.title: Riemann sum
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $T$ be a tagged partition of
$[a, b]$, with points $a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b$ and tags $\xi_k \in [x_{k-1}, x_k]$
for $k = 1, \dots, n$. The Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to $T$ is
$S_f(x, \xi) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} f(\xi_k)\,(x_k - x_{k-1})$ (an empty sum, equal to $0$, when
$n = 0$).

articles.title: Subintervals of a partition have nonnegative length
articles.statement:
If
$a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b$ is a partition of $[a, b]$, then $x_{i+1} - x_i \ge 0$ for
every $i$ with $0 \le i < n$.

articles.title: Subinterval lengths of a partition telescope
articles.statement:
If $a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b$ is
a partition of $[a, b]$, then the lengths of its subintervals sum to the length of the interval:
$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (x_{i+1} - x_i) = b - a$.

articles.title: Tags of a tagged partition lie in the interval
articles.statement:
Every tag $\xi_k$ of a tagged partition
of $[a, b]$ lies in $[a, b]$.

articles.title: Tagged partition
articles.statement:
A tagged partition of $[a, b]$ is a partition
$a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b$ of $[a, b]$ together with a choice of a tag
$\xi_k \in [x_{k-1}, x_k]$ in each subinterval, for $k = 1, \dots, n$.

articles.title: Telescoping over the fibers of an assignment
articles.statement:
Let $y_0, \dots, y_N$ be real numbers,
let $\varphi : \{0, \dots, m\} \to \{0, \dots, N\}$ be strictly increasing, and let
$\sigma : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \{0, \dots, m-1\}$ satisfy
$\varphi(\sigma(j)) \le j < \varphi(\sigma(j) + 1)$ for every $j < N$. Then for every $k < m$,

$$\sum_{j < N,\ \sigma(j) = k} (y_{j+1} - y_j) = y_{\varphi(k+1)} - y_{\varphi(k)}.$$

articles.title: Uniformly continuous integrable functions vanish at infinity
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be uniformly continuous and Lebesgue integrable on $\mathbb{R}$.
Then $f(x) \to 0$ as $|x| \to \infty$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_48`.

articles.title: The partial derivatives of $x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ are bounded
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $f(0,0)=0$ and $f(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ for $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$.
Then the partial derivatives $D_1 f$ and $D_2 f$ are bounded on $\mathbb{R}^2$: there is a real $M$
with $|D_1 f(x,y)| \le M$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$, and a real $M'$ with $|D_2 f(x,y)| \le M'$ for
all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of several variables), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_56`.

articles.title: The function $xy/(x^2+y^2)$ is discontinuous only at the origin
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be given by $f(x,y) = \frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}$ for
$(x,y) \neq (0,0)$ and $f(0,0) = 0$. Then $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{(0,0)\}$
and is not continuous at $(0,0)$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of several variables), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_93`.

articles.title: The signed radial function is not differentiable at the origin
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be the function

$$
f(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}, & y>0,\\
x, & y=0,\\
-\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}, & y<0.
\end{cases}
$$

Then $f$ is not differentiable at $(0, 0)$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of several variables), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_06`.

articles.title: Mazur's Problem 66 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
Mazur's mixed partial derivatives claim is false:
there is a function $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, at every point $(x, y)$ of the
open unit square $Q = (0, 1) \times (0, 1)$, the functions $s \mapsto f(s, y)$ and
$s \mapsto f(x, s)$ are differentiable at $x$ and at $y$ respectively, and their derivatives
$\partial_x f(\cdot, y)$ and $\partial_y f(x, \cdot)$ are again differentiable at $x$ and at $y$
respectively, but the set of points $(x, y) \in Q$ at which $s \mapsto \partial_y f(s, y)$ is not
differentiable at $x$ is not a Lebesgue null set.

## Sources

- S. Mazur, Problem 66 of the Scottish Book; refuted by V. Mykhaylyuk and A. Plichko, who construct a separately twice differentiable function on `[0, 1]²` and a set of positive measure on which the mixed derivative `f_xy` does not exist ("On a Mazur problem from 'The Scottish Book' concerning second partial derivatives", Colloq. Math. 141 (2015), 175–181, arXiv:1508.06909).

articles.title: Mazur's mixed partial derivatives claim
articles.statement:
This is the following statement, the claim of
Mazur's Problem 66 from the Scottish Book. Let $Q = (0, 1) \times (0, 1)$ be the open unit square.
For every function $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, at every point $(x, y) \in Q$, the
functions $s \mapsto f(s, y)$ and $s \mapsto f(x, s)$ are differentiable at $x$ and at $y$
respectively, and their derivatives $\partial_x f(\cdot, y)$ and $\partial_y f(x, \cdot)$ are
again differentiable at $x$ and at $y$ respectively, the mixed partial derivative
$\partial_x \partial_y f$ exists at almost every point of $Q$ for Lebesgue measure: for almost
every $(x, y) \in Q$, the function $s \mapsto \partial_y f(s, y)$ is differentiable at $x$.

Mazur asked whether a function with first partial derivatives and both pure second partial
derivatives must have its mixed second partial derivatives almost everywhere; the claim asks this
only for $\partial_x \partial_y f$.

articles.title: Smooth functions vanishing on the axes are $O(|x|\,|y|)$ near the origin
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be infinitely differentiable with $f(x,y) = 0$ whenever $xy = 0$.
Then there is a constant $C > 0$ such that $|f(x,y)| \le C\,|x|\,|y|$ for all real $x$ and $y$ with
$|x| < 1$ and $|y| < 1$, that is, on the open unit ball of $\mathbb{R}^2$ for the maximum norm.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Real functions; Functions of several variables), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_01`.

articles.title: Equal partial derivatives give a factor $x+y$
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuously differentiable with $\partial_1 f = \partial_2 f$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $f(0,0)=0$.
Then there is a continuous $g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(x,y)=g(x,y)\,(x+y)$ for all
$(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of several variables), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_02`.

articles.title: An implicit function for $x^2y_1+e^x+y_2=0$ near $(1,-1)$
articles.statement:
Let
$f(x,y_1,y_2)=x^2y_1+e^x+y_2$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$. Then there are an open set
$U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ containing $(1,-1)$ and a function $g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$,
differentiable on $U$, with $g(1,-1)=0$ and $f(g(y_1,y_2),y_1,y_2)=0$ for all $(y_1,y_2)\in U$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of several variables), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_43`.

articles.title: The dot product with a fixed vector
articles.statement:
For a finite type $\iota$ and a vector
$x \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$, this is the map $v \mapsto v \cdot x = \sum_{i \in \iota} v_i x_i$,
as a continuous linear functional $\mathbb{R}^\iota \to \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: The chain rule for gradients
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $g : E \to F$
be differentiable at $x \in E$, and let $f : F \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $g(x)$. Then
$\nabla (f \circ g)(x) = Dg(x)^* \, \nabla f(g(x))$, where $Dg(x) : E \to F$ is the Fréchet
derivative of $g$ at $x$ and $Dg(x)^*$ is its adjoint.

articles.title: Directional derivative from the gradient
articles.statement:
Let $\iota$ be a finite type, let
$f : \mathbb{R}^\iota \to \mathbb{R}$ and $g, z \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$, and suppose $f$ is Fréchet
differentiable at $z$ with derivative $w \mapsto w \cdot g$. Then for every
$v \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$, the function $t \mapsto f(z + t v)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has derivative
$v \cdot g$ at $t = 0$.

articles.title: A Fréchet derivative given by a dot product is a gradient
articles.statement:
Let $\iota$ be a finite type,
let $f : \mathbb{R}^\iota \to \mathbb{R}$ and $g, z \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$, and suppose that, for the
sup norm on $\mathbb{R}^\iota$, $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $z$ with derivative
$v \mapsto v \cdot g$. Then $f$, viewed as a function on the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^\iota$ with
inner product $\langle v, w \rangle = \sum_{i \in \iota} v_i w_i$, has gradient $g$ at $z$.

articles.title: Green's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be open, let $D \subseteq U$ be bounded and
measurable, and let $L, M : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuously differentiable on $U$.
Let $a\lt b$ and let $\gamma=(\gamma_1,\gamma_2) : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be continuous on
$[a,b]$, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, injective on $[a,b)$, with $\gamma(t)\ne\gamma(a)$ for
$a\lt t\lt b$, with image $\gamma([a,b])$ equal to the boundary of $D$, and with $\gamma(t)\in U$ for
all $t\in[a,b]$. Suppose there is a finite set $S\subseteq[a,b]$ containing $a$ and $b$ such that
$\gamma$ is continuously differentiable on $[a,b]\setminus S$ and on $[u,v]$ for any two
consecutive points $u\lt v$ of $S$, and such that for every $t\in(a,b)\setminus S$ we have
$\gamma'(t)\ne0$ and, for some $\delta>0$, $\gamma(t)+\varepsilon(-\gamma_2'(t),\gamma_1'(t))\in D$
for all $0\lt \varepsilon\lt \delta$ (so $D$ lies to the left of the curve). Then

$$
\int_a^b \bigl(L(\gamma(t))\,\gamma_1'(t)+M(\gamma(t))\,\gamma_2'(t)\bigr)\,dt
=\int_D \Bigl(\frac{\partial M}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}\Bigr)\,d(x,y).
$$

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_theorem.

articles.title: The second derivative is nonnegative at a local minimum
articles.statement:
Let $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$
be twice continuously differentiable. If $g$ has a local minimum at $x$, then $g''(x) \ge 0$.

This is the necessary direction of the one-variable second derivative test.

articles.title: Entries of the Hessian matrix
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, a point
$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and indices $i, j$, the $(i, j)$ entry of the Hessian matrix of $f$ at $x$ is
$\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=0} \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} f(x + s e_i + t e_j)$, where $e_1, \dots, e_n$ is
the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and a derivative that does not exist is taken to be $0$:
differentiate first along $e_j$, then along $e_i$.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 9.

articles.title: Hessian entries as second Fréchet derivatives
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be
twice continuously differentiable and let $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. For all indices $i, j$, the
$(i, j)$ entry of the Hessian matrix of $f$ at $x$ equals $D(Df)(x)(e_i)(e_j)$, the derivative of
the Fréchet derivative $Df$ at $x$ in the direction $e_i$, applied to $e_j$, where
$e_1, \dots, e_n$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: Symmetry of the Hessian
articles.statement:
If $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is twice continuously
differentiable, then for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the Hessian matrix of $f$ at $x$ is symmetric:
it equals its transpose.

Proof: Rewrite the matrix entries as evaluations of the second Fréchet derivative and apply
Schwarz's theorem on the symmetry of second derivatives, as proved in Mathlib, following
Wikipedia's “Symmetry of second derivatives”.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 9.41 (pp. 235–236).

articles.title: Hessian matrix
articles.statement:
For a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ and a point
$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the Hessian matrix of $f$ at $x$ is the $n \times n$ real matrix whose
$(i, j)$ entry is $\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=0} \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} f(x + s e_i + t e_j)$, where
$e_1, \dots, e_n$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and a derivative that does not exist is
taken to be $0$.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 9; stable ref https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hessian_matrix.

articles.title: Second-derivative test, necessary condition
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be twice
continuously differentiable and let $x$ be a local minimum of $f$. Then the Hessian quadratic
form of $f$ at $x$ is nonnegative: writing $H$ for the Hessian matrix of $f$ at $x$, every
$v \in \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies $\sum_{i, j} v_i H_{ij} v_j \ge 0$.

Proof: Restrict the function to the affine line through $x$ in direction $v$, apply the necessary
direction of the one-variable second derivative test, then expand the second Fréchet derivative in
the standard basis. The one-variable step argues by contradiction as in the proof of the
second-derivative test in Wikipedia's “Derivative test”: a negative second derivative makes the
first derivative negative just right of the critical point, so the function decreases there.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 9.

articles.title: A unit-norm curve in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is orthogonal to its derivative
articles.statement:
Let
