$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be a differentiable map such that $\|f(t)\| = 1$ for every real
$t$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean norm. Then $\langle f'(t), f(t) \rangle = 0$ for every
real $t$, where $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is the standard inner product on $\mathbb{R}^3$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_49`.

articles.title: Change of variables to spherical coordinates
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real Banach space and let
$f \colon \mathbb{R}^3 \to E$ be any function. Then the integral of $f$ over $\mathbb{R}^3$
equals the integral over the set of $(r, \theta, \varphi) \in \mathbb{R}^3$ with $r > 0$,
$0 < \theta < 2\pi$ and $0 < \varphi < \pi$ of
$r^2 \sin\varphi \cdot f(r \sin\varphi \cos\theta,\, r \sin\varphi \sin\theta,\, r \cos\varphi)$,
both integrals being Bochner integrals with respect to Lebesgue measure.

No integrability hypothesis is assumed; as usual for Bochner integrals, a non-integrable
function has integral $0$. This is the three-dimensional analogue of the polar-coordinate
change of variables.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, *Real and Complex Analysis*, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, Exercise 4 (spherical coordinates in `ℝ³`).
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_coordinate_system#Integration_and_differentiation_in_spherical_coordinates

articles.title: Jacobian entries at a point of differentiability
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$
be differentiable at $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Then for every row index $i$ and column index $j$, the
$(i, j)$ entry of the Jacobian matrix of $f$ at $x$ is the $i$-th coordinate of $Df(x)\, e_j$,
where $Df(x)$ is the Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$ and $e_j$ is the $j$-th standard basis
vector of $\mathbb{R}^m$.

articles.title: Entries of the Jacobian matrix are partial derivatives
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$. For every row index $i$ and column
index $j$, the $(i, j)$ entry of the Jacobian matrix of $f$ at $x$ is the derivative at $t = 0$
of $t \mapsto f_i(x + t e_j)$, where $f_i$ is the $i$-th component of $f$ and $e_j$ is the
$j$-th standard basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^m$. This derivative is taken to be $0$ when it does
not exist.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 9.

articles.title: Chain rule for Jacobian matrices
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$,
$g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^p$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$, and write $J_h(y)$ for the Jacobian
matrix of $h$ at $y$. If $f$ is differentiable at $x$ and $g$ is differentiable at $f(x)$, then
$J_{g \circ f}(x) = J_g(f(x))\, J_f(x)$, a product of a $p \times n$ and an $n \times m$ matrix.

Proof: As in Wikipedia, "Jacobian matrix and determinant" (chain rule), write each Jacobian as
the matrix of the Fréchet derivative, then use the chain rule for Fréchet derivatives and the
fact that the matrix of a composition of linear maps is the product of their matrices.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 9.15.

articles.title: The Jacobian is the matrix of the derivative
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be
differentiable at $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Then the Jacobian matrix of $f$ at $x$ is the matrix, in
the standard bases of $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$, of the Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$,
viewed as a linear map $\mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: Jacobian of a linear map given by a matrix
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a real $n \times m$ matrix. At every
point $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$, the Jacobian matrix of the map $y \mapsto M y$ from $\mathbb{R}^m$ to
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is $M$.

articles.title: The Jacobian matrix computes the derivative
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be
differentiable at $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$, and let $J$ be the Jacobian matrix of $f$ at $x$. Then for
every $v \in \mathbb{R}^m$, the product $J v$ equals $Df(x)\, v$, the Fréchet derivative of $f$ at
$x$ applied to $v$.

Proof: The Jacobian is the matrix of the Fréchet derivative (Wikipedia, "Jacobian matrix and
determinant": it represents the total derivative), and multiplying a vector by the matrix of a
linear map applies the map to that vector.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 9.

articles.title: Jacobian matrix
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$, the
Jacobian matrix of $f$ at $x$ is the $n \times m$ real matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry is the partial
derivative of the $i$-th component $f_i$ of $f$ in the $j$-th coordinate direction at $x$: the
derivative at $t = 0$ of $t \mapsto f_i(x + t e_j)$, where $e_j$ is the $j$-th standard basis
vector of $\mathbb{R}^m$. A partial derivative that does not exist is taken to be $0$.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 9; stable ref https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant.

articles.title: Length of a $C^1$ curve
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real Banach space, let $a \le b$ be real numbers,
and let $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to E$ be continuously differentiable on $[a, b]$. Then the total
variation of $\gamma$ on $[a, b]$ (its length, a priori a value in $[0, \infty]$) equals
$\int_a^b \lVert \gamma'(t) \rVert \, dt$.

Proof: Extend the derivative of $\gamma$ relative to $[a, b]$ by zero outside the interval and
identify the vector measure of its primitive with the corresponding density vector measure. The
variation of that measure is the integral of the norm, and the ordinary derivative agrees with the
derivative relative to $[a, b]$ almost everywhere on the interval.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6; stable ref https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_length.

articles.title: Length of a $C^1$ curve via its derivative within the interval
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real Banach
space, let $a \le b$ be real numbers and let $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to E$ be continuously
differentiable on $[a, b]$. Then the total variation of $\gamma$ on $[a, b]$, a priori a value in
$[0, \infty]$, equals the real number $\int_a^b \lVert \gamma'_{[a,b]}(t) \rVert \, dt$, where
$\gamma'_{[a,b]}(t)$ is the derivative of $\gamma$ at $t$ within $[a, b]$.

articles.title: Integrating the norm of a derivative within a closed interval
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed
space, let $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ be any function and let $a \le b$ be real numbers. Then
$\int_a^b \lVert f'(t) \rVert \, dt = \int_a^b \lVert f'_{[a,b]}(t) \rVert \, dt$, where $f'(t)$
is the derivative of $f$ at $t$ and $f'_{[a,b]}(t)$ is its derivative at $t$ within $[a, b]$, each
taken to be $0$ where it does not exist.

articles.title: Symmetry of mixed partial derivatives (Clairaut's theorem)
articles.statement:
For a function
$g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, write $\partial_i g$ for its partial derivative along the
$i$-th coordinate axis. If $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is twice continuously
differentiable, then for all coordinate indices $i, j$ and every point $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$,
$\partial_j (\partial_i f)(x) = \partial_i (\partial_j f)(x)$.

The proof writes both mixed partials as values of the second Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$
and applies Schwarz's theorem on the symmetry of second derivatives.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 9.41 (pp. 235–236).

articles.title: Partial derivative function of a differentiable function
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable and let $e_i$ be the $i$-th standard basis
vector of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then the partial derivative $\partial_i f$ of $f$ along the $i$-th
coordinate axis is the function $x \mapsto Df(x)\,e_i$, where $Df(x)$ is the Fréchet derivative
of $f$ at $x$.

articles.title: Partial derivative as a Fréchet derivative
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be
differentiable at a point $x$, and let $e_i$ be the $i$-th standard basis vector of
$\mathbb{R}^n$. Then the partial derivative of $f$ along the $i$-th coordinate axis at $x$ equals
$Df(x)\,e_i$, the Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$ applied to $e_i$.

The proof differentiates $f$ along the line $t \mapsto x + t e_i$ by the chain rule.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 9.

articles.title: Mixed partial derivatives via the second Fréchet derivative
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be twice continuously differentiable, write $e_k$ for the $k$-th
standard basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\partial_k g$ for the partial derivative of a
function $g$ along the $k$-th coordinate axis, and let $Df$ be the Fréchet derivative of $f$,
a map from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to the linear maps $\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$. Then for all coordinate
indices $i, j$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$,
$\partial_j (\partial_i f)(x) = \big(D(Df)(x)\,e_j\big)\,e_i$, where $D(Df)(x)$ is the Fréchet
derivative of $Df$ at $x$.

articles.title: Partial derivative as the derivative of a coordinate slice
articles.statement:
For
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, a coordinate index $i$ and a point $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, let
$e_i$ be the $i$-th standard basis vector. The partial derivative of $f$ along the $i$-th
coordinate axis at $x$ equals the derivative at $t = 0$ of the one-variable function
$t \mapsto f(x + t e_i)$, taken to be $0$ when that function is not differentiable at $0$.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 9.

articles.title: Partial derivative along a coordinate axis
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ and a
coordinate index $i$, let $e_i$ be the $i$-th standard basis vector. The partial derivative
$\partial_i f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ sends $x$ to the derivative at $t = 0$ of
$t \mapsto f(x + t e_i)$, taken to be $0$ when this function is not differentiable at $0$.

## Sources

- W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 9; stable ref https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_derivative.

articles.title: Kernel vectors are velocities of local curves in a level set
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real Banach
space and let $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$ have a strict derivative $f'$ at $x \in E$, a continuous
linear map $E \to \mathbb{R}$ that is surjective. Then for every $v \in E$ with $f'(v) = 0$ there
is a curve $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to E$ with $\varphi(0) = x$ and $\varphi'(0) = v$ such that
$f(\varphi(t)) = f(x)$ for all $t$ in some neighbourhood of $0$.

articles.title: Kernel vectors are velocities of curves in a regular level set
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real
Banach space, $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$ a $C^1$ function, $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and $x \in E$ a point
with $f(x) = c$ at which the derivative $Df(x) : E \to \mathbb{R}$ is surjective. Then for every
$v \in E$ with $Df(x)v = 0$ there is a curve $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to E$ with $\gamma(0) = x$,
$\gamma'(0) = v$ and $f(\gamma(t)) = c$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

Proof: Use the implicit function theorem to construct a local curve tangent to the kernel vector,
then compose it with a bounded arctangent reparametrization to obtain a curve on all of `ℝ`
(implicit function theorem, Banach space version:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Implicit_function_theorem).

## Sources

- J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Theorem 5.12.

articles.title: Velocities of curves in a level set lie in the kernel of the derivative
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
real normed space, $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$ a function differentiable at
$x \in E$. If a curve $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to E$ satisfies $\gamma(0) = x$, has derivative $v$ at
$0$, and satisfies $f(\gamma(t)) = c$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$, then $Df(x)v = 0$.

Proof: Apply the chain rule to `f ∘ γ`, then compare its derivative with that of the constant
function determined by the level-set equation.

## Sources

- J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Theorem 5.12; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_space.

articles.title: Taylor's theorem with little-o remainder in several variables
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be normed
vector spaces over $\mathbb{R}$, let $n$ be a natural number, and let $f : E \to F$ be $n$ times
continuously differentiable on a neighbourhood of a point $x_0 \in E$. Write $D^k f(x_0)$ for the
$k$-th Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x_0$, a continuous $k$-linear map from $E^k$ to $F$. Then, as
$x$ tends to $x_0$,

$$f(x) - \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{1}{k!}\, D^k f(x_0)(x - x_0, \ldots, x - x_0) =
o\bigl(\|x - x_0\|^n\bigr).$$

## Sources

- The integral-remainder form exists as `map_add_eq_sum_add_integral_iteratedFDeriv`.
- H. Cartan, *Differential Calculus*, Ch. III, Taylor's formula with remainder.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor%27s_theorem#Taylor's_theorem_in_several_variables

articles.title: The alternating harmonic series is not absolutely summable
articles.statement:
The series of real numbers
$\sum_{n \ge 0} \left|(-1)^n / (n + 1)\right|$ is not summable.

The series of absolute values is the harmonic series $\sum_{n \ge 0} 1 / (n + 1)$, which
diverges. In particular the convergence of the alternating harmonic series to $\log 2$ is only
conditional.

articles.title: The alternating harmonic series sums to $\log 2$
articles.statement:
The partial sums
$\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} (-1)^i / (i + 1)$ of real numbers converge to $\log 2$ as $k \to \infty$.

articles.title: Mazur's Problem 8 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
There is a convergent sequence
$(z_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of real numbers that cannot be written as
$z_n = \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} x_k y_{n-k}$ for all $n \ge 0$ with convergent sequences
$(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and $(y_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of real numbers. That is, the claim of Scottish Book
Problem 8 is false.

## Sources

- S. Mazur, Problem 8 of the Scottish Book; negative solution by V. V. Peller, "On S. Mazur's Problems 8 and 88 from the Scottish Book", arXiv:math/0703716, building on Peller, J. Operator Theory 7 (1982) 341-372; independently Kwapien-Pelczynski and Eggermont-Leung, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 96 (1986) 269-274.

articles.title: The claim of Scottish Book Problem 8
articles.statement:
This is the statement, asked about in form (b) of
Mazur's Problem 8 in the Scottish Book typescript, that every convergent sequence
$(z_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of real numbers can be written as
$z_n = \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} x_k y_{n-k}$ for all $n \ge 0$, where $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$
and $(y_n)_{n \ge 0}$ are convergent sequences of real numbers.

Indices are shifted to start at $0$.

articles.title: Power series agreeing at $1/2, 1/3, 1/4, \dots$ have equal coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $(a_k)$ and
$(b_k)$ be real sequences such that the series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k x^k$ and
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} b_k x^k$ converge absolutely for every real $x$ with $|x| < 1$. If
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k x^k = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} b_k x^k$ for $x = 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, \dots$, then
$a_k = b_k$ for all $k \ge 0$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_24`.

articles.title: Śleszyński–Pringsheim convergence criterion
articles.statement:
Let $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ and
$b_0, b_1, b_2, \dots$ be complex numbers with $1 + |a_k| \le |b_k|$ for every $k$. For $n \ge 0$
let $f_n$ be the $n$-th approximant of the continued fraction $a_0 / (b_0 + a_1 / (b_1 + \cdots))$,
that is $f_0 = 0$ and $f_n = a_0 / (b_0 + a_1 / (b_1 + \cdots + a_{n-1} / b_{n-1}))$ for $n \ge 1$.
Then there is a complex number $v$ with $|v| \le 1$ such that $f_n \to v$ as $n \to \infty$.

Zero partial numerators are admitted.

## Sources

- Carminda M. Mennen, *Möbius Maps and Continued Fractions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A52, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Convergence of an alternating weighted series in the plane
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be
real numbers. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $x_k = (\alpha, \beta) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$
if $k$ is even and $x_k = (\beta, \alpha)$ if $k$ is odd. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let
$s_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} k^{-2} x_k$ (so $s_0 = 0$). Then the sequence $(s_n)$ converges in
$\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Sequences, series, summability; Convergence and divergence of infinite limiting processes), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_46`.

articles.title: The reciprocals of $\sum_{k=0}^{n} (a_k + 1/a_k)$ tend to zero
articles.statement:
Let
$(a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive real numbers, and for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let
$x_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (a_k + 1/a_k)$. Then $1/x_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Sequences, series, summability; Convergence and divergence of infinite limiting processes), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_18`.

articles.title: Partial sums of $a_k + 1/a_k$
articles.statement:
For a real sequence $(a_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$, the sequence
$(x_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is given by $x_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (a_k + 1/a_k)$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
with the convention $1/0 = 0$.

articles.title: Monotone functions on a closed interval with a continuous pointwise limit converge uniformly
articles.statement:
**Monotone functions on a closed interval with a continuous pointwise limit converge
uniformly.** Let $a < b$ be real numbers, let $f_n : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
be nondecreasing functions, and let $g : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous with
$f_n(x) \to g(x)$ for every $x \in [a, b]$. Then $g$ is nondecreasing and $f_n \to g$ uniformly
on $[a, b]$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Real functions; Functions of one variable), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_07`.

articles.title: Local normal convergence on the empty set
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space. Every series
of functions $f_n \colon X \to E$ ($n \in \mathbb{N}$) with values in a seminormed additive
commutative group $E$ converges locally normally on the empty set.

articles.title: Local normal convergence of the zero series
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space and $E$ a
seminormed additive commutative group. For every set $S \subseteq X$, the series of functions
$X \to E$ whose terms are all zero converges locally normally on $S$.

articles.title: Local normal convergence of a series of functions on a set
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological
space and $E$ a seminormed additive commutative group. A series of functions
$f_n \colon X \to E$ ($n \in \mathbb{N}$) converges locally normally on a set $S \subseteq X$ when
every $x \in S$ has a neighbourhood $U$ such that the series converges normally on $U \cap S$.

articles.title: Normal convergence on the empty set
articles.statement:
Every series of functions $f_n \colon X \to E$
($n \in \mathbb{N}$) with values in a seminormed additive commutative group $E$ converges
normally on the empty set.

articles.title: Normal convergence of the zero series
articles.statement:
For every set $S \subseteq X$ and every seminormed
additive commutative group $E$, the series of functions $X \to E$ whose terms are all zero
converges normally on $S$.

articles.title: Normal convergence of a series of functions on a set
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a type and $E$ a
seminormed additive commutative group. A series of functions $f_n \colon X \to E$
($n \in \mathbb{N}$) converges normally on a set $S \subseteq X$ when the sum
$\sum_{n} \sup_{x \in S} \|f_n(x)\|$ is finite, where each supremum norm and the sum are taken in
the extended nonnegative reals $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: Derivative series of a locally normally convergent holomorphic series
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
normed space over $\mathbb{C}$, $S \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ an open set and $f_n \colon \mathbb{C}
\to E$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ functions that are complex differentiable on $S$. If the series
$\sum_n f_n$ converges locally normally on $S$, that is every $z \in S$ has a neighbourhood $U$
with $\sum_n \sup_{w \in U \cap S} \|f_n(w)\| < \infty$ (suprema taken in $[0, \infty]$), then
the series of derivatives $\sum_n f_n'$ also converges locally normally on $S$.

articles.title: Local normal convergence gives a neighbourhood of each point of the set
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a
topological space, $E$ a seminormed additive commutative group, $f_n \colon X \to E$
($n \in \mathbb{N}$) functions and $S \subseteq X$. If the series $\sum_n f_n$ converges locally
normally on $S$, then every $x \in S$ has a neighbourhood $U$ such that the series converges
normally on $U \cap S$.

articles.title: Termwise differentiation of locally normally convergent holomorphic series
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
complete normed space over $\mathbb{C}$, $S \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ an open set and
$f_n \colon \mathbb{C} \to E$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ functions that are complex differentiable
on $S$. If the series $\sum_n f_n$ converges locally normally on $S$, that is every $z \in S$
has a neighbourhood $U$ with $\sum_n \sup_{w \in U \cap S} \|f_n(w)\| < \infty$ (suprema taken
in $[0, \infty]$), then for every $z \in S$ the function $w \mapsto \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n(w)$
has derivative $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n'(z)$ at $z$.

articles.title: Local normal convergence passes to subsets
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space, let
$f_n \colon X \to E$ ($n \in \mathbb{N}$) be functions into a seminormed additive commutative
group $E$ and let $T \subseteq S \subseteq X$. If the series $\sum_n f_n$ converges locally
normally on $S$, then it converges locally normally on $T$.

articles.title: Normal convergence passes to subsets
articles.statement:
Let $f_n \colon X \to E$ ($n \in \mathbb{N}$) be
functions into a seminormed additive commutative group $E$ and let $T \subseteq S \subseteq X$.
If the series $\sum_n f_n$ converges normally on $S$, then it converges normally on $T$.

articles.title: Local normal convergence implies pointwise absolute convergence
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a seminormed
additive commutative group, $S$ a subset of a topological space $X$ and $f_n \colon X \to E$ for
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. If the series $\sum_n f_n$ converges locally normally on $S$, that is every
$x \in S$ has a neighbourhood $U$ with $\sum_n \sup_{y \in U \cap S} \|f_n(y)\| < \infty$ (suprema
taken in $[0, \infty]$), then for every $x \in S$ the series $\sum_n \|f_n(x)\|$ is summable.

articles.title: Normal convergence implies pointwise absolute convergence
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a seminormed
additive commutative group, $S$ a subset of a type $X$ and $f_n \colon X \to E$ for
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. If the series $\sum_n f_n$ converges normally on $S$, that is
$\sum_n \sup_{x \in S} \|f_n(x)\| < \infty$ with the suprema taken in $[0, \infty]$, then for
every $x \in S$ the series $\sum_n \|f_n(x)\|$ is summable.

articles.title: Normal convergence gives summable real sup norms
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a seminormed additive
commutative group, $S$ a subset of a type $X$ and $f_n \colon X \to E$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
If the series $\sum_n f_n$ converges normally on $S$, that is
$\sum_n \sup_{x \in S} \|f_n(x)\| < \infty$ with the suprema taken in $[0, \infty]$, then the
sequence of sup norms $\left(\sup_{x \in S} \|f_n(x)\|\right)_n$, viewed as real numbers, is
summable.

articles.title: Supremum norm over the empty set
articles.statement:
For every function $g \colon X \to E$ into a seminormed
additive commutative group $E$, the supremum norm of $g$ on the empty set, valued in
$[0, \infty]$, is $0$.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the supremum norm in the domain
articles.statement:
If $T \subseteq S \subseteq X$, then for
every function $g \colon X \to E$ into a seminormed additive commutative group $E$, the supremum
norm of $g$ on $T$ is at most the supremum norm of $g$ on $S$.

articles.title: Supremum norm of the zero function
articles.statement:
For every set $S \subseteq X$, the supremum norm on
$S$ of the zero function from $X$ to a seminormed additive commutative group $E$ is $0$.

articles.title: Extended supremum norm on a set
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a type and $E$ a seminormed additive
commutative group. For a function $g : X \to E$ and a set $S \subseteq X$, the supremum norm of
$g$ on $S$ is $\sup_{x \in S} \|g(x)\|$, taken in the extended nonnegative reals $[0, \infty]$;
in particular it is $0$ when $S$ is empty and $\infty$ when $\|g\|$ is unbounded on $S$.

articles.title: Local normal convergence implies locally uniform convergence
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complete
normed additive commutative group, $S$ a subset of a topological space $X$ and
$f_n \colon X \to E$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$. If the series $\sum_n f_n$ converges locally
normally on $S$, that is every $x \in S$ has a neighbourhood $U$ with
$\sum_n \sup_{y \in U \cap S} \|f_n(y)\| < \infty$ (suprema taken in $[0, \infty]$), then the
partial sums $x \mapsto \sum_{n < N} f_n(x)$ converge locally uniformly on $S$, as
$N \to \infty$, to the pointwise sum $x \mapsto \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n(x)$.

articles.title: Weierstrass M-test: normal convergence implies uniform convergence
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a complete
normed additive commutative group, $S$ a subset of a type $X$ and $f_n \colon X \to E$ for
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. If the series $\sum_n f_n$ converges normally on $S$, that is
$\sum_n \sup_{x \in S} \|f_n(x)\| < \infty$ with the suprema taken in $[0, \infty]$, then the
partial sums $x \mapsto \sum_{n < N} f_n(x)$ converge uniformly on $S$, as $N \to \infty$, to
the pointwise sum $x \mapsto \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n(x)$.

articles.title: Convergence in order via partial sums
articles.statement:
For a sequence $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ and
$a \in \mathbb{R}$, the series $\sum_n f(n)$ converges in order to $a$ if and only if its partial
sums $\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f(n)$ tend to $a$ as $N \to \infty$.

articles.title: Terms of a convergent series tend to zero
articles.statement:
If $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ and the
series $\sum_n f(n)$ converges in order to some $s \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f(n) \to 0$ as
$n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Convergence of a series in order
articles.statement:
For a sequence $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ and
$a \in \mathbb{R}$, the series $\sum_n f(n)$ converges in order to $a$ when its partial sums
$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f(n)$ tend to $a$ as $N \to \infty$.

articles.title: Riemann rearrangement theorem
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be such that the series
$\sum_n f(n)$ converges in order to some real number, while the series $\sum_n |f(n)|$ is not
summable. Then for every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ there is a permutation $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{N}$ such
that the rearranged series $\sum_n f(\sigma(n))$ converges in order to $a$.

## Sources

- B. Riemann, Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe, Habilitationsschrift (1854; published 1867).

articles.title: Cauchy's root test, divergence case
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ be a sequence in a
seminormed additive commutative group $\alpha$. If $\|f(n)\|^{1/n}$ tends to a real limit $l$ with
$l > 1$ as $n \to \infty$, then $f$ is not summable, that is, the series $\sum_n f(n)$ does not
converge unconditionally.

articles.title: Cauchy's root test, absolute convergence case
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ be a
sequence in a normed additive commutative group $\alpha$. If $\|f(n)\|^{1/n}$ tends to a real
limit $l$ with $l < 1$ as $n \to \infty$, then the series $\sum_n \|f(n)\|$ converges.

articles.title: Cauchy's root test, convergence case
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ be a sequence in a
complete normed additive commutative group $\alpha$. If $\|f(n)\|^{1/n}$ tends to a real limit
$l$ with $l < 1$ as $n \to \infty$, then $f$ is summable, that is, the series $\sum_n f(n)$
converges unconditionally.

articles.title: Stolz–Cesàro theorem
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and $(b_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be sequences of
real numbers such that $(b_n)$ is strictly increasing and $b_n \to +\infty$ as $n \to \infty$,
and let $L$ be a real number. If
$\frac{a_{n+1} - a_n}{b_{n+1} - b_n} \to L$ as $n \to \infty$, then
$\frac{a_n}{b_n} \to L$ as $n \to \infty$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stolz%E2%80%93Ces%C3%A0ro_theorem.

articles.title: Summability of a rising-product series
articles.statement:
Let $b$, $c$ and $x$ be complex numbers such
that $c + kb \neq 0$ for every integer $k \ge 1$. Then the series
$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-b)^j x^{j+1}}{\prod_{k=1}^{j+1} (c + kb)}$ is summable.

articles.title: Uniform convergence of $\sum (1 - \cos(x/n))$ on compact intervals
articles.statement:
For all real numbers
$a < b$ there is a function $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the partial sums
$\sum_{n=1}^{N} \bigl(1 - \cos(x/n)\bigr)$ converge to $g(x)$ uniformly for $x \in [a, b]$ as
$N \to \infty$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level I (Sequences, series, summability; Convergence and divergence of infinite limiting processes), problem `ma_proofbench_l1_05`.

articles.title: Borwein's eta–Lambert correspondence
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ be sequences of complex
numbers and let $C$ and $K$ be real numbers with $|a_n| \le C n^K$ and $|b_n| \le C n^K$ for every
$n \ge 1$. Let $\eta(s) = \sum_{n \ge 1} (-1)^{n-1} n^{-s}$ be the Dirichlet eta function. Then
$\eta(s) \sum_{n \ge 1} a_n n^{-s} = \sum_{n \ge 1} b_n n^{-s}$ for every real number
$s > \max(K + 2, 1)$ if and only if $\sum_{n \ge 1} a_n x^n / (1 + x^n) = \sum_{n \ge 1} b_n x^n$
for every real number $x$ with $0 < x < 1$.

The source quotes the correspondence from Borwein and Borwein without growth hypotheses or
ranges for $s$ and $x$; the growth bound and the ranges above make all the series involved converge
absolutely.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 18 (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-18`).

articles.title: $2$-adic dissection of the Gamma quadratic ratio
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, z$ be complex numbers such
that $m^2 + 2am + b \ne 0$ and $m^2 + 2am + b - z \ne 0$ for every integer $m$ that is nonnegative
or of the form $m = -2^j$ with $j \ge 0$ an integer. For $j \ge 0$ put $a_j = a / 2^{j+1} - 1/2$
and $b_j = 1/4 - a / 2^{j+1} + b / 2^{2j+2}$. Then the Gamma quadratic ratio $g$ satisfies
$g(a, b, z) = \prod_{j \ge 0} g(a_j, b_j, z / 2^{2j+2})$.

The source prints the parameters $a / 2^j - 1$ and $1 - a / 2^{j+1} + b / 2^{2j+2}$, which make
the identity false: for $a = 3/10$, $b = -2$, $z = 7/10$ the left side is about $1.6283$ and the
printed product about $6.18 \cdot 10^4$, while the product above matches. The parameters $a_j$,
$b_j$ come from the penultimate line of the source's proof, which writes
$m^2 + 2am + b = 2^{2j+2}(n^2 + 2 a_j n + b_j)$ for $m = (2n - 1) 2^j$. The hypotheses, absent
from the source, exclude the poles of every Gamma factor on both sides and the vanishing of $b$
and $b - z$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 23 (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-23`).

articles.title: The Gamma quadratic ratio at $z = 0$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be complex numbers with $b \ne 0$
and $\Gamma(a - \sqrt{a^2 - b})\, \Gamma(a + \sqrt{a^2 - b}) \ne 0$, where $\sqrt{\cdot}$ denotes
the principal complex square root. Then the Gamma quadratic ratio $g$ satisfies $g(a, b, 0) = 1$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 23.

articles.title: The Gamma quadratic ratio
articles.statement:
For complex numbers $a$, $b$ and $z$, the Gamma quadratic ratio
is $g(a, b, z) = \dfrac{b}{b - z} \cdot
\dfrac{\Gamma(a - \sqrt{a^2 - b})\, \Gamma(a + \sqrt{a^2 - b})}
{\Gamma(a - \sqrt{a^2 - b + z})\, \Gamma(a + \sqrt{a^2 - b + z})}$, where $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is the
principal complex square root (the value does not depend on the choice of root).

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 23.

articles.title: $2$-adic dissection of a ratio of Gamma functions
articles.statement:
For complex numbers $a$ and $z$ write
$f(a, z) = \Gamma(a + 1)^2 / \bigl(\Gamma(a + 1 - iz)\, \Gamma(a + 1 + iz)\bigr)$. If $a$ is not a
negative integer, then for every complex number $z$,
$f(a, z) = \prod_{j \ge 0} f(a / 2^{j+1} - 1/2,\ z / 2^{j+1})$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 22 (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-22`).

articles.title: Two-adic multisection of the power-weighted Lambert series
articles.statement:
For every integer $\mu \ge 1$
and every complex number $q$ with $|q| < 1$, the power-weighted Lambert series
$f_\mu(q) = \sum_{n \ge 1} n^\mu q^n / (1 - q^n)$ and
$g_\mu(q) = \sum_{n \ge 1} n^\mu q^n / (1 + q^n)$ satisfy

$$
f_\mu(q) = \sum_{j, k \ge 0} 2^{(\mu+1)j+k}
\left(g_\mu\left(q^{2^{j+k}}\right) - 2^{\mu+1} g_\mu\left(q^{2^{j+k+1}}\right)\right),
$$

the sum running over all pairs $(j, k)$ of natural numbers.

The paper prints the weight $2^{2j+k}$, its value for $\mu = 1$ (Corollary 16), which is false
for $\mu \ge 2$: for $\mu = 2$ the coefficient of $q^2$ is $\sigma_2(2) = 1^2 + 2^2 = 5$ on the
left and $1$ on the right. The weight $2^{(\mu+1)j+k}$ is what the paper's proof of Corollary 16
gives with $n^\mu$ in place of $n$: there $2^{2j+k} = 2^{j+k} \cdot 2^j$, where $2^j$ is the
factor of the index $(2n-1) 2^j$ in the summand $n$, which becomes $2^{\mu j}$ for $n^\mu$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Corollary 17 (`jis-2024-24.5.5-cor-17`).

articles.title: $2$-adic expansion of the weighted Lambert series $f$
articles.statement:
For every complex number $q$ with
$|q| < 1$, the weighted Lambert series $f(q) = \sum_{n \ge 1} n q^n / (1 - q^n)$ and
$g(q) = \sum_{n \ge 1} n q^n / (1 + q^n)$ satisfy
$f(q) = \sum_{j, k \ge 0} 2^{2j+k} \bigl(g(q^{2^{j+k}}) - 4 g(q^{2^{j+k+1}})\bigr)$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Corollary 16 (`jis-2024-24.5.5-cor-16`).

articles.title: $2$-adic multisection of the infinite $q$-Pochhammer symbol
articles.statement:
Write
$(x; y)_\infty = \prod_{k \ge 0} (1 - x y^k)$ for the infinite $q$-Pochhammer symbol, where $x$
and $y$ are complex and $|y| < 1$. For complex numbers $a$ and $q$ with $|q| < 1$,
$\prod_{j \ge 0} \bigl((a q^{2^j - 1}; q^{2^{j+1}})_\infty /
(a q^{2^{j+1} - 1}; q^{2^{j+1}})_\infty\bigr)^{2^j} = (a; q)_\infty$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 20 (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-20`).

articles.title: $3$-adic factorization of the Euler function
articles.statement:
Write
$(x; y)_\infty = \prod_{k \ge 0} (1 - x y^k)$ for the infinite $q$-Pochhammer symbol, where $x$
and $y$ are complex and $|y| < 1$. For every complex number $q$ with $|q| < 1$,
$\prod_{j \ge 0} (q^{3^j}; q^{3^{j+1}})_\infty\, (q^{2 \cdot 3^j}; q^{3^{j+1}})_\infty =
(q; q)_\infty$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 19, case `p = 1`, base 3 (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-19`).

articles.title: Parametric $3$-adic dissection of the Euler function
articles.statement:
For real numbers $x$ and $y$ with
$0 < y < 1$ write $(x; y)_\infty = \prod_{k \ge 0} (1 - x y^k)$. For all real numbers $q$ and $p$
with $0 < q < 1$,
$\prod_{j \ge 0} \bigl((q^{3^j}; q^{3^{j+1}})_\infty\, (q^{2 \cdot 3^j}; q^{3^{j+1}})_\infty /
(q^{3^{j+1}}; q^{3^{j+1}})_\infty^{\,p - 1}\bigr)^{p^j} = (q; q)_\infty$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 19, third display, real case (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-19`).

articles.title: 2-adic product factorization of the Euler function
articles.statement:
For every complex number $q$ with
$|q| < 1$, with the infinite q-Pochhammer symbol $(a; r)_\infty = \prod_{k \ge 0} (1 - a r^k)$,
the unconditional infinite product over $j \ge 0$ satisfies
$\prod_{j \ge 0} (q^{2^j}; q^{2^{j+1}})_\infty = (q; q)_\infty$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 19, case `p = 1`, base 2 (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-19`).

articles.title: Parametric 2-adic dissection of the Euler function for real q
articles.statement:
Let $q$ and $p$ be real
numbers with $0 < q < 1$, and write $(a; r)_\infty = \prod_{k \ge 0} (1 - a r^k)$ for real $a$
and $r$ (an unconditional infinite product). Then, with real exponents $p - 1$ and $p^j$,

$$\prod_{j \ge 0} \left( \frac{(q^{2^j}; q^{2^{j+1}})_\infty}
{(q^{2^{j+1}}; q^{2^{j+1}})_\infty^{\,p-1}} \right)^{p^j} = (q; q)_\infty.$$

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 19, second display, real case (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-19`).

articles.title: 2-adic dissection of the Euler function
articles.statement:
For every complex number $q$ with $|q| < 1$,
with the infinite q-Pochhammer symbol $(a; r)_\infty = \prod_{k \ge 0} (1 - a r^k)$, the
unconditional infinite product over $j \ge 0$ satisfies

$$\prod_{j \ge 0} \left( \frac{(q^{2^j}; q^{2^{j+1}})_\infty}
{(q^{2^{j+1}}; q^{2^{j+1}})_\infty} \right)^{2^j} = (q; q)_\infty.$$

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 19, first display (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-19`).

articles.title: Regrouping the multiples of B by their B-adic factorization
articles.statement:
Let $B \ge 2$ be a natural
number and let $(c_m)_{m \ge 1}$ be a sequence of complex numbers such that the family
$(c_{Bm})_{m \ge 1}$ is summable. Then

$$\sum_{j \ge 1,\, n \ge 1} \sum_{k=1}^{B-1} c_{(Bn-k) B^j} = \sum_{m \ge 1} c_{Bm},$$

where the outer sum on the left is an unconditional sum over the pairs $(j, n)$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 7, deduced identity in sum form (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-7`).

articles.title: Parametric base-B multisection of a series
articles.statement:
Let $B \ge 2$ be a natural number, let $q$
be a complex number and let $(c_m)_{m \ge 1}$ be a sequence of complex numbers. Suppose that the
family $q^j c_{(Bn-k) B^j}$ indexed by the triples $(j, n, k)$ with $j \ge 0$, $n \ge 1$ and
$1 \le k \le B - 1$ is summable, and that the family $q^j (q - 1) c_{Bn \cdot B^j}$ indexed by
the pairs $(j, n)$ with $j \ge 0$ and $n \ge 1$ is summable. Then

$$\sum_{j \ge 0,\, n \ge 1} \Bigl( q^j \sum_{k=1}^{B-1} c_{(Bn-k) B^j} -
q^j (q - 1) c_{Bn \cdot B^j} \Bigr) = \sum_{m \ge 1} c_m.$$

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 7, first display in sum form (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-7`).

articles.title: Weighted base-B multisection of a series
articles.statement:
Let $B \ge 2$ be a natural number, let
$\varphi, \chi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ be weights and let $(c_m)_{m \ge 1}$ be a sequence
of complex numbers, and for $m \ge 1$ let $\nu_B(m)$ be the largest $k$ with $B^k \mid m$.
Suppose that the family $\varphi(j) c_{(Bn-k) B^j}$ indexed by the triples $(j, n, k)$ with
$j \ge 0$, $n \ge 1$ and $1 \le k \le B - 1$ is summable, and that the family
$\chi(j) c_{Bn \cdot B^j}$ indexed by the pairs $(j, n)$ with $j \ge 0$ and $n \ge 1$ is
summable. Then

$$\sum_{j \ge 0,\, n \ge 1} \Bigl( \sum_{k=1}^{B-1} \varphi(j) c_{(Bn-k) B^j} +
\chi(j) c_{Bn \cdot B^j} \Bigr) = \sum_{m \ge 1} \Bigl( \varphi(\nu_B(m)) +
\sum_{k < \nu_B(m)} \chi(k) \Bigr) c_m.$$

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 8, base-`b` sum form (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-8`).

articles.title: Regrouping the multiples of 3 by their 3-adic factorization
articles.statement:
Let $(b_m)_{m \ge 1}$ be a
sequence of complex numbers such that the family $(b_{3m})_{m \ge 1}$ is summable. Then

$$\sum_{j \ge 1,\, n \ge 1} \bigl( b_{(3n-1) 3^j} + b_{(3n-2) 3^j} \bigr) =
\sum_{m \ge 1} b_{3m},$$

where the sum on the left is an unconditional sum over the pairs $(j, n)$.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Corollary 6, deduced identity in sum form (`jis-2024-24.5.5-cor-6`).

articles.title: Parametric 3-adic multisection of a series
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be a complex number and let
$(b_m)_{m \ge 1}$ be a sequence of complex numbers such that the three families
$q^j b_{(3n-1) 3^j}$, $q^j b_{(3n-2) 3^j}$ and $q^j (q - 1) b_{3n \cdot 3^j}$, each indexed by
the pairs $(j, n)$ with $j \ge 0$ and $n \ge 1$, are summable. Then

$$\sum_{j \ge 0,\, n \ge 1} \Bigl( q^j \bigl( b_{(3n-1) 3^j} + b_{(3n-2) 3^j} \bigr) -
q^j (q - 1) b_{3n \cdot 3^j} \Bigr) = \sum_{m \ge 1} b_m.$$

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Corollary 6, first display in sum form (`jis-2024-24.5.5-cor-6`).

articles.title: Double 2-adic multisection of a double series
articles.statement:
Let $(b_{p,q})_{p, q \ge 1}$ be a double
sequence of complex numbers such that each of the four families
$2^{j+k} b_{(2n-1) 2^j, (2m-1) 2^k}$, $2^{j+k} b_{(2n) 2^j, (2m) 2^k}$,
$2^{j+k} b_{(2n) 2^j, (2m-1) 2^k}$ and $2^{j+k} b_{(2n-1) 2^j, (2m) 2^k}$, indexed by the
quadruples $(j, k, n, m)$ with $j, k \ge 0$ and $n, m \ge 1$, is summable. Then

$$\sum_{p, q \ge 1} b_{p,q} = \sum_{j, k \ge 0,\ n, m \ge 1} 2^{j+k} \bigl(
b_{(2n-1) 2^j, (2m-1) 2^k} + b_{(2n) 2^j, (2m) 2^k} -
b_{(2n) 2^j, (2m-1) 2^k} - b_{(2n-1) 2^j, (2m) 2^k} \bigr),$$

where both sides are unconditional sums, over the pairs $(p, q)$ and the quadruples
$(j, k, n, m)$ respectively.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 15, sum version (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-15`).

articles.title: Regrouping the multiples of a power of 2 by their 2-adic factorization
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $J$ and every sequence $(c_m)_{m \ge 1}$ of complex numbers,

$$\sum_{j \ge J,\, n \ge 1} c_{(2n-1) 2^j} = \sum_{p \ge 1} c_{p 2^J},$$

where the left side is an unconditional sum over the pairs $(j, n)$. No summability is assumed:
$(j, n) \mapsto (2n-1) 2^{j-J}$ is a bijection onto the positive integers, so the two families
are summable together or not at all, and a non-summable family has sum $0$ by convention.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Corollary 14, first display in sum form (`jis-2024-24.5.5-cor-14`).

articles.title: Two-adic regrouping of the non-multiples of a power of two
articles.statement:
For every natural number $J$
and every sequence $c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$,

$$\sum_{0 \le j < J,\ n \ge 1} c_{(2n-1) 2^j} = \sum_{p \ge 1,\ 2^J \nmid p} c_p,$$

where the left side runs over the pairs $(j, n)$ of natural numbers with $j < J$ and $n \ge 1$,
the right side runs over the positive integers $p$ not divisible by $2^J$, and each side is an
unconditional sum, taken to be $0$ when its family is not summable.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Corollary 14, second display in sum form (`jis-2024-24.5.5-cor-14`).

articles.title: Parametric two-adic multisection
articles.statement:
Let $q \in \mathbb{C}$ and let $b : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{C}$ be a sequence (its value at $0$ is not used). Suppose that the families
$(q^j b_{(2n-1) 2^j})$ and $(q^j (q - 1) b_{2n \cdot 2^j})$, indexed by the pairs $(j, n)$ of
natural numbers with $n \ge 1$, are summable. Then

$$\sum_{j \ge 0,\ n \ge 1} \left(q^j b_{(2n-1) 2^j} - q^j (q - 1) b_{2n \cdot 2^j}\right)
= \sum_{m \ge 1} b_m.$$

The two summability hypotheses imply that $(b_m)_{m \ge 1}$ is summable.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 1, series version (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-1`).

articles.title: Truncated two-adic regrouping
articles.statement:
For every natural number $J$ and all sequences
$\varphi, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$,

$$\sum_{j \ge J,\ n \ge 1} \varphi(j) c_{(2n-1) 2^j}
= \sum_{p \ge 1} \varphi(J + \nu_2(p)) c_{p 2^J},$$

where $\nu_2(p)$ is the exponent of the largest power of $2$ dividing $p$, the left side runs over
the pairs $(j, n)$ of natural numbers with $j \ge J$ and $n \ge 1$, the right side runs over the
positive integers $p$, and each side is an unconditional sum, taken to be $0$ when its family is
not summable.

## Sources

- Christophe Vignat and Michael Milgram, *Curious Multisection Identities by Index Factorization*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.5, Proposition 13, in sum form (`jis-2024-24.5.5-prop-13`).

articles.title: Absolute convergence of the series in Entry 12
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be an integer and let $n$ and $a$
be complex numbers. Suppose that $|a| > e$, or that $a = e$ and $r \le -2$, and that $n + k \ne 0$
for every natural number $k$ with $r + k < 0$. Then

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left| \frac{(n+k)^{r+k}}{a^k\, k!} \right| < \infty.$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, definition (12.1) and Entry 12, printed pp. 66-67 / PDF pp. 76-77.

articles.title: Absolute convergence of the shifted series in Entry 12
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be an integer and let $n$
and $a$ be complex numbers. Suppose that $|a| > e$, or that $a = e$ and $r \le -2$, and that
$n + k \ne 0$ for every integer $k \ge 0$ with $r + k < 0$. Then

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left| \frac{(n+k)^{r+1+k}}{a^k\, k!} \right| < \infty.$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, definition (12.1) and Entry 12, printed pp. 66-67 / PDF pp. 76-77.

articles.title: Absolute convergence of the shifted series in Entry 12 for every $n$
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be an
integer and let $n$ and $a$ be complex numbers with $|a| > e$, or with $a = e$ and $r \le -2$.
Then

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left| \frac{(n+k)^{r+1+k}}{a^k\, k!} \right| < \infty,$$

where integer powers of complex numbers follow the convention $0^m = 0$ for $m < 0$.

Unlike the version that assumes $n + k \ne 0$ whenever $k \ge 0$ and $r + k < 0$, nothing is
assumed about $n$. At an index where $n + k = 0$ and the exponent $r + 1 + k$ is negative, the
term is $0^{r+1+k} = 0$, whereas the source's term is undefined there. Summability depends only
on the tail, where every exponent is nonnegative.

articles.title: Ramanujan's recurrence for the series in Entry 12
articles.statement:
Fix a complex number $a$. For an
integer $r$ and a complex number $n$, let

$$F_r(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(n+k)^{r+k}}{a^k\, k!},$$

where the sum is taken to be $0$ if the series is not summable. Suppose that $|a| > e$, or that
$a = e$ and $r \le -2$, and that $n + k \ne 0$ for every natural number $k$ with $r + k < 0$.
Then

$$F_{r+1}(n) = n F_r(n) + \frac{1}{a} F_{r+1}(n+1).$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, definition (12.1) and Entry 12, printed pp. 66-67 / PDF pp. 76-77.

articles.title: Jensen's series (Chapter 3, Entry 16, Corollary 1)
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a positive real number
with $\rho e^{\rho + 1} = 1$, let $n$ be a real number with $-\rho < n < 1$, and let $x$ be a
complex number. Then the series

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(x + kn)^k}{k!\, e^{kn}}$$

converges unconditionally to $e^x / (1 - n)$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Corollary 1, formula (16.6), printed pp. 80--81 / PDF pp. 90--91.

articles.title: Ramanujan's $\psi$-series (Chapter 3, Entry 16)
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $r$, $k$ and a complex
number $n$ define $\psi(r, k, n)$ recursively by $\psi(0, 1, n) = 1$, $\psi(0, k, n) = 0$ for
$k \ne 1$, and

$$\psi(r + 1, k, n) = (n - r - k)\, \psi(r, k, n) + (r + k - 1)\, \psi(r, k - 1, n),$$

where the last term is read as $0$ when $k = 0$. Let $r$ be a natural number and let $n$, $u$ be
complex numbers with $|u e^{1-u}| < 1$ and $|u| < 1$. Then the series

$$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(n + j)^{r+j}\, e^{-u(n+j)}\, u^j}{j!}$$

converges unconditionally to

$$\sum_{k=1}^{r+1} \frac{\psi(r, k, n)}{(1 - u)^{r+k}}.$$

The hypothesis $|u| < 1$ selects the component of $\{u : |u e^{1-u}| < 1\}$ containing $0$;
given $|u e^{1-u}| < 1$, it is equivalent to $\operatorname{Re} u < 1$. On the other component
the series converges to a different value.

Proof: Entry 12 gives absolute and locally uniform convergence, and termwise
differentiation gives the recurrence in Berndt (16.4)-(16.5). The Jensen-series
base case from Berndt (16.6) extends to the star-convex domain by analytic uniqueness.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, construction and formulas (16.4)-(16.5), printed pp. 78-79 / PDF pp. 88-89.

articles.title: Ramanujan's three-term recurrence (Chapter 3, Entry 16(a))
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $x$, $n$ be complex
numbers and $r$ an integer, where $x \ne 0$ and $x = a \log x$ with $\log$ the principal branch of
the complex logarithm. Suppose that $|a| > e$, or that $a = e$ and $r \le -2$, and that
$n + k \ne 0$ for every natural number $k$ with $r + k < 0$. For an integer $s$ and a complex
number $m$ put

$$\varphi(s, m) = e^{-m \log x} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(m + k)^{s + k}}{a^k\, k!};$$

the three series used below converge absolutely under these hypotheses. Then

$$n\, \varphi(r, n) = \varphi(r + 1, n) - \log x \cdot \varphi(r + 1, n + 1).$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, definition (12.1) printed p. 66 / PDF p. 76, Entry 12 p. 67 / PDF p. 77, and Entry 16(a) p. 78 / PDF p. 88. The series is `Entry12.F`, and the recurrence is `Entry12.ramanujan_part1_ch3_entry12` multiplied by `exp (-n * log x)`.

articles.title: Hagen–Rothe convolution for Lagrange series coefficients
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $p$, $q$,
$r$, $s$ and every natural number $m$, the Lagrange series coefficients $C_{p,q}$ satisfy

$$C_{p,q}(r + s, m) = \sum_{k=0}^{m} \binom{m}{k} C_{p,q}(r, k) \, C_{p,q}(s, m - k).$$

articles.title: Lagrange series coefficients of positive degree
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $p$, $q$, $n$ and
every natural number $k \ne 0$, the Lagrange series coefficient of degree $k$ is

$$C_{p,q}(n, k) = n \prod_{j=1}^{k-1} (n + k p - j q).$$

articles.title: Lagrange series coefficient of degree zero
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $p$, $q$, $n$, the
Lagrange series coefficient $C_{p,q}(n, 0)$ of degree $0$ equals $1$.

articles.title: Lagrange series coefficients
articles.statement:
For real numbers $p$, $q$, $n$ and a natural number $k$,
the Lagrange series coefficient $C_{p,q}(n, k)$ is $1$ if $k = 0$, and for $k \ge 1$ it is

$$C_{p,q}(n, k) = n \prod_{j=1}^{k-1} (n + k p - j q)$$

(an empty product when $k = 1$).

articles.title: Schröder's exponential series
articles.statement:
Let $z$ and $w$ be complex numbers with
$|w| \le |e^{w-1}|$ and $|w| \le 1$. Then the series

$$1 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{z (z + k w)^{k-1} e^{-k w}}{k!}$$

converges unconditionally, and its sum is $e^z$.

The set of complex numbers $w$ with $|w| \le |e^{w-1}|$ has a bounded lobe containing $0$ and an
unbounded lobe, which meet only at $w = 1$. The condition $|w| \le 1$ selects the bounded lobe
(given the first condition, it is equivalent to $\operatorname{Re} w \le 1$); on the unbounded
lobe the identity fails in general.

Proof: Following Berndt's formula (13.8), we use Abel's binomial identity, a Cauchy product and a
holomorphic ODE; radial continuity selects the unit-disk branch of $u \mapsto u e^{-u}$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Corollary to Entry 13, formula (13.8), printed p. 70 / PDF p. 80.

articles.title: Ramanujan's series for powers of a root of $x = a \log x$ (Entry 13)
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a real
number with $|a| \ge e$. Then there is a real number $x > 0$ with $x = a \log x$ such that for
every real number $n$ the series

$$1 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{n (n+k)^{k-1}}{a^k\, k!}$$

is summable with sum $x^n$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, definition (12.1), printed p. 66 / PDF p. 76, and Entry 13, printed pp. 69--70 / PDF pp. 79--80; historical attribution on printed p. 72 / PDF p. 82.

articles.title: Ramanujan's series for powers of the Catalan generating function
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $a$ be real
numbers with $|a| \le 1/4$. For a natural number $k$ put $t_k = 0$ if $k < 2$, and

$$t_k = \frac{a^k}{k!} \prod_{j=k+1}^{2k-1} (n + j)$$

if $k \ge 2$. Then the series $\sum_k t_k$ is summable and

$$\left(\frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - 4a}}\right)^{n} = 1 + n a + n \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} t_k.$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 14, Corollary 1, printed p. 71; scan PDF p. 81.

articles.title: Ramanujan's Lagrange series
articles.statement:
Let $p > 0$ and $q > 0$ be real numbers with $p \ne q$, and
let $a$ be a complex number with $|a| \le p^{-p/q} |p - q|^{(p - q)/q}$. Then there is a complex
number $L$ with $a q e^{p L} - e^{q L} + 1 = 0$ such that, for every real number $n$, the series

$$1 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{n a^k}{k!} \prod_{j=1}^{k-1} (n + k p - j q)$$

converges unconditionally to $e^{n L}$.

Proof: The argument uses the Hagen--Rothe convolution, a Stirling-type coefficient bound uniform
through the boundary circle, and a continuous exponential lift.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 14, formulas (14.1)--(14.5), printed pp. 70--71 / PDF pp. 80--81; attribution on printed p. 72 / PDF p. 82.

articles.title: Ramanujan's exponential series for powers of two
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be real numbers with
$0 < n \le 2$. Then the series

$$1 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{m}{2^{k n} \, k!} \prod_{j=1}^{k-1} (m + k n - j)$$

converges unconditionally to $2^m$.

Proof: Following Berndt and the generalized binomial series of Graham, Knuth, and Patashnik,
the series is realized as $B_n(z)^m$, where $B_n = 1 + z B_n^n$; root selection at
$z = 2^{-n}$, with the endpoint supplied by Entry 14's Catalan-power series, gives $B_n = 2$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 15, Example 1, printed pp. 73-75 / PDF pp. 83-85.

articles.title: Ramanujan's inverse series for $u - \log u$
articles.statement:
There exist a real number $r > 0$ and real
coefficients $b_0, b_1, b_2, \dots$ with $b_0 = 1$, $b_1 = -1$, $b_2 = 1/3$, $b_3 = -1/36$ and
$b_4 = -1/270$ such that the power series $\sum_k b_k x^k$ is summable for every real $x$ with
$|x| < r$, and for every real $x$ with $0 < x < r$ the sum $u$ of this series satisfies
$0 < u < 1$ and $u - \log u = 1 + x^2/2$, and the series $\sum_{j \ge 2} (1 - u)^j / j$ converges
unconditionally to $x^2/2$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 15, local inverse-series clause, printed p. 73 / PDF p. 83.

articles.title: Ramanujan's tree-function series (Chapter 3, Entry 15)
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $u$ be real numbers
with $0 < u < 1$ and $u - \log u = 1 + x^2/2$. Then the series

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(k+1)^{k-1}}{k!}\, e^{-k(1 + x^2/2)}$$

converges to $u\, e^{1 + x^2/2}$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 15, formulas (15.1)-(15.2), printed p. 73; scan PDF p. 83.

articles.title: Taylor coefficients of the solution of $x^x = a^a e^h$ (Chapter 3, Entry 17)
articles.statement:
For every
real number $a > 1/e$ there exist a real number $R > 0$ and a function
$x : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, analytic at $0$, with $x(0) = a$, such that $x(h) > 0$ and
$x(h)^{x(h)} = a^a e^h$ for all real $h$ with $|h| < R$, and such that the numbers
$A_k = (-a)^{k-1} x^{(k)}(0)$ for $k \ge 1$ satisfy, for every integer $r \ge 2$,

$$A_r = \frac{(r - 2)\, A_{r-1} + \sum_{k=1}^{r-1} \binom{r-1}{k} A_k A_{r-k}}{1 + \log a}.$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, corrected Entry 17, formulas (17.1)--(17.7), printed pp. 81--83 / PDF pp. 91--93.

articles.title: Abel's binomial identity
articles.statement:
For a complex number $w$, let $A_0(x) = 1$ and
$A_j(x) = x (x + j w)^{j-1}$ for $j \ge 1$. Then for all complex numbers $x$, $y$ and every
natural number $n$,

$$\sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{n}{j} A_j(x) A_{n-j}(y) = A_n(x + y).$$

articles.title: Newton's identities for absolutely summable sequences
articles.statement:
Let $(a_j)_{j \ge 0}$ be a sequence
of complex numbers with $\sum_j |a_j| < \infty$. Let $(e_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and $(p_k)_{k \ge 1}$ be
complex numbers such that for every $n$ the family $\prod_{j \in s} a_j$, indexed by the
$n$-element finite sets $s$ of natural numbers, is summable with sum $e_n$, and for every
$k \ge 1$ the series $\sum_{j \ge 0} a_j^k$ is summable with sum $p_k$. Then for every $n \ge 1$,

$$n e_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} p_k e_{n-k}.$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Corollary to Entry 11, printed p. 66 / PDF p. 76.

articles.title: Newton's identities for summable families
articles.statement:
Let $(a_j)_{j \ge 0}$ be a sequence of complex
numbers, and let $(e_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and $(p_k)_{k \ge 1}$ be complex numbers such that for every
$n$ the family $\prod_{j \in s} a_j$, indexed by the $n$-element finite sets $s$ of natural
numbers, is summable with sum $e_n$, and for every $k \ge 1$ the series $\sum_{j \ge 0} a_j^k$
is summable with sum $p_k$. Then for every natural number $n$,

$$n e_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} p_k e_{n-k}.$$

No absolute summability of $(a_j)$ is assumed, and the case $n = 0$, where both sides vanish,
is included.

articles.title: Powers of an absolutely summable sequence are absolutely summable
articles.statement:
Let $(a_j)_{j \ge 0}$
be a sequence of complex numbers with $\sum_j |a_j| < \infty$, and let $n \ge 1$ be an integer.
Then $\sum_j |a_j^n| < \infty$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Corollary to Entry 11, printed p. 66 / PDF p. 76.

articles.title: Recurrence for the coefficients of $e^{f(x)}$
articles.statement:
Let $(A_k)_{k \ge 1}$ and $(p_n)_{n \ge 0}$
be sequences of real numbers, let $R > 0$, and let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$. Suppose that
for every real $x$ with $|x| < R$ the series $\sum_{k \ge 1} A_k x^k / k$ is summable with sum
$f(x)$ and the series $\sum_{n \ge 0} p_n x^n$ is summable with sum $e^{f(x)}$. Then for every
integer $n \ge 1$,

$$n p_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} A_k p_{n-k}.$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 11, printed p. 66 / PDF p. 76.

articles.title: Ramanujan's binomial series transformation (Chapter 3, Entry 1, Corollary 1)
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and
$x$ be complex numbers with $|x| < 1$, write $(n)_k = n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ for the falling
factorial (with $(n)_0 = 1$), and let $Q_0, Q_1, Q_2, \ldots$ be complex numbers such that, for
some $R > 0$, the power series $\sum_k Q_k z^k$ converges absolutely for every complex $z$ with
$|z| < R$. Suppose that the double series

$$\sum_{j, m \ge 0} \frac{Q_j\, (n)_{j+m}\, x^{j+m}}{m!}$$

is absolutely summable. Then the series

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{k} \frac{Q_j}{(k-j)!}\Bigr) (n)_k\, x^k$$

and

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} Q_k\, (n)_k\, x^k\, (1 + x)^{n-k}$$

converge unconditionally to the same sum, where $(1 + x)^{n-k} = e^{(n-k) \log(1+x)}$ with the
principal branch of the logarithm.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 1, Corollary 1, printed p. 45 / PDF p. 55.

articles.title: Ramanujan's binomial series transformation without the radius hypothesis
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $x$
be complex numbers with $|x| < 1$, write $(n)_k = n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ for the falling factorial
(with $(n)_0 = 1$), and let $Q_0, Q_1, Q_2, \ldots$ be complex numbers such that the double series

$$\sum_{j, m \ge 0} \frac{Q_j\, (n)_{j+m}\, x^{j+m}}{m!}$$

is absolutely summable. Then the series

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{k} \frac{Q_j}{(k-j)!}\Bigr) (n)_k\, x^k$$

and

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} Q_k\, (n)_k\, x^k\, (1 + x)^{n-k}$$

converge unconditionally to the same sum, where $(1 + x)^{n-k} = e^{(n-k) \log(1+x)}$ with the
principal branch of the logarithm.

articles.title: Ramanujan's series transformation (Chapter 3, Entry 1)
articles.statement:
Let $R_1 > 1$, let
$f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ be analytic on the open disc $|z| < R_1$, and let
$Q_0, Q_1, Q_2, \ldots$ be complex numbers such that, for some $R_2 > 0$, the power series
$\sum_n Q_n z^n$ converges absolutely for every complex $z$ with $|z| < R_2$. Suppose that the
double series

$$\sum_{j, m \ge 0} \frac{Q_j\, f^{(j+m)}(0)}{m!}$$

is absolutely summable. Then the series

$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{n} \frac{Q_j}{(n-j)!}\Bigr) f^{(n)}(0)$$

and

$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} Q_n\, f^{(n)}(1)$$

converge unconditionally to the same sum.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 1, printed p. 45 / PDF p. 55.

articles.title: Ramanujan's series transformation without the radius hypothesis
articles.statement:
Let $R_1 > 1$, let
$f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ be analytic on the open disc $|z| < R_1$, and let
$Q_0, Q_1, Q_2, \ldots$ be complex numbers such that the double series

$$\sum_{j, m \ge 0} \frac{Q_j\, f^{(j+m)}(0)}{m!}$$

is absolutely summable. Then the series

$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{n} \frac{Q_j}{(n-j)!}\Bigr) f^{(n)}(0)$$

and

$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} Q_n\, f^{(n)}(1)$$

converge unconditionally to the same sum.

articles.title: Generalized Bell function extended to $n = -1$
articles.statement:
For an integer $n \ge -1$ and a complex
number $x$, $f(n, x) = 1$ if $n = -1$, and otherwise $f(n, x)$ is the generalized Bell function
$F(0, 1, x; n) = e^{-x} \sum_{k \ge 0} (k + 1)^n x^{k + 1} / k!$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Section 8, Example 4 and its correction, printed pp. 51--52 / PDF pp. 61--62.

articles.title: Ramanujan's generalized Bell function
articles.statement:
For complex numbers $a$, $b$, $x$ and a natural
number $n$, the generalized Bell function is
$F(a, b, x; n) = e^{-x} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(a + b(k + 1))^n x^{k+1}}{k!}$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, definition (9.1).

articles.title: Absolute convergence of Ramanujan's Bell-type series (Entry 4)
articles.statement:
For every complex
number $x$ and every natural number $n$, the series
$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(j+1)^n x^{j+1}}{j!}$ converges absolutely.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 4, formula (4.1), printed pp. 47--48 / PDF pp. 57--58.

articles.title: Exponential generating function of Ramanujan's Bell-type series (Entry 4)
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be
Ramanujan's generalized Bell function. For all complex numbers $a$ and $x$, let
$f(x, n) = F(0, 1, x; n) = e^{-x} \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(j+1)^n x^{j+1}}{j!}$ for natural
numbers $n$, and set $f(x, -1) = 1$. Then the series
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{a^n}{n!} f(x, n-1)$ converges absolutely and its sum is
$e^{x(e^a - 1)}$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 4, formula (4.1), printed pp. 47--48 / PDF pp. 57--58. The source's `f(x, n) = e^{-x} ∑_{j ≥ 0} (j + 1)ⁿ xʲ⁺¹ / j!` is `generalizedBellGenerating 0 1 x n`.

articles.title: Binomial recurrence for Ramanujan's Bell-type series (Entry 5)
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be Ramanujan's
generalized Bell function. For every natural number $n$ and every complex number $x$, write
$f(x, m) = F(0, 1, x; m)$ for natural numbers $m$, and set $f(x, -1) = 1$. Then
$f(x, n) = x \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} f(x, k-1)$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 5, printed p. 48 / PDF p. 58.

articles.title: Convergence of the generalized Bell series
articles.statement:
Let $F$ denote Ramanujan's generalized Bell
function. For complex numbers $a$, $b$, $x$ and every natural number $n$, the series
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (a + b(k + 1))^n x^{k+1} / k!$ converges absolutely and its sum is
$e^{x} F(a, b, x; n)$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, definition (9.1) printed p. 53/PDF p. 63 and Entry 9(ii), formula (9.4), printed p. 54/PDF p. 64.

articles.title: Exponential generating function of the generalized Bell function (Entry 9(ii))
articles.statement:
Let
$F(a, b, x; n)$ be Ramanujan's generalized Bell function. For all complex numbers $a$, $b$, $x$
and $y$, the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{y^n}{n!} F(a, b, x; n)$ converges to
$x e^{(a+b)y} e^{x(e^{by} - 1)}$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, definition (9.1) printed p. 53/PDF p. 63 and Entry 9(ii), formula (9.4), printed p. 54/PDF p. 64. The source's `F(a, b, x; n)` is `generalizedBellGenerating a b x n`.

articles.title: Ramanujan's integral formula with Bernoulli numbers
articles.statement:
Let $f(-1, x) = 1$ and, for natural
numbers $n$, let $f(n, x) = e^{-x} \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} (j + 1)^n x^{j+1} / j!$ for complex $x$.
Let $B_n$ be the Bernoulli numbers, with $B_1 = -1/2$. Then for every natural number $m$ and every
complex number $x$,

$$\int_0^1 x\, f(m - 1, t x)\, dt = \sum_{k=0}^{m} \binom{m}{k} B_{m-k} \frac{f(k, x)}{k + 1}.$$

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Section 8, Example 4 and its correction, printed pp. 51--52 / PDF pp. 61--62.

articles.title: Integrability of the scaled generalized Bell integrand on $(0, 1)$
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be the
generalized Bell function extended to $n = -1$. For every natural number $m$ and every complex
number $x$, the complex-valued function $t \mapsto x f(m - 1, t x)$ of a real variable $t$ is
interval integrable on $[0, 1]$ with respect to Lebesgue measure.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Section 8, Example 4 and its correction, printed pp. 51--52 / PDF pp. 61--62.

articles.title: Agreement of two definitions of the harmonic numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the
rational number $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{1}{k+1}$ equals Mathlib's harmonic number
$H_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (k+1)^{-1}$.

articles.title: Two derivative series with the same sum (Chapter 3, Entry 2, Corollary 1)
articles.statement:
Let $R > 1$, let
$f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ be analytic on the open disc $|w| < R$, and let $z$ be a complex
number with $z + n \ne 0$ for every natural number $n$. Suppose that the double series
$\sum_{j, m \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^j}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+j)} \cdot \frac{f^{(j+m)}(0)}{m!}$ converges
absolutely. Then there is a complex number $c$ such that the series
$\sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{f^{(k)}(0)}{(z+k)\, k!}$ and
$\sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^k f^{(k)}(1)}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+k)}$ both converge absolutely with sum $c$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 2, Corollary 1, printed p. 46 / PDF p. 56.

articles.title: Ramanujan's series for the harmonic numbers (Chapter 3, Entry 2, Corollary 2)
articles.statement:
Let
$H_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{1}{i}$ be the $k$-th harmonic number. For every complex number $x$, the
series $\sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{H_k x^k}{k!}$ and $\sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{(-1)^{k-1} x^k}{k!\, k}$
converge absolutely, and $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{H_k x^k}{k!} =
e^x \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k-1} x^k}{k!\, k}$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 2, formula (2.3) and Corollary 2, printed pp. 46--47 / PDF pp. 56--57.

articles.title: Ramanujan's series for the harmonic numbers, with Mathlib's harmonic numbers
articles.statement:
Let
$H_k = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} (i+1)^{-1}$ be Mathlib's $k$-th harmonic number. For every complex number
$x$, the series $\sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{H_k x^k}{k!}$ and
$\sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{(-1)^{k-1} x^k}{k!\, k}$ converge absolutely, and
$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{H_k x^k}{k!} = e^x \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k-1} x^k}{k!\, k}$.

articles.title: Ramanujan's companion series transformation (Chapter 3, Entry 2, formula (2.3))
articles.statement:
Let $x$
and $z$ be complex numbers with $z \ne -(n+1)$ for every natural number $n$. Then the series
$\sum_{j \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^j x^{j+1}}{(z+j+1)\, j!}$ converges absolutely, say with sum $S$, and
the series $\sum_{j \ge 0} \frac{x^{j+1}}{(z+1)(z+2)\cdots(z+j+1)}$ converges absolutely with sum
$e^x S$.

The identity follows from Entry 2 applied with $-x$ and $z + 1$ in place of $x$ and $z$, using
$e^x e^{-x} = 1$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 2, formula (2.3) and Corollary 2, printed pp. 46--47 / PDF pp. 56--57.

articles.title: Convergence of the left side of Ramanujan's Chapter 3, Entry 2
articles.statement:
For all complex numbers
$x$ and $z$ such that $z + r \ne 0$ for every natural number $r$, the series
$\sum_{j \ge 0} \frac{x^{j+1}}{(z+j)\, j!}$ converges absolutely.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 2, formula (2.1), printed p. 46 / PDF p. 56.

articles.title: Convergence of the right side of Ramanujan's Chapter 3, Entry 2
articles.statement:
For all complex numbers
$x$ and $z$ such that $z + r \ne 0$ for every natural number $r$, the series
$\sum_{j \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^j x^{j+1}}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+j)}$ converges absolutely.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 2, formula (2.1), printed p. 46 / PDF p. 56.

articles.title: Ramanujan's exponential transformation of a factorial series (Chapter 3, Entry 2)
articles.statement:
For all
complex numbers $x$ and $z$ such that $z + r \ne 0$ for every natural number $r$, the series
$\sum_{j \ge 0} \frac{x^{j+1}}{(z+j)\, j!}$ converges absolutely, and its sum is
$e^x \sum_{j \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^j x^{j+1}}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+j)}$.

## Sources

- Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks Part I, Chapter 3, Entry 2, formula (2.1), printed p. 46 / PDF p. 56.

articles.title: Ramanujan's extension agrees with the partial sums at natural numbers
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $F(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} f(k) - \sum_{k \ge 1} f(k + x)$,
where a series that is not summable is given the value $0$. If the series
$\sum_{k \ge 1} f(k)$ is summable, then $F(m) = f(1) + f(2) + \cdots + f(m)$ for every natural
number $m$ (for $m = 0$ the right side is the empty sum $0$).

articles.title: Difference equation for Ramanujan's extension
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and let
$F(y) = \sum_{k \ge 1} f(k) - \sum_{k \ge 1} f(k + y)$, where a series that is not summable is
given the value $0$. If $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and the series $\sum_{k \ge 0} f(k + x)$ is summable,
then $F(x) - F(x - 1) = f(x)$.

articles.title: Ramanujan's extension of partial sums
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the extension of
the partial sums of $f$ to real arguments is the function
$F(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} f(k) - \sum_{k \ge 1} f(k + x)$ on $\mathbb{R}$, where each series is an
unconditional sum and a series that is not summable is given the value $0$.

When $\sum_{k \ge 1} f(k)$ is summable, $F(m) = f(1) + \cdots + f(m)$ for every natural number
$m$.

articles.title: Ramanujan's derivative-series constants
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and a natural
number $q$, the constant $c_q$ is $\sum_{k \ge 1} f^{(q)}(k)$, the sum of the values of the
$q$-th iterated derivative of $f$ at the positive integers, where a derivative that does not
exist is taken to be $0$ and a series that is not summable is given the value $0$.

articles.title: Terms of the Taylor series in Entry 6
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
$x \in \mathbb{R}$ and a natural number $j$, the $j$-th term is $-c_{j+1} x^{j+1} / (j+1)!$, where
$c_q = \sum_{k \ge 1} f^{(q)}(k)$ with $f^{(q)}$ the $q$-th iterated derivative of $f$; a
derivative that does not exist is taken to be $0$ and a series that is not summable is given the
value $0$.

Under the smoothness, summability and domination hypotheses of Entry 6, these are the
nonconstant terms of the Taylor series at $0$ of Ramanujan's extension
$F(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} f(k) - \sum_{k \ge 1} f(k + x)$, whose constant term is $F(0) = 0$.

articles.title: Partial sums of a real function over the positive integers
articles.statement:
For
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and a natural number $n$, the partial sum is
$f(1) + f(2) + \cdots + f(n)$, which is $0$ when $n = 0$.

articles.title: Terms of the shifted derivative series
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, natural numbers
$q$ and $k$, and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the $k$-th term of the shifted series of $q$-th derivatives of
$f$ is $f^{(q)}(k + 1 + x)$, where $f^{(q)}$ is the $q$-th iterated derivative of $f$ and a
derivative that does not exist is taken to be $0$.

articles.title: Taylor expansion of Ramanujan's extension at the origin
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$
be infinitely differentiable and let $\rho > 0$. Write $c_q = \sum_{k \ge 1} f^{(q)}(k)$ and
$F(x) = c_0 - \sum_{k \ge 1} f(k + x)$, where a series that is not summable is given the value
$0$. Suppose that the series $\sum_{k \ge 1} f^{(q)}(k)$ is summable for every $q \ge 0$, that
for every $q \ge 1$ there is a summable sequence $(b_k)_{k \ge 0}$ with
$|f^{(q)}(k + 1 + x)| \le b_k$ for all $x \in [-\rho, \rho]$ and all $k \ge 0$, and that $F$ is
analytic at $0$. Then there is $r$ with $0 < r \le \rho$ such that for every real $x$ with
$|x| < r$ the series $\sum_{j \ge 0} -c_{j+1} x^{j+1} / (j+1)!$ is summable with sum $F(x)$.

articles.title: The derivative-series constant is the sum of its series
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, let $q$ be a natural number, and let $f^{(q)}$ be the $q$-th
iterated derivative of $f$, where a derivative that does not exist is taken to be $0$. If the
family $\bigl(f^{(q)}(k + 1)\bigr)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is summable, then its sum is the constant
$c_q = \sum_{k \ge 1} f^{(q)}(k)$.

articles.title: Derivatives of Ramanujan's extension at the origin
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be
infinitely differentiable and let $\rho > 0$. Write $c_q = \sum_{k \ge 1} f^{(q)}(k)$ and
$F(x) = c_0 - \sum_{k \ge 1} f(k + x)$, where a series that is not summable is given the value
$0$. Suppose that the series $\sum_{k \ge 1} f^{(q)}(k)$ is summable for every $q \ge 0$, and
that for every $q \ge 1$ there is a summable sequence $(b_k)_{k \ge 0}$ with
$|f^{(q)}(k + 1 + x)| \le b_k$ for all $x \in [-\rho, \rho]$ and all $k \ge 0$. Then
$F^{(n)}(0) = -c_n$ for every natural number $n \ge 1$.

articles.title: Ramanujan's extension of the partial sums of a smooth function
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be infinitely differentiable and let $\rho > 0$. Suppose that for
every $q \in \mathbb{N}$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}$ the series
$\sum_{k \ge 0} f^{(q)}(k + 1 + x)$ converges absolutely, and that for every $q \in \mathbb{N}$
there is a summable sequence $(b_k)_{k \ge 0}$ with $|f^{(q)}(k + 1 + x)| \le b_k$ for all
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $x \in [-\rho, \rho]$. Put $c_q = \sum_{k \ge 0} f^{(q)}(k + 1)$ and
$F(x) = c_0 - \sum_{k \ge 0} f(k + 1 + x)$, and suppose that $F$ is analytic at $0$. Then
(i) for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the series $\sum_{k \ge 0} f^{(n)}(k + 1)$ converges absolutely
with sum $c_n$; (ii) $F(0) = 0$; (iii) $F(x) - F(x - 1) = f(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$;
(iv) $F(m) = f(1) + f(2) + \dots + f(m)$ for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$, the empty sum being $0$;
(v) $F^{(n)}(0) = -c_n$ for every integer $n \ge 1$; and (vi) there is $r$ with $0 < r \le \rho$
such that for every real $x$ with $|x| < r$ the series
$\sum_{j \ge 0} -c_{j+1} x^{j+1} / (j + 1)!$ converges absolutely with sum $F(x)$.

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 6.

articles.title: Tails of the shifted series of derivatives converge
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$
and $q \in \mathbb{N}$, and write $f^{(q)}$ for the $q$-th iterated derivative of $f$, where a
derivative that does not exist is taken to be $0$. If the series
$\sum_{k \ge 0} f^{(q)}(k + 1)$ converges absolutely, then for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ the series
$\sum_{k \ge 0} f^{(q)}(k + 1 + m)$ converges absolutely.

The second series is the $m$-th tail of the first.

articles.title: Catalan's product for $\sqrt{2}$
articles.statement:
The infinite product over all natural numbers $m \ge 0$
of $\frac{(4m+2)^2}{(4m+1)(4m+3)}$ converges unconditionally to $\sqrt{2}$; that is,
$\frac{2 \cdot 2}{1 \cdot 3} \cdot \frac{6 \cdot 6}{5 \cdot 7} \cdot \frac{10 \cdot 10}{9 \cdot 11}
\cdots = \sqrt{2}$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, Journal of Integer Sequences 23, `toth46.tex`, lines 157-161. URL: <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL23/Toth/toth46.tex>.

articles.title: Catalan's constant as a series
articles.statement:
Catalan's constant $G$ equals
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{(2n+1)^2}$.

articles.title: Infinite products for exponentials of Catalan's constant
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be the sum of the series
$\sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n / (2n+1)^2$ (Catalan's constant). Then, as $m \to \infty$,

$$
\prod_{n=1}^{2m} \left(1 - \frac{2}{2n+1}\right)^{n(-1)^n} \to e^{2G/\pi - 1/2},
$$



$$
\prod_{n=1}^{2m+1} \left(1 - \frac{2}{2n+1}\right)^{n(-1)^n} \to e^{2G/\pi + 1/2},
$$

and

$$
\left(\frac{\prod_{k=0}^{m-1} (4k+3)^{4k+3}}{\prod_{k=0}^{m-1} (4k+1)^{4k+1}}\right)^2
\frac{(4m+3)^{2m+1}}{(4m+1)^{6m+1}} \to e^{4G/\pi}.
$$

The products $\prod_{k=0}^{m-1} (4k+3)^{4k+3}$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{m-1} (4k+1)^{4k+1}$ are the
source's $3^3 \cdot 7^7 \cdots (4m-1)^{4m-1}$ and $1^1 \cdot 5^5 \cdots (4m-3)^{4m-3}$.

Proof: Following Kachi and Tzermias, Proposition (catalan), dominated convergence reduces the
product limit to the cosecant integral. The substitutions $x = \pi u/2$ and $x = 2 \arctan t$,
followed by the arctangent power series, evaluate it in terms of $G$.

## Sources
